docs.title: post_reset
docs.text:
post_reset(envs_idx: slice | Tensor) -> None

Hook invoked after ALL managers have reset envs_idx.

Runs after every manager's reset(), the reset-mode events, and the zeroing of episode_length_buf — the guaranteed point to rebuild per-step caches from the final post-reset scene state, without depending on the order managers reset in. (A term's own reset() runs mid-sequence: state it derives from other entities or terms may still change before observations are computed.) No-op by default.

Managers dispatch source caches before their consumers (for example, command terms before metric terms). Runs under torch.inference_mode: mutate build()-allocated buffers in place; never rebind attributes to tensors created inside this hook.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION envs_idx

The envs that were reset — never None, but index with it, never measure it: the auto-reset path in RLEnvBase.step passes the full-length boolean reset_buf, while EnvBase.reset passes a slice or an index tensor. So buf[envs_idx] = ... and src[envs_idx] are always right, and len(envs_idx) / envs_idx.numel() silently mean num_envs rather than the reset count on the step path.

TYPE: slice | Tensor

Source code in eden/managers/base.py 
def post_reset(self, envs_idx: slice | torch.Tensor) -> None:
    """Hook invoked after ALL managers have reset ``envs_idx``.

    Runs after every manager's ``reset()``, the reset-mode events, and the zeroing of
    ``episode_length_buf`` — the guaranteed point to rebuild per-step caches from the
    *final* post-reset scene state, without depending on the order managers reset in.
    (A term's own ``reset()`` runs mid-sequence: state it derives from other entities
    or terms may still change before observations are computed.) No-op by default.

    Managers dispatch source caches before their consumers (for example, command
    terms before metric terms). Runs under ``torch.inference_mode``: mutate
    ``build()``-allocated buffers in place; never rebind attributes to tensors
    created inside this hook.

    Parameters
    ----------
    envs_idx : slice | torch.Tensor
        The envs that were reset — never ``None``, but *index with it, never measure
        it*: the auto-reset path in ``RLEnvBase.step`` passes the full-length boolean
        ``reset_buf``, while ``EnvBase.reset`` passes a slice or an index tensor. So
        ``buf[envs_idx] = ...`` and ``src[envs_idx]`` are always right, and
        ``len(envs_idx)`` / ``envs_idx.numel()`` silently mean ``num_envs`` rather
        than the reset count on the step path.
    """
    del envs_idx  # Unused.

docs.text:
post_reset(envs_idx: slice | Tensor | None = None) -> None

Fan :meth:ManagerTermBase.post_reset out once per unique term.

The env calls this from its public entry points (:meth:~eden.envs.base.EnvBase.reset, :meth:~eden.envs.base.RLEnvBase.step) right after _reset_idx returns — not from inside it, so a subclass's extra reset work finishes first (the mimic env refills the motion buffer after super()._reset_idx). By then every manager's reset(), the reset-mode events and the episode_length_buf zeroing have all run, so terms can rebuild per-step caches from the final post-reset state. The env owns that call-time contract, like CommandManager.post_physics_refresh.

Decorated @torch.inference_mode() so terms whose buffers were created under an inference-moded manager path (metric and reward terms) can mutate them here; the flip side is the in-place-only contract in :meth:ManagerTermBase.post_reset.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION envs_idx

The envs that were reset; None means all of them. Sanitized before it reaches the terms.

TYPE: slice | Tensor DEFAULT: None

@torch.inference_mode()
def post_reset(self, envs_idx: slice | torch.Tensor | None = None) -> None:
    """Fan :meth:`ManagerTermBase.post_reset` out once per unique term.

    The env calls this from its public entry points (:meth:`~eden.envs.base.EnvBase.reset`,
    :meth:`~eden.envs.base.RLEnvBase.step`) right *after* ``_reset_idx`` returns — not from
    inside it, so a subclass's extra reset work finishes first (the mimic env refills the
    motion buffer after ``super()._reset_idx``). By then every manager's ``reset()``, the
    reset-mode events and the ``episode_length_buf`` zeroing have all run, so terms can
    rebuild per-step caches from the final post-reset state. The env owns that call-time
    contract, like ``CommandManager.post_physics_refresh``.

    Decorated ``@torch.inference_mode()`` so terms whose buffers were created under an
    inference-moded manager path (metric and reward terms) can mutate them here; the flip
    side is the in-place-only contract in :meth:`ManagerTermBase.post_reset`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    envs_idx : slice | torch.Tensor, optional
        The envs that were reset; ``None`` means all of them. Sanitized before it reaches
        the terms.
    """
    envs_idx = sanitize_envs_idx(envs_idx, self._env.num_envs)
    seen: set[int] = set()
    for term in self.iter_post_reset_terms():
        term_id = id(term)
        if term_id in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(term_id)
        term.post_reset(envs_idx)

def get_term(self, name: str) -> ManagerTermBase:
    """Return the active term registered under ``name``.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If ``name`` is not an active term. The message lists the active ones, in the wording
        :meth:`eden.utils.registry.Registry.get` uses for the same miss: a caller reaching here
        with the wrong name (a term renamed in the config, a reward term naming an action term
        that was never added) has no other way to see what *is* there.
    """
    if name not in self._terms:
        available = ", ".join(self._term_names) or "none"
        raise KeyError(f"No active term named '{name}' in {type(self).__name__}. Available options: {available}")
    return self._terms[name]

def build_term(registry: Registry, env: EnvBase, options: Options, *, label: str) -> ManagerTermBase:
    """Construct the term ``options`` names from ``registry`` and ``build()`` it.

    The one place a term is built from its options — by every manager (:meth:`ManagerBase._build_term`,
    the observation manager's groups) and by the composite terms that build children of their own.

    Parameters
    ----------
    registry : Registry
        The term registry ``options.name`` is a key of.
    env : EnvBase
        The env the term is built for.
    options : Options
        The term's options; ``options.name`` is its registry key.
    label : str
        Names the config entry being built, starting with the class that holds it
        (``"RewardManager term 'lift_milk'"``, ``"MetricTermAND.terms[0]"``): the term itself only knows its
        key, and a task can hold a dozen entries of one term (``metric_reward`` ×12 in robosuite
        PickPlace), so the message alone may not say which to fix. It opens the error for a nameless term
        and is added as a note to any exception constructing or building the term raises, whose type and
        message are left unchanged.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``options.name`` is ``None`` — a legal placeholder the registry would answer with
        ``KeyError: None``, naming neither the entry nor the fix.
    """
    if options.name is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{label} names no registered term (name=None), so there is nothing to build. "
            f"Write it as <TermClass>.configure(...), which sets name, or give it name='<registry key>' — "
            f"`eden terms --grep <text>` lists them."
        )
    try:
        term = registry.get(options.name)(env=env, options=options)
        term.build()
    except Exception as e:
        e.add_note(f"while building {label} (name='{options.name}')")
        raise
    return term

docs.title: processed_action property
docs.text:
processed_action: Tensor

The command this term issued this step — what a deployment sends to the robot.

For the joint PD controllers this is the position target the controller tracks — raw_action * scale + offset + reference_offset, after any configured :class:~eden.managers.modifiers.ActionModifier's control-step modify_processed_action. Other terms command other quantities (a velocity, an effort, a binary weld flag), so both the units and the trailing width are term-specific; only the leading num_envs dimension is guaranteed.

A physics-step modifier (modify_applied_target — e.g. :class:~eden.managers.modifiers.actions.actuators.ActionDelay) is not folded in: under a delay the simulated actuator tracks an earlier processed_action, exactly as the real robot tracks the command it received a latency ago.

Read this rather than recomputing the target at the call site — a recomputation silently drops whatever control-step modifiers are configured, so the logged target diverges from the one the controller issued.

Whether this term only stands in, in simulation, for something the real robot does itself.

True means the physical effect follows from another term's command (or from physics) on hardware, so a deployment has nothing to send for this term: :class:~eden.managers.terms.actions.welding_actions.ParallelJawWelding welds the object to the gripper because sim contact friction is unreliable, while on the robot the gripper joints closing — commanded by a separate joint term — hold it.

def verify_command_shape(self, command: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    """Fail loud — naming this term — the first time a control command's width != the DOF count.

    A wrong-width joint command otherwise reaches the raw Genesis call and surfaces as an opaque
    ``GenesisException: Invalid input shape: (N, W)... required size D`` naming neither the term,
    the entity, nor the DOF set. Controllers call this from ``apply_actions``
    with the exact tensor they hand to ``entity.control_dofs_*`` — the only layer that knows both
    the term identity and the true (post-slice) command width.

    Checked once per term, not every step: the command width is structural (fixed by the term's
    ``dofs_name`` and controller), so a first-step check catches a misconfiguration without any
    steady-state cost. No-op for a shape-less command (a Python scalar Genesis handles itself).
    """
    if self._command_shape_checked:
        return
    self._command_shape_checked = True
    shape = getattr(command, "shape", None)
    if shape is None or len(shape) == 0:
        return
    width = shape[-1]
    if width != self._n_dofs:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Action term {term_subject(self)} produced a command of "
            f"width {width}, but it controls {self._n_dofs} DOFs ({self.dofs_name}). The command's last "
            f"dimension must equal the number of controlled DOFs — check the term's `dofs_name` and its "
            f"controller output size."
        )

def __init__(self, env: EnvBase, options: ActionManagerOptions):
    super().__init__(env=env, options=options)

    self._reject_no_op_terms()
    self._reject_overlapping_dofs()

    # Create action slices after terms are prepared
    self._term_slice = {}
    idx = 0
    for term_name, term in self._terms.items():
        self._term_slice[term_name] = slice(idx, idx + term.action_dim)
        idx += term.action_dim

    # Create buffers to store actions.
    self._action = torch.zeros((self.num_envs, self.total_action_dim), device=self.device)
    self._prev_action = torch.zeros_like(self._action)

    # Cached once: the dict-action width check runs only in smoke mode (a process-level flag
    # set before construction), so real training pays nothing — not even the env lookup — per step.

def clear_action_history(self, envs_idx: (slice | torch.Tensor) | None = None) -> None:
    """Zero the raw actions :meth:`reset` zeroes, the manager's and each term's, current and previous.

    For a caller that restarts what a policy observes without resetting the env: a deployment's
    START or policy switch, where the robot keeps running. A ``last_action`` observation then reads
    zeros, as it does after an env reset. :meth:`reset` itself does more, which such a caller must
    not: it resets every term's modifiers and an ``ACCUMULATE`` target, state a reset-mode DR event
    rewrites right after it in an env reset and that nothing rewrites on a robot.
    """
    if envs_idx is None:
        envs_idx = slice(None)
    self._prev_action[envs_idx] = 0.0
    self._action[envs_idx] = 0.0
    for term in self._terms.values():
        if term._raw_action is not None:
            term._raw_action[envs_idx] = 0.0
            term._prev_action[envs_idx] = 0.0

def reset(self, envs_idx: (slice | torch.Tensor) | None = None) -> dict[str, float]:
    if envs_idx is None:
        envs_idx = slice(None)

    # Reset action history.
    # NOTE: use assignment here (it works for both slice and tensor index), not .zero_()
    self._prev_action[envs_idx] = 0.0
    self._action[envs_idx] = 0.0

    # Reset action terms.
    for term in self._terms.values():
        term.reset(envs_idx=envs_idx)
    return {}

compute(action: Tensor | dict[str, Tensor]) -> None
Source code in eden/managers/action_manager.py 
def compute(self, action: torch.Tensor | dict[str, torch.Tensor]) -> None:
    if isinstance(action, dict):
        if self._smoke:
            # Smoke-only: name the offending term before term.compute turns a width mismatch
            # into a bare torch broadcast error (or an unknown key into a bare KeyError).
            self._validate_dict_action(action)
        for term_name, term_action in action.items():
            # The tensor form below copies into the device buffer, so a host-built action works there; the
            # dict form hands each term its tensor as given. Moved here (a no-op for one already on the
            # device) so both forms accept `torch.tensor([...])` — a CPU tensor, since Eden sets no torch
            # default device.
            term_action = term_action.to(self.device)
            term = self._terms[term_name]
            term.compute(term_action)
            if term._accepts_missing_command_:
                term_action = torch.where(torch.isnan(term_action), term.action, term_action)
            self._prev_action[:, self._term_slice[term_name]] = self._action[:, self._term_slice[term_name]]
            self._action[:, self._term_slice[term_name]] = term_action
    else:
        if self.total_action_dim != action.shape[1]:
            # Name the per-term layout so the caller can see which term owns which columns —
            # the mismatch is otherwise reported only as two totals.
            layout = ", ".join(f"{name}={term.action_dim}" for name, term in self._terms.items())
            raise ValueError(
                f"Invalid action shape, expected: {self.total_action_dim}, received: {action.shape[1]}. "
                f"Expected per-term layout: [{layout}]."
            )
        self._prev_action[:] = self._action
        self._action[:] = action
        for term_name, term in self._terms.items():
            term_actions = self._action[:, self._term_slice[term_name]]
            term.compute(term_actions)
            if term._accepts_missing_command_:
                self._action[:, self._term_slice[term_name]] = torch.where(
                    torch.isnan(term_actions), term.action, term_actions
                )

docs.title: ObservationTerm
docs.text:
ObservationTerm(env: EnvBase, options: ObservationTermOptions)

Bases: ConfigurableTermBase[ObservationTermOptions], _ObservationTermFields

Base class for observation terms.

compute() is a read, not a tick. The manager calls it more often than once per control step and never promises which call is "the" step: once per term at build to learn the output shape (before any reset()), from EnvBase.reset(), at phase 19 of RLEnvBase.step, again at phase 12 for the final-observation snapshot when record_final_observations is on, from RslRlVecEnvWrapper.get_observations() outside the step, and from the deploy pre-flight probe. The cross-group raw cache goes the other way and may call compute() on only one of several identically configured instances. A term that advances state inside compute() — an integral, a counter, a latch — therefore double-counts under any of those, silently: the failure is a wrong number, not an exception.

Per-step state lives on the term and moves in the lifecycle hooks instead: build() allocates the buffer, :meth:post_physics_refresh advances it exactly once per control step on the post-physics state (phase 7 — the same hook, epoch and reasoning as a command term's measurement state at 5, and after the metrics at 6 so a term may integrate one), reset(envs_idx) zeroes the rows of the envs that restart, post_reset(envs_idx) rebuilds what the post-reset scene determines, and compute() returns the buffer. :class:~eden.managers.terms.observations.locomotion.VelocityTrackingErrorIntegral is the shipped worked example. Function terms have none of these hooks — see :class:ObservationTermFuncWrapper.

The post-compute fields (modifiers/noise/clip/scale/history) are options-only (see ObservationTermOptions.POST_COMPUTE_FIELDS): configure() accepts them and stores them on the options, but they are NOT mirrored as term attributes — the manager applies them from outside so a compute() can't accidentally read (and be wrongly deduped on) a modifier value.

When each modifier is read. clip and history_length are read off self._options on every step, so a post-build write to them takes effect immediately. noise and scale are resolved once at build — into self._noise and self._resolved_scale — because both need setup the hot path must not repeat (a noise model instance; a length check against the term's feature dim plus a device tensor). Writing term._options.scale after env.build() therefore has no effect: it is not the value the manager multiplies by, and nothing detects the divergence for you. Read what is actually applied off :attr:effective_scale; to retune it at runtime, call :meth:~eden.managers.observation_manager.ObservationManager.set_term_scale, which re-runs the feature-dim check. Modifiers stay the manager's business in both directions — that is what keeps them off this class.

docs.title: post_physics_refresh
docs.text:
post_physics_refresh() -> None

Advance per-step state on the post-physics scene (phase 7 — the grading epoch).

No-op by default. The one call per control step that a stateful term may count on: it runs after the physics sub-steps, after command_manager.post_physics_refresh (5) and metric_manager.compute (6) — so a term may integrate a refreshed command cache or a shared metric and see this step's value — and before termination/reward; and, unlike compute(), exactly once, whatever else reads the observation this step. Accumulate here (add_ into a build()-time buffer, in place), and return the buffer from compute().

Running above the auto-reset (phase 13) is what gives a stateful observation the semantics one expects of it: the final-observation snapshot at phase 12 carries this step's increment, reset() then zeroes the envs that restart, and the fresh episode's first observation at phase 19 reads zero rather than one post-reset increment. EnvBase.reset() and the build-time shape probe run no phase 7 at all, so a term reads as zero there too.

Invoked by :meth:ObservationManager.post_physics_refresh from RLEnvBase.step and EnvBase.step, and, on hardware, once per control tick from DeploymentBase.state_to_observation after the robot state is synced (a command term's post_physics_refresh does not run there; this one does, because the policy's observations are the hardware path). Never from compute(), and never from a reset.

def post_physics_refresh(self) -> None:
    """Advance per-step state on the post-physics scene (phase 7 — the *grading* epoch).

    No-op by default. The one call per control step that a stateful term may count on: it runs
    after the physics sub-steps, after ``command_manager.post_physics_refresh`` (5) and
    ``metric_manager.compute`` (6) — so a term may integrate a refreshed command cache or a shared
    metric and see this step's value — and before termination/reward; and, unlike ``compute()``,
    exactly once, whatever else reads the observation this step. Accumulate here (``add_`` into a
    ``build()``-time buffer, in place), and return the buffer from ``compute()``.

    Running *above* the auto-reset (phase 13) is what gives a stateful observation the semantics
    one expects of it: the final-observation snapshot at phase 12 carries this step's increment,
    ``reset()`` then zeroes the envs that restart, and the fresh episode's first observation at
    phase 19 reads zero rather than one post-reset increment. ``EnvBase.reset()`` and the build-time
    shape probe run no phase 7 at all, so a term reads as zero there too.

    Invoked by :meth:`ObservationManager.post_physics_refresh` from ``RLEnvBase.step`` and
    ``EnvBase.step``, and, on hardware, once per control tick from
    ``DeploymentBase.state_to_observation`` after the robot state is synced (a command term's
    ``post_physics_refresh`` does **not** run there; this one does, because the policy's
    observations are the hardware path). Never from ``compute()``, and never from a reset.
    """

Stateless by construction. def __init__(self, env: EnvBase, options: ObservationManagerOptions):
    super().__init__(env=env, options=options)

    self._group_obs_dim: dict[str, tuple[int, ...] | list[tuple[int, ...]]] = dict()
    self._obs_buffer: dict[str, torch.Tensor | dict[str, torch.Tensor]] | None = None

    for group_name, group_term_dims in self._group_obs_term_dim.items():
        if self._group_obs_options[group_name].concatenate_terms:
            try:
                term_dims = torch.stack(
                    [torch.tensor(dims, device="cpu") for dims in group_term_dims],
                    dim=0,
                )
                if len(term_dims.shape) > 1:
                    dim = self._group_obs_options[group_name].concatenate_dim
                    dim_sum = torch.sum(term_dims[:, dim], dim=0)
                    term_dims[0, dim] = dim_sum
                    term_dims = term_dims[0]
                else:
                    term_dims = torch.sum(term_dims, dim=0)
                self._group_obs_dim[group_name] = tuple(term_dims.tolist())
            except RuntimeError:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Unable to concatenate observation terms in group `{group_name}`.") from None
        else:
            self._group_obs_dim[group_name] = group_term_dims

    # Cross-group raw-output cache. Many tasks reuse the same observation term in multiple groups (e.g. an
    # identical `policy` and `critic` group that differ only in noise/corruption); the raw `term.compute()` is then
    # computed once per group even though it's identical. Terms whose raw output is provably identical (same
    # registered term + same compute params, ignoring post-compute noise/clip/scale/history) compute once per step
    # and the result is reused. Safe because compute() is contractually a pure read of env state (see
    # ``ObservationTerm``): a stateful term advances in ``post_physics_refresh``, which reaches every instance,
    # so two identically configured instances hold identical state and either one's compute() stands for both.
    self._raw_cache: dict = {}
    self._build_dup_signatures()

    # ``(group, term)`` pairs that ``nan_policy="warn"`` has already warned about. Each pair is warned
    # about once and after that only sanitized, with no host read: a warning every step would flood a
    # training log.
    self._non_finite_warned: set[tuple[str, str]] = set()

def summary(self) -> str:
    msg = f"<ObservationManager> contains {len(self._group_obs_term_names)} groups.\n"
    for group_name, group_dim in self._group_obs_dim.items():
        title = f"Active Observation Terms in Group: '{group_name}'"
        if self._group_obs_options[group_name].concatenate_terms:
            title += f" (shape: {group_dim})"
        rows = []
        obs_terms = zip(
            self._group_obs_term_names[group_name],
            self._group_obs_term_dim[group_name],
            self._group_obs_terms[group_name],
            strict=False,
        )
        for index, (name, dims, term) in enumerate(obs_terms):
            if term._options.history_length > 0 and term._options.flatten_history_dim:
                # Flattened history: show (9,) ← 3×(3,)
                original_size = int(np.prod(dims)) // term._options.history_length
                original_shape = (original_size,) if len(dims) == 1 else dims[1:]
                shape_str = f"{dims}  ← {term._options.history_length}×{original_shape}"
            else:
                shape_str = str(tuple(dims))
            rows.append([index, name, shape_str])
        msg += format_table(title, ["Index", "Name", "Shape"], rows, align={"Name": "l"})
        msg += "\n"
    return msg

def get_term(self, name: str) -> ObservationTermLike:
    # term_keys() (not keys()) so declared config fields aren't iterated as obs groups.
    for group_name in self._options.term_keys():
        for term_name, term in zip(
            self._group_obs_term_names[group_name],
            self._group_obs_terms[group_name],
            strict=True,
        ):
            if term_name == name:
                return term
    # Available options listed for the same reason ``Registry.get`` and
    # ``FlatManagerBase.get_term`` list theirs: the caller has the wrong name and no other way
    # to see the right one. Terms are grouped here, so the groups are named too.
    available = ", ".join(
        f"{group}: {', '.join(names) or 'none'}" for group, names in self.group_term_names.items()
    )
    raise ValueError(f"Term '{name}' not found in observation manager. Available options: {available or 'none'}")

set_term_scale(group_name: str, term_name: str, scale: float | list[float]) -> None

Retune one term's post-compute scale after the env is built.

scale is resolved once during env construction (see :func:_resolve_term_scale), so assigning term._options.scale afterwards changes what the options report but not what the manager multiplies by. This is the supported way to change it: the value goes through exactly the check the build-time resolution ran — feature dim, length, identity short-circuit — and both halves are written together, so a term can never report a scale it is not applying. A rejected value leaves both untouched, because the resolution runs first.

Addressed by (group_name, term_name) rather than a term handle because the same term name in two groups is two independent instances with their own scale, which :meth:get_term cannot distinguish.

Call this once, at setup. Scale is applied per frame before the frame enters a history buffer, so retuning a term whose window already holds frames would leave the older ones at the previous scale and the newer ones at the new one — one feature carrying two scales for history_length steps, which nothing in the config can show. That is refused. The window counts as empty before the first compute() and again after a full reset(), so the usual setup orders — retune before the first step, or after env.reset(), which is where the training wrappers leave you — are all allowed.

A term with no history holds no cross-step state in the observation pipeline, so it stays retunable at any point as far as this manager is concerned. That is not a licence to retune mid-training: the RL side holds state derived from the old scale (an observation normalizer's running statistics, most obviously) that nothing here can see or invalidate.

The observation group holding the term.

TYPE: str

term_name

The term to retune, as named in the group.

TYPE: str

scale

The new scale. A list is matched against the term's raw feature dim, as at build.

def set_term_scale(self, group_name: str, term_name: str, scale: float | list[float]) -> None:
    """Retune one term's post-compute ``scale`` after the env is built.

    ``scale`` is resolved once during env construction (see :func:`_resolve_term_scale`), so assigning
    ``term._options.scale`` afterwards changes what the options report but not what the manager
    multiplies by. This is the supported way to change it: the value goes through exactly the check the
    build-time resolution ran — feature dim, length, identity short-circuit — and both halves are written
    together, so a term can never report a scale it is not applying. A rejected value leaves both
    untouched, because the resolution runs first.

    Addressed by ``(group_name, term_name)`` rather than a term handle because the same term name in two
    groups is two independent instances with their own scale, which :meth:`get_term` cannot distinguish.

    **Call this once, at setup.** Scale is applied per frame *before* the frame enters a history buffer,
    so retuning a term whose window already holds frames would leave the older ones at the previous scale
    and the newer ones at the new one — one feature carrying two scales for ``history_length`` steps,
    which nothing in the config can show. That is refused. The window counts as empty before the first
    ``compute()`` and again after a full ``reset()``, so the usual setup orders — retune before the first
    step, or after ``env.reset()``, which is where the training wrappers leave you — are all allowed.

    A term with no history holds no cross-step state in the *observation* pipeline, so it stays retunable
    at any point as far as this manager is concerned. That is not a licence to retune mid-training: the
    RL side holds state derived from the old scale (an observation normalizer's running statistics, most
    obviously) that nothing here can see or invalidate.

    Parameters
    ----------
    group_name: str
        The observation group holding the term.
    term_name: str
        The term to retune, as named in the group.
    scale: float or list[float]
        The new scale. A list is matched against the term's raw feature dim, as at build.
    """
    if group_name not in self._group_obs_term_names:
        available = ", ".join(self._group_obs_term_names) or "none"
        raise ValueError(f"Observation group '{group_name}' not found. Available options: {available}")
    names = self._group_obs_term_names[group_name]
    if term_name not in names:
        available = ", ".join(names) or "none"
        raise ValueError(
            f"Term '{term_name}' not found in observation group '{group_name}'. Available options: {available}"
        )
    self._assert_history_not_started(group_name, term_name)
    index = names.index(term_name)
    term = self._group_obs_terms[group_name][index]
    resolved = _resolve_term_scale(
        term_name, group_name, scale, self._group_obs_term_raw_dim[group_name][index], self._env.device
    )
    term._resolved_scale = resolved
    # Assignment on an options model is not validated (``validate_assignment`` is off), so normalize to
    # the declared ``float | list[float]`` rather than letting a tuple survive into the options.
    term._options.scale = float(scale) if isinstance(scale, (int, float)) else [float(v) for v in scale]

def reset(self, envs_idx: torch.Tensor | slice | None = None) -> dict[str, float]:
    history_batch_ids = (
        None if envs_idx is None else sanitize_envs_idx(envs_idx, self._env.num_envs, prefer_slice=False)
    )

    for group_name in self._group_obs_term_names:
        for _, term in self._group_obs_class_terms.get(group_name, ()):
            term.reset(envs_idx=envs_idx)

        for term in self._group_obs_terms[group_name]:
            if term._noise is not None:
                term._noise.reset(envs_idx=envs_idx)
            # Modifier state is per-step state like the history window, so it restarts with it, on
            # the same indices.
            for modifier in term._modifiers:
                modifier.reset(envs_idx=history_batch_ids)

        history = self._group_obs_term_history_buffer[group_name]
        if isinstance(history, dict):
            for buffer in history.values():
                buffer.reset(batch_ids=history_batch_ids)
        else:
            # Group-level history: one CircularBuffer for the concatenated group.
            history.reset(batch_ids=history_batch_ids)
    return {}

def post_physics_refresh(self) -> None:
    """Advance every class term's per-step state on the post-physics scene — phase 7, once per control step.

    The once-per-step tick that ``compute()`` is not (see :class:`ObservationTerm`). Called by the
    env's step after ``command_manager.post_physics_refresh()`` (5) and ``metric_manager.compute()``
    (6), before the graded layer and above the auto-reset; and once per control tick from the deploy
    loop. This method owns that call-time contract; terms override the no-op
    :meth:`ObservationTerm.post_physics_refresh`.

    Reaches class terms only: a function term is stateless by construction
    (:class:`ObservationTermFuncWrapper`). Every instance is ticked, including the duplicates the
    cross-group raw cache computes only once — that is what keeps their state identical and the
    cache sound.
    """
    for terms in self._group_obs_class_terms.values():
        for _, term in terms:
            term.post_physics_refresh()

def compute(self, update_history: bool = False) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor | dict[str, torch.Tensor]]:
    # Reset the per-step cross-group cache so reused raw outputs reflect the current state. Cleared (not just
    # overwritten) to avoid pinning tensors.
    self._raw_cache.clear()
    obs_buffer: dict[str, torch.Tensor | dict[str, torch.Tensor]] = dict()
    # One pass for `compute_once` (ManagerBase): terms share an intermediate within it, across groups too.
    with self.compute_pass():
        for group_name in self._group_obs_term_names:
            obs_buffer[group_name] = self.compute_group(group_name, update_history)
    self._obs_buffer = obs_buffer
    return obs_buffer

compute_group(group_name: str, update_history: bool = False) -> Tensor | dict[str, Tensor]
Source code in eden/managers/observation_manager.py 
def compute_group(self, group_name: str, update_history: bool = False) -> torch.Tensor | dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
    # The frames ``nan_policy`` "warn" / "error" still has to check, read back together once the
    # group's terms are computed: one host read per group rather than one per term.
    unchecked: list[tuple[str, torch.Tensor]] = []

    # Fast path: pre-allocated concatenation buffer (no history, 1-D obs, concatenate_terms).
    concat_buf = self._group_concat_buffer.get(group_name)
    if concat_buf is not None:
        slices = self._group_concat_slices[group_name]
        for i, (term_name, term) in enumerate(
            zip(self._group_obs_term_names[group_name], self._group_obs_terms[group_name], strict=True)
        ):
            start, end = slices[i]
            concat_buf[:, start:end].copy_(self._term_frame(group_name, term_name, term, update_history, unchecked))
        self._check_non_finite(group_name, unchecked)
        return concat_buf.clone()

    # General path
    group_obs: dict[str, torch.Tensor] = OrderedDict()

    for term_name, term in zip(
        self._group_obs_term_names[group_name],
        self._group_obs_terms[group_name],
        strict=True,
    ):
        obs = self._term_frame(group_name, term_name, term, update_history, unchecked)
        if self._group_obs_options[group_name].history_length is not None:
            group_obs[term_name] = obs
        elif term._options.history_length > 0:
            circular_buffer = self._group_obs_term_history_buffer[group_name][term_name]
            if update_history or not circular_buffer.is_initialized:
                circular_buffer.append(obs)
                buf = circular_buffer.buffer
            else:
                # Snapshot path: produce the buffer that *would* result from
                # appending ``obs`` now, without mutating the underlying state.
                # The canonical once-per-step advance happens elsewhere
                # (post-reset compute in ``RLEnvBase.step``); doing it here
                # too would skip a frame for non-done envs, while skipping
                # it entirely would drop the freshly-computed post-physics
                # frame from the snapshot.
                buf = circular_buffer.peek_buffer(obs)

            if term._options.flatten_history_dim:
                group_obs[term_name] = buf.reshape(self._env.num_envs, -1)
            else:
                group_obs[term_name] = buf
        else:
            group_obs[term_name] = obs

    self._check_non_finite(group_name, unchecked)

    if self._group_obs_options[group_name].history_length is not None:
        group_obs = torch.cat(
            list(group_obs.values()),
            dim=self._group_obs_options[group_name].concatenate_dim,
        )
        circular_buffer = self._group_obs_term_history_buffer[group_name]
        if update_history or not circular_buffer.is_initialized:
            circular_buffer.append(group_obs)
            buf = circular_buffer.buffer
        else:
            # Snapshot path: see term-level branch above.
            buf = circular_buffer.peek_buffer(group_obs)

        if self._group_obs_options[group_name].flatten_history_dim:
            return buf.reshape(self._env.num_envs, -1)
        else:
            return buf

    if self._group_obs_options[group_name].concatenate_terms:
        return torch.cat(
            list(group_obs.values()),
            dim=self._group_obs_options[group_name].concatenate_dim,
        )
    return group_obs

RewardManager(env: RLEnvBase, options: RewardManagerOptions)

Bases: FlatManagerBase[RewardManagerOptions]

Computes the scalar step reward as the weighted sum of all active terms.

Terms are declared flat (:class:RewardTermOptions) or inside named groups (:class:RewardGroupOptions); flat terms implicitly belong to :data:DEFAULT_REWARD_GROUP. Grouping never changes the scalar reward the environment returns — :meth:compute always sums over all groups — it adds a per-group readout (:meth:get_group_reward, :meth:get_group_episode_sum) for multi-channel consumers (CMDP-style task/style/penalty critics, per-group logging). Groups partition the active terms, so summing :meth:get_group_reward over :attr:group_term_names reconstructs the value :meth:compute returned for the same step (up to floating-point summation order).

Unlike observation groups (which may share a term across groups), reward groups are a strict partition of one flat term set — duplicate term names across groups raise at construction. That is why this stays a :class:FlatManagerBase: the terms, buffers, and the flat API (terms, active_terms, get_term, iter_terms, get_episode_sum) are unchanged; groups are a labeling on top.

def __init__(self, env: RLEnvBase, options: RewardManagerOptions):
    super().__init__(env=env, options=options)
    num_terms = len(self._term_names)

    # Whether reset() emits the per-term reward log keys. None auto-selects:
    # off when explicit groups give a group-sum readout, on otherwise (a flat config has
    # nothing to summarize to). _has_explicit_groups is set by _prepare_terms above.
    log_pref = self._options.log_per_term_rewards
    self._log_per_term = (not self._has_explicit_groups) if log_pref is None else bool(log_pref)
    if not self._log_per_term and log_pref is None:
        # Declaring the first reward group silently flips this default, so every
        # ``Episode_Reward/<term>`` key a flat config was logging disappears. Say so once at
        # build rather than leaving it to be noticed as a gap in wandb.
        en.logger.info(
            f"RewardManager: per-term reward log keys (Episode_Reward/<term>) are off because this config "
            f"declares reward groups; logging Episode_Reward_Group/<group> for "
            f"{list(self._group_term_names)} instead. Set `log_per_term_rewards=True` to keep both."
        )

    # 2D episode sums for vectorized accumulation.
    # ``_episode_sums`` is the weighted+masked accumulation; ``_episode_raw_sums``
    # mirrors the raw (unweighted) term outputs for diagnostic logging.
    self._episode_sums = torch.zeros((self.num_envs, num_terms), dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)
    self._episode_raw_sums = torch.zeros((self.num_envs, num_terms), dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)
    self._reward_buf = torch.zeros(self.num_envs, dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)
    self._step_reward = torch.zeros((self.num_envs, num_terms), dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)
    # Unweighted (but temporally masked) term outputs of the last step: compute() fills it and
    # multiplies it into _step_reward; get_term_value() reads it.
    self._step_raw_reward = torch.zeros((self.num_envs, num_terms), dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)

    # Per-group column indices into the flat term buffers.
    self._group_col_idx: dict[str, torch.Tensor] = {
        group: torch.tensor([self._term_name_to_idx[name] for name in names], dtype=torch.long, device=self.device)
        for group, names in self._group_term_names.items()
    }
    # dt of the last compute() call; 0.0 until then so the group readout is
    # zeros before the first step, matching the zero-filled buffers.
    self._last_dt = 0.0
    # Constant zero scalar: sum-start for the per-group reset logs so empty groups
    # stay tensor-typed without a per-reset allocation. Read-only by contract —
    # it is returned as-is as the log value of an empty group.
    self._log_zero = torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)

    # Pre-compute weights vector for vectorized multiply. ``_weights_host`` is the same list on
    # the host: compute() compares against it and uploads only on a change (a curriculum moving
    # a weight), since writing a Python float into a CUDA tensor is a GPU->CPU sync.
    self._weights_host = [term.weight for term in self._terms.values()]
    self._weights = torch.tensor(self._weights_host, dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)

    # Pre-allocate temporal mask (1.0 for non-temporal terms, updated per-step for temporal).
    # ``range_s`` is in seconds; convert to integer step bounds once here so the per-step
    # compare uses ``episode_length_buf`` directly (rounding keeps both ends inclusive).
    self._temporal_mask = torch.ones((self.num_envs, num_terms), dtype=torch.float, device=self.device)
    self._temporal_term_info: list[tuple[int, list[tuple[int, int]]]] = []
    for term_idx, term in enumerate(self._terms.values()):
        if term.is_temporal_dependent:
            step_range = [(round(lo / self._env.dt), round(hi / self._env.dt)) for lo, hi in term.range_s]
            self._temporal_term_info.append((term_idx, step_range))

    """Return the reward of group ``group`` for the last computed step as a ``(num_envs,)`` tensor.

@staticmethod
def is_timestep_in_range(timestep: torch.Tensor, ranges: list[tuple[float, float]]) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Check whether a batch of timesteps falls within any of the given intervals.

    Parameters
    ----------
    timestep : torch.Tensor
        ``(batch_size,)`` tensor of timesteps.
    ranges : list of tuple of float
        List of ``(lower, upper)`` tuples defining valid intervals, in the same
        units as ``timestep`` (step counts, not seconds).

    Returns
    -------
    torch.Tensor
        ``(batch_size,)`` boolean tensor indicating membership.
    """
    is_valid = torch.zeros_like(timestep, dtype=torch.bool, device=timestep.device)
    for lower, upper in ranges:
        is_valid |= (timestep >= lower) & (timestep <= upper)
    return is_valid

def reset(self, envs_idx: torch.Tensor | None = None) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
    if envs_idx is None:
        envs_idx = slice(None)
    extras = {}
    # Per-term episode averages are computed for every term (the group readout below is
    # derived from them), but only surfaced as log keys when _log_per_term is set —
    # otherwise a term-heavy config's per-iteration log is dominated by them.
    # One reduction over every term's column rather than a gather per term: on the auto-reset
    # path ``envs_idx`` is the bool ``reset_buf``, and each gather with it is a GPU->CPU sync.
    max_episode_length_s = self._env.max_episode_length_s
    episode_means = mean_over_envs(self._episode_sums, envs_idx) / max_episode_length_s
    per_term: dict[str, torch.Tensor] = dict(zip(self._term_names, episode_means.unbind()))
    if self._log_per_term:
        raw_episode_means = mean_over_envs(self._episode_raw_sums, envs_idx) / max_episode_length_s
        for key, raw_mean in zip(self._term_names, raw_episode_means.unbind()):
            extras["Episode_Reward/" + key] = per_term[key]
            extras["Episode_Reward_Raw/" + key] = raw_mean
    # Always cleared, even when not logged — the accumulators must reset every episode.
    self._episode_sums[envs_idx] = 0.0
    self._episode_raw_sums[envs_idx] = 0.0
    # Per-group episode averages, derived from the per-term scalars above: groups
    # partition the terms, so a group's average is exactly the sum of its members' —
    # no extra buffer indexing on the auto-reset hot path, and one normalization
    # convention instead of two. Only when groups are declared — ungrouped envs
    # log no group keys. Group sums are emitted regardless of
    # _log_per_term (they are the terse default readout, not per-term detail).
    if self._has_explicit_groups:
        for group, names in self._group_term_names.items():
            extras["Episode_Reward_Group/" + group] = sum((per_term[name] for name in names), self._log_zero)
    for terms in self._reset_terms:
        terms.reset(envs_idx=envs_idx)
    return extras

compute(dt: float) -> Tensor
Source code in eden/managers/reward_manager.py 
@torch.inference_mode()
def compute(self, dt: float) -> torch.Tensor:
    # _step_raw_reward is filled and masked in-place through phases 1-2a; phase 2c writes its
    # weighted copy into _step_reward. After compute() returns, _step_raw_reward holds
    # compute() * mask and _step_reward holds compute() * mask * weight.
    self._last_dt = dt

    # Phase 1: Fill raw term outputs and sync weights (curriculum may modify them).
    # _step_raw_reward[:, i] = term_i.compute()
    # One pass for `compute_once` (ManagerBase): terms share an intermediate within it.
    with self.compute_pass():
        for term_idx, term in enumerate(self._terms.values()):
            self._step_raw_reward[:, term_idx] = term.compute()
    # An env Genesis flagged as corrupt this step is reset in the same step, but its terms just read that state
    # (a NaN contact force, say): the transition carries no signal, and a NaN would end the run in the learner's
    # NaN check and poison the episode sums. ``masked_fill_``, not a multiply: NaN * 0 is NaN.
    self._step_raw_reward.masked_fill_(self._env.get_solver_error_envs_mask()[:, None], 0.0)
    self.sync_device_fields()

    # Phase 2a: Apply temporal mask in-place. Raw episode sums respect this
    # mask too — accumulating before masking would log term outputs from
    # timesteps where range_s makes the term inactive.
    if self._temporal_term_info:
        for idx, step_range in self._temporal_term_info:
            self._temporal_mask[:, idx] = self.is_timestep_in_range(
                self._env.episode_length_buf, step_range
            ).float()
        # _step_raw_reward *= mask  →  now holds compute() * mask
        self._step_raw_reward.mul_(self._temporal_mask)

    # Phase 2b: Accumulate raw episode sums (compute() * mask, no weights).
    self._episode_raw_sums.add_(self._step_raw_reward, alpha=dt)

    # Phase 2c: Apply per-term weights into the weighted buffer; the raw one is kept for
    # get_term_value(). An out-of-place multiply, so keeping it costs no extra copy.
    # _step_reward = _step_raw_reward * weights  →  compute() * mask * weight
    torch.mul(self._step_raw_reward, self._weights, out=self._step_reward)

    # Phase 3: Reduce to scalar reward and accumulate episode sums.
    torch.sum(self._step_reward, dim=1, out=self._reward_buf)
    self._reward_buf.mul_(dt)
    self._episode_sums.add_(self._step_reward, alpha=dt)
    return self._reward_buf

def sync_device_fields(self) -> None:
    """Copy the terms' current ``weight`` onto the device, when one changed since the last call.

    A curriculum may move a term's weight between steps. ``compute()`` calls this; the CUDA graph of the
    graded phase (``EnvOptions.cuda_graph_options``) calls it before each replay instead, since a host-side
    comparison is exactly what a replay skips.
    """
    weights = [term.weight for term in self._terms.values()]
    if weights != self._weights_host:
        self._weights.copy_(torch.tensor(weights, dtype=torch.float))
        self._weights_host = weights

compute() -> Tensor
Source code in eden/managers/termination_manager.py 
def compute(self) -> torch.Tensor:
    self._truncated_buf[:] = False
    self._terminated_buf[:] = False
    # NOTE: reset corrupted state (call set_qpos to reset), per
    # https://github.com/Genesis-Embodied-AI/Genesis/issues/2239; truncated, not terminated, and without
    # any term's verdict (see `solver_errors`).
    self._solver_error_buf[:] = self._env.get_solver_error_envs_mask()
    healthy = ~self._solver_error_buf
    # One pass for `compute_once` (ManagerBase): terms share an intermediate within it.
    with self.compute_pass():
        for name, term in self._terms.items():
            dones = torch.logical_and(term.compute(), healthy, out=self._term_dones[name])  # written in place
            if term.time_out:
                self._truncated_buf |= dones
            else:
                self._terminated_buf |= dones
    self._truncated_buf |= self._solver_error_buf
    return self._truncated_buf | self._terminated_buf

In :meth:RLEnvBase.step this runs after the auto-reset and below the reward, so what it produces is the command the next action is chosen from and phase 19's observations carry — not the command this step was graded against. :meth:_update_command says what belongs here and what does not.

On the deployment path it is one of two command hooks that run: DeploymentBase.step drives :meth:advance_reference first — so a time-advancing reference keeps moving on hardware — then this method and :meth:draw_vis. :meth:post_physics_refresh does not run there at all. def compute(self, dt: float) -> None:
    """Tick the resampling clock, then resample and publish (phase 17 — the *preparation* epoch).

    In :meth:`RLEnvBase.step` this runs after the auto-reset and below the reward, so what it
    produces is the command the next action is chosen from and phase 19's observations carry —
    not the command this step was graded against. :meth:`_update_command` says what belongs
    here and what does not.

    On the deployment path it is one of **two** command hooks that run: ``DeploymentBase.step``
    drives :meth:`advance_reference` first — so a time-advancing reference keeps moving on
    hardware — then this method and :meth:`draw_vis`. :meth:`post_physics_refresh` does not run
    there at all. A deployed term must produce whatever the policy's observations read from here
    or from the advance — see ``docs/guides/terms.md``.
    """
    self.time_left -= dt
    resample_envs_mask = self.time_left <= 0.0
    # NOTE: no `.any()` gate here. `_resample` already counts the mask — its one GPU→CPU
    # sync — and returns early on an empty one, so a gate would only pay that sync twice.
    self._resample(resample_envs_mask)
    self._update_command()

post_physics_refresh() -> None

Refresh state derived from the post-physics robot pose (phase 5 — the grading epoch).

No-op by default; override to refresh caches. This runs after the physics sub-steps and before metric/termination/reward, which makes it the hook for everything that grades this step: pose and contact caches, progress counters, hold latches, tracking errors. A value written here is read by phase 9's reward in the same step — no lag, and nothing to snapshot across the auto-reset. Writing it in :meth:_update_command instead is the bug class docs/guides/terms.md documents under "Which hook: grade the step, or prepare the next one".

Invoked by :meth:CommandManager.post_physics_refresh, which owns the call-time contract — which means it is not invoked on the deployment path: DeploymentBase.step drives :meth:advance_reference and :meth:compute, and nothing between them, because on hardware there are no physics sub-steps to bracket and no reward to grade. State a deployed term's observations read has to be produced from :meth:compute too; an idempotent cache refresh can simply live in both, the way :class:~eden.managers.terms.commands.mimic.MotionCommand refreshes its robot-state cache.

Restart a time-advancing reference at its first frame, for every env (no-op by default).

The reset-side twin of :meth:advance_reference, and it exists for the deployment path alone: DeploymentBase.reset_motion_reference drives it at deploy reset, at the operator's START and on every policy switch, so a clip hands over from its beginning the way the manager path already does through MotionManager.rewind_to_start. docs.title: swap_term
docs.text:
swap_term(name: str, options: CommandTermOptions) -> CommandTerm

Replace the built term name with one configured by options; return the old one.

The post-build counterpart of what the config does before build: a deployment substitutes a task's trained command generator for one an operator drives (:class:~eden.managers.terms.commands.velocity.OperatorVelocityCommand) or one that simply holds a value, the way it substitutes the simulated entity for a :class:~eden.extensions.deployment.utils.state.RobotStateEntity. The caller owns the returned term and can pass its options back here to undo the swap.

The replacement is built and build()-ed exactly as _prepare_terms would, and its command must have the same shape as the one it replaces: the observation buffers and the trained policy's input width were fixed by the old term, so a different width would reach the policy as a silently misaligned observation vector.

Nothing here repoints terms that cached the replaced term in their own build() (the pattern self._command = env.command_manager.get_term(...)). A caller that needs those to follow the swap must repoint them — see :meth:~eden.extensions.deployment.base.DeploymentBase._repoint_command_term_refs.

RAISES DESCRIPTION KeyError

If name is not an active term (the message lists the active ones).

ValueError

If the replacement's command shape differs from the replaced term's.

Source code in eden/managers/command_manager.py 
def swap_term(self, name: str, options: CommandTermOptions) -> CommandTerm:
    """Replace the built term ``name`` with one configured by ``options``; return the old one.

    The post-build counterpart of what the config does before build: a deployment
    substitutes a task's trained command generator for one an operator drives
    (:class:`~eden.managers.terms.commands.velocity.OperatorVelocityCommand`) or one that
    simply holds a value, the way it substitutes the simulated entity for a
    :class:`~eden.extensions.deployment.utils.state.RobotStateEntity`. The caller owns the
    returned term and can pass its options back here to undo the swap.

    The replacement is built and ``build()``-ed exactly as ``_prepare_terms`` would, and its
    command must have the **same shape** as the one it replaces: the observation buffers and
    the trained policy's input width were fixed by the old term, so a different width would
    reach the policy as a silently misaligned observation vector.

    Nothing here repoints terms that cached the *replaced* term in their own ``build()``
    (the pattern ``self._command = env.command_manager.get_term(...)``). A caller that needs
    those to follow the swap must repoint them — see
    :meth:`~eden.extensions.deployment.base.DeploymentBase._repoint_command_term_refs`.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If ``name`` is not an active term (the message lists the active ones).
    ValueError
        If the replacement's command shape differs from the replaced term's.
    """
    old_term = self.get_term(name)
    new_term = self._build_term(name, term_option=options)
    # ``build()`` has already run, so the replacement may own something by now — an
    # OperatorVelocityCommand holds a *process-global* keyboard grab. Release it if we
    # end up rejecting it, or a config error leaves that grab behind with nothing
    # holding a reference to close it.
    try:
        if new_term.command.shape != old_term.command.shape:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Cannot swap command term '{name}': {type(new_term).__name__} commands "
                f"{tuple(new_term.command.shape)} but {type(old_term).__name__} commands "
                f"{tuple(old_term.command.shape)}. The observation width the policy was trained "
                "on comes from the replaced term, so the two must agree."
            )
    except BaseException:
        close = getattr(new_term, "close", None)
        if close is not None:
            close()
        raise
    self._terms[name] = new_term
    return old_term

def restore_term(self, name: str, term: CommandTerm) -> None:
    """Put back a term :meth:`swap_term` returned, undoing that swap.

    Deliberately narrow — it takes an already-built term rather than options, because the
    only correct argument is the exact object ``swap_term`` displaced. Rebuilding the
    original from its options instead would drop whatever state it had accumulated and
    leave any reference the caller repointed pointing at a third object.
    """
    if name not in self._terms:
        available = ", ".join(self._term_names) or "none"
        raise KeyError(f"No active term named '{name}' in {type(self).__name__}. Available options: {available}")
    self._terms[name] = term

@classmethod
def compute_batch(cls, terms: Sequence[EventTerm], envs_idx: slice | torch.Tensor | None) -> None:
    """Fire ``terms``, RESET terms of this kind adjacent in priority order, on the same ``envs_idx``.

    The default fires them one by one. A kind whose terms each write simulator state overrides it
    to write once for all of them (the reference-state-initialization terms: one Genesis write and
    one forward-kinematics pass per reset, not one per entity). The event manager hands a run
    of adjacent RESET terms to one call when each term's class takes both ``compute`` and
    ``compute_batch`` from the same class (a subclass that overrides ``compute`` alone runs alone)
    and none sets ``min_step_count_between_reset`` (so every term fires on exactly ``envs_idx``). A
    throttle set on a batched term after the build splits its batch back into single terms.
    """
    for term in terms:
        term.compute(envs_idx=envs_idx)

def get_term(self, name: str) -> ManagerTermBase:
    """Return the active event term registered under config key ``name``, whatever its mode.

    For a term another one reads from, e.g. ``ResetFromStateBuffer.current_column`` serving a goal stored
    with the reset states.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If ``name`` is not an active term. The message lists the active ones, worded as the flat
        managers' ``get_term`` words it.
    """
    for _, term_name, term in self.iter_terms():
        if term_name == name:
            return term
    available = ", ".join(self.active_terms) or "none"
    raise KeyError(f"No active term named '{name}' in {type(self).__name__}. Available options: {available}")

def reset(self, envs_idx: (slice | torch.Tensor) | None = None):
    for mode_terms in self._mode_reset_terms.values():
        for term in mode_terms:
            term.reset(envs_idx=envs_idx)

        if not state.term.is_global_time:
            assert state.term.interval_range_s is not None
            lower, upper = state.term.interval_range_s
            sampled_interval = torch.rand(self._env.num_envs, device=self.device) * (upper - lower) + lower
            assign_over_envs(state.time_left, envs_idx, sampled_interval)
    return {}

compute(mode: EventMode, envs_idx: slice | Tensor | None = None, dt: float | None = None, global_env_step_count: int | None = None, n_envs: int | None = None)
Source code in eden/managers/event_manager.py 
def compute(
    self,
    mode: EventMode,
    envs_idx: (slice | torch.Tensor) | None = None,
    dt: float | None = None,
    global_env_step_count: int | None = None,
    n_envs: int | None = None,
):
    # ``n_envs``: how many envs ``envs_idx`` selects, when the caller has already counted them (the
    # auto-reset has — it is the gate in ``EnvBase._reset_scene_and_events``). Counting a bool mask
    # is a GPU->CPU sync, so a known count is not paid for twice.
    # Dispatch per mode rather than re-checking ``mode`` for every term. The
    # per-term bodies live in ``_step_{interval,reset}_term`` so each mode's
    # trigger logic reads independently.
    if mode == _INTERVAL:
        if dt is None:
            raise ValueError(f"Event mode '{mode}' requires the time-step of the environment.")
        if envs_idx is not None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Event mode '{mode}' does not require environment indices. This is an undefined behavior"
                " as the environment indices are computed based on the time left for each environment."
            )
        for state in self._interval_states:
            self._step_interval_term(state, dt)
    elif mode == _RESET:
        if global_env_step_count is None:
            raise ValueError(f"Event mode '{mode}' requires the total number of environment steps to be provided.")
        if n_envs is None:
            envs_idx, n_envs = sanitize_envs_idx(envs_idx, self._env.num_envs, return_n_envs=True)
        else:
            envs_idx = sanitize_envs_idx(envs_idx, self._env.num_envs)
        if n_envs == 0:
            return
        for run in self._reset_runs:
            if isinstance(run, ResetTermBatch):
                self._step_reset_batch(run, envs_idx, global_env_step_count)
            else:
                self._step_reset_term(run, envs_idx, global_env_step_count)
    elif mode == _STARTUP:
        for term in self._mode_terms[_STARTUP]:
            term.compute(envs_idx=envs_idx)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid event mode: {mode}")

def __init__(self, env: EnvBase, options: CurriculumManagerOptions):
    super().__init__(env=env, options=options)

    # Keyed only once a term has actually computed, so "never computed" is a missing key
    # rather than a ``None`` value indistinguishable from "computed and published nothing".
    # :meth:`get_state` turns each of those into its own raise.
    self._curriculum_state: dict[str, Any] = dict()
    #: Name of the term currently inside :meth:`compute`, or ``None`` outside the loop. Lets
    #: :meth:`get_state` tell "declared after its consumer" from "read before the run's first
    #: compute()" exactly, rather than guessing from an empty cache -- the cache is *also*
    #: empty for the first term in the loop on the first step, which is the common ordering bug.
    self._computing: str | None = None
    #: ``common_step_counter`` at each term's last publish, written beside the value it dates.
    #: Per-term rather than one stamp for the loop so a term whose ``compute()`` *raised* keeps
    #: the date of the step it last succeeded on, instead of being credited with the step it
    #: died on -- the loop's bookkeeping must not lie to a caller that caught the exception.
    self._published_at: dict[str, int] = dict()

reset(envs_idx: Tensor | slice | None = None) -> dict[str, float | Tensor]

Publish the cached per-term state, then feed the finished episodes to the terms.

The term half is frozen at eval, exactly like :meth:compute — a curriculum term's reset() is how it accumulates the statistics compute() would adapt from (an episode- length EMA, a success rate), so running one without the other would have the internal state drift away from the published one for the whole rollout, on evidence nothing is allowed to act on.

The publish half reports whatever the last :meth:compute cached — and an eval env has no last compute(): env.training is fixed at construction, so an eval rollout logs no Curriculum/* key at all, from its first reset to its last. That is deliberate: the level an eval was graded at is the one its config pins, which the saved config already records; publishing it from here would mean running compute() at build, and the two terms whose compute() has side effects — StageRewardWeightCurriculum and VelocityCommandCurriculum — would then overwrite the configured reward weights and command ranges with their step-0 stage.

def reset(self, envs_idx: torch.Tensor | slice | None = None) -> dict[str, float | torch.Tensor]:
    """Publish the cached per-term state, then feed the finished episodes to the terms.

    The term half is frozen at eval, exactly like :meth:`compute` — a curriculum term's
    ``reset()`` is how it accumulates the statistics ``compute()`` would adapt from (an episode-
    length EMA, a success rate), so running one without the other would have the internal state
    drift away from the published one for the whole rollout, on evidence nothing is allowed to
    act on.

    The publish half reports whatever the last :meth:`compute` cached — and **an eval env has
    no last compute()**: ``env.training`` is fixed at construction, so an eval rollout logs no
    ``Curriculum/*`` key at all, from its first reset to its last. That is deliberate: the
    level an eval was graded at is the one its config pins, which the
    saved config already records; publishing it from here would mean running ``compute()`` at
    build, and the two terms whose ``compute()`` has side effects —
    ``StageRewardWeightCurriculum`` and ``VelocityCommandCurriculum`` — would then *overwrite*
    the configured reward weights and command ranges with their step-0 stage.
    """
    extras = {}
    for term_name, term_state in self._curriculum_state.items():
        if term_state is not None:
            if isinstance(term_state, dict):
                for key, value in term_state.items():
                    extras[f"Curriculum/{term_name}/{key}"] = _published(value)
            else:
                extras[f"Curriculum/{term_name}"] = _published(term_state)
    if not self._env.training:
        return extras
    for term in self._reset_terms:
        term.reset(envs_idx=envs_idx)
    return extras

docs.title: compute
docs.text:
compute() -> None

Adapt every term and cache what it published — a no-op at eval.

Curricula adapt task difficulty from training statistics, so an eval rollout freezes them: otherwise its difficulty is non-stationary, e.g. an EMA-gated goal curriculum at num_envs=1 collapses its window to a single episode, so one failed episode retreats the level mid-rollout and every later episode is graded on an easier task than the one being reported. Terms still apply their configured initial level at build, so eval entry points pin difficulty through the term's own config.

The freeze is all-or-nothing and lives here rather than at the call site so it cannot go asymmetric: :meth:reset is gated the same way. Nothing is cached either, so :meth:get_state raises for every term for the whole rollout rather than handing a consumer a None that reads like "not ready yet".

Source code in eden/managers/curriculum_manager.py 
def compute(self) -> None:
    """Adapt every term and cache what it published — a no-op at eval.

    Curricula adapt task difficulty from training statistics, so an eval rollout freezes them:
    otherwise its difficulty is non-stationary, e.g. an EMA-gated goal curriculum at
    ``num_envs=1`` collapses its window to a single episode, so one failed episode retreats the
    level mid-rollout and every later episode is graded on an easier task than the one being
    reported. Terms still apply their configured initial level at build, so eval entry points
    pin difficulty through the term's own config.

    The freeze is all-or-nothing and lives here rather than at the call site so it cannot go
    asymmetric: :meth:`reset` is gated the same way. Nothing is cached either, so
    :meth:`get_state` raises for every term for the whole rollout rather than handing a
    consumer a ``None`` that reads like "not ready yet".
    """
    if not self._env.training:
        return
    try:
        for name, term in self._terms.items():
            # Recorded so a term that reads a not-yet-computed sibling gets an error naming
            # *which config entry* to move -- the traceback carries the consumer's class, but a
            # task can hold several entries of one class (``penalty_torques`` and
            # ``penalty_smoothness`` in docs/guides/curricula.md), and the entry key is what you edit.
            self._computing = name
            self._curriculum_state[name] = term.compute()
            self._published_at[name] = self._env.common_step_counter
    finally:
        self._computing = None

docs.title: get_state
docs.text:
get_state(term_name: str) -> dict

Return the most recent compute() output cached for the named term.

Never returns None. Every way there can be no state is a raise, because the one thing a consumer must not do is read the absence as "not ready yet" and fall back to a default: that fallback then stands for the whole run, with nothing logged and nothing raised. When you want a level that is correct in both modes, read it off the term itself — curriculum_manager.get_term(name) — which is what ObjectVelocityDisturbance does; get_state is only for consuming what another term published this step, and it enforces that rather than only asking for it: a cached value from an earlier step raises too. Without that the same read is treated two ways -- the run's first step raises, and every step after silently serves the previous step's level, which is the intermittency this contract exists to remove.

Freshness is dated against env.common_step_counter, which advances once per step with the physics (:meth:RLEnvBase.step), so a read from phases 5-20 is placed exactly. Phases 1-3 run before that advance and so still date as the previous step; there is no earlier per-step marker to key off, and what they would read is in any case the newest publish that can exist, since this step's :meth:compute has not run.

RAISES DESCRIPTION KeyError

If no curriculum term is named term_name, so a typo cannot pass for "not computed yet" and leave a consumer that treats that as "not ready" on its default for the whole run.

RuntimeError

If the named term has no state this step. The five causes get five messages, each naming the one edit that fixes it: the env is at eval, so nothing ever computes; the term is declared after the consumer now reading it; the read happens before the run's first compute() at all; the term's compute() returns None; or the read runs earlier in the step than phase 16, so the cache still holds the previous step's publish.

Source code in eden/managers/curriculum_manager.py 
def get_state(self, term_name: str) -> dict:
    """Return the most recent ``compute()`` output cached for the named term.

    **Never returns ``None``.** Every way there can be no state is a raise, because the one
    thing a consumer must not do is read the absence as "not ready yet" and fall back to a
    default: that fallback then stands for the whole run, with nothing logged and nothing
    raised. When you want a level that is correct in *both* modes, read it off the term
    itself — ``curriculum_manager.get_term(name)`` — which is what ``ObjectVelocityDisturbance``
    does; ``get_state`` is only for consuming what another term *published* this step, and it
    enforces that rather than only asking for it: a cached value from an *earlier* step raises
    too. Without that the same read is treated two ways -- the run's first step raises, and
    every step after silently serves the previous step's level, which is the intermittency this
    contract exists to remove.

    Freshness is dated against ``env.common_step_counter``, which advances once per step with
    the physics (:meth:`RLEnvBase.step`), so a read from phases 5-20 is placed exactly. Phases
    1-3 run *before* that advance and so still date as the previous step; there is no earlier
    per-step marker to key off, and what they would read is in any case the newest publish that
    can exist, since this step's :meth:`compute` has not run.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If no curriculum term is named ``term_name``, so a typo cannot pass for "not computed
        yet" and leave a consumer that treats that as "not ready" on its default for the whole run.
    RuntimeError
        If the named term has no state this step. The five causes get five messages, each
        naming the one edit that fixes it: the env is at eval, so nothing ever computes; the
        term is declared after the consumer now reading it; the read happens before the run's
        first ``compute()`` at all; the term's ``compute()`` returns ``None``; or the read runs
        earlier in the step than phase 16, so the cache still holds the previous step's
        publish.
    """
    if term_name not in self._terms:
        # One line on purpose: KeyError.__str__ is repr(args[0]), so a newline here would
        # reach the reader as a literal "\n" in an escaped blob.
        raise KeyError(
            f"No curriculum term named '{term_name}'. Declared curriculum terms: "
            f"{', '.join(self._terms) or '(none)'}. Fix: use one of those keys, or add "
            f"'{term_name}' to curriculum_options."
        )
    if term_name in self._curriculum_state:
        state = self._curriculum_state[term_name]
        if state is None:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Curriculum term '{term_name}' ({self._term_label(term_name)}) computed but published "
                f"nothing: its compute() returned None.\n"
                f"Fix: return a dict of scalars from {self._term_label(term_name)}.compute() — it is both "
                f"what get_state() serves and what is logged as Curriculum/{term_name}/<key>.\n"
                "A term that publishes on some steps and not others raises here intermittently; publish "
                "every step, or do not let anything read this term's state."
            )
        published_at = self._published_at[term_name]
        step = self._env.common_step_counter
        if published_at != step:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Curriculum term '{term_name}' last published at step {published_at}, and it is now step "
                f"{step}: this cached value is one control step stale.\n"
                "reading from: a phase earlier in the step than CurriculumManager.compute(), which is "
                "phase 16 (docs/guides/environments.md) — a curriculum term's reset(), a metric, a "
                "termination and a reward all run before it\n"
                f"Fix: read the level off the term itself — curriculum_manager.get_term('{term_name}'), a "
                f"{self._term_label(term_name)} — which is current at every phase; or move this read into "
                "a hook that runs after phase 16, where get_state() serves the current step's publish.\n"
                "Do NOT call CurriculumManager.compute() yourself to refresh it: terms adapt as a side "
                "effect of computing — PenaltyCurriculum steps its scale by `degree` toward a threshold "
                "bound on each call — so a second call inside one step advances the curriculum twice."
            )
        return state
    if not self._env.training:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Curriculum term '{term_name}' has no state: this env was built with eval_mode=True, and "
            "CurriculumManager.compute() is a no-op at eval, so no term computes and nothing is ever "
            "cached — for the whole rollout, not just this step.\n"
            f"Fix: read the level off the term itself — curriculum_manager.get_term('{term_name}'), a "
            f"{self._term_label(term_name)} — which holds the configured level in training and at eval "
            "alike; that is what ObjectVelocityDisturbance._adaptive_scale does.\n"
            "Do NOT catch this and fall back to a default: the default would stand for every step of the "
            "eval, grading it at a difficulty no training step used, with nothing logged and nothing "
            "raised. Closing that silent fallback is why this raises at all."
        )
    if self._computing is not None:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Curriculum term '{term_name}' has not computed yet, so it has no state to read.\n"
            f"curriculum_options order: {', '.join(self._term_names)}\n"
            f"'{self._computing}' is reading '{term_name}', but '{term_name}' is declared after it\n"
            f"Fix: move '{term_name}' above '{self._computing}' in curriculum_options — "
            "CurriculumManager computes terms in declaration order, so a producer declared after its "
            "consumer would feed it a value one control step stale."
        )
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"Curriculum term '{term_name}' has no state yet: this read happens before the run's first "
        "CurriculumManager.compute(), which is step phase 16 (docs/guides/environments.md).\n"
        "reading from: outside the curriculum compute loop — build(), the first reset(), or task setup\n"
        f"Fix: read the term's own level off curriculum_manager.get_term('{term_name}'), a "
        f"{self._term_label(term_name)}, which is valid from build() onward. get_state() only ever "
        "serves what a term has already published."
    )

SuccessCheckerMixin(options: T)

Bases: ConfigurableMixin

The configurable fields every metric term has, class or function, and the success check they drive.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION success_threshold

The threshold for success. The threshold is inclusive. Defaults to 1.0.

direction

The metric direction. Defaults to MetricDirection.HIB ("hib").

metric_mode

The metric success mode. Defaults to MetricMode.INTERVAL ("interval").

is_cumulative

Whether the metric is cumulative. Defaults to False.

contributes_to_success

Whether this term participates in task-success accounting (success_buf, Metrics/Success, Metrics/Progress, and the per-episode success label the recorder stamps). Defaults to True. Set False for a term that exists only to share a computed quantity with other terms (via metric_manager.get_value — see metric_reward / metric_observation) and has no notion of succeeding: such a term would otherwise pin Metrics/Success to its own trivially-true (or trivially-false) verdict for the whole task. is_success is never called on a non-contributing term, so its success_threshold / direction are unused.

Notes

These five settings are fixed once the metric manager is built: it reads them into its batched reset() then, so a later write to one (from a curriculum, say) would not take effect. Set them through configure.
