docs.title: tcp_offset property
docs.text:
tcp_offset: tuple[float, float, float]

The tool point — pad midpoint with the gripper open — in the ee_link frame (m).

The gripper's own tcp_offset (declared in its base-link frame) carried through the mounting pose the weld applies, so a rig with an attach_offset / attach_quat reports the point where the pads actually are. The config-time twin of the grasp frame the robosuite terms measure on the built rig.

docs.title: max_substep_dt property
docs.text:
max_substep_dt: float | None

Finest substep either half of the rig needs (None when neither declares one).

A rig is only as stiff as its stiffest constraint allows: welding a Robotiq onto an arm that imposes nothing still means the rig cannot be stepped above the Robotiq's limit. Read it when choosing EnvOptions.sim_dt / sim_substeps for a scene that holds the rig.

docs.title: hold_width
docs.text:
hold_width(width: float, clearance: float = 0.002) -> dict[str, float]

Finger DOF targets that put the pads width + 2 * clearance apart.

Linear between gripper_open (pads :attr:stroke apart) and gripper_close (pads touching), clamped to that range — so a Franka Hand holding a 4 cm peg gets each prismatic finger at ~2.2 cm, and a Robotiq the matching driver angle. Meant for objects welded to the hand; a free object is grasped by the gripper action instead.

def hold_width(self, width: float, clearance: float = 0.002) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Finger DOF targets that put the pads ``width + 2 * clearance`` apart.

    Linear between ``gripper_open`` (pads :attr:`stroke` apart) and ``gripper_close`` (pads
    touching), clamped to that range — so a Franka Hand holding a 4 cm peg gets each prismatic
    finger at ~2.2 cm, and a Robotiq the matching driver angle. Meant for objects welded to the
    hand; a free object is grasped by the gripper action instead.
    """
    closed = min(max(1.0 - (width + 2.0 * clearance) / self.stroke, 0.0), 1.0)
    return {
        dof: self.gripper_open[dof] + closed * (self.gripper_close[dof] - self.gripper_open[dof])
        for dof in self.gripper_dofs
    }

docs.title: preset_hold
docs.text:
preset_hold(width: float, clearance: float = 0.002) -> None

Start the gripper closed on an object width m wide: writes :meth:hold_width into its defaults.

Unlike :meth:hold_width, which clamps because it is asked for a pose and a pose always exists, this refuses a width the gripper cannot close on. The two differ because the outcomes differ: a clamped query is a number the caller can inspect, whereas a clamped preset silently starts the episode with the gripper wide open around an object welded into it — a rig that looks like it is holding something it is not, with nothing to notice.

Source code in eden/options/robots/composite/base.py 
def preset_hold(self, width: float, clearance: float = 0.002) -> None:
    """Start the gripper closed on an object ``width`` m wide: writes :meth:`hold_width` into its defaults.

    Unlike :meth:`hold_width`, which clamps because it is asked for a pose and a pose always
    exists, this refuses a width the gripper cannot close on. The two differ because the
    outcomes differ: a clamped *query* is a number the caller can inspect, whereas a clamped
    *preset* silently starts the episode with the gripper wide open around an object welded into
    it — a rig that looks like it is holding something it is not, with nothing to notice.
    """
    if width <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{type(self).__name__}.preset_hold needs the width of an object to hold, got {width} m. "
            f"To start the gripper simply shut, set its defaults from gripper_close instead."
        )
    opening = width + 2.0 * clearance
    if opening > self.stroke:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{type(self).__name__} cannot hold a {width} m object at {clearance} m clearance: that needs a "
            f"{opening} m opening and {type(self.gripper).__name__}'s stroke is {self.stroke} m. Widths up to "
            f"{self.stroke - 2.0 * clearance} m fit at this clearance."
        )
    self.gripper.default_dofs_pos.update(self.hold_width(width, clearance))

docs.title: HumanoidOptions
docs.text:
HumanoidOptions(**data)

Bases: CompositeEntityOptions

Shared base for a bimanual humanoid rig: a hand-stripped humanoid + an end-effector per wrist.

The bimanual counterpart of :class:_ArmCompositeOptions. Where an arm rig welds one end-effector to one arm, a humanoid rig welds a left and a right one — a dexterous hand or a two-finger gripper, whichever the embodiment carries — onto the flange frames the humanoid asset declares, and so expands into three scene entities rather than two::

rig = HumanoidOptions(robot=OliNoHands(), left_hand=..., right_hand=...,
                      left_ee_link="left_hand_mount", right_ee_link="right_hand_mount")
scene = en.scenes.Empty(robot=rig)
# -> entities "robot", "left_hand", "right_hand"

The humanoid is the composite's primary body, so the scene placement key must equal :attr:robot_name. Concrete rigs (LimX Oli + Wuji hands, …) subclass this with default fields and register in :data:COMPOSITE_ROBOT_REGISTRY; the useful default is the hand-stripped humanoid variant (OliNoHands, G1Dofs29NoHands), so the arms carry the real end-effector's mass and not that plus a moulded phantom one.

Everything a controller needs is a shortcut property over the sub-options, so the DOF lists and grasp links cannot drift from the robot definitions::

JointPositionAction.configure(entity_name=rig.robot_name, dofs_name=rig.robot_dofs)
DifferentialIKController.configure(entity_name=rig.robot_name, ee_link_name=rig.right_ee_link)

A gripper-ended rig reads its open/close targets off the sub-option (rig.left_hand.open_dofs_pos): unlike :class:ManipulatorOptions, this base stays end-effector agnostic, since a humanoid can wear a different one per side.

The mount transform is likewise shared by default (:attr:mount_offset / :attr:mount_quat) but overridable per wrist (:attr:left_mount_quat and friends), because "both flanges take the same transform" holds only where the asset frames are mirror images — true of Oli's *_hand_mount pair, not a property of humanoids in general.

What the rig stands on follows the same shape: :attr:feet_links reads the humanoid's own feet_links_name unless :attr:feet_links_name overrides it, for a rig whose ground contact is not the humanoid's declared feet.

docs.title: weld_quat
docs.text:
weld_quat(child: EntityOptions, mount_quat: UnitVec4FType) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]

The attach_quat that makes mount_quat a rotation of URDF link frames.

Genesis applies a weld's quaternion before the morph frame offset, and Eden keeps the child's up/front alignment in that offset (Entity._create_morph_from_options), so the parent link gets attach @ align. Right-multiplying by align^-1 cancels it, making mount_quat mean the child's base-link orientation in the parent link frame — the identity when the two URDF frames coincide.

A no-op for a child with the Eden default axes. The Wuji hands' alignment is a 180 deg rotation, so leaving it in welds the hand pointing back up the forearm, silently.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION child

The entity being welded, read for its up / front declaration. A primitive has no asset axes to align and is not a supported end-effector.

TYPE: EntityOptions

mount_quat

Intended (w, x, y, z) orientation of the child's base link in the parent link frame. Scaling is harmless (quat_to_R normalizes); zero raises, since Genesis would only surface a bare ZeroDivisionError.

TYPE: array - like[float, float, float, float]

RETURNS DESCRIPTION tuple[float, float, float, float]

The (w, x, y, z) quaternion to pass as the weld's attach_quat.

Source code in eden/options/robots/composite/base.py 
def weld_quat(child: EntityOptions, mount_quat: UnitVec4FType) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    """The ``attach_quat`` that makes ``mount_quat`` a rotation of URDF *link* frames.

    Genesis applies a weld's quaternion **before** the morph frame offset, and Eden keeps the
    child's ``up``/``front`` alignment in that offset (``Entity._create_morph_from_options``), so
    the parent link gets ``attach @ align``. Right-multiplying by ``align^-1`` cancels it, making
    ``mount_quat`` mean the child's base-link orientation in the parent link frame — the identity
    when the two URDF frames coincide.

    A no-op for a child with the Eden default axes. The Wuji hands' alignment is a 180 deg
    rotation, so leaving it in welds the hand pointing back up the forearm, silently.

    Parameters
    ----------
    child : EntityOptions
        The entity being welded, read for its ``up`` / ``front`` declaration. A primitive has no
        asset axes to align and is not a supported end-effector.
    mount_quat : array-like[float, float, float, float]
        Intended (w, x, y, z) orientation of the child's base link in the parent link frame.
        Scaling is harmless (``quat_to_R`` normalizes); zero raises, since Genesis would only
        surface a bare ``ZeroDivisionError``.

    Returns
    -------
    tuple[float, float, float, float]
        The (w, x, y, z) quaternion to pass as the weld's ``attach_quat``.
    """
    quat = np.asarray(mount_quat, dtype=np.float64)
    if np.linalg.norm(quat) < 1e-12:
        raise ValueError(f"mount_quat must be a non-zero quaternion (w, x, y, z); got {tuple(mount_quat)}.")
    align = align_up_and_front(child.up, child.front)
    return tuple(float(v) for v in gu.R_to_quat(gu.quat_to_R(quat) @ align.T))

def has_frame_alignment(child: EntityOptions) -> bool:
    """Whether ``child``'s ``up``/``front`` rotate its asset at load, so a weld must cancel them."""
    return not np.allclose(align_up_and_front(child.up, child.front), np.eye(3), atol=1e-9)

Franka Emika Panda arm + Franka Hand, as a composite rig.

The same robot as :class:~eden.options.robots.FrankaEmikaPanda (one MJCF, arm and fingers in one entity) but assembled the way every other manipulator rig is: the arm-only :class:~eden.options.robots.FrankaEmikaPandaNoHand with the :class:~eden.options.robots.FrankaHand welded onto its attachment flange. docs.title: FrankaXHand
docs.text:
FrankaXHand(**data)

Bases: DexManipulatorOptions

Franka arm + RobotEra XHand1 (left) on the LeFranX right-angle coupling, a 12-DOF dexterous manipulator.

The dexterous counterpart of :class:~eden.options.robots.composite.droid.Droid: same Franka arm and home pose, but the two-finger gripper is swapped for the XHand1 hand, welded to the Franka's attachment frame and driven in joint space. The grasp point is the fingertip centroid. Construct like any Options preset — FrankaXHand(base_pos=(0, 0, 0.4)) — and add it to a scene by name (en.scenes.Empty(robot=FrankaXHand(...))); the scene expands it into the robot (arm) and hand entities.

The hand hangs on the coupling (wengmister/xhand-coupling <https://github.com/wengmister/xhand-coupling>_, the mount of the LeFranX Franka + XHand teleoperation stack), a plate bolted to the flange plus a holder hanging off it. The hand's finger axis is perpendicular to the flange axis and its palm faces along it, so with the flange pointing down the fingers are horizontal and the palm faces down. Both CAD parts are exported in one assembly frame, which fixes the transform: the hand's Ø38 wrist bore slides over the holder's 13 mm boss and the wrist face rests on the seat around it, 46 mm out from the flange face and 37 mm off the flange axis; the fingers point back across that axis.

The clocking about the flange axis is the one measured on a lab robot: at the Franka ready pose (0, -pi/4, 0, -3pi/4, 0, pi/2, pi/4) the fingertips point along the base frame's -y, the palm faces down and the thumb is on the base's side. That is one 90-degree bolt step off the coupling's dowel-pin hole. A coupling mounted on its pin instead hangs the hand at attach_offset=(-0.037, 0.0, 0.046), attach_quat=(0.0, 0.7071068, 0.0, 0.7071068) (fingertips along -x at the ready pose). A hand on another mount takes that mount's attach_offset / attach_quat the same way.

Only the weld is modelled. The coupling itself (75 x 77 x 95 mm envelope) has no geometry here, so nothing collides with it.

docs.title: xArm7 + XHand
docs.text:
XArm7XHand = UFACTORY xArm7 + RobotEra XHand1 (left/right), ConTrack's rig.

ConTrack ships the arm and hand pre-welded in one URDF (assets/urdf/xarm_xhand_{left,right}.urdf). This composite reproduces that chain from Eden's own unit robots — :class:~eden.options.robots.ufactory_xarm7.Xarm7 plus :class:~eden.options.robots.robotera_xhand.XHand1_L/XHand1_R — welded at the arm flange, so the rig needs no ConTrack-specific asset. Genesis attach removes the hand's root joint and merges both bodies into a single kinematic tree, so this is a true fixed joint, not a constraint-based weld.

Equivalence to ConTrack's combined URDF (verified in tests/options/robots/composite/test_xarm_xhand.py):

  • The xArm7 chain (link_base..link7: joint origins, axes, limits, masses, inertias, dynamics) is bit-identical between Eden's arms/ufactory_xarm7/xarm.urdf and the combined file.
  • ConTrack welds the hand with joint_eef: link7 -> {side}_hand_link at xyz=(0, 0, 0.007) rpy=(3.14, 0, ±1.57). Eden's link_eef is a zero-offset fixed child of link7, and Eden's XHand1 assets carry that rpy rotation inside the asset (their base frame is the flange-aligned convention), so the mount reduces to :data:_MOUNT_OFFSET with an identity rotation.
  • rpy="3.14 0 ±1.57" truncates π and π/2, i.e. ConTrack's weld is 1.781 mrad off the exact rotation. Mount at ConTrack's own truncated value and all 38 link positions agree to 292 nm — the chains are the same geometry. This rig mounts at the exact rotation instead, which leaves a 0.37 mm systematic offset at the fingertips versus the released clips. That is deliberate: this is a general-purpose preset, so it describes the real robot rather than reproducing one dataset's typo, and 0.37 mm is ~80x below the tightest std any ConTrack reward uses (3 cm contact distance). Override attach_quat if you need the truncated frame bit-for-bit.
  • Every hand link frame is rotated by a constant 180° ((1, ±1, 0)/√2) relative to the combined URDF: the two XHand1 revisions use mirrored per-link frame conventions. Link positions, joint values, and dynamics are unaffected; only link quaternions differ, so terms that read a hand link's orientation are not frame-comparable with the source implementation.

Known asset-revision deltas (Eden's XHand1 is a later revision than ConTrack's copy): per-link masses differ by ≤ 8 g (largest: right thumb_rota_link2, 35 g vs 43 g), the *back*/*tip* massless stubs carry different placeholder inertias, and thumb_rota_joint1/2 cap at 1.570 rad instead of 1.745. The bundled clips peak at 1.505 rad on thumb_rota_joint1, so the reference stays reachable — but the residual policy's ±0.25 rad finger action clips ~0.07 rad earlier than in the source.

SimToolReal's merged 29-DOF URDF (iiwa14_left_sharpa_adjusted_restricted.urdf) reaches the hand through two intermediate frames::

iiwa14_link_7
  --[iiwa14_joint_ee     xyz=(0, 0, 0.045)  rpy=(0, 0, 0)      ]--> iiwa14_link_ee
  --[iiwa14_sharpa       xyz=(0, 0, 0)      rpy=(0, 0, +15 deg)]--> sharpa_mount
  --[sharpa_mount_joint  xyz=(0, 0, 0.05)   rpy=(0, 0, -90 deg)]--> left_hand_C_MC

Both are pure frames (sharpa_mount carries only a 50 g placeholder mass) and every rotation is about z, so the chain collapses to the one attach_offset / attach_quat weld below. Verified against that URDF: 36/36 links, forward kinematics <= 9e-7 m / 2.5e-4 deg, per-DOF dynamics exact, and a 200-step 29-DOF PD rollout agreeing to 0.002 deg. Three deliberate differences: the 0.05 kg sharpa_mount has no counterpart (leaving the arm's M(q) block 0.5-0.7% low), arm collision is 46 MJCF spheres vs 8 URDF meshes (hand geometry is identical), and :data:SIMTOOLREAL_HAND_DOFS_POS_LIMITS is opt-in.

That agreement also depends on the joint damping and effort limit the iiwa14 MJCF omits; those are hardware properties so they live on :class:~eden.options.robots.kuka_iiwa14.Iiwa14 and are inherited here.

docs.title: G1 + Inspire hands
docs.text:
G1Inspire = Unitree G1 29DoF body + an Inspire RH56DFQ hand welded to each wrist (Weave's G1-Inspire-HOI rig).

The composite form of Weave's merged g1_29dof_rev_1_0_with_inspire_hand_DFQ.urdf, cut at its two fixed hand joints so each hand is its own scene entity with its own DOFs while the assembled rig is the one the Weave reference motions were retargeted onto.

The body is :class:~eden.options.robots.unitree_g1.G1Dofs29NoHands on the bare-wrist URDF: the same G1 rev 1.0 joints, frames and masses, except that each *_wrist_yaw_link carries the bare wrist (0.0846 kg) rather than the no-hand MJCF's wrist-plus-rubber-hand (0.2546 kg), so the arms carry the welded hands' real mass and no phantom payload on top.

The mount is the fixed hand joint the split cut (*_base_link_joint): the hand base link sits 0.0415 m along the wrist, rotated rpy (0, 0, π/2) left and (π, 0, -π/2) right. Those two rotations are not mirror images, so the rig sets them per side. :class:~eden.datasets.weave_dataset.WeaveG1InspireHOIDataset rebuilds the hand base pose of the reference from the same constants.

The hands are not gravity-compensated: the G1 is a floating-base humanoid whose arms carry the 0.19 kg per hand.

docs.title: G1 + Wuji hands
docs.text:
G1Wuji = Unitree G1 29-DOF (hands stripped) + a Wuji Hand2 beta2 bolted to each wrist.

The G1 counterpart of :class:~eden.options.robots.composite.oli_wuji.OliWuji. The flange is the *_ee_link frame the no-hand G1 MJCF declares 4 cm past each *_wrist_yaw_link, along the forearm (+x of the wrist frame).

The orientation. Unlike Oli, the G1 wrist frame runs its forearm along +x, while a Wuji hand's fingers run along its base link's -z. The mount is therefore -90 deg about the flange's y axis, which takes the hand's -z onto the flange's +x: fingers continue the forearm, palm toward the body midline and thumb on the wrist frame's +z (forward in the arms-down pose). One quaternion serves both sides, because the per-side chirality lives in the _L / _R hand assets.

docs.title: Oli + Wuji hands
docs.text:
OliWuji = LimX Oli (hands stripped) + a Wuji Hand2 beta2 bolted to each wrist flange.

A :class:~eden.options.robots.composite.base.HumanoidOptions rig: a humanoid root with two dexterous hands, rather than the one-arm-one-end-effector shape of :class:~eden.options.robots.composite.base._ArmCompositeOptions. Both welds are identities, so this module is entirely defaults — the entity names, the pelvis knob, the mount transform, the DOF shortcuts and the two welds all come from the base.

The flange. Carried by the asset, not by this file: :class:~eden.options.robots.limx_oli.OliNoHands declares a pure *_hand_mount frame on each exposed wrist flange, so the hands seat on it with no offset and nothing here re-derives one.

The orientation. Also the identity, because both assets already share the wrist convention: Oli's arm and its moulded hand run along -Z, which is the Wuji finger axis (up=(0, 0, -1)); and the moulded hand is wide across X (8.6 cm), thin across Y (5.5 cm), with its distal geometry drifting +Y right / -Y left — fingers curling toward the palm — which is the palm normal the Wuji hand declares per side. Palm inboard, thumb forward.

The catch. A Wuji hand's up/front rotate its asset 180 deg at load, and a weld has to cancel that or the hand ends up pointing back up the forearm — see :func:~eden.options.robots.composite.base.weld_quat, which :meth:~eden.options.robots.composite.base.HumanoidOptions._mount_spec applies to every humanoid weld.

The hands are deliberately not gravity-compensated (unlike the industrial-arm rigs here): Oli is a floating-base humanoid whose arms must carry the payload they are given.

docs.title: Scene Presets
docs.text:
Scene presets are functions that return a SceneOptions with a ground plane (or a full room) already in it. The robot is the robot argument (left_robot / right_robot on the two-arm BimanualEmpty and LBMEval), and every other entity is a keyword argument named after it. The core presets are also exported as short names: en.scenes.Empty, BimanualEmpty, Tabletop, KitchenCountertop and LBMEval. The scenes and terrains guide covers scenes, objects and terrain.

import eden as en

# excerpted from eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py
scene_options = en.scenes.Empty(
    is_support_enabled=True,
    robot=en.robots.Yam(default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), default_root_quat=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
)

docs.title: Core presets
docs.text:
Empty scene presets (plane-only, single and bimanual).

These are factory functions, not SceneOptions subclasses: each returns a plain SceneOptions with the ground plane and robot(s) added as named children. A factory (rather than a builder __init__ on a subclass) keeps the saved/reconstructed type a base SceneOptions, so a config round-trips through validated load — a builder __init__ that takes non-persisted args (is_support_enabled/surface) and injects entities cannot be reconstructed from the serialized entity list.

Tabletop and kitchen-countertop scene options.

These are factory functions, not SceneOptions subclasses: each returns a plain SceneOptions with the table/countertop and ground plane added as named children, so a config round-trips through validated load (the saved/reconstructed type is a base SceneOptions).

LBM-eval scene options.

def EmptySceneOptions(
    robot: EntityOptions,
    *,
    is_support_enabled: bool = False,
    surface: SurfaceLike | None = None,
    **entities: EntityOptions,
) -> SceneOptions:
    """Basic scene with a robot and a ground plane.

    Parameters
    ----------
    robot : EntityOptions
        The robot entity configuration.
    is_support_enabled : bool
        Whether to enable support-surface tracking on the plane.
    surface : SurfaceLike | None
        Surface for the plane, e.g. ``PlasticSurfaceOptions(color=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0))``.
    **entities : EntityOptions
        Additional named entities to add to the scene. Passing ``plane=`` replaces the flat
        ground with that entity (e.g. ``TerrainOptions``) under the same name.
    """
    ground = _ground(entities, is_support_enabled, surface)  # pops a `plane` override out of entities
    return SceneOptions(robot=robot, plane=ground, **entities)

docs.text:
LBMEvalSceneOptions(left_robot: EntityOptions | None = None, right_robot: EntityOptions | None = None, plane: PlaneOptions | None = None, **kwargs: EntityOptions) -> SceneOptions

Bimanual scene built around the Riverway dual-Franka station.

The two arms default to :class:FrankaEmikaPanda. The scene re-poses them onto the station's left (+x site) and right (-y site) gantry base plates, orients each one so its forward (+x) points into the workspace (left=180° about z, right=90° about z), and applies a ±π/4 offset to joint1 (the base DOF) so the two arms splay away from each other at init instead of meeting in the middle of the table.

Returns a plain :class:SceneOptions (station + re-posed robots as named children) so the config round-trips through validated load.

Source code in eden/options/scenes/lbm_eval.py 
def LBMEvalSceneOptions(
    left_robot: EntityOptions | None = None,
    right_robot: EntityOptions | None = None,
    plane: PlaneOptions | None = None,
    **kwargs: EntityOptions,
) -> SceneOptions:
    """Bimanual scene built around the Riverway dual-Franka station.

    The two arms default to :class:`FrankaEmikaPanda`. The scene re-poses them
    onto the station's left (+x site) and right (-y site) gantry base plates,
    orients each one so its forward (+x) points into the workspace
    (left=180° about z, right=90° about z), and applies a ±π/4 offset to
    ``joint1`` (the base DOF) so the two arms splay away from each other at
    init instead of meeting in the middle of the table.

    Returns a plain :class:`SceneOptions` (station + re-posed robots as named
    children) so the config round-trips through validated load.
    """
    if left_robot is None or right_robot is None:
        # Lazy import: a robot module loads the whole ``eden.options.robots`` package,
        # which this scene needs only for the default arms.
        from eden.options.robots.franka_emika_panda import FrankaEmikaPanda

        if left_robot is None:
            left_robot = FrankaEmikaPanda()
        if right_robot is None:
            right_robot = FrankaEmikaPanda()

    scene_kwargs: dict[str, EntityOptions] = {
        "station": LBMRiverwayStation(),
        "left_robot": left_robot.model_copy(
            update={
                "default_root_pos": LBM_LEFT_ROBOT_POS,
                "default_root_quat": LBM_LEFT_ROBOT_QUAT,
                "default_dofs_pos": _with_joint1_offset(left_robot, _LBM_LEFT_JOINT1_OFFSET),
            }
        ),
        "right_robot": right_robot.model_copy(
            update={
                "default_root_pos": LBM_RIGHT_ROBOT_POS,
                "default_root_quat": LBM_RIGHT_ROBOT_QUAT,
                "default_dofs_pos": _with_joint1_offset(right_robot, _LBM_RIGHT_JOINT1_OFFSET),
            }
        ),
    }
    if plane is not None:
        scene_kwargs["plane"] = plane
    return SceneOptions(**scene_kwargs, **kwargs)

def CalvinPlayTableSceneOptions(robot: EntityOptions | None = None, **kwargs: EntityOptions) -> SceneOptions:
    """CALVIN play-table scene built from the original table-D and block URDFs.

    Returns a plain :class:`SceneOptions` with the play table and the three
    colored blocks added as named children so the config round-trips through
    validated load.

        "plane": PlaneOptions(),
        "table": CalvinPlayTable(default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
        "block_red": CalvinRedBlock(default_root_pos=(-0.12, -0.12, 0.49)),

docs.title: Sensor and Camera Options
docs.text:
SensorsOptions and CamerasOptions are the sensors_options and cameras_options fields of a config. Each holds named children: one SensorOptions or CameraOptions per sensor or camera, keyed by the name the env exposes it under (env.sensors[...], env.cameras[...]). A SensorOptions wraps any Genesis sensor options (gs.sensors.*, or one of Eden's engine sensors) and says which entity and link to attach it to. The sensors and rendering guide explains each sensor and camera mode.

from eden.options.camera import CameraOptions, CamerasOptions
from eden.options.sensors import SensorOptions, SensorsOptions

Configuration for a single camera.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION model

Camera model.

Camera position.

cam_lookat

Camera lookat.

cam_resolution

Camera resolution in (width, height).

cam_up

Camera up vector.

cam_intrinsic

Camera intrinsic matrix, used to set the camera's field of view and resolution. If provided, cam_fov and cam_resolution will be ignored.

cam_extrinsic

Camera extrinsic matrix, used to set the camera's position, lookat, and up. The extrinsic matrix is the inverse of the transform from the camera frame to the world frame. If provided, cam_pos, cam_lookat, and cam_up will be ignored.

cam_aperture

Camera aperture.

cam_fov

Vertical field of view, in degrees.

cam_near

Near clipping plane in meters. None leaves Genesis's default (rasterizer/batch renderer only).

cam_far

Far clipping plane in meters. None leaves Genesis's default (rasterizer/batch renderer only).

debug

Whether to enable debug mode.

follow_entity_name

Name of the entity to follow.

attach_entity_name

Name of the entity to attach the camera to.

attach_link_name

Name of the link to attach the camera to.

attach_offset

Offset of the camera from the link.

attach_quat

Quaternion of the camera from the link (w, x, y, z).

overlays

What :meth:~eden.entities.camera.Camera.render_rgb paints onto every frame after the renderer made it, in order: a background composite (BackgroundImageComposite for a backdrop image, SplatComposite for a splat env's Gaussian splat), then state the task tracks but the scene does not render, such as the ink on a whiteboard. Reaches the recording and anything else built on render_rgb; an overlay leaves the pixels a composite before it replaced. An overlay that reads the point cloud costs a second render of the view per frame. See :mod:eden.entities.camera_overlays.

sensor_options

Genesis sensor options (e.g. RasterizerCameraOptions, NyxCameraOptions). When provided, the camera uses scene.add_sensor() instead of scene.add_camera(). The sensor backend only supports RGB rendering; depth/segmentation/normal/pointcloud are not available. Fields pos/lookat/fov/res/up are auto-populated from cam_pos/cam_lookat/cam_fov/cam_resolution/cam_up during build if not explicitly set.

Built with the overlay class's configure(), e.g. PlanePaintOverlay.configure(metric_name="drawing", color=(0, 0, 0)), which fills name with the overlay's registry key and carries its parameters as extras. docs.title: Splat and Renderer Options
docs.text:
Options for photorealistic backgrounds and the non-default renderers. SplatOptions configures a Gaussian-splat background rendered with gsplat and NyxSplatOptions one rendered with the Nyx path tracer; PCDOptions loads a raw point cloud. RayTracerOptions and BatchRendererOptions are Eden's versions of Genesis' ray tracer and Madrona batch renderer options. The sensors and rendering guide explains when to use each renderer, and the scenes guide covers real-to-sim splat scenes.

from eden.options.splat import SplatOptions
from eden.options.renderer import BatchRendererOptions

A camera shows the splat only when its CameraOptions.overlays declares a SplatComposite (camera overlays).

docs.title: PCDOptions
docs.text:
PCDOptions(**data)

Bases: ConfigurableOptions

PCD options for Eden.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION path

Path to the ply file, fetched from registry/dataset when it is not a local file.

local_dir

Where the file is cached. Unset, it is assets_subdir under the asset root, resolved when the options are built (:meth:resolve_local_dir), so a saved config's local_dir stays unset.

assets_subdir

The subdirectory of the asset root that an unset local_dir means; empty is the root. A field, and so saved with the config, unlike EntityOptions' class constant: PCDs have no per-family subclasses to carry one, and saving it is harmless here. It is a relative name, never a machine's path, and it is read only while the options are built, since path is resolved to the local file then and saved resolved. What the class-constant rule elsewhere keeps out of saved configs is an absolute default path.

scale

Scale factor.

pos

Translation of the pcd.

quat

Rotation of the pcd (w, x, y, z).

multiplier

Per-splat radiance scale. Maps to LightFieldAsset.multiplier on the Nyx backend; ignored by the gsplat backend (SplatOptions). 1.0 leaves the splat unchanged, >1 brightens, <1 darkens.

tint

Per-channel multiplicative tint applied on top of multiplier. Maps to LightFieldAsset.tint on the Nyx backend; ignored by the gsplat backend.

attach_entity

Name of the entity whose pose drives this splat. Requires SplatOptions(per_env_gaussians=True): when set, the splat is treated as a dynamic rigid body that follows this entity per environment. None marks a static background splat. Ignored by the Nyx backend (which renders a static background).

attach_link

Optional link name on attach_entity to bind to (defaults to the entity's base link).

docs.title: SplatOptions
docs.text:
SplatOptions(**data)

Bases: DynamicConfigurableOptions

Gaussian-splat options for Eden, consumed by :class:~eden.envs.splat.SplatEnvBase (non-RL) and :class:~eden.envs.splat.SplatRLEnvBase (RL).

The one gsplat backend (:class:~eden.utils.batch_splat_renderer.BatchSplatRenderer), composited over the sim pass by segmentation mask. There is no sh_degree field (SH is read from each PLY) and no bg_color field (the background is the composite, not a fill). Shadows that sim objects cast on the background entities are carried onto the splat per camera, with the shadow_strength of the camera's SplatComposite overlay. Nyx is the separate path-traced backend (:class:NyxSplatOptions).

Which camera renders each view is selected by camera_mode — :class:~eden.entities.camera.SplatCamera renders one env-invariant pose and broadcasts it (cheap; a fixed camera over a shared background), :class:~eden.entities.camera.BatchSplatCamera renders every env's camera (needed for an attached/following camera or per_env_gaussians).

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION per_env_gaussians

The shared / per-env Gaussian switch. False (shared) stores one Gaussian set and renders every env's camera from it — memory-light, scales to many envs, but the splat scene is identical across envs. True (per-env) gives each env its own Gaussians so splats bound to entities (PCDOptions.attach_entity) follow that env's sim poses; memory is O(num_envs * G), fitting tens–hundreds of envs. Forces the batched camera.

minibatch

Chunk size over the env/view axis, bounding peak VRAM (gsplat evaluates view-dependent SH per rendered view). None renders all envs at once.

camera_mode

How each splat camera renders. "auto" (default) picks per camera: the batched camera when per_env_gaussians or the camera is attached/following (per-env poses), else the single-view camera. "single" / "batched" force one class for every camera ("single" is rejected with per_env_gaussians=True). This is env-wide: with two or more splat cameras the forced modes apply to all of them; per-camera control would need the knob on CameraOptions, so rely on "auto" when different cameras need different modes.

NyxSplatOptions(**data)

Bases: DynamicConfigurableOptions

Nyx-based splat rendering options.

Uses Nyx's native light field support to render gaussian-splat backgrounds inside the path tracer, instead of the gsplat rasterize-and-segmentation-composite approach of :class:SplatOptions.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION spp

Samples per pixel for path tracing.

denoise

Whether to apply denoising.

near

Near clipping plane distance.

far

Far clipping plane distance.

max_pt_depth

Must stay None. gs-nyx-plugin exposes no path-depth control, so a depth set here could never take effect; it is rejected rather than ignored.

lights

Light definitions in Z-up coordinates. Each dict should have a "type" key ("point", "directional", or "spot") and type-specific parameters.

env_map_paths

Paths to HDR environment map textures.

tone_mapper

Name of the gs_nyx.nyx_py_sdk.EToneMapper member to use. Use "Off" or "Reinhard" while tuning lighting to see closer-to- linear radiance feedback. Written into each camera's profile (see :func:eden.envs.nyx_splat.write_nyx_camera_profile), including a camera's own NyxCameraOptions that sets no camera_profile; one that does keeps its own.

exposure_compensation

Exposure, in EV, relative to unit exposure (a pixel shows the radiance it receives; +1 doubles the image). 0 keeps the brightness that light intensities and env-map brightnesses were tuned against; Nyx's own default camera renders 0.53 EV darker.

docs.title: BatchRendererOptions
docs.text:
Bases: BatchRenderer

Options for the gs-madrona batch renderer, with declarative scene lights.

Madrona renders ambient-only until lights are added (cameras come out near-black), and it bakes the light count at scene.build() time — so lights must be registered via gs.Scene.add_light before the build. The raw genesis gs.renderers.BatchRenderer has no lights field, so this eden subclass carries them declaratively (mirroring :class:RayTracerOptions.lights); :class:eden.envs.base.EnvBase applies them right after scene creation.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION lights

One kwargs dict per gs.Scene.add_light call, e.g. {"pos": (0.5, 0.5, 2.0), "dir": (0, 0, -1), "intensity": 3.0, "directional": True, "castshadow": False}.

TYPE: list of dict

def to_genesis_surface(self) -> Surface:
    """Materialize the Genesis surface. Must be called after ``gs.init()``."""
    # Forward every set value (declared fields + dynamic extras), dropping unset
    # ``None`` shortcuts so the Genesis surface keeps its own defaults.
    kwargs = {key: value for key, value in self.dict().items() if value is not None}
    return self._genesis_surface_cls(**kwargs)

docs.title: Built-in Terms
docs.text:
Eden ships ready-made terms for every manager: action controllers, observations, rewards, terminations, commands, events, curricula, metrics and recorders, plus the modifiers that post-process term inputs and outputs. This section renders their API docs, one page per kind and one section per module.

To find what a term accepts, use the term catalog. It is generated from the registries, so it lists every registered term with its parameters, their types and defaults, and which are required. In a terminal:

eden terms --grep height           # terms whose name, parameters or summary match a regex
eden terms --kind reward           # one kind only
eden terms --json                  # the whole catalog, for tooling

docs.title: Using a built-in term
docs.text:
Configure a term in a config with .configure(...), which returns its serializable options. A class term takes its parameters as keyword arguments. A function term goes through the kind's function wrapper (short aliases in eden.terms), with its parameters in params={...}. Those aliases are the function wrappers only: eden.terms.RewardTerm is RewardTermFuncWrapper, not the class-term base eden.managers.reward_manager.RewardTerm that shares its name (the same holds for EventTerm and MetricTerm). Subclass the base from its manager module. Excerpted from eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py and eden/tasks/benchmark/move_forward/config.py:

from eden import observations, rewards
from eden.terms import RewardTerm

dofs_pos = observations.DofsPos.configure(entity_name="robot")
joint_vel_hinge = RewardTerm.configure(
    func=rewards.dofs_vel_limits,
    weight=-0.01,
    params={"entity_name": "robot", "max_vel": 0.5},
)
tracking_lin_vel = rewards.TrackingLinVel.configure(
    weight=1.0,
    command_name="velocity_command",
    entity_name="robot",
    sigma=0.25,
)

from eden import observations, rewards, terminations, ... imports the built-in term modules lazily, on first use. A term is looked up by its registry key, never by object identity, so a class term you write yourself must be registered with @<KIND>_TERM_REGISTRY.register(). See the terms guide.

Base class for observation terms defined as function. See :class:ObservationTerm for the modifier fields (options-only, not mirrored as attributes), for when each one is read, and for :attr:effective_scale.

Stateless by construction. A function term is a pure forward of env state: the manager never dispatches reset(), post_reset() or post_physics_refresh() to it (the inherited reset and post_reset are no-ops, and there is no refresh hook to call), so state kept in a closure or a module global is never zeroed at episode reset and advances on every one of the several compute() calls a step may make. A term that needs per-episode or per-step state is a class term.

docs.title: Shared term helpers
docs.text:
Building blocks the built-in terms reuse: resolve-once helpers for build() (resolve_link_idx, resolve_terrain, resolve_metric_manager, ...) and cheap math helpers for compute() (projected_gravity, base_height_above_ground, ...).

Shared helpers for manager terms.

Small building blocks reused across observation / reward term build() and compute() so the same idiom (gravity projection, link-index resolution, base height over the ground, per-DOF std from a regex dict) isn't re-implemented per term. Resolve-once helpers (resolve_link_idx / resolve_terrain / resolve_per_dof_std / resolve_metric_manager) are meant to be called in build() — a function term, which has none, calls them per step; the math helpers (gravity_vec / projected_gravity / base_height_above_ground) are cheap enough for the hot path.

docs.title: gravity_vec
docs.text:
gravity_vec(num_envs: int, device) -> Tensor

World-frame down vector [0, 0, -1] expanded to (num_envs, 3).

Cache once in build(); pass to :func:projected_gravity as the gravity input and/or use directly as the upright reference vector. Built on the device rather than copied from a host list, so a function term that has no build() can call it per step without a GPU->CPU sync.

Source code in eden/managers/terms/utils.py 
def gravity_vec(num_envs: int, device) -> torch.Tensor:
    """World-frame down vector ``[0, 0, -1]`` expanded to ``(num_envs, 3)``.

    Cache once in ``build()``; pass to :func:`projected_gravity` as the gravity input and/or use directly as
    the upright reference vector. Built on the device rather than copied from a host list, so a function term
    that has no ``build()`` can call it per step without a GPU->CPU sync.
    """
    down = torch.zeros(3, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    down[2:].fill_(-1.0)  # a slice fill; `down[2] = -1.0` would copy a host scalar, which syncs
    return down.expand(num_envs, -1)

resolve_metric_manager(env: EnvBase, *, term: str, metric_name: str) -> MetricManager

Return env.metric_manager after checking that it exists and that metric_name is one of its terms.

For a metric pull term's build(): the metric manager is constructed ahead of the termination, reward and observation managers (RLEnvBase._manager_order), so these mistakes surface at env construction rather than on the first step. term is the pulling term's registry key. An empty metric_name — the class terms' default, i.e. a configure() that forgot it — raises a ValueError saying so; an unknown one raises the manager's own KeyError. Both list the active metrics.

Source code in eden/managers/terms/utils.py 
def resolve_metric_manager(env: EnvBase, *, term: str, metric_name: str) -> MetricManager:
    """Return ``env.metric_manager`` after checking that it exists and that ``metric_name`` is one of its terms.

    For a metric pull term's ``build()``: the metric manager is constructed ahead of the termination, reward
    and observation managers (``RLEnvBase._manager_order``), so these mistakes surface at env construction
    rather than on the first step. ``term`` is the pulling term's registry key. An empty ``metric_name`` —
    the class terms' default, i.e. a ``configure()`` that forgot it — raises a ``ValueError`` saying so; an
    unknown one raises the manager's own ``KeyError``. Both list the active metrics.
    """
    if env.metric_manager is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{term}(metric_name='{metric_name}') requires a metric term, but no metric manager is configured."
        )
    if not metric_name:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{term}: metric_name is not set — pass metric_name=<one of the active metrics> to configure(). "
            f"Active metrics: {env.metric_manager.active_terms}"
        )
    env.metric_manager.get_value(metric_name)
    return env.metric_manager

resolve_metric_term(env: EnvBase, *, term: str, metric_name: str, expected: type[MetricT]) -> MetricT

The metric term metric_name, checked to be an expected: for a term whose build() reads a task's metric (its ink, its grade) through the metric's own attributes rather than its value.

Fails as :func:resolve_metric_manager does for a missing manager or name, and with a TypeError naming the metrics that are an expected when metric_name is some other metric. term is the reading term's name.

Source code in eden/managers/terms/utils.py 
def resolve_metric_term(env: EnvBase, *, term: str, metric_name: str, expected: type[MetricT]) -> MetricT:
    """The metric term ``metric_name``, checked to be an ``expected``: for a term whose ``build()`` reads a task's
    metric (its ink, its grade) through the metric's own attributes rather than its value.

    Fails as :func:`resolve_metric_manager` does for a missing manager or name, and with a ``TypeError`` naming the
    metrics that are an ``expected`` when ``metric_name`` is some other metric. ``term`` is the reading term's name.
    """
    metrics = resolve_metric_manager(env, term=term, metric_name=metric_name)
    metric = metrics.get_term(metric_name)
    if not isinstance(metric, expected):
        matching = [name for name in metrics.active_terms if isinstance(metrics.get_term(name), expected)]
        raise TypeError(
            f"{term} reads a {expected.__name__} metric, but metric '{metric_name}' is a {type(metric).__name__}. "
            f"Set metric_name to one of the {expected.__name__} metrics: {matching}."
        )
    return metric

docs.text:
soft_dof_pos_violation(dofs_pos: Tensor, soft_limits: Tensor) -> Tensor

Per-DOF distance outside the soft [lower, upper] position band (>= 0, zero inside).

dofs_pos is (..., num_dofs) and soft_limits is (..., num_dofs, 2) ([..., 0] lower, [..., 1] upper). Sum over the DOF axis for a scalar penalty; compare > 0 for a limit-exceeded mask.

Source code in eden/managers/terms/utils.py 
def soft_dof_pos_violation(dofs_pos: torch.Tensor, soft_limits: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Per-DOF distance outside the soft ``[lower, upper]`` position band (``>= 0``, zero inside).

    ``dofs_pos`` is ``(..., num_dofs)`` and ``soft_limits`` is ``(..., num_dofs, 2)`` (``[..., 0]`` lower,
    ``[..., 1]`` upper). Sum over the DOF axis for a scalar penalty; compare ``> 0`` for a limit-exceeded mask.
    """
    lower = -(dofs_pos - soft_limits[..., 0]).clip(max=0.0)
    upper = (dofs_pos - soft_limits[..., 1]).clip(min=0.0)
    return lower + upper

docs.title: parallel_jaw_is_grasping
docs.text:
parallel_jaw_is_grasping(entity: Entity, contact_info: dict[str, Tensor], left_gripper_link_idx: int, right_gripper_link_idx: int, gripper_idx_local: list[int], force_threshold: float, object_link_idx: int | Tensor | None = None) -> Tensor

Per-env bool (num_envs,): both gripper pads carry contact force aligned with the closing direction above force_threshold — a parallel-jaw grasp.

Detects a grasp even when the fingers can't fully close (an object is held between them). Shared by the IsGrasping metric/termination and the ParallelJawWelding action, so both apply the same force test. They differ only in which contacts it sums:

  • object_link_idx=None (IsGrasping): each pad's force over all its contacts, so a grasp across two links of one multi-link object counts. So do pads pressing two different objects.
  • object_link_idx given (ParallelJawWelding, once per candidate link): only contacts with that link, so both pads must press the one link that would be welded.

contact_info is entity.get_contacts(exclude_self_contact=True). gripper_idx_local is [left_pad, right_pad] (local link indices) and defines the left→right closing direction; the pad link indices (entity.get_link(...).idx) are the global indices matched against the contact pairs.

Source code in eden/managers/terms/utils.py 
def parallel_jaw_is_grasping(
    entity: Entity,
    contact_info: dict[str, torch.Tensor],
    left_gripper_link_idx: int,
    right_gripper_link_idx: int,
    gripper_idx_local: list[int],
    force_threshold: float,
    object_link_idx: int | torch.Tensor | None = None,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Per-env bool ``(num_envs,)``: both gripper pads carry contact force aligned with the closing
    direction above ``force_threshold`` — a parallel-jaw grasp.

    Detects a grasp even when the fingers can't fully close (an object is held between them). Shared by
    the ``IsGrasping`` metric/termination and the ``ParallelJawWelding`` action, so both apply the same
    force test. They differ only in which contacts it sums:

    * ``object_link_idx=None`` (``IsGrasping``): each pad's force over all its contacts, so a grasp
      across two links of one multi-link object counts. So do pads pressing two different objects.
    * ``object_link_idx`` given (``ParallelJawWelding``, once per candidate link): only contacts with
      that link, so both pads must press the one link that would be welded.

    ``contact_info`` is ``entity.get_contacts(exclude_self_contact=True)``. ``gripper_idx_local`` is
    ``[left_pad, right_pad]`` (local link indices) and defines the left→right closing direction; the pad
    link indices (``entity.get_link(...).idx``) are the global indices matched against the contact pairs.
    """
    link_a = contact_info["link_a"]
    link_b = contact_info["link_b"]
    force_a = contact_info["force_a"]
    force_b = contact_info["force_b"]
    valid_mask = contact_info["valid_mask"]

    # Net contact force on each pad, summed over contacts (from whichever side of the pair is the pad).
    # When an object link is supplied, require both pad forces to come from that same candidate. This
    # prevents contacts with two different objects from being combined into a false grasp.
    if object_link_idx is None:
        left_a = link_a == left_gripper_link_idx
        left_b = link_b == left_gripper_link_idx
        right_a = link_a == right_gripper_link_idx
        right_b = link_b == right_gripper_link_idx
    else:
        left_a = (link_a == left_gripper_link_idx) & (link_b == object_link_idx)
        left_b = (link_b == left_gripper_link_idx) & (link_a == object_link_idx)
        right_a = (link_a == right_gripper_link_idx) & (link_b == object_link_idx)
        right_b = (link_b == right_gripper_link_idx) & (link_a == object_link_idx)

    left_forces = torch.sum(force_a * (left_a & valid_mask)[..., None], dim=1)
    left_forces += torch.sum(force_b * (left_b & valid_mask)[..., None], dim=1)
    right_forces = torch.sum(force_a * (right_a & valid_mask)[..., None], dim=1)
    right_forces += torch.sum(force_b * (right_b & valid_mask)[..., None], dim=1)

    # Closing direction (left pad → right pad); project each pad's net force onto its inward direction.
    gripper_pos = entity.get_links_pos(ls_idx_local=gripper_idx_local)
    close_dir = gripper_pos[:, 1] - gripper_pos[:, 0]
    close_dir = close_dir / close_dir.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-8)
    left_proj = torch.bmm(left_forces.unsqueeze(1), close_dir.unsqueeze(2)).reshape(-1)
    right_proj = torch.bmm(right_forces.unsqueeze(1), (-close_dir).unsqueeze(2)).reshape(-1)

    return (left_proj.abs() > force_threshold) & (right_proj.abs() > force_threshold)

docs.title: resolve_link_idx
docs.text:
resolve_link_idx(entity: Entity, names: list[str], device, *, preserve_order: bool = True, term: str | None = None, field: str = 'links_name') -> Tensor

Resolve link name patterns to a local-index long tensor (call once in build()).

preserve_order=True matches RigidEntity.find_named_links_idx_local's default.

The entity must be a rigid one. Named links are a RigidEntity API, and so is every reason to ask for their indices (get_links_pos / get_links_net_contact_force), so a particle or FEM entity named here has neither the links nor the per-link readings the caller is about to take. Checking it at this one chokepoint is what spares each link term its own copy — the same reason :func:resolve_terrain checks get_height rather than leaving it to every height term.

An empty selection always raises. A pattern matching nothing already raises from the inner resolve_matching_names, but an empty names matches nothing without raising, and every caller is per-link by design: the silent result is a zero-width observation, a never-firing mask, or — for the feet_link_names rewards, whose field defaults to [] — a penalty that reads zero for a whole training run. That is the config mistake this helper exists to catch, so the check is not opt-in; a caller that genuinely tolerates an empty selection branches before calling, as :class:~eden.managers.terms.observations.contact.GroupedContactFlags does for its optional partner links. term (the calling term's class name) and field (the config field the patterns came from — not links_name on every term) only label the error.

Source code in eden/managers/terms/utils.py 
def resolve_link_idx(
    entity: Entity,
    names: list[str],
    device,
    *,
    preserve_order: bool = True,
    term: str | None = None,
    field: str = "links_name",
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Resolve link name patterns to a local-index ``long`` tensor (call once in ``build()``).

    ``preserve_order=True`` matches ``RigidEntity.find_named_links_idx_local``'s default.

    The entity must be a rigid one. Named links are a ``RigidEntity`` API, and so is every reason to
    ask for their indices (``get_links_pos`` / ``get_links_net_contact_force``), so a particle or FEM
    entity named here has neither the links nor the per-link readings the caller is about to take.
    Checking it at this one chokepoint is what spares each link term its own copy — the same reason
    :func:`resolve_terrain` checks ``get_height`` rather than leaving it to every height term.

    An *empty* selection always raises. A pattern matching nothing already raises from the inner
    ``resolve_matching_names``, but an empty ``names`` matches nothing *without* raising, and every
    caller is per-link by design: the silent result is a zero-width observation, a never-firing mask,
    or — for the ``feet_link_names`` rewards, whose field defaults to ``[]`` — a penalty that
    reads zero for a whole training run. That is the config mistake this helper exists to catch, so
    the check is not opt-in; a caller that genuinely tolerates an empty selection branches before
    calling, as :class:`~eden.managers.terms.observations.contact.GroupedContactFlags` does for its
    optional partner links. ``term`` (the calling term's class name) and ``field`` (the config field
    the patterns came from — not ``links_name`` on every term) only label the error.
    """
    prefix = f"{term}: " if term else ""
    if not hasattr(entity, "find_named_links_idx_local"):
        raise TypeError(
            f"{prefix}entity '{entity.name}' is a {type(entity).__name__}, which has no named links (no "
            f"find_named_links_idx_local) and so reports no per-link pose or contact force. Selecting links by "
            f"name needs a rigid entity (eden.entities.rigid.RigidEntity); a particle or FEM entity is made of "
            f"particles, not links. "
            f"Check that entity_name points at the robot rather than at a deformable object in the scene."
        )
    _, link_idx = entity.find_named_links_idx_local(names, preserve_order=preserve_order)
    if not link_idx:
        available = [link.name for link in entity.links]
        raise ValueError(
            f"{prefix}{field}={names} matched no links on entity '{entity.name}'. This term is per-link, so an "
            f"empty selection is not a disabled term — it is a zero-width observation, a never-firing mask, or a "
            f"penalty that reads zero for a whole training run. "
            f"Set {field} to the link patterns you meant; to not use the term at all, remove it from the config "
            f"rather than leaving its link selection empty. Available links: {available}"
        )
    return torch.tensor(link_idx, dtype=torch.long, device=device)

resolve_terrain(entities: dict, name: str | None) -> Entity | None

Resolve an optional terrain_entity_name to an entity that can report ground height.

None passes through as None — measure against the world-frame z, which is what a flat scene wants and what Isaac Lab's height terms do. A name is looked up with :func:~eden.utils.misc.resolve_named_entity, so a typo lists the scene's entities, and the result is then checked for the one thing :func:base_height_above_ground needs from it: get_height. Without that check the plausible mistake — naming the flat ground plane rather than a :class:~eden.entities.terrain.Terrain — reaches the hot path and surfaces as an AttributeError on the first step, which for a termination term means mid-run rather than at env construction.

def resolve_terrain(entities: dict, name: str | None) -> Entity | None:
    """Resolve an optional ``terrain_entity_name`` to an entity that can report ground height.

    ``None`` passes through as ``None`` — measure against the world-frame ``z``, which is what a flat
    scene wants and what Isaac Lab's height terms do. A name is looked up with
    :func:`~eden.utils.misc.resolve_named_entity`, so a typo lists the scene's entities, and the result
    is then checked for the one thing :func:`base_height_above_ground` needs from it: ``get_height``.
    Without that check the plausible mistake — naming the flat ground plane rather than a
    :class:`~eden.entities.terrain.Terrain` — reaches the hot path and surfaces as an ``AttributeError``
    on the first step, which for a termination term means mid-run rather than at env construction.
    """
    if name is None:
        return None
    terrain = resolve_named_entity(entities, name)
    if not hasattr(terrain, "get_height"):
        raise TypeError(
            f"terrain_entity_name='{name}' names a {type(terrain).__name__}, which reports no ground height "
            f"(no get_height). It must be a Terrain (eden.entities.terrain.Terrain). A flat scene needs no "
            f"terrain entity at all — leave terrain_entity_name unset to measure the world-frame z."
        )
    return terrain

Height of an entity's base link above the ground, (num_envs,).

With terrain=None this is the world-frame z of the base — correct on a flat plane and what Isaac Lab's root_height_below_minimum / base_pos_z measure. Pass a :class:~eden.entities.terrain.Terrain to subtract the terrain height sampled under the base's xy instead, which is what makes a height threshold meaningful on rough ground: on a slope the world z of a perfectly-postured robot tracks the hill, so a fixed floor on it fires at the bottom and never at the top.

relative selects the frame the base pose is read in, exactly as on :func:~eden.managers.terms.observations.proprio.base_pos: False (the default, and what :func:~eden.managers.terms.rewards.locomotion.base_height_l2 uses) is the solver frame, which Genesis re-origins onto the body's inertial frame; True is the frame the asset was authored in — the frame default_root_pos and Isaac Lab's root_pos_w are in. The two differ by the base link's centre-of-mass offset, so a threshold tuned in one frame is wrong in the other.

def base_height_above_ground(entity: Entity, terrain: Entity | None = None, *, relative: bool = False) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Height of an entity's base link above the ground, ``(num_envs,)``.

    With ``terrain=None`` this is the world-frame ``z`` of the base — correct on a flat plane and
    what Isaac Lab's ``root_height_below_minimum`` / ``base_pos_z`` measure. Pass a
    :class:`~eden.entities.terrain.Terrain` to subtract the terrain height sampled under the base's
    ``xy`` instead, which is what makes a height threshold meaningful on rough ground: on a slope the
    world ``z`` of a perfectly-postured robot tracks the hill, so a fixed floor on it fires at the
    bottom and never at the top.

    ``relative`` selects the frame the base pose is read in, exactly as on
    :func:`~eden.managers.terms.observations.proprio.base_pos`: ``False`` (the default, and what
    :func:`~eden.managers.terms.rewards.locomotion.base_height_l2` uses) is the solver frame, which
    Genesis re-origins onto the body's inertial frame; ``True`` is the frame the asset was authored
    in — the frame ``default_root_pos`` and Isaac Lab's ``root_pos_w`` are in. The two differ by the
    base link's centre-of-mass offset, so a threshold tuned in one frame is wrong in the other.
    """
    pos = entity.get_pos(relative=relative)
    if terrain is None:
        return pos[:, 2]
    # get_height wants a (B, h_out, w_out, 2) sample grid; one point per env is the 1x1 case.
    ground = terrain.get_height(pos[:, :2].reshape(-1, 1, 1, 2)).reshape(-1)
    return pos[:, 2] - ground

docs.text:
resolve_per_dof_std(std_dict: dict[str, float], robot: Entity, device, *, default: float | None = None, field: str = 'std') -> Tensor

Per-DOF std tensor from a regex -> value dict over the robot's DOF names.

Every DOF must be matched by some pattern (later patterns override earlier ones); DOFs no pattern matches raise a ValueError naming them, so a std map written for one robot cannot silently mis-weight another's extra DOFs. An explicit ".*" entry is the opt-in for "everything else gets this value"; passing default= instead fills unmatched DOFs with that value without raising. The reverse is deliberately tolerated: a pattern matching no DOF is NOT an error, so one std map can be shared across robots and carry entries for DOFs only some of them have (e.g. .*head.* in a map used by both the G1 and the LimX Oli). field names the offending config field in the error. Call once in build().

Source code in eden/managers/terms/utils.py 
def resolve_per_dof_std(
    std_dict: dict[str, float],
    robot: Entity,
    device,
    *,
    default: float | None = None,
    field: str = "std",
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Per-DOF std tensor from a ``regex -> value`` dict over the robot's DOF names.

    Every DOF must be matched by some pattern (later patterns override earlier ones); DOFs no pattern
    matches raise a ``ValueError`` naming them, so a std map written for one robot cannot silently
    mis-weight another's extra DOFs. An explicit ``".*"`` entry is the opt-in for "everything else gets
    this value"; passing ``default=`` instead fills unmatched DOFs with that value without raising.
    The reverse is deliberately tolerated: a pattern matching no DOF is NOT an error, so one std map
    can be shared across robots and carry entries for DOFs only some of them have (e.g. ``.*head.*``
    in a map used by both the G1 and the LimX Oli). ``field`` names the offending config field in the
    error. Call once in ``build()``.
    """
    dofs_name = robot.dofs_name
    fill = 0.0 if default is None else default  # placeholder only: unmatched DOFs raise below when default is None
    result = torch.full((len(dofs_name),), fill, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    matched = [False] * len(dofs_name)
    for pattern, value in std_dict.items():
        for i, name in enumerate(dofs_name):
            if re.match(pattern, name):
                result[i] = value
                matched[i] = True
    if default is None and not all(matched):
        unmatched = [name for name, hit in zip(dofs_name, matched) if not hit]
        raise ValueError(
            f"{field} does not cover {len(unmatched)} of {len(dofs_name)} DOFs on '{robot.name}': "
            f"{', '.join(unmatched)}\n"
            f"patterns tried: {list(std_dict)}\n"
            f"Add a pattern for them, or '.*': <value> as an explicit catch-all."
        )
    return result

docs.title: ExplicitPDController
docs.text:
ExplicitPDController(env: EnvBase, options: ActionTermOptions)

Bases: _JointPDControllerBase

Explicit joint PD controller using manual torque computation.

Computes PD torques explicitly and applies them via control_dofs_force. This is more physically accurate as it matches real-world motor control where only torque commands are valid. Better suited for sim2real transfer and easier to extend with domain randomization (e.g., randomizing kp/kd, adding motor delays).

An optional modifier can be provided to compose post-processing steps (delay, backlash, DC saturation, friction, effort clipping, motor strength scaling) on top of the PD controller::

ExplicitPDController.configure(
    entity_name="robot",
    dofs_name=["joint1", "joint2"],
    modifier=Compose.configure(
        modifiers=[
            ActionDelay.configure(delay_range_steps=(1, 3)),
            FrictionModel.configure(static_friction=2.4, dynamic_friction=0.24),
            EffortClip.configure(driving_torque_limit=111.0, ...),
            MotorStrength.configure(motor_strength=0.8),
        ]
    ),
)
Note

Requires sim_substeps=1 so that PD torques are recomputed at every physics substep. Adjust decimation accordingly to maintain the desired control frequency.

The -kd * qdot term is explicit under every EnvOptions.integrator: Genesis' implicit passes only damp the DOFs it drives itself (:class:ImplicitPDController), and the entity's kd * substep_dt armature fold runs under "euler" only. A kd stable through ImplicitPDController at a given substep can therefore diverge here.

def reset(self, envs_idx: (slice | torch.Tensor) | None = None) -> None:
    super().reset(envs_idx)
    if envs_idx is None:

def apply_actions(self) -> None:
    target = self._applied_command()
    dofs_vel = self.entity.get_dofs_vel(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)
    pos_err = target - self.entity.get_dofs_pos(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)

    # PD control
    ctrl_torque = self._kp * pos_err - self._kd * dofs_vel

    # Apply modifiers to the computed torques (e.g., backlash, friction, effort clip)
    if self._modifier is not None:
        ctrl_torque = self._modifier.modify_ctrl_torque(ctrl_torque, dofs_vel, pos_err=pos_err)

    self.verify_command_shape(ctrl_torque)
    self.entity.control_dofs_force(ctrl_torque, dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)

VelocityFeedforwardPDController(env: EnvBase, options: ActionTermOptions)

Bases: _JointPDControllerBase

Explicit joint PD controller with velocity feedforward.

Extends the explicit PD controller by accepting both target joint positions and target joint velocities as actions. The torque is computed as:

.. math:: \tau = k_p (q_{target} + q_{offset} - q_{current} + q_{motor_offset}) + k_d (-\dot{q}{current} + \dot{q})} \cdot r_{ff

where :math:r_{ff} is the velocity feedforward ratio. Post-processing (motor strength scaling, torque offset injection, effort clipping, etc.) is opt-in via the modifier parameter — see the composable modifiers in :mod:eden.managers.modifiers.actions.actuators.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION entity_name

The name of the entity to control.

dofs_name

The names of the DOFs to control.

reference_source

Source of the reference offset added on top of the position action.

scale

The scale to apply to the position actions; None (the default) applies none.

offset

The offset to apply to the position actions.

velocity_scale

The scale to apply to the velocity actions.

feed_forward_ratio

The ratio for the velocity feedforward term.

def build(self) -> None:
    if self.reference_source == ReferenceSource.ACCUMULATE:
        # ACCUMULATE is honored only by controllers that use the base ``compute``;
        # this one overrides it, so accumulation would silently never happen.
        raise ValueError(
            f"{term_subject(self)}: reference_source='accumulate' is not supported "
            f"(its overridden compute() does not integrate the action)."
        )
    super().build()

    # Re-allocate _processed_action to hold both position and velocity
    self._processed_action = torch.zeros(self.num_envs, self._n_dofs * 2, device=self.device)

    # The solver's flag: Genesis batches a heterogeneous entity's DOF info by itself in some scenes.
    self._batch_dofs_info = self.entity.has_batched_dofs_info

    # Cache PD gains
    self._kp = self.entity.get_dofs_kp(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)
    self._kd = self.entity.get_dofs_kd(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)

def compute(self, actions: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    self._prev_action[:] = self._raw_action
    self._raw_action[:] = actions
    n_dofs = self._n_dofs
    if self._delta_reference is not None:
        # Capture once per env step; constant across decimation substeps.
        self._delta_reference[:] = self.entity.get_dofs_pos(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)
    joint_pos = self._compute_pos_target(self._raw_action[:, :n_dofs])
    joint_vel = self._raw_action[:, n_dofs:] * self.velocity_scale

    # Apply the control-step modifiers to the position half (e.g., envelope clip); a delay acts
    # on the whole command per physics step, in `apply_actions`.
    if self._modifier is not None:
        joint_pos = self._modifier.modify_processed_action(joint_pos)

    self._processed_action[:, :n_dofs] = joint_pos
    self._processed_action[:, n_dofs:] = joint_vel

def apply_actions(self) -> None:
    n_dofs = self._n_dofs

    command = self._applied_command()
    target_pos = command[:, :n_dofs]
    target_vel = command[:, n_dofs:]
    dofs_vel = self.entity.get_dofs_vel(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)
    pos_err = target_pos - self.entity.get_dofs_pos(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)

    ctrl_torque = self._kp * pos_err + self._kd * (target_vel * self.feed_forward_ratio - dofs_vel)

    # Apply modifier to ctrl torque (e.g., backlash, friction, effort clip)
    if self._modifier is not None:
        ctrl_torque = self._modifier.modify_ctrl_torque(ctrl_torque, dofs_vel, pos_err=pos_err)

    self.verify_command_shape(ctrl_torque)
    self.entity.control_dofs_force(ctrl_torque, dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)

ExplicitVelocityController(env: EnvBase, options: ActionTermOptions)

Bases: _JointPDControllerBase

Explicit joint velocity controller using manual torque computation.

The policy action is interpreted as a target joint velocity. Torque is computed as a proportional law on the velocity error:

.. math:: \tau = k_p (\dot{q}_{target} - \dot{q})

This matches the behavior of MuJoCo's velocity actuator and the implicit counterpart :class:ImplicitVelocityController. Use this variant when an explicit, auditable torque is required (e.g., sim2real, modifier composition, domain randomization of the gain).

The gain is derived from the DOF force range so it is automatically scaled to each joint's effort capacity:

.. math:: k_p = (F_{max} - F_{min}) \cdot \text{velocity_gain}

action_dim: int

No policy output: this term pins its DOFs rather than steering them.

The base class returns the DOF count, which would have ActionManager reserve a slice of the action vector per pinned DOF — columns the policy would learn to emit and compute would discard, since it is a no-op. num_dofs is left alone: the term commands those DOFs, it just takes no input for them. def is_joint_position_controller(term: type | ActionTerm) -> bool:
    """Whether ``term`` (a term class or instance) is a joint PD controller that commands positions.

    True for :class:`ImplicitPDController`, :class:`ExplicitPDController`,
    :class:`VelocityFeedforwardPDController` and their subclasses; False for the velocity
    controllers, which share the PD base for its scale/offset plumbing but command a velocity, and
    for every other action term. This is the set a robot's position action scale, and a joint-zero
    offset such as :class:`~eden.managers.terms.events.domain_rand.RandomizeDofsPosOffset`, apply to.

    Parameters
    ----------
    term: type | ActionTerm
        An action term class, or a built term instance.

DifferentialIKController(env: EnvBase, options: ActionTermOptions)

Bases: ActionTerm

Action term that maps task-space commands to joint targets via differential IK.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION entity_name

The name of the entity to control.

dofs_name

The names of the DOFs to control.

ee_link_name

The name of the end-effector link.

ee_local_pos

Control-point position in the end-effector link frame, in metres: the point the position rows move, and the point a rotation command turns the link about. The default is the link origin.

position_scale

Metres per normalized action unit for the position axes. A scalar applies to x, y, and z; a length-3 list configures the axes independently.

orientation_scale

Radians per normalized action unit for the orientation axes. A scalar applies to rx, ry, and rz; a length-3 list configures the axes independently.

damping

Levenberg-Marquardt damping lambda for the differential-IK least squares Jt (J Jt + lambda I)^-1. Larger values trade tracking accuracy for stability near singularities, where an under-damped solve produces large delta_q spikes (visible as end-effector jitter). mjlab's DifferentialIKActionCfg uses 0.1 (the default here); an under-damped value like 1e-4 is effectively undamped.

max_dq

Optional per-step clamp (rad) on the IK joint delta, mirroring mjlab's max_dq. Caps how far any joint may move in a single control step, which bounds end-effector speed and smooths motion. None disables it.

position_weight

Task-space weight on the position (x, y, z) rows of the IK solve.

orientation_weight

Task-space weight on the orientation (rx, ry, rz) rows of the IK solve, mirroring mjlab's DifferentialIKActionCfg.orientation_weight. The damped least squares weights both the Jacobian rows and the task error per axis, so orientation_weight=0.0 makes it position-only — the wrist orientation is left uncontrolled (free in the nullspace) rather than driven by the policy, which removes wrist jitter without pinning the wrist. Defaults to 1.0 (full 6-DOF). Relies on damping > 0 to keep zero-weighted rows of J Jt invertible.

def build(self) -> None:
    super().build()

    self._ee_link = self.entity.get_link(self.ee_link_name)
    if len(self.ee_local_pos) != 3 or not all(math.isfinite(value) for value in self.ee_local_pos):
        raise ValueError(
            f"{term_subject(self)}: ee_local_pos must contain three finite values, got {self.ee_local_pos}"
        )
    self._ee_local_pos = torch.tensor(self.ee_local_pos, dtype=gs.tc_float, device=self.device)

    # Jacobian columns are in dofs_name order; build indices to select
    # this action's DOF subset from the reordered Jacobian. A welded child (a
    # composite's gripper / dex hand) has no base columns either — Genesis ``attach``
    # removed its root joint — so gate on ``has_immobile_base``, matching ``_jac_perm``.
    base_offset = 0 if self.entity.has_immobile_base else 6
    self._jac_dofs_idx = torch.as_tensor(
        [base_offset + self.entity.dofs_idx_map[idx] for idx in self.dofs_idx_local.tolist()],
        dtype=gs.tc_int,
        device=self.device,
    )

    self._scale = torch.cat(
        (
            _resolve_axis_parameter(self.position_scale, 3, device=self.device),
            _resolve_axis_parameter(self.orientation_scale, 3, device=self.device),
        )
    )

    # Per-axis task weights; None means uniform 1.0 and skips the weighting.
    if self.position_weight != 1.0 or self.orientation_weight != 1.0:
        self._task_weight = torch.tensor(
            [self.position_weight] * 3 + [self.orientation_weight] * 3,
            device=self.device,
            dtype=gs.tc_float,
        ).unsqueeze(0)  # (1, 6)

docs.text:
compute(actions: Tensor) -> None
Source code in eden/managers/terms/actions/task_space_actions.py 
def compute(self, actions: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    assert actions.shape == (
        self.num_envs,
        self.action_dim,
    ), f"Expected actions shape: (num_envs, {self.action_dim}), got {actions.shape=}"
    self._prev_action[:] = self._raw_action
    self._raw_action[:] = actions

    delta_target = self._scale * torch.tanh(actions)  # (n_envs, 6)
    # (n_envs, 6, n_dofs), the linear rows at the control point.
    J = self.entity.get_jacobian(link=self._ee_link, local_point=self._ee_local_pos)[:, :, self._jac_dofs_idx]
    if self._task_weight is not None:
        # Weighted damped least squares: weight the Jacobian rows and task
        # error per axis. orientation_weight=0 zeros the orientation rows
        # (damping keeps J Jt invertible) -> position-only IK, wrist free.
        J = J * self._task_weight.unsqueeze(-1)  # (n_envs, 6, n_dofs)
        delta_target = delta_target * self._task_weight  # (n_envs, 6)
    J_T = J.transpose(1, 2)  # (n_envs, n_dofs, 6)
    # `solve_ex`, not `solve`: `solve` reads the LU info back to raise on a singular system, a GPU->CPU
    # sync every control step. `J Jt + damping * I` is positive definite, so there is nothing to catch.
    delta_q = J_T @ torch.linalg.solve_ex(J @ J_T + self.diag, delta_target)[0].unsqueeze(-1)
    delta_q = delta_q.squeeze(-1)  # (n_envs, n_dofs)

    # Per-step joint-delta clamp (mjlab's max_dq): bounds joint speed.
    if self.max_dq is not None:
        delta_q = delta_q.clamp(-self.max_dq, self.max_dq)

    self._processed_action = delta_q + self.entity.get_dofs_pos(dofs_idx_local=self.genesis_dofs_idx)

docs.title: OperationalSpaceController
docs.text:
OperationalSpaceController(env: EnvBase, options: ActionTermOptions)

Bases: ActionTerm

Operational-space control to a persistent relative position/pose target.

Policy actions are clipped, scaled, and composed with the measured world-frame control-point pose in :meth:compute. The resulting absolute target stays fixed while :meth:apply_actions recomputes feedback, Jacobian, inertia, nullspace, and DOF force on every physics substep. Gravity compensation is configured on the rigid material of the kinematic-tree root, including the root parent rather than only the controlled child in a welded tree. This controller does not add Coriolis or centrifugal bias forces. The entity's configured force range saturates the controller command, not the total effective effort including material gravity compensation.

The controller supports fixed entities and entities welded through a static parent chain. dofs_name defines one ordered controller space shared by the Jacobian, mass matrix, DOF state, nullspace objective, and output force. When dynamics are enabled, build rejects a selected DOF set that omits an ancestor DOF of the control-point link. The selected mass submatrix further assumes remaining excluded branch DOFs are fixed or held so their acceleration can be neglected, or are dynamically decoupled; assigning them another controller does not by itself remove dynamic coupling. Operational inertia uses a relative Tikhonov approximation to the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, so a rank-deficient Jacobian has a finite damped minimum-norm response.

Planned extensions

TODO(generic-osc-extensions): Add absolute pose targets, configurable task/root/world command frames, per-axis motion selection, absolute wrench and hybrid motion-force control, variable impedance, and command interpolation as concrete Eden callers require them. Extend the dynamics contract to floating bases and passive coupled coordinates only with an explicit generalized-coordinate index space. Keep multi-end-effector, mobile-manipulator, and whole-body coordination in a composite layer above this single-control-point action term.

Control-point position in the end-effector link frame, in metres.

orientation_scale

def compute(self, actions: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    expected_shape = (self.num_envs, self.action_dim)
    if tuple(actions.shape) != expected_shape:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{term_subject(self)}: actions must have shape {expected_shape}, got {tuple(actions.shape)}"
        )
    self._prev_action[:] = self._raw_action
    self._raw_action[:] = actions
    self._scaled_action.copy_(actions)
    torch.clamp(self._scaled_action, min=-self._action_clip, max=self._action_clip, out=self._scaled_action)
    self._scaled_action[:, :3].mul_(self._position_scale)
    if self.control_mode == "pose":
        self._scaled_action[:, 3:].mul_(self._orientation_scale)

    entity = self.resolve_entity(self.entity_name)
    current_pos, current_quat = self._control_point_pose(entity)
    self._update_goal_from_action(current_pos, current_quat, self._scaled_action)
