def __init__(
    self,
    name: str,
    term_class: Type[ManagerTermBase],
    term_fn_wrapper_class: Type[ManagerTermFuncWrapperBase] | None = None,
    populated_by: Sequence[str] = (),
) -> None:
    super().__init__(name, populated_by)
    self._term_class = term_class
    self._term_fn_wrapper_class = term_fn_wrapper_class
    if term_fn_wrapper_class is not None:
        # Let ``configure(func=...)`` verify the function is registered here (see
        # ConfigurableFuncWrapperMixin._build_config_dict). Stamped on the wrapper *class*, so a
        # wrapper shared by two registries would make one registry's terms validate against the
        # other's — refuse it (each registry needs its own func-wrapper subclass). Re-stamping the
        # same registry (e.g. a re-import) is a harmless no-op.
        existing = getattr(term_fn_wrapper_class, "_term_registry", None)
        if existing is not None and existing is not self:
            raise ValueError(
                f"func-wrapper class {term_fn_wrapper_class.__name__} is already bound to registry "
                f"'{existing._name}'; a wrapper class must belong to a single registry (give "
                f"registry '{name}' its own {term_fn_wrapper_class.__name__} subclass)."
            )
        term_fn_wrapper_class._term_registry = self
    # Stamp this registry onto the kind's term-options class so ManagerTermOptions can
    # validate parameter names at construction time (see
    # ManagerTermOptions._validate_param_names). First stamp wins: a second registry built
    # over the same options class (e.g. a user registry whose terms subclass a built-in
    # term) leaves the original binding intact — names it can't resolve simply skip the
    # construction-time check and fall back to the build-time one. ``__dict__`` (not
    # getattr) so a subclassed options class can still be bound to its own registry.
    for term_or_wrapper in filter(None, (term_class, term_fn_wrapper_class)):
        options_class = getattr(term_or_wrapper, "_options_class_", None)
        if options_class is not None and options_class.__dict__.get("_term_registry_") is None:
            options_class._term_registry_ = self

def registered_class(self, key: str) -> type:
    """The class the term registered under ``key`` is built as, which is where its defaults live.

    A class term is stored as its class — the defaults-carrying subclass when ``register`` was
    given keyword defaults (:meth:`_with_defaults`). A function term is stored as
    ``partial(wrapper, func=...)``, and ``wrapper`` is the per-registration subclass carrying
    *its* keyword defaults, not the kind's shared ``*FuncWrapper``: that subclass is the only
    place ``@METRIC_TERM_REGISTRY.register(direction=MetricDirection.LIB)`` on a function is
    recorded, so a default read off the shared wrapper is the kind's, not the term's.

    key : str

    Returns
    -------
    type

    """
    registered = self.get(key)
    return registered.func if isinstance(registered, partial) else registered

def register(self, obj: Any = None, *, name: str | None = None, **term_defaults: Any) -> Any:
    """Register a class term, a function term, or a func-wrapper subclass.

    Takes no ``name``: a term's key is always its own ``to_snake_case(__name__)`` — see
    :data:`_WHY_THE_KEY_IS_THE_NAME`, the cause this refusal shares with :func:`_derive_name`.
    ``name`` is declared only so it can be *refused* — ``**term_defaults`` would otherwise
    swallow it and quietly set a class attribute called ``name`` on the term instead.
    """
    if name is not None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{self._name}_REGISTRY.register() takes no name=: a term's key is always its own "
            f"name, because {_WHY_THE_KEY_IS_THE_NAME}. Passing '{name}' cannot change that. "
            f"Drop it, and rename the term itself if you want a different key."
        )
    if obj is None:
        # used as a decorator
        def deco(func_or_class: Any) -> Any:
            key = _derive_name(func_or_class, None, self._name)
            return self._register_term(func_or_class, key, term_defaults)

        return deco

    # used as a function call
    return self._register_term(obj, _derive_name(obj, None, self._name), term_defaults)

Bases: Registry

Registry for asset families with multiple mesh-file variants.

A single decorated class declares its source directory name and the list of available variant ids. The decorator stamps _base_name and _default_variant (the first id in variant_list) onto the class, merges family metadata into cls.metadata, and registers one partial(cls, variant=N) callable per variant under the key f"{base_name}_{N}". The decorated class itself is also returned so it stays importable for type-level use.

Asset families (objaverse, ...) follow this contract by declaring a base options class that defines _base_name/_default_variant as ClassVar and an __init__ (or model_post_init) that materializes file from those + the requested variant.

Calling register() with neither base_name nor variant_list falls through to :class:Registry's plain-name registration, so procedural primitives (boxes, spheres) can share the same registry as variant assets.

register(obj: Any = None, *, name: str | None = None, base_name: str = '', variant_list: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> Any
Source code in eden/utils/registry.py 
def register(
    self,
    obj: Any = None,
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    base_name: str = "",
    variant_list: Sequence[int] | None = None,
) -> Any:
    if base_name == "" and variant_list is None:
        return super().register(obj, name=name)

    if not variant_list:
        raise ValueError(f"variant_list is required when base_name is set (base_name={base_name!r})")

    def _register(options):
        options._base_name = base_name
        options._default_variant = variant_list[0]
        merged_metadata = dict(getattr(options, "metadata", None) or {})
        merged_metadata.update(
            {
                "base_name": base_name,
                "variant_list": list(variant_list),
                "num_variants": len(variant_list),
                "variants_name": [f"{base_name}_{variant}" for variant in variant_list],
            }
        )
        options.metadata = merged_metadata
        for variant in variant_list:
            self._do_register(f"{base_name}_{variant}", partial(options, variant=variant))
        return options

    if obj is None:
        return _register
    return _register(obj)

module_is_initializing(module: Any) -> bool

Whether module is still executing its own body — a partial import, not a finished one.

importlib.import_module returns immediately, with the half-built module, when the calling thread is already importing it; only a different thread blocks until the body is done. This is the flag the import system itself reads to tell those apart (importlib._bootstrap._find_and_load), and two callers need it for the same reason — to know whether what they just got back is complete enough to draw a conclusion from: :meth:Registry._populate before it memoizes _populated, and ManagerTermOptions._resolve_term_registry before it reports "no registry claims this class".

ModuleSpec._initializing is private, hence the defensive getattr chain — though not obscure: it has been there since the spec protocol landed in 3.4. Absent (or an object with no __spec__, such as a C extension loaded the old way) reads as finished.

def module_is_initializing(module: Any) -> bool:
    """Whether ``module`` is still executing its own body — a partial import, not a finished one.

    ``importlib.import_module`` returns immediately, with the half-built module, when the calling
    thread is already importing it; only a *different* thread blocks until the body is done. This
    is the flag the import system itself reads to tell those apart
    (``importlib._bootstrap._find_and_load``), and two callers need it for the same reason — to
    know whether what they just got back is complete enough to draw a conclusion from:
    :meth:`Registry._populate` before it memoizes ``_populated``, and
    ``ManagerTermOptions._resolve_term_registry`` before it reports "no registry claims this
    class".

    ``ModuleSpec._initializing`` is private, hence the defensive ``getattr`` chain — though not
    obscure: it has been there since the spec protocol landed in 3.4. Absent (or an object with
    no ``__spec__``, such as a C extension loaded the old way) reads as finished.

    Parameters
    ----------
    module : ModuleType
        The module :func:`importlib.import_module` returned.

    Returns
    -------
    bool
        ``True`` while the module's body is still running.
    """
    return bool(getattr(getattr(module, "__spec__", None), "_initializing", False))

docs.title: ConfigurableMixin
docs.text:
ConfigurableMixin(options: T)

Bases: Generic[T]

Bind a runtime object (term / entity) to its declarative Options class.

The binding is reflection-driven, so subclasses just declare class attributes and get a matching options class "for free":

  • Options class discovery — :meth:__init_subclass__ reads the ConfigurableMixin[T] type argument off __orig_bases__ and stores it as _options_class_.
  • Parameter discovery — :meth:get_parameter_names walks the MRO and collects every plain (non-function, non-underscore, non-property/classmethod/staticmethod) class attribute, minus _non_parameter_names; those are the configurable parameters.
  • Options ↔ attribute mirroring — :meth:configure packs the parameters into an _options_class_ instance, and __init__ mirrors them back onto the runtime object via :func:mirror_options_onto (deep-copying both the options' values and the class-level defaults, so an instance never aliases either).

_extra_option_params (below) are the one documented exception to the mirroring.

Source code in eden/utils/common.py 
def __init__(self, options: T) -> None:
    self._uid = gs.UID()
    self._options: T = options

    mirror_options_onto(self, self._options)

    # Deferred, not module-scope — see the NOTE above this module's imports.
    from eden.options._metadata import OPTION_METADATA_KEYS

    # check if there are unused parameters in the options. ``_extra_option_params`` are legitimate
    # options-only fields (not mirrored as attrs), so they are expected to be "unused" here.
    unused_params = set(self._options.keys()) - set(self.get_parameter_names())
    tolerated = {"name", "class_name"} | set(OPTION_METADATA_KEYS) | self._extra_option_params
    # ``params`` is a declared framework field on function-capable term options. An *empty* one is
    # legitimately unused when the same options class configures a class-based term; a non-empty
    # ``params`` on a class-based term would be silently ignored, so it stays invalid.
    if not getattr(self._options, "params", None):
        tolerated.add("params")
    invalid_params = unused_params - tolerated
    if invalid_params:
        # Name the term, not only the class: for a function term the class is the shared
        # ``*FuncWrapper``, which cannot tell the author which of a dozen terms is wrong.
        # Same wording as the construction-time check (``ManagerTermOptions._validate_param_names``).
        term_name = getattr(self._options, "name", None)
        subject = f"term '{term_name}' ({type(self).__name__})" if term_name else type(self).__name__
        raise ValueError(
            invalid_parameters_message(subject, invalid_params, self.get_configure_specs(), self._retired_params)
        )

@classmethod
def get_parameter_names(cls) -> list[str]:
    params = set()
    excluded: set[str] = set()
    # Only collect attributes from classes in the ConfigurableMixin
    # hierarchy, skipping unrelated bases like nn.Module.
    for base_cls in cls.__mro__:
        excluded |= base_cls.__dict__.get("_non_parameter_names", frozenset())
        if base_cls is ConfigurableMixin or not issubclass(base_cls, ConfigurableMixin):
            continue
        for name, value in base_cls.__dict__.items():
            if name.startswith("__") or name.startswith("_"):
                continue
            if isinstance(value, (property, cached_property, classmethod, staticmethod)):
                continue
            if isinstance(value, FunctionType):
                continue
            params.add(name)
    return list(params - excluded)

def configured_fingerprint(
    self, exclude: Iterable[str] = (), names: tuple[str, ...] | None = None
) -> tuple[tuple[str, Hashable], ...]:
    """Every configured parameter's current value, by name, as :func:`frozen_value` makes it comparable.

    Two objects with equal fingerprints are configured alike right now; one fingerprint taken twice
    differs exactly when a parameter changed in between (a curriculum moving it, a nested options model
    edited in place, a tensor rebound). Name-sorted, so the pairs line up between two calls. ``exclude``
    leaves parameters out; ``names`` gives the parameters as :meth:`fingerprint_names` already resolved them,
    instead of ``exclude``.
    """
    excluded = frozenset(exclude)  # once: a generator is truthy even when it yields nothing
    if names is None:
        names = self.fingerprint_names(excluded)
    elif excluded:
        raise ValueError(
            f"configured_fingerprint of {type(self).__name__} takes exclude or names, not both: names are "
            f"already resolved without the excluded ones (fingerprint_names(exclude={sorted(excluded)!r}))."
        )
    return tuple((name, frozen_value(getattr(self, name, None))) for name in names)

@classmethod
def get_parameter_specs(cls) -> tuple[ParamInfo, ...]:
    """:meth:`get_parameter_names` with each parameter's declared type and default.

    Name-sorted, because ``get_parameter_names`` collects into a set and its order is
    therefore arbitrary — while an error message quoting the accepted set, and the generated
    catalogue page, both have to be reproducible.

    Nothing is ever reported ``required``: a class parameter *is* a class attribute, so it
    always has a default (an annotation-only declaration is not a parameter at all — see
    :meth:`get_parameter_names`). The required/optional split exists only for function terms,
    in :meth:`ConfigurableFuncWrapperMixin.get_function_parameter_specs`.
    """
    annotations: dict[str, Any] = {}
    # Reversed MRO so a subclass's annotation wins over the base's, and ``__dict__`` rather
    # than ``getattr`` because ``cls.__annotations__`` silently falls back to the nearest
    # annotated base — which would attribute a base's type to an unannotated override.
    for base_cls in reversed(cls.__mro__):
        annotations.update(base_cls.__dict__.get("__annotations__") or {})
    return tuple(
        ParamInfo(name, render_annotation(annotations.get(name)), render_default(getattr(cls, name)))
        for name in sorted(cls.get_parameter_names())
    )

@classmethod
def get_configure_specs(cls) -> tuple[ParamInfo, ...]:
    """Every parameter :meth:`configure` accepts — what an "invalid parameter" error must quote.

    :meth:`get_parameter_specs` plus the options-only :attr:`_extra_option_params`, whose type
    and default are read off the options class because they have no class attribute to read one
    from (that is exactly what makes them options-only).
    """
    fields = getattr(cls._options_class_, "model_fields", None) or {}
    extras = []
    for name in sorted(cls._extra_option_params):
        field = fields.get(name)
        if field is None:
            extras.append(ParamInfo(name))
            continue
        required = field.is_required()
        extras.append(
            ParamInfo(
                name,
                render_annotation(field.annotation),
                # ``get_default`` (not ``field.default``) so a ``default_factory`` field renders
                # its value, not the ``PydanticUndefined`` sentinel.
                "" if required else render_default(field.get_default(call_default_factory=True)),
                required=required,
            )
        )
    return cls.get_parameter_specs() + tuple(extras)

@classmethod
def configure(cls, **kwargs) -> T:
    """
    Configure the class with the given parameters.

    Parameters
    ----------
    **kwargs: dict
        The parameters to configure the class with.

    Returns
    -------
    T
        The options instance for the class.
    """
    config = cls._build_config_dict(**kwargs)
    if cls._options_class_ is None:
        raise TypeError(
            f"{cls.__name__} must parameterize ConfigurableMixin[T] with a concrete Options type "
            f"or set _options_class_ explicitly."
        )
    # ``name`` is framework-injected so managers can resolve terms by registry key
    # (``ManagerBase._build_term`` reads ``term_option.name``). Manager-term options always
    # subclass the extra="allow" ``*TermOptions`` bases and carry it as an extra. Every other
    # configure target (Camera, Sensor, Entity, extension options) never reads it, so for an
    # extra="forbid" options class that doesn't declare a ``name`` field we drop it instead of
    # tripping the forbid validation.
    options_class = cls._options_class_
    if options_class.model_config.get("extra") == "forbid" and "name" not in options_class.model_fields:
        config.pop("name", None)
    return options_class(**config)

def __init__(self, options: T) -> None:
    super().__init__(options=options)

    :func:`~eden.utils.params.function_param_specs` — because describing a term means naming
    every key it accepts, not only the ones ``configure()`` will refuse to go without.
    """
    return function_param_specs(func, exclude=cls._manager_injected_params)

@classmethod
def get_required_function_parameter_names(cls, func: FunctionType) -> set[str]:
    """Parameters of ``func`` without a default that the author must supply via ``params``.

    Keyword-only and positional-or-keyword params both count (``compute`` calls
    ``func(env=..., **params)``, so either is supplied by keyword), matching what
    :meth:`get_function_parameter_specs` advertises as required. ``_manager_injected_params``
    (``env``, ``envs_idx``) are excluded.
    """
    return {
        name
        for name, param in inspect.signature(func).parameters.items()
        if param.kind in (inspect.Parameter.POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD, inspect.Parameter.KEYWORD_ONLY)
        and param.default is inspect.Parameter.empty
    } - cls._manager_injected_params

@classmethod
def configure(cls, func: FunctionType, **kwargs) -> T:
    """
    Configure the class with the given parameters.

    Parameters
    ----------
    func: FunctionType
        The function to configure the class with.
    **kwargs: dict
        The parameters to configure the class with.

    Returns
    -------
    T
        The options instance for the class.
    """
    config = cls._build_config_dict(func=func, **kwargs)

        raise TypeError(

docs.text:
frozen_value(value: Any, depth: int = 0) -> Hashable

value as a hashable constant that compares equal exactly when the value is the same configuration.

For keying or fingerprinting what a term was configured with (:meth:ConfigurableMixin.configured_fingerprint). A scalar, string or enum is itself. A tensor is where it lives (its storage address, shape, strides and dtype), not its values: two terms reading one tensor are configured alike, and a tensor written in place is the same configuration while one rebound to another tensor is not. A numpy array is its values (a host array is read as a constant, so one edited in place is another configuration). A list, tuple, set or dict is its items, and an options model or a dataclass is its fields, so a value edited in place inside one is seen; past _FROZEN_DEPTH levels, and for any other object, a value is its identity.

Source code in eden/utils/common.py 
def frozen_value(value: Any, depth: int = 0) -> Hashable:
    """``value`` as a hashable constant that compares equal exactly when the value is the same configuration.

    For keying or fingerprinting what a term was configured with (:meth:`ConfigurableMixin.configured_fingerprint`).
    A scalar, string or enum is itself. A tensor is where it lives (its storage address, shape, strides and dtype),
    not its values: two terms reading one tensor are configured alike, and a tensor written in place is the same
    configuration while one rebound to another tensor is not. A numpy array is its values (a host array is read
    as a constant, so one edited in place is another configuration). A list, tuple, set or dict is its items,
    and an options model or a dataclass is its fields, so a value edited in place inside one is seen; past
    ``_FROZEN_DEPTH`` levels, and for any other object, a value is its identity.
    """
    if value is None or isinstance(value, (bool, int, float, str, Enum)):
        return value
    if isinstance(value, torch.Tensor):
        return ("tensor", value.data_ptr(), tuple(value.shape), value.stride(), value.dtype)
    if isinstance(value, np.ndarray):
        return ("ndarray", value.shape, value.dtype.str, value.tobytes())
    if isinstance(value, np.generic):
        return value.item()
    if depth >= _FROZEN_DEPTH:
        return ("object", id(value))
    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
        return tuple(frozen_value(item, depth + 1) for item in value)
    if isinstance(value, (set, frozenset)):
        return frozenset(frozen_value(item, depth + 1) for item in value)
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return tuple((key, frozen_value(item, depth + 1)) for key, item in value.items())
    if isinstance(value, BaseModel):
        items = [(name, getattr(value, name)) for name in type(value).model_fields]
        items += list((value.model_extra or {}).items())
        return (type(value), tuple((name, frozen_value(item, depth + 1)) for name, item in items))
    if is_dataclass(value) and not isinstance(value, type):
        return (
            type(value),
            tuple((f.name, frozen_value(getattr(value, f.name), depth + 1)) for f in dataclass_fields(value)),
        )
    return ("object", id(value))

docs.title: mirror_options_onto
docs.text:
mirror_options_onto(obj: ConfigurableMixin, options: ConfigurableOptions) -> None

Mirror every configurable parameter of obj from options onto obj itself.

A parameter the options do not carry falls back to obj's own class attribute. Both sources are deep-copied, so a runtime object never shares a mutable value with

  • its class — otherwise every instance is handed the same list/dict, and mutating one instance leaks into all the others and permanently corrupts the class default for the rest of the process; or
  • its options — otherwise mutating the runtime attribute in place rewrites the config EnvBase.config serializes, and two objects built from one options instance (a config reused across envs) silently share state.

:class:Entity, :class:Sensor and :class:Camera call this directly rather than delegating __init__ to :class:ConfigurableMixin: their options also carry fields that are consumed instead of mirrored (morph construction, the nested Genesis sensor/camera options), which the mixin's unused-parameter check would reject.

Two consequences of copying the options' side. A mirrored attribute and obj._options.<name> are independent from here on, so code that mutates one must not expect the other to follow — read a mirrored field off obj, not off the options. And a built Genesis :class:Surface (the non-SurfaceOptions half of SurfaceLike) is aliased, not copied — see :func:_copy_mirrored_value for why.

Source code in eden/utils/common.py 
def mirror_options_onto(obj: ConfigurableMixin, options: ConfigurableOptions) -> None:
    """Mirror every configurable parameter of ``obj`` from ``options`` onto ``obj`` itself.

    A parameter the options do not carry falls back to ``obj``'s own class attribute. Both
    sources are deep-copied, so a runtime object never shares a mutable value with

    * its **class** — otherwise every instance is handed the *same* list/dict, and mutating
      one instance leaks into all the others *and* permanently corrupts the class default
      for the rest of the process; or
    * its **options** — otherwise mutating the runtime attribute in place rewrites the
      config ``EnvBase.config`` serializes, and two objects built from one options instance
      (a config reused across envs) silently share state.

    :class:`Entity`, :class:`Sensor` and :class:`Camera` call this directly rather than
    delegating ``__init__`` to :class:`ConfigurableMixin`: their options also carry fields
    that are *consumed* instead of mirrored (morph construction, the nested Genesis
    sensor/camera options), which the mixin's unused-parameter check would reject.

    Two consequences of copying the options' side. A mirrored attribute and
    ``obj._options.<name>`` are independent from here on, so code that mutates one must not
    expect the other to follow — read a mirrored field off ``obj``, not off the options. And a
    built Genesis :class:`Surface` (the non-``SurfaceOptions`` half of ``SurfaceLike``) is
    *aliased*, not copied — see :func:`_copy_mirrored_value` for why.
    """
    # Field names only. ``keys()`` is a cached, value-free enumeration; ``model_dump()`` would
    # recursively serialize the entire options subtree (material, surface, every default_dofs_*
    # table) once per call, and emit serializer warnings for arbitrary-typed fields.
    option_fields = set(options.keys())
    # ``ManagerTermOptions.params`` defaults to ``None``, meaning "not a function term".
    # Mirroring that ``None`` would shadow the wrapper's ``{}`` class default and every function
    # term would die at its first ``compute()`` with "argument after ** must be a mapping", so an
    # empty ``params`` falls through to the class default. Same predicate the unused-parameter
    # check below uses, deliberately.
    if not getattr(options, "params", None):
        option_fields.discard("params")
    for name in obj.get_parameter_names():
        source = options if name in option_fields else obj
        setattr(obj, name, _copy_mirrored_value(getattr(source, name)))

docs.title: Parameter descriptions
docs.text:
How a configurable's parameters are described, shared by eden terms, the term catalog and the configure() errors so all three word a parameter identically.

How a configurable's parameters are described — and the wording that describes them.

A term's accepted parameter set has to be visible outside its signature: an author who guessed a parameter name wrong learns nothing from an error that names only the offending key. This module is the single place that renders a parameter (name, type, default) and the single place that words the "that parameter is not accepted" errors, so:

  • the three checks that run at construction (ManagerTermOptions._validate_param_names), at configure() and at build (ConfigurableFuncWrapperMixin) cannot drift in wording, and
  • eden terms and :mod:eden.managers.catalog describe a term exactly the way its errors do.

No eden imports (only :mod:inspect, :mod:typing and pydantic's TypeAdapter), so both :mod:eden.options.managers.base and :mod:eden.utils.common can reach it — which is also why invalid_function_param_keys lives here rather than with the manager options (see its docstring).

def render_annotation(annotation: Any) -> str:
    """``annotation`` as source text, or ``""`` when it is absent.

    An annotation of literal ``None`` also renders as ``""``: it is indistinguishable from
    "unannotated" for a class attribute (``dict.get`` returns ``None`` for both) and no term
    declares one.
    """
    if annotation is inspect.Parameter.empty or annotation is None:
        return ""
    return annotation if isinstance(annotation, str) else _format_type(annotation)

def render_default(value: Any) -> str:
    """``value`` as a one-line literal an author could paste back into a config.

    Enum members by name — ``repr`` gives ``<ReferenceSource.DEFAULT: 'default'>``, which is not
    something you can write — and any line breaks collapsed to single spaces, so a multi-line repr
    cannot split the markdown table row or terminal line it is rendered into.
    """
    if isinstance(value, Enum):
        return f"{type(value).__name__}.{value.name}"
    # Collapse only line breaks, not every space run (which would corrupt a string default's content).
    return repr(value).replace("\r\n", " ").replace("\r", " ").replace("\n", " ")

function_param_specs(func: FunctionType, *, exclude: Collection[str] = ()) -> tuple[ParamInfo, ...]

The params={...} entries an author supplies for function term func, in signature order.

Every named parameter except those in exclude (the manager-injected env / envs_idx) is listed, because every one of them is a legal params key: compute calls func(env=..., **params) and invalid_function_param_keys validates against the whole signature. That deliberately includes positional-or-keyword params — Eden's built-ins declare author-supplied params keyword-only, but nothing stops an out-of-tree term from doing otherwise, and omitting one from the listing would describe the term wrongly.

*args / **kwargs are dropped: neither is a parameter an author can name. A **kwargs term accepts any key (see invalid_function_param_keys), which a name list cannot express.

Source code in eden/utils/params.py 
def function_param_specs(func: FunctionType, *, exclude: Collection[str] = ()) -> tuple[ParamInfo, ...]:
    """The ``params={...}`` entries an author supplies for function term ``func``, in signature order.

    Every named parameter except those in ``exclude`` (the manager-injected ``env`` / ``envs_idx``)
    is listed, because every one of them is a legal ``params`` key: ``compute`` calls
    ``func(env=..., **params)`` and ``invalid_function_param_keys`` validates against the whole
    signature. That deliberately includes positional-or-keyword params — Eden's built-ins declare
    author-supplied params keyword-only, but nothing stops an out-of-tree term from doing otherwise,
    and omitting one from the listing would describe the term wrongly.

    ``*args`` / ``**kwargs`` are dropped: neither is a parameter an author can name. A ``**kwargs``
    term accepts *any* key (see ``invalid_function_param_keys``), which a name list cannot express.
    """
    return tuple(
        ParamInfo(
            name,
            render_annotation(param.annotation),
            "" if param.default is inspect.Parameter.empty else render_default(param.default),
            required=param.default is inspect.Parameter.empty,
        )
        for name, param in inspect.signature(func).parameters.items()
        if param.kind in (inspect.Parameter.POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD, inspect.Parameter.KEYWORD_ONLY)
        and name not in exclude
    )

def render_params(specs: Iterable[ParamInfo]) -> str:
    """``specs`` as one comma-separated line, required first — or ``"(none)"``.

    Required first because that is the part an author is missing when this text appears in an
    error; the rest is reference. Stable within each half (input order is signature order).
    """
    ordered = sorted(specs, key=lambda spec: not spec.required)
    return ", ".join(str(spec) for spec in ordered) or "(none)"

def invalid_function_param_keys(func, params) -> set[str]:
    """Return the ``params`` keys that are not parameters of ``func``.

    Empty when every key is a parameter of ``func`` — or when ``func`` accepts ``**kwargs``,
    in which case any key is legal. Shared by the construction-time check
    (:meth:`~eden.options.managers.base.ManagerTermOptions._validate_param_names`) and the
    build-time backstop (``ConfigurableFuncWrapperMixin.__init__``) so the two can't drift.
    Callers that need the accepted set for a message build it from :func:`function_param_specs`,
    which also carries the types and defaults a bare name list cannot.

    Here rather than in :mod:`eden.options.managers.base` because :mod:`eden.utils.common` is its
    other caller and ``eden.options.entities`` reaches back into ``eden.utils`` (via
    ``eden.utils.terrains``) — so a utils module that imports ``eden.options`` at module scope is a
    cycle as soon as it is the first of the three to be imported.
    This module's contract is exactly that: no eden imports, reachable from either side.

    Parameters
    ----------
    func : Callable
        The function term whose signature defines the legal keys.
    params : Mapping | None
        The ``params`` dict to check; ``None`` and ``{}`` are both legal and yield no keys.

    Returns
    -------
    set[str]
        The offending keys, empty when there are none.
    """
    signature_params = inspect.signature(func).parameters
    if any(p.kind is inspect.Parameter.VAR_KEYWORD for p in signature_params.values()):
        return set()
    return set(params or {}) - set(signature_params)

def unknown_parameter_names(extras: Iterable[str], configurable: type, *, tolerated: Collection[str] = ()) -> set[str]:
    """The names in ``extras`` (an options object's extra fields) that ``configurable`` takes no parameter for.

    The one check behind every options class that carries a configurable's parameters as extras (term options,
    camera overlay options): a parameter is a class parameter (``get_parameter_names``) or an options-only one
    (``_extra_option_params``). The options' own metadata (``_option_*``) always passes, and ``tolerated`` names what
    else a caller's options carry that is not a parameter (term options' ``class_name``).
    """
    allowed = set(configurable.get_parameter_names()) | set(getattr(configurable, "_extra_option_params", ()))
    return {key for key in extras if not key.startswith("_option_")} - allowed - set(tolerated)

The counterpart of :func:invalid_params_message for top-level parameters, shared by the same three checks. def invalid_parameters_message(
    subject: str,
    invalid_keys: Collection[str],
    accepted: Iterable[ParamInfo],
    retired: Mapping[str, str],
) -> str:
    """The one wording for "these are not parameters of ``subject``" — a class term or configurable.

    The counterpart of :func:`invalid_params_message` for top-level parameters, shared by the same
    three checks. A key in ``retired`` (a class's ``_retired_params``) also gets that class's
    migration note: a retired name is still invalid, but a config saved before it was retired should
    fail with directions, not only with the list of what is accepted now.
    """
    message = (
        f"The following parameters are invalid: {sorted(invalid_keys)} for {subject}, "
        f"allowed parameters: {render_params(accepted)}"
    )
    retired_keys_by_note: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
    for key in sorted(invalid_keys):
        if key in retired:
            retired_keys_by_note.setdefault(retired[key], []).append(key)
    notes = [f"Retired {keys}: {note}" for note, keys in retired_keys_by_note.items()]
    return ". ".join([message, *notes])

For options that carry a configurable's parameters as extras, which pydantic leaves exactly as written. A key that is not a parameter passes through untouched; :func:unknown_parameter_names is what refuses those.

def validated_parameter_values(configurable: type, values: Mapping[str, Any], *, subject: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """``values`` with each of ``configurable``'s parameters validated against its declared type and converted the way
    pydantic converts a declared options field: a list a JSON file read back becomes the declared tuple, ``"0.5"``
    becomes ``0.5``.

    For options that carry a configurable's parameters as extras, which pydantic leaves exactly as written. A key that
    is not a parameter passes through untouched; :func:`unknown_parameter_names` is what refuses those.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        For a value the declared type does not admit (``None`` or a bool for a number, a string for a list), naming
        ``subject``, the parameter, its type and its default.
    TypeError
        For a parameter whose annotation cannot be resolved (a type imported only for type checking) or validated.
    """
    params = set(configurable.get_parameter_names())
    validated = dict(values)
    for key, value in values.items():
        if key not in params:
            continue
        validator = _parameter_validator(configurable, key)
        if validator is None:
            continue
        annotation, adapter = validator
        try:
            # Lax, as an options field converts (``"0.5"`` to 0.5, a list to a tuple), except that a bool counts as a
            # number only where the type admits a bool: ``shadow_strength: yes`` in a YAML file is a mistake, not 1.0.
            validated[key] = adapter.validate_python(value, strict=True if isinstance(value, bool) else None)
        except ValidationError as e:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{subject} needs {key} as {render_annotation(annotation)}; got {value!r} ({type(value).__name__}): "
                f"{e.errors()[0]['msg']}. E.g. {key}={render_default(getattr(configurable, key))} (the default)."
            ) from None
    return validated

docs.title: Multi-GPU (DDP)
docs.text:
Rank and world-size queries and process-group setup. Also reachable as eden.distributed. See the multi-GPU guide.

Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) utilities for Eden.

This module provides a simple, universal interface for multi-GPU training with PyTorch DDP. Eden uses the NCCL backend for collective communication.

import eden restricts each process's CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to one physical GPU so that Genesis and PyTorch both see cuda:0. The NCCL process group is initialized early in eden.init() — right after gs.init() and before any scene building — so that NCCL gets a clean CUDA context.

Usage with torchrun::

torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=2 my_script.py

The module reads LOCAL_RANK, RANK, and WORLD_SIZE environment variables set by torchrun (or any compatible launcher).

docs.title: Run identity and provenance
docs.text:
The per-run reproducibility manifest (run.json).

Eden's canonical run identity is the log-directory basename <timestamp>-<run id> (resolved in :mod:eden.__init__). This module writes a sibling run.json recording everything needed to reproduce or trace a run: the applied seed, the eden and Genesis versions, the eden working-tree git state, the RL library that wrote the checkpoints, the full command line, and the task.

It is deliberately separate from the per-config config.json envelope (_meta), which is re-stamped on every save_as_json — including deploy_config.json — and describes the task, not the run instance. run.json is written exactly once, at launch, into the (lazily created) log directory.

The name pip install and importlib.metadata know Eden by (not its import name), and how to install an extra.

Eden imports as eden and is distributed as eden-world: the PyPI name eden belongs to an unrelated Kivy project, so pip install eden installs the wrong package. [project].name in pyproject.toml is the source of truth; tests/test_pyproject.py pins :data:DISTRIBUTION_NAME to it, and checks that every pip install "<name>[<extra>]" written in eden/, docs/ and examples/ names this distribution and an extra it declares.

A message that tells the reader how to install an extra says it with :func:install_hint, which names both commands: whoever reads it may have Eden from PyPI or a clone. An extra in :data:UV_ONLY_EXTRAS gets the checkout's command alone, with the reason pip cannot install it.

This module is the one home for what is particular about installing an extra: each such fact is a table here, which :func:pip_install_extra / :func:uv_sync_extra read and tests/test_pyproject.py ties to pyproject.toml. A call site never writes its own install command. It imports nothing beyond the standard library, so import eden can read :func:get_eden_version without loading torch.

def get_rl_library(backend: str | None) -> dict[str, str | None] | None:
    """The RL library record for ``backend``, or ``None`` when there is nothing to record.

    Parameters
    ----------
    backend : str | None
        Eden's runner-backend key — a key of :data:`RL_LIBRARY_DISTRIBUTIONS`
        (``"rsl_rl"`` / ``"rl_games"``), or ``None`` when the caller doesn't know.

    Returns
    -------
    dict | None
        ``{"backend": ..., "distribution": ..., "version": ...}``, with ``version``
        ``None`` if the distribution isn't installed under that name. ``None`` for an
        unknown or missing ``backend`` — provenance is best-effort and never fabricated.
    """
    distribution = RL_LIBRARY_DISTRIBUTIONS.get(backend or "")
    if distribution is None:
        return None
    # The backend can be known (the config named it) while the distribution is absent under
    # that name — a source checkout on PYTHONPATH, say: the version is None, the backend recorded anyway.
    return {"backend": backend, "distribution": distribution, "version": installed_version(distribution)}

def read_run_manifest(log_dir: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    """Read ``<log_dir>/run.json``, or ``None`` if it is missing or unreadable.

    Best-effort by contract: callers enrich diagnostics with this, so a run predating the
    manifest must degrade to "unrecorded", never to an error.

    Parameters
    ----------
    log_dir : str
        A run's log directory (the one holding ``run.json`` and the checkpoints).

    Returns
    -------
    dict | None
        The parsed manifest, or ``None``.
    """
    path = os.path.join(log_dir, RUN_MANIFEST_FILENAME)
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            manifest = json.load(f)
    except (OSError, ValueError):  # missing/unreadable, or truncated JSON
        return None
    return manifest if isinstance(manifest, dict) else None

def build_run_manifest(
    *,
    log_dir: str,
    run_id: str | None,
    timestamp: str | None,
    task: str,
    seed: int | None,
    world_size: int,
    run_name: str,
    argv: list[str],
    resumed_from: str | None = None,
    rl_backend: str | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Assemble the run-manifest dict, resolving the eden/Genesis/RL-library versions.

    Split from :func:`write_run_manifest` so the field set can be asserted without
    touching the filesystem. Not pure: resolving the versions shells out to git and reads
    installed-package metadata, which is why tests stub those three lookups.

    Parameters
    ----------
    log_dir : str
        The run's log directory (its basename is the canonical run identity).
    run_id : str | None
        This run's base-36 id, from :func:`eden.get_run_id`. Taken as an argument rather
        than parsed out of ``log_dir`` so the manifest never has to guess how the basename
        is composed (a later run_name decoration would break basename parsing).
    timestamp : str | None
        This run's creation timestamp, from :func:`eden.get_run_timestamp`.
    task : str
        The registered task name being trained.
    seed : int | None
        The base seed applied to the run's RNGs (``None`` when the backend exposes no seed
        field). Under DDP this is rank 0's seed; rank ``r`` uses ``seed + r`` (see
        ``world_size``), so the whole run reproduces from this base plus the topology.
    world_size : int
        Number of DDP ranks (1 for single-GPU). Makes ``seed`` unambiguous: the per-rank
        seeds are ``seed`` through ``seed + world_size - 1``.
    run_name : str
        The human-facing run name (``""`` when unset).
    argv : list[str]
        The full process command line (typically ``sys.argv``).
    resumed_from : str | None
        Basename of the parent run this one resumed from (``--resume``), or ``None`` for a
        fresh run. Records the fork lineage a resume creates (a resume trains in a new run
        directory rather than continuing the parent in place).
    rl_backend : str | None
        Eden's runner-backend key (``"rsl_rl"`` / ``"rl_games"``) — the library that will
        write this run's checkpoints. Its installed version is resolved and recorded under
        ``rl_library`` (see :func:`get_rl_library`); ``None`` records ``rl_library: null``.

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        The JSON-serializable manifest.
    """
    return {
        "schema_version": RUN_MANIFEST_SCHEMA_VERSION,
        "run_id": run_id,
        "run_name": run_name,
        "timestamp": timestamp,
        "log_dir": os.path.abspath(log_dir),
        "task": task,
        "seed": seed,
        "world_size": world_size,
        "resumed_from": resumed_from,
        "argv": list(argv),
        # The release version, the commit (a clone's HEAD, else null) and whether that tree
        # was dirty. Genesis is a dependency with no working tree of its own, so it has no
        # dirty flag; its commit is the one a git+ or editable install records.
        "eden": get_eden_run_provenance(),
        "genesis": get_package_provenance("genesis-world"),
        # The RL library owns the checkpoint layout, so replaying a `.pt` needs a
        # compatible version of *it*, not just of eden/genesis.
        "rl_library": get_rl_library(rl_backend),
    }

def write_run_manifest(log_dir: str, manifest: dict[str, Any]) -> str:

def editable_checkout(dist: metadata.Distribution) -> Path | None:
    """The checkout an editable install of ``dist`` points at, as its ``direct_url.json`` records it, or ``None`` when
    ``dist`` is not an editable install of a local directory. The directory may since have moved.
    """
    record = direct_url_record(dist)
    url = urlparse(str(record.get("url", "")))
    if not (record.get("dir_info", {}).get("editable") and url.scheme == "file"):
        return None
    return Path(url2pathname(url.path))

The shell command that installs Eden with extra, e.g. pip install "eden-world[vis]".

For an extra with :data:UNPUBLISHED_REQUIREMENTS the command installs those too, so it is complete as printed. For one in :data:REINSTALLED_PACKAGES whose wheel is already installed, it then reinstalls that wheel alone at the installed version: pip install "eden-world[onnx]" && pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps "onnxruntime==1.27.0" (--no-deps, or pip would reinstall torch with it). So the command reads this environment. Each requirement is double-quoted: single quotes reach pip verbatim from Windows cmd, double quotes work in every shell.

Source code in eden/utils/distribution.py 
def pip_install_extra(extra: str) -> str:
    """The shell command that installs Eden with ``extra``, e.g. ``pip install "eden-world[vis]"``.

    For an extra with :data:`UNPUBLISHED_REQUIREMENTS` the command installs those too, so it is complete as printed.
    For one in :data:`REINSTALLED_PACKAGES` whose wheel is already installed, it then reinstalls that wheel alone at
    the installed version: ``pip install "eden-world[onnx]" && pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps
    "onnxruntime==1.27.0"`` (``--no-deps``, or pip would reinstall torch with it). So the command reads this
    environment. Each requirement is double-quoted: single quotes reach pip verbatim from Windows ``cmd``, double
    quotes work in every shell.
    """
    command = " ".join(
        [
            "pip install",
            f'"{DISTRIBUTION_NAME}[{extra}]"',
            *(f'"{req}"' for req in UNPUBLISHED_REQUIREMENTS.get(extra, ())),
        ]
    )
    package = REINSTALLED_PACKAGES.get(extra)
    installed = installed_version(package) if package else None
    if installed:
        command += f' && pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps "{package}=={installed}"'
    return command

The command that adds extra to a checkout's environment, e.g. uv sync --inexact --extra vis.

--inexact because uv sync is exact by default: it uninstalls every extra and group the command does not name, so a reader synced with --all-extras --all-groups who pasted a sync of --extra vis alone from an error message would lose everything else. tests/test_pyproject.py holds the docs and examples to the same rule.

For an extra with :data:UNPUBLISHED_REQUIREMENTS it also syncs the extra's <extra>-git dependency group, which holds them: uv sync --inexact --extra flashsac --group flashsac-git. For one in :data:REINSTALLED_PACKAGES it reinstalls that wheel: uv sync --inexact --extra onnx --reinstall-package onnxruntime.

def uv_sync_extra(extra: str) -> str:
    """The command that adds ``extra`` to a checkout's environment, e.g. ``uv sync --inexact --extra vis``.

    ``--inexact`` because ``uv sync`` is exact by default: it uninstalls every extra and group the command does not
    name, so a reader synced with ``--all-extras --all-groups`` who pasted a sync of ``--extra vis`` alone from an
    error message would lose everything else. ``tests/test_pyproject.py`` holds the docs and examples to the same rule.

    For an extra with :data:`UNPUBLISHED_REQUIREMENTS` it also syncs the extra's ``<extra>-git`` dependency group,
    which holds them: ``uv sync --inexact --extra flashsac --group flashsac-git``. For one in
    :data:`REINSTALLED_PACKAGES` it reinstalls that wheel: ``uv sync --inexact --extra onnx --reinstall-package
    onnxruntime``.
    """
    group = [f"--group {extra}-git"] if extra in UNPUBLISHED_REQUIREMENTS else []
    reinstall = [f"--reinstall-package {REINSTALLED_PACKAGES[extra]}"] if extra in REINSTALLED_PACKAGES else []
    return " ".join(["uv sync --inexact", f"--extra {extra}", *group, *reinstall])

def install_hint(extra: str) -> str:
    """How to install ``extra``, for an error message or a help text, in both the ways a reader may need: with Eden
    from PyPI, and in a clone. For ``vis`` it reads::

        `pip install "eden-world[vis]"`, or `uv sync --inexact --extra vis` in a checkout

    Both commands are complete as printed (see :func:`pip_install_extra` and :func:`uv_sync_extra`). An extra in
    :data:`UV_ONLY_EXTRAS` gets the checkout's command alone, and why pip cannot install it.
    """
    if extra in UV_ONLY_EXTRAS:
        return f"`{uv_sync_extra(extra)}` in a checkout of Eden (pip cannot install it: {UV_ONLY_EXTRAS[extra]})"

docs.title: Smoke runs
docs.text:
Lightweight build-and-step smoke harness for any registered task.

build_and_step("<task>") (or eden smoke --task <name>) constructs a task config by name, builds its Genesis env, and steps it a few times with no action — a one-call end-to-end sanity check for refactors and cheap coverage. Task variants take the same route as the CLI's mod flags: build_and_step("move_forward", modifier_kwargs={"robot": "go1"}) is eden smoke --task move_forward --robot go1.

It encapsulates the steps that are otherwise easy to get wrong:

  • initialize Genesis first (done here if the caller hasn't),
  • pick MimicRLEnvBase vs RLEnvBase from the config type,
  • build() then reset() before stepping,
  • step(None) advances the sim with no action tensor.

is_smoke() -> bool

True in "smoke" mode — the few-step, headless run used for CI/sanity checks.

Controlled by EDEN_SMOKE (the canonical knob, set to 1 by eden examples smoke and the recipe test harness); PYTEST_VERSION (set by pytest) is a fallback so a bare test run is treated as smoke. Examples branch their step horizon on it: horizon = 5 if en.is_smoke() else 1000.

EDEN_SMOKE is parsed as a boolean, not by presence: EDEN_SMOKE=0 / false / no is a real off-switch. An explicitly-set value is authoritative — it wins over PYTEST_VERSION, so a test can opt back out of smoke mode with EDEN_SMOKE=0. An unset or empty value falls through to the PYTEST_VERSION presence check. (Falsey vocabulary matches eden.extensions.policies.onnx._env_bool.)

def is_smoke() -> bool:
    """True in "smoke" mode — the few-step, headless run used for CI/sanity checks.

    Controlled by ``EDEN_SMOKE`` (the canonical knob, set to ``1`` by ``eden examples smoke``
    and the recipe test harness); ``PYTEST_VERSION`` (set by pytest) is a fallback so a bare
    test run is treated as smoke. Examples branch their step horizon on it:
    ``horizon = 5 if en.is_smoke() else 1000``.

    ``EDEN_SMOKE`` is parsed as a boolean, not by presence: ``EDEN_SMOKE=0`` / ``false`` / ``no``
    is a real off-switch. An explicitly-set value is authoritative — it wins over
    ``PYTEST_VERSION``, so a test can opt back out of smoke mode with ``EDEN_SMOKE=0``. An unset
    or empty value falls through to the ``PYTEST_VERSION`` presence check. (Falsey vocabulary
    matches ``eden.extensions.policies.onnx._env_bool``.)
    """
    eden_smoke = os.environ.get("EDEN_SMOKE", "").strip().lower()
    if eden_smoke:
        return eden_smoke not in ("0", "false", "no")
    return bool(os.environ.get("PYTEST_VERSION"))

def build_and_step(
    task: "Union[str, EdenConfig]",
    *,
    modifier_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    num_envs: int = 2,
    num_steps: int = 2,
    eval_mode: bool = False,
    show_viewer: bool = False,
    backend=None,
) -> "RLEnvBase":
    """Build a task's env and step it ``num_steps`` times with no action.

    One-shot: each call builds a fresh scene and does not destroy it, so it is
    meant for a single sanity check (or a session-scoped test), not a tight
    loop over many tasks in one process.

    Parameters
    ----------
    task : str | EdenConfig
        A registered task name, or an already-constructed config object. A name
        goes through ``TASK_REGISTRY.build`` so the task's TaskMods run — a
        mod-bound task is not buildable without them.
    modifier_kwargs : dict[str, Any], optional
        TaskMod overrides forwarded to ``TASK_REGISTRY.build(task, **modifier_kwargs)``
        — the Python side of ``eden smoke --task <name> --<flag> <value>``, e.g.
        ``{"robot": "go1"}``. Unknown flags raise the registry's ``ValueError``. Only
        a task *name* can take them: a config object is already built, mods included,
        so passing both raises ``TypeError`` rather than silently ignoring the kwargs.
    num_envs : int
        Number of parallel envs to build.
    num_steps : int
        Number of no-action ``step(None)`` calls to run after the initial reset.
    eval_mode : bool
        Build in eval mode (training/randomization off). Defaults to False so the
        full training path is exercised.
    show_viewer : bool
        Open the Genesis viewer.
    backend : genesis backend, optional
        Passed to ``en.init`` only when Genesis isn't initialized yet. ``None``
        leaves ``en.init``'s default; pass ``gs.gpu`` / ``gs.cpu`` to choose.

    Returns
    -------
    RLEnvBase
        The built, stepped env — returned so callers can inspect it. Any error
        in the build/step path propagates; surfacing it is the point.
    """
    import eden as en
    import genesis as gs

    from eden.envs.base import env_class_for_config
    from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY
    from eden.utils.configs import EdenConfig

    if isinstance(task, EdenConfig) and modifier_kwargs:
        raise TypeError(
            f"build_and_step() got modifier_kwargs {sorted(modifier_kwargs)} together with an already-built "
            f"{type(task).__name__}. TaskMods run while a task is built from its name, so either pass the task "
            "name here or apply them yourself with TASK_REGISTRY.build(name, **modifier_kwargs) and pass the result."
        )

    if not getattr(gs, "_initialized", False):
        en.init(**({"backend": backend} if backend is not None else {}))

    cfg = task if isinstance(task, EdenConfig) else TASK_REGISTRY.build(task, **(modifier_kwargs or {}))
    cfg.env_options.num_envs = num_envs

    env = env_class_for_config(cfg).from_config(cfg, show_viewer=show_viewer, eval_mode=eval_mode)
    env.build()
    env.reset()
    for _ in range(num_steps):
        env.step(None)
    return env

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text:
Per-term cost profilers for the step loop.

On-demand, one-shot per-term cost profiler for a single task.

Why this exists

A term that is correct but slow is invisible. Nothing in a normal run tells the author that the observation term they just wrote allocates a torch.tensor(...) constant every step and now dominates rollout collection — the only symptom is a training run that feels slow. Measured on the Go1 backflip benchmark, two runs of the same task on the same GPU differed 35x in throughput purely because of per-call allocations inside a task's own terms (see docs/guides/terms.md).

This profiler makes that cost investigable on demand. eden smoke --task <name> --profile builds the task, steps it a bounded window, attributes wall time to each term the per-step managers run, and writes a ranked, machine-readable term_cost.json — so an author (or a coding agent that just wrote the term) can see which term is the bottleneck and what fraction of the step it costs.

Relationship to :class:~eden.utils.profiling.step_profiler.RLStepProfiler

That profiler attaches to a caller-driven loop (training / rollout) and also rolls up per-manager overhead; this one owns a short self-driven window and emits a compact ranking with no manager rollup. They share the term-discovery and timing mechanism in :mod:eden.utils.profiling.core, so both stay faithful to the same manager internals and the same both-sides CUDA sync.

Purely additive, zero overhead when off

Nothing here runs unless a caller asks for it. The profiler wraps term.compute from the outside for the measurement window only, times it with a CUDA sync on both sides so the number reflects the term's own GPU work, then restores every original method. A run without --profile creates no profiler object and wraps no method anywhere in the framework.

Live-loop per-term profiler for the RL step loop.

Instruments every manager term's compute() — plus each manager's top-level compute(), reset() and post_reset() and the other hooks the step loop calls on it (the action manager's apply_actions(), the motion manager's fill_data(), ...) — so the wall-clock cost of observations / rewards / terminations / commands / events / curriculum / metrics / actions / motion can be attributed term by term while a real loop drives the env. Use it to surface the framework-level overhead Eden spends dispatching and composing terms on top of the raw Genesis physics step.

The headline numbers are:

  • per-term mean/total wall time and share of the step,
  • per-manager time split into terms (its term calls) and overhead (the manager's own methods around them) — no split for a manager whose terms are not timed (the motion manager's run inside fill_data, not through compute),
  • the step-loop work no manager owns: the Genesis scene.step physics tick (physics) and the env's own reset work around the managers' resets (reset: scene.reset, solver bookkeeping, buffer zeroing, index handling), and
  • the unattributed remainder of the step — the Python in env.step between instrumented calls.

The per-term table and :meth:RLStepProfiler.as_dict's total_ms_per_step are inclusive: a call's wall time counts every instrumented call nested inside it. The rollup instead charges each call only its own time (its wall time minus that of the instrumented calls nested inside it), and only inside :meth:RLStepProfiler.step windows, so its rows partition the measured step exactly. A RESET event that fills the motion window is charged its own work under event and the fill under motion; reset excludes everything instrumented inside it. With sync=True the syncs around a nested call land in its caller's own time. A call that raises is still recorded, with its wall time up to the raise (no closing sync).

For the one-shot "profile the term I just wrote" workflow, see :func:eden.utils.profiling.term_profiler.profile_terms. Both share the term-discovery and timing mechanism in :mod:eden.utils.profiling.core.

GPU note

Manager terms launch CUDA kernels asynchronously, so naive host-side timing measures launch cost, not execution. With sync=True (default) the profiler calls :func:torch.cuda.synchronize around every measured call, yielding true wall time per term at the cost of serializing kernels that would otherwise overlap — absolute numbers run high but the relative breakdown is faithful. With sync=False you instead measure pure Python dispatch cost (useful for spotting per-term CPU overhead). The two views answer different questions.

Shared instrumentation core for the per-term profilers.

Both front-ends attribute wall time to individual manager terms by the same mechanism: find every term the step loop runs, wrap its compute() with a CUDA-synced timer, and restore it afterwards. That mechanism lives here so there is a single source of truth for

  • the coupling to manager term storage (:func:iter_terms), and
  • the reversible, sync-both-sides timing wrapper (:func:time_call times one call, :class:Patch installs and removes a wrapper, :func:time_method joins the two). The one-shot profiler uses :func:time_method; the live-loop one builds its own wrapper from :func:time_call and :class:Patch, to subtract the calls nested inside a call from its own time.

The two front-ends differ only in policy — what they measure and how they report it — not in this mechanism:

  • :class:eden.utils.profiling.step_profiler.RLStepProfiler attaches to a caller-driven loop (training / rollout), also times manager-level methods, and produces a full per-manager rollup. Use it to profile terms in an actual loop.
  • :func:eden.utils.profiling.term_profiler.profile_terms owns a short, self-driven window and produces a compact, agent-readable ranking. Use it to profile a term you just wrote, in isolation.

def render(self, top: int | None = 15) -> str:
    """Human-readable table, costliest term first (``top`` rows, then a rollup)."""
    term_total = sum(r.us_per_step for r in self.rows)
    lines = [
        f"Per-term compute cost — {self.num_steps} steps, "
        f"{self.step_us:.0f} us/env-step ({term_total:.0f} us/step in terms).",
        f"  {'us/step':>10}  {'%step':>6}  {'calls':>5}  term",
    ]
    shown = self.rows if top is None else self.rows[:top]
    for r in shown:
        lines.append(
            f"  {r.us_per_step:>10.0f}  {r.pct_step:>5.1f}%  {r.calls_per_step:>5.1f}  {r.manager}:{r.term}"
        )
    if top is not None and len(self.rows) > top:
        rest = sum(r.us_per_step for r in self.rows[top:])
        lines.append(f"  {rest:>10.0f}  {'':>6}  {'':>5}  ({len(self.rows) - top} more terms)")
    lines.append("  " + self.HINT)
    if self.sync:
        lines.append("  " + self.NOTE)
    return "\n".join(lines)

Attribute wall time to each per-step term over a bounded window.

Runs warmup steps uninstrumented (kernel compilation and lazy allocation land there), then wraps every term's compute, runs measure steps, and restores the originals. The env is left stepped, not reset — the caller owns it.

Event terms are excluded (they fire on reset / interval, not per step) and so are action terms (their dominant cost is in apply_actions, not the timed compute). The reported step_us is the whole env.step() measured under the same both-sides sync, so it runs high in absolute terms but the per-term pct_step shares are faithful (see :class:~eden.utils.profiling.step_profiler.RLStepProfiler for the same caveat).

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION env

A built, reset env.

TYPE: EnvBase

Uninstrumented steps before measuring.

TYPE: int DEFAULT: 10

measure

Instrumented steps; per-term cost is normalized by this (a term computed more than once per step accumulates all its calls into that step's cost).

TYPE: int DEFAULT: 50

step

Zero-arg step to call each iteration. Defaults to lambda: env.step(None).

TYPE: callable DEFAULT: None

Synchronize CUDA around each timed call. Defaults to whether CUDA is present.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: None

RETURNS DESCRIPTION ProfileReport

Ranked per-term cost plus the measured env-step time.

def profile_terms(
    env: "EnvBase",
    *,
    warmup: int = 10,
    measure: int = 50,
    step: Callable[[], object] | None = None,
    sync: bool | None = None,
) -> ProfileReport:
    """Attribute wall time to each per-step term over a bounded window.

    Runs ``warmup`` steps uninstrumented (kernel compilation and lazy allocation
    land there), then wraps every term's ``compute``, runs ``measure`` steps, and
    restores the originals. The env is left stepped, not reset — the caller owns it.

    Event terms are excluded (they fire on reset / interval, not per step) and so
    are action terms (their dominant cost is in ``apply_actions``, not the timed
    ``compute``). The reported ``step_us`` is the whole ``env.step()`` measured
    under the same both-sides sync, so it runs high in absolute terms but the
    per-term ``pct_step`` shares are faithful (see
    :class:`~eden.utils.profiling.step_profiler.RLStepProfiler` for the same caveat).

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : EnvBase
        A built, reset env.
    warmup : int
        Uninstrumented steps before measuring.
    measure : int
        Instrumented steps; per-term cost is normalized by this (a term computed
        more than once per step accumulates all its calls into that step's cost).
    step : callable, optional
        Zero-arg step to call each iteration. Defaults to ``lambda: env.step(None)``.
    sync : bool, optional
        Synchronize CUDA around each timed call. Defaults to whether CUDA is present.

    Returns
    -------
    ProfileReport
        Ranked per-term cost plus the measured env-step time.
    """
    synchronize = resolve_sync(sync)
    step = step or (lambda: env.step(None))

    for _ in range(warmup):
        step()

    timeable, skipped = discover_timeable(env, include_event=False, include_action=False)
    warn_untimed("profile_terms", skipped)

    records: dict[tuple[str, str], _Timing] = {}
    patches = []  # list[core.Patch]
    for manager, label, term in timeable:
        rec = records.setdefault((manager, label), _Timing())
        patches.append(time_method(term, "compute", rec.add, synchronize))

    step_time = _Timing()
    try:
        for _ in range(measure):
            time_call(step, step_time.add, synchronize)
    finally:
        for patch in patches:
            patch.restore()

    steps = max(measure, 1)
    step_us = step_time.total_s / steps * 1e6
    rows = [
        TermCost(
            manager=manager,
            term=label,
            us_per_step=rec.total_s / steps * 1e6,
            calls_per_step=rec.calls / steps,
        )
        for (manager, label), rec in records.items()
    ]
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: r.us_per_step, reverse=True)
    for r in rows:
        r.pct_step = (r.us_per_step / step_us * 100.0) if step_us > 0 else 0.0
    return ProfileReport(num_steps=measure, step_us=step_us, sync=synchronize is not None, rows=rows)

Attribute RL-step wall time to individual manager terms.

Typical usage::

profiler = RLStepProfiler(env)
profiler.attach()
for _ in range(warmup):
    env.step(sample_action())
profiler.reset()            # discard warmup, keep instrumentation

    with profiler.step():   # times the whole env.step()
        env.step(sample_action())

    ...

def __init__(self, env: EnvBase, *, sync: bool = True):
    self._env = env
    # Only sync when there's actually a CUDA device to wait on.
    self._synchronize = resolve_sync(sync)
    self._stats: dict[tuple[str, str, str], TermTiming] = {}
    self._patches: list[Patch] = []
    # One entry per instrumented call in progress: the wall time of the instrumented calls
    # nested inside it so far, subtracted from its own to give its self time.
    self._nested_s: list[float] = []
    self._step = TermTiming(manager="", label="step", kind="step")
    # Whether a ``step()`` window is open. Own time accrues only inside one, so the rollup
    # partitions the measured step; instrumented calls outside (an ``env.reset()`` between
    # timed steps) still reach the per-term table, and their wall time is ``_outside_s``.
    self._in_step = False
    self._outside_s = 0.0
    self._attached = False

attach() -> RLStepProfiler
Source code in eden/utils/profiling/step_profiler.py 
def attach(self) -> RLStepProfiler:
    if self._attached:
        return self
    hooks = self._step_loop_hooks()
    # discover_timeable dedups a term shared across groups so it is wrapped once, not
    # double-counted, and drops any term that can't carry the timing override.
    timeable, skipped = discover_timeable(self._env, include_event=True)
    warn_untimed("RLStepProfiler", skipped)
    # A run of RESET terms that fires as one ``compute_batch`` never calls its terms' own ``compute``:
    # time the batch as one row, ``reset.<a>+<b>+...``, in their place.
    event_manager = getattr(self._env, "event_manager", None)
    batches = list(event_manager.iter_reset_batches()) if event_manager is not None else []
    batched = {id(term) for batch in batches for term in batch.terms}
    for mgr_name, label, term in timeable:
        if id(term) not in batched:
            self._wrap((mgr_name, label, "term"), term, "compute")
    for batch in batches:
        self._wrap(("event", f"reset.{'+'.join(batch.names)}", "term"), batch, "compute")
    for key, owner, method in hooks:
        self._wrap(key, owner, method)
    self._attached = True
    return self

def as_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Machine-readable summary (JSON-serializable).

    ``terms``, ``managers`` (by manager) and ``loop`` (by step-loop row: ``physics``,
    ``reset``) hold one record per instrumented callable: every call, inclusive of the calls
    nested inside it (``total_ms_per_step``, ``pct_step``), plus its own time inside step
    windows (``self_ms_per_step``). ``rollup`` is the report's rollup table: own time per
    row, summing to ``step_ms``. ``outside_step_ms`` is the wall time of instrumented calls
    made outside :meth:`step`, which only the records count.
    """
    n = max(self.num_steps, 1)
    step_total = self._step.total_s

    def pack(r: TermTiming) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {
            "manager": r.manager,
            "label": r.label,
            "kind": r.kind,
            "calls_per_step": r.calls / n,
            "mean_ms": r.mean_s * 1e3,
            "total_ms_per_step": r.total_s / n * 1e3,
            "self_ms_per_step": r.self_s / n * 1e3,
            "std_ms": r.std_s * 1e3,
            "max_ms": r.max_s * 1e3,
            "pct_step": (r.total_s / step_total * 100.0) if step_total > 0 else 0.0,
        }

    def pack_by_owner(kind: str) -> dict[str, dict[str, dict[str, Any]]]:
        return {
            owner: {label: pack(r) for label, r in entries.items()}
            for owner, entries in self._records_by_owner(kind).items()
        }

    terms = sorted(self._term_records(), key=lambda r: r.total_s, reverse=True)
    manager_rows, other_rows = self._rollup()
    return {
        "num_steps": self.num_steps,
        "sync": self._sync,
        "step_ms": self._step.mean_s * 1e3,
        "steps_per_s": (n / step_total) if step_total > 0 else 0.0,
        "terms": [pack(r) for r in terms],
        "managers": pack_by_owner("manager"),
        "loop": pack_by_owner("loop"),
        "rollup": {
            row: {
                "ms_per_step": own_s / n * 1e3,
                "terms_ms_per_step": None if t is None else t / n * 1e3,
                "overhead_ms_per_step": None if o is None else o / n * 1e3,
                "pct_step": (own_s / step_total * 100.0) if step_total > 0 else 0.0,
            }
            for row, own_s, t, o in [*manager_rows, *other_rows]
        },
        "outside_step_ms": self._outside_s * 1e3,
    }

def report(self, *, top: int | None = None, sort_by: str = "total") -> str:
    """Build human-readable breakdown tables.

    Parameters
    ----------
    top : int, optional
        If given, only show the ``top`` slowest terms.
    sort_by : str, optional
        Term ordering, either ``"total"`` (default) or ``"mean"``.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        The formatted breakdown tables.
    """
    n = max(self.num_steps, 1)
    step_total = self._step.total_s
    step_ms = self._step.mean_s * 1e3

    key = (lambda r: r.mean_s) if sort_by == "mean" else (lambda r: r.total_s)
    terms = sorted(self._term_records(), key=key, reverse=True)
    if top is not None:
        terms = terms[:top]

    def pct(total_s: float) -> str:
        return f"{(total_s / step_total * 100.0):.1f}" if step_total > 0 else "-"

    term_tbl = PrettyTable()
    # Calls outside a step window still count here, over the timed steps: say so on the table itself.
    outside = ", incl. calls outside step()" if self._outside_s > 0.0 else ""
    term_tbl.title = f"Per-Term Timing  ({self.num_steps} steps, sync={self._sync}{outside})"
    term_tbl.field_names = ["Manager", "Term", "Calls/step", "Mean (ms)", "Total/step (ms)", "% step"]
    term_tbl.align["Term"] = "l"
    term_tbl.align["Manager"] = "l"
    for r in terms:
        term_tbl.add_row(
            [
                r.manager,
                r.label,
                f"{r.calls / n:.2f}",
                f"{r.mean_s * 1e3:.4f}",
                f"{r.total_s / n * 1e3:.4f}",
                pct(r.total_s),
            ]
        )

    # Per-manager rollup, by own time so the rows sum to the step: each manager's terms and its
    # own methods around them (dispatch/bookkeeping), then the step-loop rows no manager owns,
    # and whatever no instrumented call covers.
    mgr_tbl = PrettyTable()
    mgr_tbl.title = "Per-Manager Rollup  (own time; rows sum to the step)"
    mgr_tbl.field_names = ["Manager", "Own/step (ms)", "Terms (ms)", "Overhead (ms)", "% step"]
    mgr_tbl.align["Manager"] = "l"

    def add_rollup_row(row: str, own_s: float, terms_s: float | None, overhead_s: float | None) -> None:
        split = ["-", "-"] if terms_s is None else [f"{terms_s / n * 1e3:.4f}", f"{overhead_s / n * 1e3:.4f}"]
        mgr_tbl.add_row([row, f"{own_s / n * 1e3:.4f}", *split, pct(own_s)])

    manager_rows, other_rows = self._rollup()
    for rollup_row in manager_rows:
        add_rollup_row(*rollup_row)
    mgr_tbl.add_row(["─" * 7, "─" * 13, "─" * 10, "─" * 13, "─" * 6])
    for rollup_row in other_rows:
        add_rollup_row(*rollup_row)

    steps_per_s = (n / step_total) if step_total > 0 else 0.0
    header = (
        f"RL step profile — {self.num_steps} steps, {self._env.num_envs} envs, "
        f"sync={self._sync}\n"
        f"  step: {step_ms:.3f} ms/step  ({steps_per_s:,.0f} steps/s, "
        f"{steps_per_s * self._env.num_envs:,.0f} env-steps/s)\n"
    )
    if self._outside_s > 0.0:
        header += (
            f"  {self._outside_s * 1e3:.3f} ms of instrumented calls ran outside profiler.step() "
            "(e.g. an env.reset() between timed steps): counted in the per-term table, not the rollup\n"
        )
    return header + "\n" + mgr_tbl.get_string() + "\n\n" + term_tbl.get_string() + "\n"

def restore(self) -> None:
    """Undo the patch, restoring the original bound/class method."""
    if self._had_own:

    elif self._name in self._owner.__dict__:

def resolve_sync(sync: bool | None) -> Callable[[], None] | None:
    """Return the CUDA-synchronize callable to use around timed calls, or ``None``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    sync : bool or None
        ``True`` to synchronize, ``False`` to skip, ``None`` to auto-enable only
        when a CUDA device is present. In every case a synchronize callable is
        returned only if CUDA is actually available (there is nothing to wait on
        otherwise).

    Returns
    -------
    callable or None
        ``torch.cuda.synchronize`` when syncing, else ``None``.
    """
    import torch

    if sync is None:
        sync = torch.cuda.is_available()
    return torch.cuda.synchronize if (sync and torch.cuda.is_available()) else None

An action term's dominant cost is in apply_actions (per decimation substep), not the compute this module times, so a compute-only view (the one-shot profiler) excludes it to avoid reporting a misleading ~0; the live-loop profiler, which also times apply_actions, includes it.

def iter_terms(
    env: "EnvBase", *, include_event: bool = True, include_action: bool = True
) -> Iterator[tuple[str, str, Any]]:
    """Yield ``(manager, label, term)`` for every term the step loop runs.

    Composes the public term iterators of the three manager shapes: the
    observation manager's ``iter_terms()`` (per group), the event manager's
    ``iter_terms()`` (per mode), and the flat ``terms`` dict every
    :class:`~eden.managers.base.FlatManagerBase` exposes. Managers absent on this
    env (e.g. a task with no command manager) are skipped.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : EnvBase
        A built environment.
    include_event : bool
        Whether to include event-manager terms. They fire on reset / interval
        through mode dispatch rather than once per step, so a per-step cost view
        (the one-shot profiler) excludes them; the live-loop profiler includes
        them.
    include_action : bool
        Whether to include action-manager terms. An action term's dominant cost
        is in ``apply_actions`` (per decimation substep), not the ``compute`` this
        module times, so a compute-only view (the one-shot profiler) excludes it
        to avoid reporting a misleading ~0; the live-loop profiler, which also
        times ``apply_actions``, includes it.

    Yields
    ------
    tuple of (str, str, object)
        The owning manager's name, a human-readable label (``"group.term"`` for
        observations, ``"mode.term"`` for events, the bare term name otherwise),
        and the term instance.
    """
    om = getattr(env, "observation_manager", None)
    if om is not None:
        for group, name, term in om.iter_terms():
            yield "observation", f"{group}.{name}", term
    if include_event:
        ev = getattr(env, "event_manager", None)
        if ev is not None:
            for mode, name, term in ev.iter_terms():
                yield "event", f"{mode}.{name}", term
    for mgr_name in FLAT_TERM_MANAGERS:
        if mgr_name == "action" and not include_action:
            continue
        mgr = getattr(env, f"{mgr_name}_manager", None)
        if mgr is None:
            continue
        for name, term in mgr.terms.items():
            yield mgr_name, name, term

def can_time(owner: Any) -> bool:
    """Whether ``owner`` can carry the per-instance ``compute`` override the timers install.

    :func:`time_method` shadows the method with an instance attribute, so the owner
    needs a writable ``__dict__``. A term defining ``__slots__`` without one cannot
    be wrapped — the ``setattr`` would raise. No built-in term is slotted, but an
    author could write one, so :func:`discover_timeable` skips such a term instead
    of crashing the profiler. Manager instances always qualify.
    """
    return hasattr(owner, "__dict__")
