def compute(self, subterrain: tu.SubTerrain) -> tu.SubTerrain:
    from eden.utils.terrains.io import load_height_field

    if not self.file:
        raise ValueError("HeightFieldFileTerrain: 'file' is required (path of an exported height-field .npz).")
    data = load_height_field(self.file)
    expected = (subterrain.width, subterrain.length)
    if data.height_field_m.shape != expected:
        raise ValueError(
            f"HeightFieldFileTerrain: '{self.file}' grid is {data.height_field_m.shape} but the "
            f"TerrainOptions imply {expected}; set subterrain_size=((H-1)*hs, (W-1)*hs) with the "
            "file's horizontal_scale."
        )
    if abs(subterrain.horizontal_scale - data.horizontal_scale) > 1e-9:
        raise ValueError(
            f"HeightFieldFileTerrain: horizontal_scale mismatch — file has {data.horizontal_scale}, "
            f"TerrainOptions has {subterrain.horizontal_scale}."
        )
    # The stored grid is meters; raw values are meters/vertical_scale.
    subterrain.height_field_raw[:] = data.height_field_m / subterrain.vertical_scale
    return subterrain

Height-field terrain export/import.

Eden terrains are generated in memory (:func:generate_height_field) and normally live only inside the Genesis morph. This module defines a small on-disk .npz format so a terrain's height field can be exported once and re-used by offline tools (e.g. the TCRS terrain-adaptive motion retargeter) without re-running the generators.

Format (version 1)

height_field float32 [H, W] grid of heights in meters (vertical_scale is already applied). Axis 0 maps to world +x, axis 1 to world +y — the same convention as :func:generate_height_field and :class:~eden.entities.terrain.Terrain. horizontal_scale float64 cell size in meters: x = origin[0] + i * horizontal_scale. origin float64 [3] world position of grid corner [0, 0]. _format_version Integer format tag; loaders must reject unknown versions.

Source code in eden/utils/terrains/io.py 
def export_height_field(
    path: str,
    height_field_m: np.ndarray,
    horizontal_scale: float,
    origin: tuple[float, float, float] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
) -> None:
    """Save a height field (in meters) to ``path`` in the versioned ``.npz`` format."""
    if not str(path).endswith(".npz"):
        # np.savez would silently append ".npz", breaking a later load with the
        # original path string.
        raise ValueError(f"Height-field export path must end with '.npz'; got '{path}'.")
    data = HeightFieldData(height_field_m=height_field_m, horizontal_scale=horizontal_scale, origin=origin)
    np.savez_compressed(
        path,
        height_field=data.height_field_m,
        horizontal_scale=np.float64(data.horizontal_scale),
        # float64: world coordinates can be large, and float32 loses ~1 m of
        # precision near 1e7 — the height grid itself stays float32.
        origin=np.asarray(data.origin, dtype=np.float64),
        _format_version=np.int64(HEIGHT_FIELD_FORMAT_VERSION),
    )

def load_height_field(path: str) -> HeightFieldData:
    """Load a height field previously written by :func:`export_height_field`."""
    with np.load(path) as raw:
        missing = {"height_field", "horizontal_scale", "origin", "_format_version"} - set(raw.files)
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(
                f"'{path}' is not an Eden height-field npz: missing key(s) {sorted(missing)}. "
                f"Found keys: {sorted(raw.files)}."
            )
        version = int(raw["_format_version"])
        if version != HEIGHT_FIELD_FORMAT_VERSION:
            raise ValueError(
                f"'{path}' has height-field format version {version}; this Eden version reads "
                f"version {HEIGHT_FIELD_FORMAT_VERSION}. Re-export the terrain."
            )
        return HeightFieldData(
            height_field_m=raw["height_field"],
            horizontal_scale=float(raw["horizontal_scale"]),
            origin=tuple(raw["origin"].tolist()),
        )

def terrain_options_from_height_field_file(path: str) -> "TerrainOptions":
    """Build a ``TerrainOptions`` that reconstructs an exported height field verbatim.

    The returned options place the terrain at the file's origin and reproduce
    the stored grid exactly (float raw field, ``vertical_scale=1.0``), so a
    scene built from them matches what the TCRS
    ``HeightFieldTerrain`` queried during adaptation.
    """
    from eden.options.entities import TerrainOptions
    from eden.utils.terrains.height_field_file_terrain import HeightFieldFileTerrain

    data = load_height_field(path)
    height, width = data.height_field_m.shape
    return TerrainOptions(
        horizontal_scale=data.horizontal_scale,
        vertical_scale=1.0,
        subterrain_size=(
            (height - 1) * data.horizontal_scale,
            (width - 1) * data.horizontal_scale,
        ),
        terrain_generators=[[HeightFieldFileTerrain.configure(file=path)]],
        default_root_pos=data.origin,
    )

def height_field_from_terrain_options(options: "TerrainOptions") -> HeightFieldData:
    """Materialize the height field a :class:`TerrainOptions` would build, in meters.

    Runs the same :func:`generate_height_field` call as
    :meth:`eden.entities.terrain.Terrain._create_morph_from_options`, applies
    ``vertical_scale``, and stamps ``options.default_root_pos`` as the origin.
    """
    import genesis as gs

    from eden.utils.terrains.base import generate_height_field

    if gs.EPS is None:
        # generate_height_field reads gs.EPS, which Genesis only sets at init;
        # without this guard the failure is an opaque TypeError deep inside.
        raise RuntimeError("height_field_from_terrain_options requires an initialized Genesis — call en.init() first.")
    if not options.terrain_generators or not options.terrain_generators[0]:
        raise ValueError(
            "height_field_from_terrain_options: options.terrain_generators must be a non-empty "
            f"rectangular grid of generators; got {options.terrain_generators!r}."
        )
    n_subterrains = (len(options.terrain_generators), len(options.terrain_generators[0]))
    height_field = generate_height_field(
        terrain_generators=options.terrain_generators,
        subterrain_size=options.subterrain_size,
        n_subterrains=n_subterrains,
        horizontal_scale=options.horizontal_scale,
        vertical_scale=options.vertical_scale,
        randomize=options.randomize,
    )
    return HeightFieldData(
        height_field_m=height_field.astype(np.float32) * options.vertical_scale,
        horizontal_scale=options.horizontal_scale,
        origin=tuple(options.default_root_pos),
    )

def cell_of(self, uv: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """``(row, col)`` of the cell holding each point ``uv (..., 2)``; may lie outside the grid."""
    uv = np.asarray(uv, dtype=np.float64)
    return np.stack(
        [np.floor((self.v0 - uv[..., 1]) / self.cell), np.floor((uv[..., 0] - self.u0) / self.cell)], -1
    ).astype(np.int64)

def centers(self) -> np.ndarray:
    """``(u, v)`` of every cell's centre, ``(rows, cols, 2)``."""
    u = self.u0 + (np.arange(self.cols) + 0.5) * self.cell
    v = self.v0 - (np.arange(self.rows) + 0.5) * self.cell
    return np.stack(np.meshgrid(u, v, indexing="xy"), axis=-1)

docs.text:
get_asset_path(file: str, registry: str | None = 'Kashu7100', dataset: str | None = 'eden_assets', local_dir: str | None = None) -> str

Resolve an asset to a local file, fetching it and its dependencies from the Hub if needed.

file is one of:

  • a path inside local_dir, cached or not: the repo path below local_dir, resolved as that repo path is (so a missing dependency of a cached file is fetched too);
  • any other existing local path, returned as is (an absolute one that does not exist raises, without a fetch);
  • the file's full path in the registry/dataset Hub repo, e.g. models/eggplant/object.urdf.

local_dir defaults to :func:eden.utils.misc.get_assets_dir, the download root EDEN_ASSETS_DIR moves. A repo path is matched exactly, never by its tail. local_dir can hold other datasets' caches (the download root holds ycb/, simpler/, ...), so a bare name or a path suffix could name another dataset's file; the error for one lists the repo paths that end in it.

With registry or dataset set to None nothing is fetched: file is returned if it exists locally, else None.

Source code in eden/utils/assets.py 
def get_asset_path(
    file: str,
    registry: str | None = "Kashu7100",
    dataset: str | None = "eden_assets",
    local_dir: str | None = None,
) -> str:
    """Resolve an asset to a local file, fetching it and its dependencies from the Hub if needed.

    ``file`` is one of:

    - a path inside ``local_dir``, cached or not: the repo path below ``local_dir``, resolved as that
      repo path is (so a missing dependency of a cached file is fetched too);
    - any other existing local path, returned as is (an absolute one that does not exist raises,
      without a fetch);
    - the file's full path in the ``registry/dataset`` Hub repo, e.g. ``models/eggplant/object.urdf``.

    ``local_dir`` defaults to :func:`eden.utils.misc.get_assets_dir`, the download root ``EDEN_ASSETS_DIR``
    moves. A repo path is matched exactly, never by its tail. ``local_dir`` can hold other datasets' caches
    (the download root holds ``ycb/``, ``simpler/``, ...), so a bare name or a path suffix could name
    another dataset's file; the error for one lists the repo paths that end in it.

    With ``registry`` or ``dataset`` set to ``None`` nothing is fetched: ``file`` is returned if it exists
    locally, else ``None``.
    """
    local_dir = resolve_local_dir(local_dir)
    if registry is None or dataset is None:
        return file if os.path.exists(file) else None

    asset_path = local_dir
    repo_id = f"{registry}/{dataset}"
    local_dir_abs = os.path.abspath(local_dir)
    file_abs = os.path.abspath(file)
    if file_abs.startswith(local_dir_abs + os.sep) and not os.path.isdir(file_abs):
        # A path inside local_dir is the cached copy of the repo path below it, so it resolves
        # (and has its dependencies fetched) exactly as that repo path does.
        repo_file = os.path.relpath(file_abs, local_dir_abs)
    elif os.path.exists(file):
        return file
    elif os.path.isabs(file):
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"No such local file: {file!r}. An absolute path is read from disk, never fetched; only a path "
            f"inside local_dir ({local_dir}) or a repo path names a file of the Hub repo {repo_id!r}."
        )
    else:
        repo_file = file

    matched_file_path = os.path.join(local_dir, repo_file)
    if not os.path.isfile(matched_file_path):
        # Escaped: ``allow_patterns`` are fnmatch patterns, and a name is matched literally.
        _snapshot_download_locked(
            repo_type="dataset",
            repo_id=repo_id,
            allow_patterns=[glob.escape(repo_file)],
            local_dir=local_dir,
        )
        if not os.path.isfile(matched_file_path):
            raise FileNotFoundError(_not_fetched_message(file, repo_file, repo_id, local_dir))

    # Download asset dependencies (meshes, textures, materials, etc.)
    # Walk the dep graph layer by layer, BFS: every file at the current
    # depth is parsed for refs, then ALL missing refs are downloaded in a
    # single batched ``snapshot_download`` call before advancing to the
    # next layer. URDFs in particular reference dozens of ``.obj`` files,
    # which each reference one ``.mtl`` — batching avoids one HF round-trip
    # per file (laptop URDF: 1 + 37 + 37 + textures ≈ 4 batched calls instead
    # of ~100 single-file ones).
    checked_files: set[str] = {matched_file_path}
    current_layer: list[str] = [matched_file_path]

    while current_layer:
        next_missing_patterns: list[str] = []
        next_local_paths: list[str] = []
        already_local: list[str] = []
        # (referring file, ref, candidates) for each ref this layer's fetch asks for.
        requested: list[tuple[str, str, list[tuple[str, str]]]] = []

        for current_file in current_layer:
            dep_paths = _get_asset_dependencies(current_file)
            if not dep_paths:
                continue

            file_dir = os.path.dirname(current_file)
            file_dir_relative = os.path.relpath(file_dir, asset_path)

            for dep_path in dep_paths:
                candidates = _resolve_dep(dep_path, file_dir, file_dir_relative, asset_path)
                found_local = False
                for _dep_pattern, dep_local_path in candidates:
                    if os.path.exists(dep_local_path):
                        if dep_local_path not in checked_files:
                            already_local.append(dep_local_path)
                        found_local = True
                        break
                if not found_local:
                    requested.append((current_file, dep_path, candidates))
                    for dep_pattern, dep_local_path in candidates:
                        # An absolute ref's primary candidate is a host path, not a repo path.
                        if not os.path.isabs(dep_pattern):
                            next_missing_patterns.append(dep_pattern.replace(os.sep, "/"))
                            next_local_paths.append(dep_local_path)

        # Dedup patterns + their matched local paths, preserving order.
        seen: set[str] = set()
        unique_patterns: list[str] = []
        unique_local_paths: list[str] = []
        for pattern, local_path in zip(next_missing_patterns, next_local_paths):
            if pattern not in seen:
                seen.add(pattern)
                unique_patterns.append(pattern)
                unique_local_paths.append(local_path)

        if unique_patterns:
            _snapshot_download_locked(
                repo_type="dataset",
                repo_id=repo_id,
                allow_patterns=[glob.escape(pattern) for pattern in unique_patterns],
                local_dir=local_dir,
            )
        for referrer, dep_path, candidates in requested:
            if not any(os.path.exists(dep_local_path) for _, dep_local_path in candidates):
                patterns = [p.replace(os.sep, "/") for p, _ in candidates if not os.path.isabs(p)]
                _warn_dependency_not_delivered(repo_id, local_dir, referrer, dep_path, patterns)

        next_layer: list[str] = []
        for p in already_local:
            if p not in checked_files:
                checked_files.add(p)
                next_layer.append(p)
        for p in unique_local_paths:
            if p not in checked_files and os.path.exists(p):
                checked_files.add(p)
                next_layer.append(p)
        current_layer = next_layer

    return matched_file_path

def sample_data_path(task: str, filename: str) -> str:
    """Resolve one of ``task``'s sample files, fetching it from HuggingFace on first use.

    The one way in to the shared example-data repo, so a checkout and an installed wheel
    behave identically. The task name *is* the directory holding that task's files, which
    stops a task widening its fetch to another's.

    Parameters
    ----------
    task : str
        Registered task name, and the directory holding that task's files in the repo.
    filename : str
        File to resolve, relative to that directory. Only this one file is downloaded.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Local path to the file.
    """
    return get_asset_path(
        f"{task}/{filename}",
        registry=SAMPLE_DATA_REGISTRY,
        dataset=SAMPLE_DATA_REPO,
        # A directory of its own rather than the asset root (the default): tasks write beside their
        # clip — contrack caches the exported object mesh in a ``.cache/`` there. It must also be
        # stable, not a HuggingFace snapshot dir whose name tracks the revision, or those caches
        # cold-start every run.
        local_dir=get_cache_dir(SAMPLE_DATA_REPO),
    )

    else:
        return candidates[-1][1]

Resolve a --resume reference to a run directory under runs_root.

runs_root is a task's run root (logs/<task>); each child is a run directory named <timestamp>[-<run_name>]-<id>. ref selects one of them:

  • "latest" — the most recently modified run directory;
  • an exact run id — the trailing -<id> segment of a run's basename;
  • a substring — matched against the whole basename (e.g. part of a run_name).

Fails loud, listing the available runs, when nothing matches or a substring is ambiguous, so a typo never silently resumes the wrong run. This is the run-directory analogue of :func:find_latest_checkpoint (which selects a checkpoint within one run); callers chain the two: find_latest_checkpoint(resolve_run_dir(root, ref)).

def resolve_run_dir(runs_root: str, ref: str) -> str:
    """Resolve a ``--resume`` reference to a run directory under ``runs_root``.

    ``runs_root`` is a task's run root (``logs/<task>``); each child is a run directory
    named ``<timestamp>[-<run_name>]-<id>``. ``ref`` selects one of them:

    - ``"latest"`` — the most recently modified run directory;
    - an exact run id — the trailing ``-<id>`` segment of a run's basename;
    - a substring — matched against the whole basename (e.g. part of a run_name).

    Fails loud, listing the available runs, when nothing matches or a substring is
    ambiguous, so a typo never silently resumes the wrong run. This is the run-directory
    analogue of :func:`find_latest_checkpoint` (which selects a checkpoint *within* one
    run); callers chain the two: ``find_latest_checkpoint(resolve_run_dir(root, ref))``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    runs_root : str
        The task's run root, e.g. ``logs/<task>``.
    ref : str
        ``"latest"``, an exact run id, or a basename substring.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Path (joined onto ``runs_root``) of the resolved run directory.

    Raises
    ------
    FileNotFoundError
        If ``runs_root`` has no run directories, or ``ref`` matches none.
    ValueError
        If ``ref`` is a substring matching more than one run.
    """
    if not os.path.isdir(runs_root):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No runs directory {runs_root!r} to resume from — train the task first.")
    run_dirs = sorted(d for d in os.listdir(runs_root) if os.path.isdir(os.path.join(runs_root, d)))
    if not run_dirs:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No runs under {runs_root!r} to resume from — train the task first.")

    def _full(name: str) -> str:
        return os.path.join(runs_root, name)

    if ref == "latest":
        # Not max(run_dirs): the "%y%b%dT..." timestamp prefix (Aug/Sep/...) does not sort
        # chronologically as a string, so pick the most recently written run by mtime.
        return _full(max(run_dirs, key=lambda d: os.path.getmtime(_full(d))))

    # Exact run-id match (the trailing base-36 segment); ids are unique, so 0 or 1 hit.
    id_matches = [d for d in run_dirs if d.rsplit("-", 1)[-1] == ref]
    if id_matches:
        return _full(id_matches[0])

    sub_matches = [d for d in run_dirs if ref in d]
    if len(sub_matches) == 1:
        return _full(sub_matches[0])
    if len(sub_matches) > 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"--resume {ref!r} is ambiguous under {runs_root!r}; it matches "
            + ", ".join(sub_matches)
            + ". Use 'latest', a full run id, or a longer substring."
        )
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"--resume {ref!r} matched no run under {runs_root!r}. Available runs: " + ", ".join(run_dirs)
    )

def load_text(filepath: str) -> dict:
    try:
        if filepath.endswith(".yaml") or filepath.endswith(".yml"):
            with open(filepath, "r") as f:
                return yaml.safe_load(f)
        elif filepath.endswith(".json"):
            with open(filepath, "r") as f:
                return json.load(f)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported file type: {filepath}")
    except OSError as e:
        # Provide a clearer error message while preserving the original exception context.
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Unable to open file '{filepath}': {e}") from e

docs.title: Kinematics-only robot envs
docs.text:
Genesis runtime helpers — transient kinematics envs for preprocessing.

Shared infrastructure for any Eden preprocessing code that needs to spin up a Genesis scene just to run forward kinematics or query a Jacobian, without the full training-loop machinery. Callers include:

  • :meth:eden.datasets.base.DatasetBase._forward_velocity_kinematics — fills in per-link velocity fields after dataset prepare.
  • :class:eden.datasets.modifiers.smooth_start_end.SmoothStartTransition — builds a single-env scene for the smooth-start IK.
  • :class:eden.datasets.modifiers.ground.GroundFirstFrame — FK of each clip's first frame to put the robot on the floor.
  • :class:eden.extensions.teleop.sonic.g1_fk.G1KeyFrameFk — a scene held open for the process's FK queries.

docs.title: transient_robot_env
docs.text:
transient_robot_env(robot_options: 'EntityOptions', *, num_envs: int = 1, sim_dt: float = 0.005) -> 'Iterator[tuple[EnvBase, RigidEntity]]'

Yield (env, robot) for a single-shot kinematics scene.

Destroys the env on exit. Use for preprocessing code that needs FK / Jacobian queries but doesn't run physics simulation.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION robot_options

Eden RobotOptions (or any EntityOptions) for the robot to spawn.

TYPE: 'EntityOptions'

num_envs

Scene env count. Most preprocessing wants 1; _forward_velocity_kinematics uses len(motion_seq.buffer_length) to vectorise over clips.

TYPE: int DEFAULT: 1

sim_dt

Doesn't affect kinematics queries, only matters for the constraint solver warmup. Set to the clip's dt when relevant, otherwise leave at the small default.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 0.005

Wall

compile

compile

Source code in eden/utils/genesis_runtime.py 
@contextmanager
def transient_robot_env(
    robot_options: "EntityOptions",
    *,
    num_envs: int = 1,
    sim_dt: float = 0.005,
) -> "Iterator[tuple[EnvBase, RigidEntity]]":
    """Yield ``(env, robot)`` for a single-shot kinematics scene.

    Destroys the env on exit. Use for preprocessing code that needs FK /
    Jacobian queries but doesn't run physics simulation.

    Parameters
    ----------
    robot_options:
        Eden ``RobotOptions`` (or any ``EntityOptions``) for the robot to
        spawn.
    num_envs:
        Scene env count. Most preprocessing wants 1; ``_forward_velocity_kinematics``
        uses ``len(motion_seq.buffer_length)`` to vectorise over clips.
    sim_dt:
        Doesn't affect kinematics queries, only matters for the constraint
        solver warmup. Set to the clip's dt when relevant, otherwise leave
        at the small default.

    Wall time: ~5–30 s on first call per Python process due to the Quadrants kernel
    compile; subsequent invocations within the same process reuse the
    compile cache.
    """
    _ensure_genesis_initialized()

    # Imports here (not at module scope) because ``EnvBase`` pulls in heavy
    # Genesis machinery — this helper should be cheap to ``from … import``
    # without paying the cost when the consumer doesn't actually need a
    # scene.
    from eden.envs.base import EnvBase
    from eden.options import EnvOptions, SceneOptions

    env = EnvBase(
        env_options=EnvOptions(num_envs=num_envs, sim_dt=sim_dt),
        scene_options=SceneOptions(robot=robot_options),
    )
    env.build()
    try:
        yield env, env.entities["robot"]
    finally:
        env.destroy()

docs.title: clear_rigid_query_caches
docs.text:
clear_rigid_query_caches(rigid_solver) -> None

Drop the rigid solver's per-step query caches, so the next query of the step is answered afresh.

The part of Genesis' RigidSolver._restart that Eden needs, and only that part: _restart also re-arms every drone's once-per-step propeller guard, which a mid-step call must not do. Genesis exposes no public call for this, so the cache attributes are named here, in one place, and a Genesis that renamed one raises rather than leaving a cache that would be served stale.

Source code in eden/utils/genesis_runtime.py 
def clear_rigid_query_caches(rigid_solver) -> None:
    """Drop the rigid solver's per-step query caches, so the next query of the step is answered afresh.

    The part of Genesis' ``RigidSolver._restart`` that Eden needs, and only that part: ``_restart`` also re-arms
    every drone's once-per-step propeller guard, which a mid-step call must not do. Genesis exposes no public
    call for this, so the cache attributes are named here, in one place, and a Genesis that renamed one raises
    rather than leaving a cache that would be served stale.
    """
    for owner_name, cache_name in _RIGID_QUERY_CACHES:
        owner = getattr(rigid_solver, owner_name, None)
        if owner is None:  # a solver with nothing of this kind built (no collider in an all-Mochi scene, say)
            continue
        cache = getattr(owner, cache_name, None)
        if not isinstance(cache, dict):
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Genesis' {type(owner).__name__} has no per-step query cache '{cache_name}' (a dict) any more, "
                f"so eden.utils.genesis_runtime.clear_rigid_query_caches cannot drop it: this Genesis renamed or "
                "restructured it. Update _RIGID_QUERY_CACHES to the new attribute (see RigidSolver._restart in "
                "Genesis); skipping the clear would serve a cached query stale."
            )
        cache.clear()

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Bug reports, fixes, new tasks, terms, robots and documentation are all welcome. This page covers setting up a development checkout, the lint and test commands, how to title and describe a pull request, and where each kind of change lives. Every change also follows the rules in AGENTS.md at the repository root. It is short, and it is what coding agents read first, so read it before your first pull request.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
Eden needs Python 3.12 or 3.13 (requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.14") and uv. Linux with an NVIDIA GPU is the primary platform.

git clone https://github.com/embodied-ai-nexus/Eden.git
cd Eden
uv sync                    # the core dependencies plus the dev group (ruff, pre-commit, pytest)
uv run pre-commit install  # run the hooks on every commit

Add the extras your change touches with --inexact, for example uv sync --inexact --extra vis --extra docs. Without --inexact, uv sync installs exactly what you name and removes every extra you installed earlier, so a later bare uv sync strips them too. For everything at once, run uv sync --all-extras --all-groups: some extras need a package that is not on PyPI, and it lives in a <extra>-git dependency group (uv sync --inexact --extra flashsac --group flashsac-git). The installation page lists the extras.

Run everything through uv run (or the checkout's .venv/bin/python), which keeps the environment in step with uv.lock:

uv run eden list                                       # the CLI
uv run python examples/<path>/<script>.py              # a script
uv run pytest tests/managers/test_reward_manager.py    # one test file
uv run pre-commit run --files <changed files>          # lint and format what you touched
Working in several git worktrees

If you keep one git worktree per branch, give each worktree its own virtual environment (env -u VIRTUAL_ENV uv sync inside it). Eden is installed in editable mode, so a shared environment imports eden from whichever checkout synced it last. Two things lead there by accident: uv run --active (or a VIRTUAL_ENV left over from another checkout), which also rewrites that environment's editable finder to point at the current worktree; and uv pip install without --python .venv/bin/python, which installs into whatever VIRTUAL_ENV names. Check with .venv/bin/python -c "import eden; print(eden.__file__)".

docs.title: Lint and format
docs.text:
.pre-commit-config.yaml runs four hooks: ruff-check and ruff-format (ruff 0.14.11), yamlfmt for YAML files and toml-sort-fix for TOML files. CI runs the same hooks on every file (uvx pre-commit run --all-files), so a pull request that skips them fails the lint job.

Ruff is configured in pyproject.toml:

  • the line length is 120;
  • on top of ruff's default rules it enables pydocstyle (D) with the NumPy convention, so every package needs a docstring in its __init__.py (D104), and any docstring you write must be valid NumPy style and document all of its parameters (D417). Modules, classes, methods and functions are not required to have one (D100-D103 are ignored), though most modules carry one.

Code conventions that ruff cannot check are in AGENTS.md: absolute imports outside __init__.py, Eden imported before genesis and torch, geometry through eden.utils.geom rather than re-implemented at the call site, quaternions in wxyz order, and failing fast with an error message that says how to fix the problem.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
tests/ mirrors eden/: the tests of eden/utils/geom.py live in tests/utils/test_geom.py. Tests are Detroit style: they build real options, managers, entities and envs, and use test doubles only at hardware, network and clock boundaries. Testing covers the layout, what to assert, and how to keep the cost of scene builds down.

Run the test files your change touches, one file at a time. The full suite builds many Genesis scenes and takes a long time.

Some checked-in files are generated, and a test fails when one drifts from the code. If you add, rename or re-parameterize a term, regenerate the term catalog:

uv run python -m eden.managers.catalog          # rewrites docs/api/terms/catalog.md and eden/resources/term_catalog.md
uv run python -m eden.managers.catalog --check  # exits 1 if either page is stale

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
• Branch from main, open the pull request against main, and keep one change per pull request.

  • Tag the title with one or more of the tags the history uses, then a scope and a summary, for example [BUG FIX] tasks registry: override=True keeps the shadowed task's mods.

    Tag For [FEATURE] a new capability [BUG FIX] a fix to wrong behaviour [BREAKING] a change to a public API, a config field, a CLI flag or a checkpoint layout; add it next to the main tag [PERF] a measured speedup; put the numbers in the description [REFACTOR] restructuring with no change in behaviour [TEST] tests only, or next to the main tag when the pull request also adds tests [DOCS] documentation [EXAMPLES] changes under examples/ [MISC] dependency pins, tooling, anything else

  • Fill in the pull request template: describe the change and why it is needed, link the issue it resolves, and say how you tested it, with the exact commands.

  • A misconfiguration must fail at the earliest well-defined point (Pydantic validation, a term's configure() or build()) with a message that names the bad value and what is accepted. Do not let it fail on the first step(), and do not fall back silently to a default. Error Messages says what such a message must contain.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
You are changing Where it goes Read first A task eden/tasks/<package>/config.py, a config class registered with @TASK_REGISTRY.register() Task configuration, your first task A task variant a TaskMod registered with the task TaskMods A reusable term eden/managers/terms/<kind>/, registered with @<KIND>_TERM_REGISTRY.register() Terms A term only one task uses the task's own package (eden/tasks/<package>/custom_terms/ or its config.py), registered the same way Terms A robot eden/options/robots/<robot>.py, a RobotOptions subclass registered with @ROBOT_REGISTRY.register() Robots A sensor or solver Genesis does not ship eden/engine/ Engine addons A custom RL algorithm eden/learning/wrappers/<library>/<algorithm>/, never examples/ Training runs A frozen policy eden/extensions/policies/<name>/ Extending policies A deployment backend eden/extensions/deployment/ Deployment A CLI subcommand a handler in eden/utils/cli/<area>.py plus an entry in COMMANDS in eden/__main__.py CLI internals A runnable example examples/ examples/AGENTS.md, examples Documentation docs/ Writing the docs

Tasks, terms and robots register themselves where they are defined; there is no central index to update. A term is looked up by its registry key, which is always its snake-cased class or function name, so a term class you write must be registered to be found.

docs.title: Reporting bugs
docs.text:
Open bugs and feature requests with the issue templates. Include the exact command, the full traceback, and the output of:

uv run python -c "import eden, genesis, torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"

docs.title: Writing the Docs
docs.text: This page is for anyone editing Eden's documentation: how to build and preview the site, which pages are generated or checked by tests, the style the pages follow, and how the site is published.

docs.title: Build and preview
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs Material and mkdocstrings from mkdocs.yml at the repository root. Install the docs extra and serve the site locally:

uv sync --inexact --extra docs
uv run mkdocs serve        # live-reloading preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000/Eden/
uv run mkdocs build --strict   # a one-off build into site/, as CI runs it

mkdocstrings reads the package source with griffe, which does not import it, so the build needs only the docs extra's packages: CI installs just those, without torch or Genesis, at the versions pinned in .github/actions/docs-toolchain/constraints.txt. In a development checkout, the uv sync above adds them to the environment you already have. --strict fails the build on any warning: a link to a page or anchor that does not exist, or a page missing from nav:. The one exception is griffe's docstring and signature warnings, which the tree still carries by the thousand: docs/hooks/griffe_warnings.py lowers them to DEBUG and prints how many there were. Their number may not grow: a build with more than the hook's MAX_GRIFFE_WARNINGS fails. uv run mkdocs build -v shows them, so you can find the ones your change added. When you fix some, lower the ceiling in the same change. The count depends on the griffe version, so a local build with other versions than CI's pins can differ; bump the pins and the ceiling together.

docs.title: Where pages live
docs.text:
Directory Contents docs/getting-started/ installation, quickstart, concepts, the first-task tutorial, assets, troubleshooting docs/guides/ one guide per subsystem; AGENTS.md cites these as the authoritative prose docs/tasks/ the task suites docs/api/ the API reference: short intros around ::: blocks docs/reference/ the CLI and environment-variable references docs/contributing/ this section docs/assets/ images, videos and stylesheets

The navigation is the nav: tree in mkdocs.yml; a new page needs an entry there.

docs.title: Generated and test-pinned content
docs.text:
Some pages, or parts of them, are produced from the code or parsed by tests. Edit them the way the table says, or a test fails.

Content Rule Checked by docs/api/terms/catalog.md Generated. Never edit it by hand: run uv run python -m eden.managers.catalog after adding, renaming or re-parameterizing a term. It also rewrites eden/resources/term_catalog.md, the index that ships in the wheel. eden terms --markdown prints the same page. tests/resources/test_term_catalog.py The <!-- step-order-table --> block and the manager-order rows of docs/guides/environments.md Parsed and compared with the env classes; keep the columns and their formatting. tests/envs/test_base.py The inherited_members: [...] lists in docs/api/managers.md Each must name every field the term kind's mixin declares. tests/managers/test_base.py Every install command in docs/**/*.md pip install 'eden-world[<extra>]', never eden[<extra>]; only extras declared in pyproject.toml; never pip for an extra in UV_ONLY_EXTRAS; every uv sync that names an extra or group needs --inexact, and an extra that has a -git group needs that group too. tests/test_pyproject.py

Code and tests also cite guide paths and sections (docs/guides/testing.md, docs/guides/error-messages.md, the "Task Package Layout" section of docs/guides/task-config.md, and others). Before you rename or move a guide, grep the repository for its path.

docs.title: API pages
docs.text:
An API page is a short introduction followed by mkdocstrings blocks:

::: eden.managers.terms.rewards.locomotion
    options:
      show_root_heading: false

The handler's defaults are in mkdocs.yml (NumPy docstrings, private names and Pydantic's model_* methods filtered out, members in source order). The options used most on these pages are show_root_heading: false to render a module's members without a heading for the module itself, members: [...] to pick members, and show_bases: true with inherited_members: false for a subclass that should not repeat its base class.

Every ::: path must resolve. Griffe, the library mkdocstrings uses (installed with the docs extra), loads the source statically, so you can check a path without importing Eden:

uv run python -c "import griffe; griffe.load('eden.envs.base', search_paths=['.'])['EnvBase']"

A directory without an __init__.py is invisible to that loader under its eden. path: eden/envs/wrappers/, eden/utils/motion_reference/, eden/utils/buffers/, eden/options/objects/ and a few others. Name their classes in prose instead of using :::, or give the directory an __init__.py with a docstring. Render each object on one page only; a second ::: for the same object gives it two anchors.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Write plainly and directly, in the second person and the present tense. Leave out marketing words. Prefer a longer sentence a newcomer can read once over a compressed one they have to decode.
  • Open each page with # Title and one to three sentences saying what it covers and who needs it. Use ## and ### sections, and end with a short ## See also list where it helps.
  • Lead with the common case and a working example; put edge cases and internals further down.
  • Put code identifiers in backticks. Link the first mention of a major class to its API page. Link between pages with relative .md paths, never with absolute URLs to the published site.
  • Use admonitions for gotchas (!!! warning, !!! note, !!! tip), collapsible ??? note "..." blocks for long asides, content tabs (=== "uv" / === "pip") where two variants matter, and Mermaid diagrams only where a picture explains a flow better than prose.
  • Use tables only for facts that are really tabular, and only with values you checked.
  • Check every class name, import path, field, default, command and flag against the source or --help before you write it. Write commands as eden <command> .... Snippets use absolute imports and wxyz quaternions; prefer an excerpt of real code from eden/tasks/ or examples/, with its path, to an invented example.
  • Use only numbers that are in the repository (the README, code comments, tests), and say where they come from.
  • Do not reference issue or pull-request numbers, private repositories, people or internal hosts: they mean nothing to a reader of the public site.
  • Reuse media under docs/assets/ (from a page in docs/guides/, ../assets/readme/<file>.webp).

pymdownx.snippets can include a file into a page with --8<-- "<path>", relative to the repository root; a missing path fails the build.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
The site is published to GitHub Pages at https://embodied-ai-nexus.github.io/Eden from a branch named docs of embodied-ai-nexus/Eden:

  1. Every push to main that touches docs/, mkdocs.yml, eden/ or the workflow itself runs .github/workflows/docs.yml. You can also start it by hand from the Actions tab (Docs → Run workflow). Only embodied-ai-nexus/Eden publishes; in a fork the job is skipped.
  2. The workflow installs the docs extra and runs mkdocs gh-deploy --strict --force --remote-branch docs, which builds the site and force-pushes the HTML to docs as a single commit. A build that warns is not published: the site stays on the last good build, and GitHub reports the failed run to whoever pushed.
  3. GitHub Pages serves that branch. To set it up once, open the repository's Settings → Pages, choose Deploy from a branch as the source, and select the docs branch and the / (root) folder.

The docs branch holds only generated HTML; never edit it by hand. Pull requests do not publish: the docs job in .github/workflows/ci.yml runs the same mkdocs build --strict without deploying.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The examples/ directory of the repository holds runnable scripts for most of Eden's features, from complete trainable projects to one-concept recipes. This page explains how they are organized, how to find and run one, and lists them all. The scripts are in the repository only, so you need a clone; a PyPI install does not include them.

docs.title: Three tiers
docs.text:
Tier Where What it is Projects examples/projects/<area>/ End-to-end task templates that build an environment, train and evaluate. Fork one to start a real task. Policies examples/policies/<name>/ Run a published, pretrained policy in simulation; most can also run it on hardware. Recipes examples/recipes/<capability>/ Short scripts that each show one capability: a sensor, a solver, a teleop device, a term.

A registered task trains with eden train --task <name>, so a project script only adds what eden train and eden inference do not: an interactive viewer, keyboard control, recordings, data preparation. The published policies also run without a script, through eden inference --policy <name> and eden deploy --policy <name> (Policy zoo).

docs.title: Finding an example
docs.text:
Every runnable example carries a small metadata block in its module docstring: its tier, its capabilities, the hardware it needs, any optional dependencies, and the command that runs it. eden examples list reads those blocks without importing the scripts:

eden examples list                              # every example
eden examples list --tier recipe                # one tier
eden examples list --capability sensor          # a capability namespace...
eden examples list --capability sensor.lidar    # ...or one capability
eden examples list --hardware cpu               # what runs without a GPU
eden examples list --search splat               # substring search over key, purpose and capabilities
eden examples list --json                       # machine-readable records

The hardware values are cpu, gpu, gpu-fp64 (a GPU and double precision, en.init(precision="64")) and real-robot. Capabilities are namespace.leaf tags in a fixed set of namespaces: solver, sensor, robot, teleop, dataset, pose, retarget, term, render, planning, task, scene, deploy, collision, terrain and rl.

docs.title: Running an example
docs.text:
Run an example with the command in its metadata (run:), which eden examples list --json prints, from the repository root:

uv run python examples/recipes/sensors/sensors_lidar_go2.py -v
uv run python examples/projects/reaching/reacher.py train

The examples share one set of short flags, and each letter means the same thing in every script:

Short Long Meaning -v --vis Open the viewer -c --cpu Run on the CPU (examples default to the GPU) -b --num-envs Number of parallel environments -s --steps Number of steps or iterations -t --seconds Simulated seconds -e --exp-name Experiment name -r --record Record a video -o --output-dir / --output Where the script writes its output -d --debug-vis Draw debug visualizations

A script whose whole point is its viewer takes --no-vis instead of -v. Each script's --help, docstring or README gives its other flags.

docs.title: Smoke-running
docs.text:
eden examples smoke runs one example headless for a few steps, with EDEN_SMOKE=1, which shortens the example's horizon:

eden examples smoke recipes/physics/mpm_tutorial
eden examples smoke recipes/physics/mpm_tutorial --timeout 300

It refuses, with exit code 2 and the reason, an example that needs real hardware, a teleoperation device, a missing optional dependency (the reason includes how to install it), or a GPU the machine lacks, and one that is not instrumented for smoke mode or whose canonical command needs arguments. To smoke-test a registered task rather than an example, use eden smoke --task <name>.

docs.title: Optional dependencies
docs.text: Some examples need a package that is not part of Eden's core install. The metadata names them, and eden examples list --json shows them as optional_deps; the most common are onnx (most published policies), nyx, viser, gello, metaquest, pico, wuji, sb3, skrl, graspgen and graspgenx, which are Eden extras (Installation), and libuipc, curobo, ompl, spacemouse and metamotivo, which are installed separately. eden examples smoke prints the install command for a missing one.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Example What it does Run projects/reaching/reacher Train and evaluate the reacher task on a Yam arm with rsl_rl uv run python examples/projects/reaching/reacher.py train projects/locomotion/move_forward Train and evaluate move_forward, with the robot, controller and runner picked on the command line uv run python examples/projects/locomotion/move_forward.py --task move_forward projects/locomotion/velocity_tracking/main Velocity-tracking training and interactive play for humanoids (G1 29-DOF, LimX Oli) uv run python examples/projects/locomotion/velocity_tracking/main.py train projects/locomotion/mujoco_playground/getup/main Train and evaluate a Go1 get-up policy uv run python examples/projects/locomotion/mujoco_playground/getup/main.py train projects/locomotion/mujoco_playground/handstand/main Train and evaluate a Go1 handstand policy uv run python examples/projects/locomotion/mujoco_playground/handstand/main.py train projects/locomotion/extreme_parkour/main Extreme-parkour playback on a Go2 (teacher, or the distilled depth student) uv run python examples/projects/locomotion/extreme_parkour/main.py play projects/locomotion/husky_skate/main Play a trained HUSKY skateboarding policy (G1 23-DOF and a skateboard) uv run python examples/projects/locomotion/husky_skate/main.py play --steps 50 projects/manipulation/main Train and run inference for the manipulation tasks uv run python examples/projects/manipulation/main.py train --task manipulation_reach_droid projects/manipulation/piano/main Train two Wuji Hand 2 hands to play the piano, then watch and hear them uv run python examples/projects/manipulation/piano/main.py train --song twinkle_twinkle projects/manipulation/polaris/main Keyboard-teleoperate a DROID arm across the PolaRiS Gaussian-splat scenes uv run python examples/projects/manipulation/polaris/main.py --task polaris_block_stack_kitchen projects/manipulation/simpler/main Keyboard-teleoperate a WidowX-250 across the SIMPLER Bridge tasks uv run python examples/projects/manipulation/simpler/main.py --vis projects/mimic/beyondmimic/main BeyondMimic motion imitation uv run python examples/projects/mimic/beyondmimic/main.py train projects/mimic/mimic_beyondmimic/main BeyondMimic on MimicRLEnvBase uv run python examples/projects/mimic/mimic_beyondmimic/main.py train projects/mimic/general_mimic/main General-mimic inference, with a ghost overlay of the reference uv run python examples/projects/mimic/general_mimic/main.py inference --model /path/to/general_mimic.pt projects/mimic/assistmimic/main AssistMimic: a caregiver humanoid helps a weakened one up (SMPL humanoids) uv run python examples/projects/mimic/assistmimic/main.py train projects/mimic/contrack/render Render a trained ConTrack checkpoint to a video see its docstring projects/sysid/xhand1/collect_data, identify, verify System identification of an XHand1: collect real trajectories, identify DOF parameters, verify them see examples/projects/sysid/xhand1/

The BeyondMimic, AssistMimic and TWIST2 directories also hold data-preparation scripts under scripts/ (CSV or PKL to Eden's .npz motion format, replaying a converted clip). Several projects have a README next to the script.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
Each script builds an environment from the policy's own specification and rolls it out in simulation. See the policy zoo for what each policy is and needs.

Example Policy Needs policies/amo/main AMO whole-body G1 control, with live keyboard commands policies/beyondmimic_moves/main Any of the BeyondMimic G1-Moves motion-tracking policies (--clip) policies/gmt/main GMT general motion tracking on a G1 policies/holosoma/main Holosoma velocity-command locomotion on a G1 onnx policies/homie/main, keyboard_teleop HOMIE walk/stand tracker on a G1, with keyboard teleoperation (simulation or real G1) policies/humanoid_gpt/main Humanoid-GPT motion tracker on a kinematic reference; analyze_record reads an eden deploy --debug_record file onnx policies/husky/main HUSKY skateboarding on a G1 onnx, GPU policies/metamotivo/main MetaMotivo (FB-CPR) on Eden's SMPL humanoid metamotivo policies/omnireset/main UWLab's OmniReset peg-insertion expert, measuring its success rate GPU policies/omnixtreme/main OmniXtreme motion tracking on a G1 onnx policies/policy_switch/main Hot-swap between Holosoma locomotion and SONIC tracking on one G1 onnx policies/protomotionv3/main ProtoMotions v3 motion tracker on a kinematic reference policies/simtoolreal/main Sim-to-sim check of the SimToolReal policy port policies/sonic/main GEAR-SONIC universal-token policy on a kinematic reference onnx policies/twist2/main TWIST2 motion tracking on an Eden .npz motion (scripts/pkl_to_npz converts its data) onnx

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Recipes are grouped by the capability they show. eden examples list --tier recipe prints each one's purpose.

docs.title: Physics recipes
docs.text:
examples/recipes/physics/ ports the examples of the Genesis physics catalogue (all but Stable Fluid: smoke) to Eden's options. Each script builds an EnvBase from EnvOptions and SceneOptions and steps it. The material on an entity picks its solver, and coupling with rigid bodies is enabled per entity. Run any of them with -v to open the viewer:

uv run python examples/recipes/physics/mpm_tutorial.py -v
Genesis example Eden script Solvers Rigid: franka cube rigid_franka_cube.py Rigid Rigid: collision tower rigid_collision_tower.py Rigid Rigid: contype rigid_contype.py Rigid FEM: hard and soft constraint fem_hard_soft_constraint.py FEM MPM: tutorial mpm_tutorial.py MPM MPM: sand wheel mpm_sand_wheel.py MPM + rigid SPH: rigid sph_rigid.py SPH + rigid SPH + MPM sph_mpm.py SPH + MPM PBD: liquid pbd_liquid.py PBD PBD: cloth pbd_cloth.py PBD IPC: robot cloth teleop ipc_robot_cloth_teleop.py IPC + FEM + rigid Coupler: cloth on rigid coupler_cloth_on_rigid.py PBD + rigid Coupler: rigid + MPM coupler_rigid_mpm.py MPM + rigid Coupler: cut dragon coupler_cut_dragon.py MPM + rigid Coupler: water wheel coupler_water_wheel.py SPH or MPM + rigid Coupler: flush cubes coupler_flush_cubes.py MPM SAP: franka grasp rigid cube sap_franka_grasp_cube.py SAP + rigid

Beyond the catalogue: ipc_objects_falling.py, ipc_robot_grasp_cube.py, and coupler_cut_dragon_teleop.py, a keyboard-teleoperated version of the cut dragon.

Most of these need the GPU backend; the metadata's hardware tag says which. The SAP grasp also needs double precision (en.init(precision="64")), and the IPC scripts need the libuipc bindings. Genesis' particle emitters have no Eden wrapper yet, so the sand, water-wheel and flush-cubes scripts call env.scene.add_emitter(...) directly. examples/recipes/physics/README.md has per-script notes.

docs.title: Writing an example
docs.text:
examples/AGENTS.md in the repository is the contract for adding one: the metadata block and its closed vocabularies, the flag convention, how to make a script smoke-runnable, and the tests that check all three (tests/utils/test_examples_catalog.py, tests/utils/test_example_flags.py). Two rules matter most:

  • Construct a registered task with TASK_REGISTRY.build(name), never TASK_REGISTRY.get(name)() or the bare config class, which skip the task's mods.
  • Shorten the horizon in smoke mode: horizon = 5 if en.is_smoke() else 1000.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
New to Eden? These pages take you from an empty machine to a policy you trained and a task you wrote yourself. Read them in order the first time; each one ends by pointing at the next.

Once you are past these pages, the command reference lists every eden command, and the examples hold runnable scripts for most features.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Install eden-world from PyPI or from a clone with uv, choose optional extras, and check that it works.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: GPU and driver problems, uv sync pitfalls, asset downloads, headless rendering and other common errors.

docs.title: Assets and the download cache
docs.text: Eden ships code, not meshes. Robot models, objects, scenes, published policy checkpoints and motion datasets are downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub the first time something needs them, and read from disk after that. This page says where those files go, how to move them, how to run without network access, and how to fetch everything in advance for a cluster.

docs.title: Where files go
docs.text:
What Where, by default Moved by Robots, objects, scenes, splat scans, benchmark-suite assets, published policy checkpoints, MuJoCo models for eden deploy --mujoco ~/.cache/eden/assets/ EDEN_ASSETS_DIR Motion datasets (eden.datasets: AMASS, LAFAN1, PHUMA, Weave, ...) the Hugging Face cache, ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/ HF_HOME, or the dataset's raw_data_path Per-task sample clips, processed motion caches, generated meshes and other files Eden writes ~/.cache/eden/ XDG_CACHE_HOME Genesis' compiled kernels ~/.cache/quadrants/ (Genesis)

~/.cache is $XDG_CACHE_HOME when that variable is set. The asset root is shared by every virtual environment and reinstall of Eden on the machine, and needs no root access to write.

To print the asset root of the Eden you are running:

python -c "from eden.utils.misc import get_assets_dir; print(get_assets_dir())"

Assets are fetched file by file, not as whole repositories. A robot's URDF or MJCF file comes first, then the meshes, materials and textures it references, so the cache holds only what the tasks you built actually used. Families of objects keep their files in a subdirectory of the asset root: YCB objects in ycb/, LIBERO in libero/, robosuite in robosuite/, published policies in policies/, and so on.

Deleting ~/.cache/quadrants/ is safe: nothing in it is downloaded, but the next run compiles its kernels again.

docs.title: Moving the asset root
docs.text:
Set EDEN_ASSETS_DIR to an absolute path to put every asset somewhere else, for example on a larger disk:

export EDEN_ASSETS_DIR=/data/eden_assets

It is read every time a path is resolved, so it applies to everything the process downloads after you set it, and to every entity whose local_dir is unset. A relative path raises a ValueError that prints the absolute path to export instead, because a relative one would point somewhere different whenever the working directory changed.

An entity's local_dir option, when set, overrides the root for that entity alone. EDEN_ASSETS_DIR does not move an explicit local_dir, and a config saved on another machine carries that machine's explicit paths; leave local_dir unset unless you mean to pin a location.

If the asset root cannot be written, the first download fails with a PermissionError that names the directory and says whether EDEN_ASSETS_DIR chose it. A read-only cache that already holds every file keeps working.

docs.title: Which Hub repositories Eden reads
docs.text:
All of them are dataset repositories. The repository an entity reads from is its registry and dataset options (<registry>/<dataset>), so you can point any entity at a mirror. The defaults:

Repository Holds Read by Kashu7100/eden_assets robots, grippers, hands, scene assets, splat scans robot and most object options (eden/options/entities.py) Kashu7100/eden_policies published policy checkpoints eden inference --policy and eden deploy --policy (eden/extensions/policies/) Kashu7100/eden_example small per-task sample files tasks with a default sample clip Kashu7100/mujoco_menagerie MuJoCo Menagerie and vendor MJCF models eden deploy --mujoco --menagerie Kashu7100/eden_libero, eden_robosuite, eden_simpler, eden_polaris, eden_robocasa, eden_robocasa365, eden_lbm_eval, eden_robolab, eden_calvin benchmark-suite scenes and objects eden/options/objects/ and the matching tasks Kashu7100/eden_ycb, eden_objaverse, eden_dextoolbench, eden_arctic, eden_omomo_holosoma object meshes eden/options/objects/ Kashu7100/eden_art reference pictures for the painting tasks eden/tasks/art/painting/ haosulab/ReplicaCAD ReplicaCAD scenes eden/options/objects/replica_cad.py ember-lab-berkeley/AMASS_Retargeted_for_G1, lvhaidong/LAFAN1_Retargeting_Dataset, DAVIAN-Robotics/PHUMA, bones-studio/seed, appolyn/Weave, jose-barreiros-tri/hhi-assist, exptech/g1-moves retargeted motion data eden/datasets/, the beyondmimic_moves policy UW-Lab/uwlab-assets (pinned revision) OmniReset reset states and checkpoints the omnireset tasks and policy

A failed fetch names the repository and the file in its error, so you can look the file up on the Hub directly.

docs.title: Running offline
docs.text:
Once a machine holds everything a task needs, it runs with no network access. A file that is already on disk is read without contacting the Hub. Set HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 so that a missing file fails at once, with a message naming it, instead of waiting for a network timeout:

export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
eden train --task reacher

The error for a missing file reads ... could not be fetched: the Hub repo ... cannot be reached ... Offline (HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1) or no network?. Fetch that file once on a machine with network access, then copy or share the cache as described below.

docs.title: Pre-fetching for a cluster
docs.text:
Compute nodes often have no internet access, or a home directory with a small quota that each node sees separately. Fetch on a machine with network access (a login node) into storage every node mounts:

  1. Put the caches on shared storage. Point the asset root and the Hugging Face cache at a shared path, and the Eden cache too if you use motion datasets or sample clips:

    export EDEN_ASSETS_DIR=/shared/$USER/eden_assets
export HF_HOME=/shared/$USER/huggingface
export XDG_CACHE_HOME=/shared/$USER/cache

  2. Build every task you will run, once. Building a task fetches every file it uses, and a CPU build with one environment is enough:

    eden smoke --task velocity_tracking_flat --cpu --num_envs 1
eden smoke --task robosuite_lift --cpu --num_envs 1

    Pass the same variant flags the job will use (--robot, --task_name, ...), because they can change which assets load. For a published policy, roll it out for one step the same way: eden inference --policy <name> --cpu --steps 1.

  3. Run the job offline. Export the same variables in the job script, plus HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1.

Several processes, such as the ranks of a multi-GPU run, can share one cache safely: huggingface_hub locks each file while it downloads, so one process fetches it and the others wait for the finished file.

To mirror a whole repository instead, use the hf command that comes with huggingface_hub. Asset repositories are large, so prefer step 2 unless you need everything:

hf download Kashu7100/eden_assets --repo-type dataset --local-dir "$EDEN_ASSETS_DIR"

docs.title: When a download fails
docs.text:
The error names the file and the repository. The common cases:

  • ... the Hub repo ... cannot be reached ...: the machine cannot reach the Hub, or HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 is set. Behind a proxy, export it (export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:3128). On a node without internet, pre-fetch as above. If the Hub rate-limits you (HTTP 429), log in so requests are authenticated: hf auth login.
  • Asset ... is not a file in the Hub repo ...: the path does not exist in that repository. Asset paths are full repository paths (models/eggplant/object.urdf), never a bare file name, and the message lists the repository paths that end in the name you gave.
  • A warning that a dependency was not delivered: a model references a file its repository lacks, and loads without it (a missing texture renders untextured). Report it with the warning's text. Copying the file into your cache fixes only your machine.
  • An interrupted download left a broken file: delete the file named in the error and run again, so that it is fetched again.

Troubleshooting covers the rest.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
Every Eden task is built from the same few pieces: a config that describes the task, an environment that builds it, entities that live in its scene, and managers that run the task's terms on every step. This page explains each piece and how they fit together, so that the rest of the docs read as detail on a picture you already have.

graph LR
    Config["Task config<br/>(EdenRLConfig subclass)"] -->|from_config| Env["Environment<br/>(RLEnvBase)"]
    Env --> Scene["Scene"]
    Scene --> Entities["Entities<br/>robot, objects, terrain"]
    Env --> Managers["Managers<br/>action, command, observation,<br/>reward, termination, event, ..."]
    Managers --> Terms["Terms<br/>one function or class each"]
    Terms -.->|read and write| Entities

docs.title: Configs
docs.text:
A task is a subclass of a config class whose fields are option groups: env_options (simulation settings), scene_options (what is in the scene), one *_options field per manager, and, for a trainable task, runner_options (the learning algorithm). All of them are Pydantic models. They validate when they are constructed, save to and load from JSON or YAML, and refuse unknown fields: a misspelled field name raises immediately instead of being ignored. Only the classes that hold children under names you choose, such as SceneOptions (entities) and the manager options (terms), accept extra keys.

There are three config classes you subclass, and each is built by its own environment class:

Config Environment For EdenConfig EnvBase A scene with actions and observations, no rewards EdenRLConfig RLEnvBase An RL task: adds rewards, terminations, commands, curricula and runner_options EdenMimicConfig MimicRLEnvBase Motion imitation: adds motion_options, a reference motion

The splat variants (EdenSplatConfig, EdenSplatRLConfig, EdenNyxSplatConfig) pair with environments that render Gaussian-splat scenes. A config must be built by its own environment class: RLEnvBase.from_config(mimic_config) raises a TypeError instead of building a mimic task with no motion reference. When the class is not known in advance, env_class_for_config(config) from eden.envs.base picks it.

The options a task sets are described in Task configuration, and the field-by-field reference is in the API reference.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
An environment is a batch of num_envs copies of the task, simulated in parallel. You construct it from a config and then build and reset it yourself:

import eden as en
import genesis as gs

en.init(backend=gs.gpu)

from eden.envs.base import RLEnvBase
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY

config = TASK_REGISTRY.build("reacher")
config.env_options.num_envs = 16

env = RLEnvBase.from_config(config)
env.build()
obs, info = env.reset()             # step() returns (obs, reward, terminated, timeouts, info)

Two rules apply to every script:

  • Import eden before genesis and torch. Importing eden assigns each multi-GPU rank its GPU, and that must happen before anything initializes CUDA. Multi-GPU training explains why.
  • Call en.init() once per process, before building anything. It initializes Genesis, the log directory and logging. Its backend defaults to the CPU, so pass backend=gs.gpu to simulate on the GPU.

The training wrappers (such as RslRlVecEnvWrapper from eden.envs.wrappers.rsl_rl_env) build and reset inside their own from_config, and eden train does all of this for you. Environments covers construction, stepping and resets in detail.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
Entities are the things in the scene: robots, rigid objects, terrain, and deformable bodies (MPM, SPH, PBD, FEM and Mochi). The scene option you pick is a preset, and each extra keyword argument becomes an entity under that name:

import eden as en
from eden.options import BoxOptions

scene_options = en.scenes.Empty(                  # a ground plane
    robot=en.robots.Yam(),                         # a robot preset, under the name "robot"
    cube=BoxOptions(size=(0.05, 0.05, 0.05), default_root_pos=(0.4, 0.0, 0.025)),
)

Once the environment is built, look an entity up by that name. Every getter returns a batch, one row per environment:

robot = env.entities["robot"]
pos = robot.get_pos()       # (num_envs, 3)
quat = robot.get_quat()     # (num_envs, 4), w x y z

Quaternions are w, x, y, z

Every quaternion in Eden, config fields such as default_root_quat included, is ordered (w, x, y, z). The identity is (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0).

Entities covers pose frames, the two DOF index spaces, armature, contacts and the deformable entity types; Robots covers the robot catalog.

docs.title: Managers and terms
docs.text:
A manager owns one aspect of the task and computes it from a set of terms. A term is one small piece of behavior: one observation, one reward, one termination condition. A task config lists the terms each manager runs, by name:

Manager Its terms Config field Action Turn the policy's action into actuator commands (PD, OSC, IK controllers, ...) action_options Command Generate goals: target poses, velocities, reference motions command_options Observation Compute observation groups (policy, critic, ...), with noise and history observation_options Reward Compute weighted reward terms, summed into the step reward reward_options Termination Decide which episodes end, and whether each ending is a time-out termination_options Event Randomize and reset the scene at startup, on reset, or at intervals event_options Curriculum Change the task's difficulty as training progresses curriculum_options Metric Share a computation between terms, and report success metric_options Recorder Record episodes to a dataset recorder_options

EnvBase runs the action, metric, event, observation and recorder managers; RLEnvBase adds the rest, and MimicRLEnvBase adds a motion manager for the reference motion.

A term is either a function or a class:

import torch

from eden.managers import REWARD_TERM_REGISTRY
from eden.managers.reward_manager import RewardTerm


@REWARD_TERM_REGISTRY.register()
def base_height_error(env, *, entity_name: str, target: float) -> torch.Tensor:
    """A function term: stateless, its parameters come from params={...}."""
    return torch.square(env.entities[entity_name].get_pos()[:, 2] - target)


@REWARD_TERM_REGISTRY.register()
class BaseHeightPenalty(RewardTerm):
    """A class term: its fields are its parameters, and build() runs once at env construction."""

    entity_name: str = "robot"
    target: float = 0.3

    def build(self) -> None:
        self.resolve_entity(self.entity_name)  # a wrong name raises now, not on the first step

    def compute(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        return torch.square(self.resolve_entity(self.entity_name).get_pos()[:, 2] - self.target)

A config refers to a term through .configure(...). A function term goes through its kind's wrapper with func= and params=; a class term is configured directly:

from eden.options import RewardManagerOptions
from eden.terms import RewardTerm

reward_options = RewardManagerOptions(
    height_fn=RewardTerm.configure(func=base_height_error, weight=-1.0, params={"entity_name": "robot", "target": 0.3}),
    height_cls=BaseHeightPenalty.configure(weight=-1.0, target=0.3),
)

eden.terms holds the wrappers for function terms: ObsTerm, RewardTerm, DoneTerm, EventTerm, CurrTerm and MetricTerm. (The RewardTerm there is the function wrapper; the class-term base above has the same name and lives in eden.managers.reward_manager.) Eden's own terms are in eden.observations, eden.rewards, eden.terminations, eden.actions, eden.commands, eden.events, eden.curricula and eden.metrics, and eden terms --grep <text> searches all of them with their parameters.

Use a function when the term only reads state; use a class when it has parameters to validate, names to resolve once, or state to keep between steps. Writing terms explains that choice and the lifecycle of a class term.

docs.title: Registries
docs.text:
Eden finds terms and tasks by name, through registries.

Term registries. Each kind of term has one (REWARD_TERM_REGISTRY, OBSERVATION_TERM_REGISTRY, ... in eden.managers). A term's key is always its name in snake case: BaseHeightPenalty registers as base_height_penalty, and the function action_rate_l2 as action_rate_l2. Two terms whose names give the same key cannot both be registered in one registry, and that includes Eden's built-in terms: registering your own base_height_l2 reward raises a ValueError naming the built-in that holds the key. register() takes no name= argument; rename the term to change its key. A class term that was never registered configures without complaint but fails when the environment is built.

The task registry. TASK_REGISTRY (in eden.tasks) maps a task name to its config class. A task registers itself where it is defined, with @TASK_REGISTRY.register(), and the registry finds every such decorator by scanning the source of eden/tasks/ without importing it, so there is no central list to update and eden list stays fast. The name is the class name in snake case without the Config suffix: ReacherConfig is reacher.

from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY

config = TASK_REGISTRY.build("reacher")                     # the config, with its task mods applied
config = TASK_REGISTRY.build("reacher", difficulty="hard")  # with a variant flag set

TASK_REGISTRY.get("reacher") returns the bare class instead. Instantiating it yourself skips the task's mods, which for some tasks leaves required settings (such as which robot to load) empty, so construct a registered task with build().

Task mods are the variants of a task. A TaskMod is a small class whose constructor arguments become CLI flags (--difficulty above) and whose apply() edits the config. TaskMods covers them.

Tasks outside Eden's own tree register the same way; Your first task shows how to make eden train find them.

docs.title: One control step
docs.text:
env.step(action) runs one control step. In outline, for an RL environment:

graph LR
    A["apply action"] --> P["physics<br/>(decimation substeps)"]
    P --> T["terminations"]
    T --> R["rewards"]
    R --> X["reset finished<br/>episodes"]
    X --> C["curricula,<br/>commands, events"]
    C --> O["observations"]

Three consequences are worth knowing before you write a term:

  • Auto-reset runs before the observation. Finished environments are reset inside step(), after rewards and terminations, so the observation step() returns for them is the first observation of the new episode, not the terminal one.
  • The policy runs at the control rate. Each step applies the action, then advances physics decimation times by sim_dt (both in EnvOptions), so the control period is sim_dt * decimation.
  • Observation compute() is a read. The observation manager computes its terms at several points (at build, at reset, during the step), so a counter advanced inside an observation's compute() advances more than once per step. Per-step state goes in a hook that runs once per step.

The full sequence has twenty phases; The step loop lists them, and Writing terms says which hook each kind of per-step state belongs in.

  • Task configuration: every option group.
