docs.title: Your first task
docs.text:
This tutorial builds a task from scratch and trains it with eden train: a Yam arm learns to bring its gripper to a target. On the way it writes a custom reward term, adds a variant flag with a TaskMod, and checks the task before training. It follows the reacher task, eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py, which is the template every built-in task is written to.

You need Eden installed (Installation) and the ideas from Key concepts.

docs.title: Where the task lives
docs.text:
A task is a config class in a Python module, registered with @TASK_REGISTRY.register(). Eden finds tasks by scanning packages for that decorator, so the module has to be in a package Eden scans. There are two places:

  • Your own package (this tutorial). The package declares itself to Eden through an entry point, and works the same with Eden from PyPI or from a clone.
  • Inside a clone of Eden, under eden/tasks/, if you are adding a task to Eden itself. See Adding the task to Eden itself at the end.

Create this layout:

my_tasks/
├── pyproject.toml
└── my_tasks/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── tasks/
        ├── __init__.py
        └── reach/
            ├── __init__.py
            └── config.py

The __init__.py files can be empty. The scan skips __init__.py files and any module whose name starts with an underscore, so the task itself goes in config.py.

pyproject.toml names the package to scan under the eden.tasks entry-point group:

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=77"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "my-tasks"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["eden-world"]

[project.entry-points."eden.tasks"]
my_tasks = "my_tasks.tasks"

The entry point's value is the dotted name of a package (not a module, and without a :attribute). Eden scans every .py file under it.

docs.title: Write the config
docs.text: The rest of the tutorial fills in my_tasks/tasks/reach/config.py. The complete file is at the end of this section.

docs.title: The scene, the actions and the command
docs.text:
Start with the imports, the simulation settings, the scene and the action. These are the reacher's, unchanged:

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Annotated

import torch

import eden as en
from eden import actions, observations, rewards, terminations
from eden.constants import ReferenceSource
from eden.managers import REWARD_TERM_REGISTRY
from eden.managers.reward_manager import RewardTerm as RewardTermBase
from eden.managers.terms.commands.oracle import UniformT3Command
from eden.managers.terms.observations.manipulation import ObjectToOracleDistance
from eden.managers.terms.utils import resolve_link_idx
from eden.options import ObservationGroupOptions
from eden.options.learning.rsl_rl import (
    RslRlActorOptions,
    RslRlCriticOptions,
    RslRlGaussianDistributionOptions,
    RslRlOnPolicyRunnerOptions,
    RslRlPpoAlgorithmOptions,
)
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY
from eden.tasks.registry import TaskMod
from eden.terms import DoneTerm, ObsTerm, RewardTerm
from eden.utils.configs import (
    ActionManagerOptions,
    CommandManagerOptions,
    EdenRLConfig,
    EnvOptions,
    ObservationManagerOptions,
    RewardManagerOptions,
    SceneOptions,
    TerminationManagerOptions,
)
from eden.utils.string import term_subject

The config class declares each option group as an annotated field with a default:

class MyReachConfig(EdenRLConfig):
    env_options: EnvOptions = EnvOptions(
        num_envs=4096,
        episode_length_s=9.0,
        iterations=10,
        ls_iterations=20,
        sim_dt=0.01,
        sim_substeps=2,
        decimation=1,
        max_collision_pairs=30,
        multiplier_collision_broad_phase=12,
        enable_multi_contact=True,
    )

    scene_options: SceneOptions = en.scenes.Empty(
        is_support_enabled=True,
        robot=en.robots.Yam(default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), default_root_quat=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
    )

    action_options: ActionManagerOptions = ActionManagerOptions(
        joint_pos_controller=actions.ImplicitPDController.configure(
            entity_name="robot",
            dofs_name="joint*",
            scale=0.05,
            reference_source=ReferenceSource.DELTA,
        ),
    )

    command_options: CommandManagerOptions = CommandManagerOptions(
        reaching_target=UniformT3Command.configure(
            x_range=(0.3, 0.5),
            y_range=(-0.1, 0.1),
            z_range=(0.25, 0.35),
            resampling_time_range=(2.0, 3.0),
        ),
    )

What each part does:

  • env_options: 4096 parallel environments, 9-second episodes, and a 0.01 s physics step with no decimation, so the policy acts at 100 Hz. The solver settings (iterations, max_collision_pairs, ...) are the reacher's.
  • scene_options: a ground plane and the Yam arm, placed at the origin under the name robot. Quaternions are (w, x, y, z), so (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) is no rotation.
  • action_options: one action term, an implicit PD controller on every joint whose name matches joint*. With ReferenceSource.DELTA the target is the current joint position plus 0.05 * action, a small increment each step.
  • command_options: a 3D target point sampled uniformly in a box in front of the arm, resampled every 2 to 3 seconds. Other terms find it by its name, reaching_target. The arm sits at the origin without rotation, so the point is in both the world frame and the arm's base frame.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
The policy sees the joint positions and velocities, the vector from the gripper to the target, and its own last action. The reacher defines the terms once and uses them in two groups: policy for the actor and critic for the value function.

_OBSERVATIONS = dict(
    dofs_pos=observations.DofsPos.configure(entity_name="robot"),
    dofs_vel=observations.DofsVel.configure(entity_name="robot"),
    gripper_to_target=ObjectToOracleDistance.configure(
        entity_name="robot",
        entity_link_name="link_left_finger",
        command_name="reaching_target",
        robot_name="robot",
    ),
    last_action=ObsTerm.configure(func=observations.last_action, params={"action_name": "joint_pos_controller"}),
)

Inside the class:

    observation_options: ObservationManagerOptions = ObservationManagerOptions(
        policy=ObservationGroupOptions(**_OBSERVATIONS),
        critic=ObservationGroupOptions(**_OBSERVATIONS),
    )

DofsPos and DofsVel are class terms, configured directly. last_action is a function term, configured through the ObsTerm wrapper with func= and params=. To find other observation terms and their parameters, run eden terms --kind observation.

docs.title: A custom reward term
docs.text:
The reward pays for bringing the gripper to the target: exp(-d² / std²), where d is the distance from the midpoint of the two fingers to the target. It is a class term, because it has names to resolve once (two links and a command) and a parameter worth validating:

@REWARD_TERM_REGISTRY.register()
class GripperToTarget(RewardTermBase):
    """exp(-d^2 / std^2) of the distance d between the midpoint of the gripper's fingers and the target."""

    entity_name: str = "robot"
    links_name: list[str] = ["link_left_finger", "link_right_finger"]
    command_name: str = "reaching_target"
    std: float = 0.2

    def build(self) -> None:
        if self.std <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{term_subject(self)}: std={self.std} must be positive; it is the distance (m) at which the "
                f"reward has fallen to exp(-1)."
            )
        robot = self.resolve_entity(self.entity_name)
        self._links_idx = resolve_link_idx(robot, self.links_name, self.device, term=type(self).__name__)
        self._command = self._env.command_manager.get_term(self.command_name)

    def compute(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        robot = self.resolve_entity(self.entity_name)
        gripper_pos = robot.get_links_pos(ls_idx_local=self._links_idx).mean(dim=1)  # (num_envs, 3)
        target_pos = self._command.command[..., :3]
        dist_sq = torch.sum(torch.square(gripper_pos - target_pos), dim=-1)
        return torch.exp(-dist_sq / self.std**2)  # (num_envs,)

How the term is put together:

  • The class fields are its parameters, each with a default. The config sets them through GripperToTarget.configure(...), and a misspelled one raises when the config is constructed.
  • build() runs once, when the environment is built. Everything that can be resolved ahead of time is resolved here: the link indices and the command term. A wrong link or command name raises now, with a message that lists what exists, instead of on the first training step.
  • compute() runs every step and returns one value per environment. It looks the robot up again with resolve_entity() rather than keeping the handle from build(): deployment swaps the simulated robot for the real one, and a handle kept from build() would keep reading the simulation.
  • The key is the class name in snake case, gripper_to_target. register() takes no name=.

The base class is imported as RewardTermBase because eden.terms also exports a RewardTerm, the wrapper for function terms that the next section uses for the two built-in penalties. Writing terms covers the other hooks a class term can implement (reset(), post_reset(), post_physics_refresh()) and when each is the right place for state.

docs.title: Rewards, terminations and the runner
docs.text:
Inside the class, weight the custom reward against two built-in penalties, end each episode on a time-out, and set up PPO:

    reward_options: RewardManagerOptions = RewardManagerOptions(
        reach=GripperToTarget.configure(weight=1.0, std=0.2),
        action_rate=RewardTerm.configure(func=rewards.action_rate_l2, weight=-0.01),
        joint_pos_limits=RewardTerm.configure(
            func=rewards.dofs_pos_limits, weight=-10.0, params={"entity_name": "robot"}
        ),
    )

    termination_options: TerminationManagerOptions = TerminationManagerOptions(
        timeout=DoneTerm.configure(func=terminations.time_out, time_out=True),
    )

    runner_options: RslRlOnPolicyRunnerOptions = RslRlOnPolicyRunnerOptions(
        algorithm=RslRlPpoAlgorithmOptions(
            value_loss_coef=1.0,
            use_clipped_value_loss=True,
            clip_param=0.2,
            entropy_coef=0.005,
            num_learning_epochs=5,
            num_mini_batches=4,
            learning_rate=1.0e-3,
            schedule="adaptive",
            gamma=0.99,
            lam=0.95,
            desired_kl=0.01,
            max_grad_norm=1.0,
        ),
        actor=RslRlActorOptions(
            activation="elu",
            hidden_dims=[256, 128],
            distribution_cfg=RslRlGaussianDistributionOptions(init_std=1.0),
        ),
        critic=RslRlCriticOptions(activation="elu", hidden_dims=[256, 128]),
        max_iterations=100,
        save_interval=100,
        experiment_name="my_reach",
    )

time_out=True marks the termination as a time limit rather than a failure, which the learner treats differently when it bootstraps the value of the last state.

docs.title: A variant flag
docs.text:
A TaskMod turns a choice into a command-line flag. Its constructor arguments become flags, and apply() edits the config. This one sets how far from the centre of the box the target may be sampled:

class TargetSpreadMod(TaskMod):
    """How far from the centre of the workspace the reaching target may be sampled."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        target_spread: Annotated[float, "Half-width (m) in x and y of the box the target is sampled in."] = 0.1,
    ):
        self.target_spread = target_spread

    def apply(self, config: MyReachConfig) -> MyReachConfig:
        if self.target_spread <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"--target_spread={self.target_spread} must be positive; it is a half-width in metres.")
        target = config.command_options.reaching_target
        target.x_range = (0.4 - self.target_spread, 0.4 + self.target_spread)
        target.y_range = (-self.target_spread, self.target_spread)
        return config

Three rules make a TaskMod work:

  • A positional-or-keyword argument with a type annotation becomes a flag (--target_spread). Arguments after a bare * are keyword-only and are not flags; use them for settings fixed at registration time.
  • Annotated[T, "help text"] gives the flag its --help text. A Literal[...] type becomes a flag with fixed choices.
  • The default must describe the same task as the bare config. Here 0.1 reproduces the config's own x_range=(0.3, 0.5) and y_range=(-0.1, 0.1), so MyReachConfig() and TASK_REGISTRY.build("my_reach") agree.

docs.title: Register the task
docs.text:
Decorate the config class and attach the mod. The decorator goes on the class, the mod is passed as an instance (a bare class is instantiated with no arguments), and the task name is the class name in snake case without the Config suffix:

@TASK_REGISTRY.register(modifiers=(TargetSpreadMod(),))
class MyReachConfig(EdenRLConfig):
    ...

TASK_REGISTRY must be imported with from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY (or from eden.tasks.registry): the scan recognizes the decorator only through those imports, and warns when it sees the name used without one.

docs.text:

from typing import Annotated

from eden import actions, observations, rewards, terminations
from eden.constants import ReferenceSource
from eden.managers import REWARD_TERM_REGISTRY
from eden.managers.reward_manager import RewardTerm as RewardTermBase
from eden.managers.terms.commands.oracle import UniformT3Command

from eden.terms import DoneTerm, ObsTerm, RewardTerm
from eden.utils.configs import (

_OBSERVATIONS = dict(

docs.title: Install the package
docs.text:
Install my_tasks in editable mode into the environment Eden is installed in, so that edits to config.py take effect without reinstalling:

pipuv (Eden from a clone) 
cd my_tasks
pip install -e .

source /path/to/Eden/.venv/bin/activate    # the environment Eden is installed in
cd my_tasks
uv pip install -e .

Reinstall only when you change pyproject.toml, for example to rename the entry point.

docs.title: Check the task
docs.text:
eden list

my_reach appears with my-tasks, the distribution's name, as its source and TargetSpreadMod as its modifier. If it is missing, the scan did not find the package: check the entry point's value, and that the decorated class is not in an __init__.py or a module whose name starts with _. A broken entry point (a package that does not import) is reported with a warning when the registry scans.

Then build the task and step it, which runs every term's build() and a few compute() calls:

eden smoke --task my_reach                 # GPU, 2 environments, 2 steps
eden smoke --task my_reach --cpu
eden smoke --task my_reach --profile       # also time each term, and write term_cost.json

A wrong entity, link or command name fails here, with a message naming what exists. Building the task takes a fraction of the time a training run does, so run it after every change.

docs.title: Train it
docs.text:
eden train --task my_reach
eden train --task my_reach --target_spread 0.15     # the variant flag
eden train --task my_reach --help                   # every flag, --target_spread with its help text

The run lands in logs/my_reach/<timestamp>-<id>/, with the checkpoint, config.json and run.json described in the Quick start. On an RTX 3080 the 100 iterations take about 30 s once the kernels are compiled, and the reach term's episode reward climbs from about 0.01 to 0.3 and is still rising at the last iteration. Raise max_iterations to train further.

docs.title: Watch it
docs.text:
eden inference --task my_reach --checkpoint "$(ls -t logs/my_reach/*/model_*.pt | head -n1)" --vis

eden inference rebuilds the task from the config.json next to the checkpoint, so it plays the variant you trained. Passing a variant flag such as --target_spread together with that checkpoint is an error, because the saved config already decides it; --override still applies on top of the saved config. The saved config names your classes by their import path, so my_tasks must stay installed for the run to replay.

docs.title: Using the task from a script
docs.text:
The entry point is what makes eden commands see the task. A script of your own can also add a package to the scan for its own process only:

import eden as en
import genesis as gs

from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY

en.init(backend=gs.gpu)
TASK_REGISTRY.add_search_path("my_tasks.tasks")
config = TASK_REGISTRY.build("my_reach", target_spread=0.15)

build() takes the mod's flags as keyword arguments. Always construct a registered task with build(), never by calling MyReachConfig() or TASK_REGISTRY.get("my_reach")(): those skip the task's mods, which for many tasks leaves required settings empty. A script that trains directly instead of through eden train also has to set the logger itself, since RslRlOnPolicyRunnerOptions.logger defaults to "wandb" (eden train passes its own --logger, which defaults to tensorboard). Training runs shows a complete training script.

docs.title: Adding the task to Eden itself
docs.text:
To contribute a task to Eden, put it in a clone under eden/tasks/. Built-in tasks follow conventions that the tests in tests/tasks/test_init.py check:

  • The config class is defined in eden/tasks/<package>/config.py, or eden/tasks/<suite>/<task>/config.py for a task in a suite.
  • The task name starts with the package's name: name the class <Package><Task>Config, so that the key derives as <package>_<task> (PolarisPanCleanConfig in eden/tasks/polaris is polaris_pan_clean). A task named exactly like its package is fine too.
  • Task names are snake case.

No entry point is needed: eden/tasks/ is always scanned. Task configuration describes the package layout in full, and Contributing covers tests and pull requests.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Writing terms: the term lifecycle, per-step hooks, validation and the gotchas.
  • TaskMods: composable variants, prefixes, mods that change the robot.
  • Task configuration: every option group a config can set.
  • Events and domain randomization: randomize the scene on reset.
  • Training runs: resuming, loggers, other runners.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page installs Eden, either from PyPI into your own project or from a clone of the repository, and explains the optional extras that add rendering, teleoperation, retargeting and other features. It ends with a check that the install works.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or 3.13. pyproject.toml declares requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.14"; Eden has not been run on Python 3.14 yet.
  • Linux x86_64 with an NVIDIA GPU is the primary platform, and the one GPU-parallel training is built for.
  • macOS on Apple silicon and Windows AMD64 are supported on a best-effort basis: the dependency resolution is required to stay installable on both, but a few extras need more than they have. Nyx path tracing has no macOS build, onnx-gpu has no macOS wheels, Gaussian-splat rendering needs CUDA, and the Wuji Glove SDK is Linux-only.

Eden runs on the CPU too (every command takes --cpu), which is enough to build tasks and try things with a few environments, but training at scale needs a GPU.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
Eden is published on PyPI as eden-world. The import name is eden, and the command it installs is eden:

pipuv project 
pip install eden-world
pip install "eden-world[vis]"        # with an optional extra

uv add eden-world
uv add "eden-world[vis,onnx]"        # with optional extras

pip install eden installs a different package

The PyPI name eden belongs to an unrelated project. Always install eden-world, and write extras as eden-world[<extra>]. Only the distribution name differs: you still import eden and run eden.

A PyPI install carries the eden package only. The examples/ directory, the tests and these docs live in the repository, so eden examples list and the example scripts need a clone.

docs.title: Install from a clone
docs.text:
A clone is the way to run the examples, work on Eden itself, or follow main. uv creates the virtual environment and installs Eden into it in editable mode:

git clone https://github.com/embodied-ai-nexus/Eden.git
cd Eden
uv sync                              # the core, plus the dev tools (ruff, pre-commit, pytest)
source .venv/bin/activate            # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

To install every extra instead:

uv sync --all-extras --all-groups

--all-groups matters: two extras need a package that is not on PyPI, and those packages come from dependency groups (see Extras that need a git package).

To add one extra to what is already installed:

uv sync --inexact --extra vis

uv sync removes what you do not name

Without --inexact, uv sync is exact: it uninstalls every extra and group the command does not name. After uv sync --all-extras --all-groups, a later sync that names only vis (and not --inexact) removes every other extra. Use --inexact to add an extra, or repeat the full set of flags every time you sync. Troubleshooting covers repairing an environment this has already happened to.

With plain pip in a clone, pip install -e ".[vis]" works for most extras, but pip ignores the [tool.uv] settings in pyproject.toml, so the soma-retargeter extra cannot be installed that way.

docs.title: Running eden
docs.text:
Inside an activated virtual environment, eden is on your PATH. Without activating it, prefix every command with uv run (in a clone) or call the module directly:

uv run eden list          # in a clone, without activating .venv
python -m eden list       # any environment where Eden is installed

The rest of these docs write commands as eden <command>.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
The core install covers building tasks, training with rsl_rl, inference, export to TorchScript and the asset cache. Everything else is an extra. Each row gives the packages it adds, read from [project.optional-dependencies] in pyproject.toml.

Despite its name, all is not every extra. To install genuinely everything in a clone, use uv sync --all-extras --all-groups.

docs.title: Extras with special install rules
docs.text:
onnx and onnx-gpu exclude each other. Their runtime wheels, onnxruntime and onnxruntime-gpu, both own the onnxruntime/ directory, so whichever is installed last provides it. Pick one. uv sync --all-extras --all-groups installs both, and the CPU wheel usually ends up on top; to use the GPU wheel, reinstall it last:

uv sync --inexact --extra onnx-gpu --reinstall-package onnxruntime-gpu

Do not uninstall either wheel to fix this: removing one deletes files the other needs. If the GPU runtime falls back to the CPU, a policy still runs, only slower, and Eden warns once.

soma-retargeter installs only with uv, in a clone: uv sync --inexact --extra soma-retargeter. eden-soma-retargeter 0.4.0 pins trimesh==4.11.3 while Genesis needs trimesh>=5, and only the clone's [tool.uv] override-dependencies reconciles the two. pip ignores that table, so a pip install of this extra fails to resolve.

batch-splat compiles CUDA code on first use. gsplat JIT-compiles a CUDA extension the first time it is imported, so the CUDA toolkit (nvcc) has to be installed.

graspgen is under a non-commercial license. GraspGen ships under NVIDIA's non-commercial license; GraspGenX (graspgenx) is Apache-2.0. Both download their models on first use (grasp_gen download for GraspGen).

pose needs separate checkpoints. GVHMR's checkpoints are a separate download (gvhmr-download-checkpoints), and the SMPL and SMPL-X body models are licence-gated, so you obtain them yourself.

docs.title: Extras that need a git package
docs.text:
Two extras depend on a package that is not on PyPI. PyPI refuses to publish a package whose requirements point at a git URL, so the pinned git requirement lives in a dependency group named after the extra:

Extra Git package In a clone metaquest televuer uv sync --inexact --extra metaquest --group metaquest-git flashsac rsl-rl-flashsac uv sync --inexact --extra flashsac --group flashsac-git

With pip, install the extra and the pinned git requirement in one command. When the package is missing, the error Eden raises prints that command in full; the pins themselves are eden.utils.distribution.UNPUBLISHED_REQUIREMENTS.

docs.title: Hardware SDKs Eden cannot declare
docs.text:
Some device SDKs cannot be a dependency at all:

  • PICO: the pico extra covers Eden's side of the link only. Tracking also needs the xrobotoolkit_sdk extension module, which you build from source against the XRoboToolkit PC Service. See examples/recipes/teleop/pico/README.md in the repository.
  • Franka Panda: panda-python wheels ship inside a zip per libfranka version on the panda-py GitHub releases, so you install the one that matches your robot's firmware by hand. The comment above the franka extra in pyproject.toml gives the commands for libfranka 0.8.0.
  • Wuji Glove: wuji-sdk publishes Linux wheels only (x86_64 and aarch64). Off Linux the wuji extra installs nothing.

The Wuji SDK sends telemetry

Importing wuji_sdk starts a background worker that batches anonymous usage events to a third-party analytics host. Set WUJI_TELEMETRY_DISABLE=1 in your environment to turn it off. Eden does not set it for you.

docs.title: GPU and CUDA
docs.text:
Eden installs PyTorch from PyPI, whose Linux wheels bundle their own CUDA libraries. What your machine needs is an NVIDIA driver new enough for the CUDA version that torch was built for. Compare the two:

nvidia-smi                                               # top right: the newest CUDA the driver supports
python -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())"

The driver's version must be at least torch's, and the second command should print True.

When a script or command asks for the GPU (gs.gpu, the default of every eden command), Genesis tries CUDA, then AMD GPUs, then Metal on macOS, and falls back to the CPU with the warning Backend gpu not available on this machine. Falling back to CPU. If you see that warning on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU, torch cannot see the GPU; see Troubleshooting.

The first run of a task compiles Genesis' kernels, which takes a while; the compiled kernels are cached under ~/.cache/quadrants/ and later runs start much faster.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
python -c "import eden; print(eden.__version__, eden.__file__)"
eden --help
eden list

The first line prints the installed version (for example 0.1.0) and where eden is imported from: a path inside your clone for a source install. eden list prints a table of every registered task. Neither command builds a scene, so both finish in a few seconds.

To check that simulation works too, build a task and step it twice:

eden smoke --task reacher             # GPU
eden smoke --task reacher --cpu       # no GPU

It ends with ✅ smoke OK: built 'reacher' with 2 env(s) and ran 2 step(s). The first time, it also downloads the robot's assets (Assets explains where they go).

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page trains a policy, watches it, and then takes it further: export, a MuJoCo sim-to-sim check, and a published policy you can run without training. It uses reacher, the smallest built-in task: a 6-DOF Yam arm learns to move its gripper to target points sampled in front of it.

You need Eden installed (Installation). The commands default to the GPU; add --cpu to any of them on a machine without one.

docs.title: 1. Find a task
docs.text:
eden list

This prints every registered task with its source (eden for a built-in task) and the task mods that give it variant flags. reacher has one mod, ReacherDifficultyMod, which adds --difficulty. To see every flag a task accepts, its variant flags included:

eden train --task reacher --help

Task suites describes the built-in tasks by family.

docs.title: 2. Train it
docs.text:
eden train --task reacher

reacher builds 4096 parallel environments and runs 100 PPO iterations with rsl_rl (its runner_options set max_iterations=100). The first run compiles Genesis' kernels before training starts and caches them for later runs, and it downloads the Yam arm's model files (Assets). While training, rsl_rl prints a summary per iteration; the mean episode reward should rise as the arm learns to reach.

The run writes to a new directory, logs/reacher/<timestamp>-<id>/, relative to the directory you ran the command from:

File What it is model_<iteration>.pt The policy checkpoint. Only the newest is kept (keep_last_checkpoints=1 by default). config.json The full config the run trained with. eden inference, eden export and eden deploy rebuild the task from it. run.json The seed, the command line and the Eden and Genesis versions, for reproducing the run. progress.json A small summary of the run's progress, rewritten every iteration. events.out.tfevents.* TensorBoard logs: tensorboard --logdir logs/reacher

Useful flags (all of them are in eden train --task reacher --help):

eden train --task reacher --num_envs 1024                    # fewer environments, e.g. for a smaller GPU
eden train --task reacher --difficulty hard                  # a variant flag from the task's mod
eden train --task reacher --override 'runner_options: {max_iterations: 300}'
eden train --task reacher --resume latest                    # continue the newest run, in a new run directory
eden train --task reacher --logger wandb                     # log to Weights & Biases instead of TensorBoard
eden train --task reacher --run_name first_try               # logs/reacher/<timestamp>-first_try-<id>/
eden train --task reacher --cpu --num_envs 64                # no GPU

--override takes a YAML mapping that is merged into the task's config, and can be repeated. --config <file> does the same from a .json or .yaml file.

docs.title: 3. Watch the trained policy
docs.text:
Point eden inference at a checkpoint. This picks the newest one:

eden inference --task reacher --checkpoint "$(ls -t logs/reacher/*/model_*.pt | head -n1)" --vis

--vis opens the Genesis viewer and runs one episode in one environment. eden inference loads the config.json next to the checkpoint, so it rebuilds the task exactly as it was trained, in evaluation mode. For the same reason a variant flag such as --difficulty cannot be combined with a checkpoint that has a config.json; --override still applies on top.

On a machine without a display, record a video instead of opening the viewer:

eden inference --task reacher --checkpoint <path/to/model_100.pt> --rec

--rec adds a recording camera and writes an .mp4 into the new run directory that eden inference creates under logs/reacher/. --steps N, --episodes N and --num_envs N change how long and how wide the rollout is.

docs.title: 4. Export it
docs.text:
eden export --task reacher --checkpoint <path/to/model_100.pt>

This writes the policy as ONNX and TorchScript, plus a policy_spec.json that describes its observations, actions and control rate, into exported/<checkpoint name>/ next to the checkpoint. Each exported graph is checked against the policy on the environment's observations; the ONNX check needs the onnx extra, and --no_verify skips the checks. Exporting a policy describes the files.

docs.title: 5. Check it against MuJoCo, then hardware
docs.text:
eden deploy runs the policy through the same loop it uses on a real robot. With --mujoco, the robot is a MuJoCo model instead, which checks the policy against a second physics engine before you touch hardware:

eden deploy --task <task> --checkpoint model.pt --mujoco --vis     # sim-to-sim
eden deploy --task <task> --checkpoint model.pt                    # real hardware

The robot and its hardware backend come from the task's scene. Deployment has many safety-relevant flags (gain scaling, joint ramps, a simulated gantry); read Deployment before running a policy on a robot.

docs.title: 6. Run a published policy
docs.text:
Eden ships ports of published controllers that run without any training:

eden inference --policy homie --vis                         # HOMIE walk/stand controller on a Unitree G1
eden inference --policy homie --vis --base_command 0.5 0 0  # a constant velocity command (vx, vy, yaw rate)

--policy accepts a package name from eden/extensions/policies/ (for example holosoma or homie). Without --task, Eden builds a scene from the policy's own robot, observations and actions. The checkpoint downloads on first use. Some policies need more: motion-tracking policies such as sonic need --motion_file, and the ONNX ones need the onnx or onnx-gpu extra. The policy zoo lists every policy and what it needs.

docs.text:

  • Your first task: write a task of your own and train it with eden train.
  • Training runs: checkpoints, resuming, loggers, other runners.
  • Multi-GPU training: torchrun and SLURM.
  • eden terms --grep friction: find a built-in term and its parameters (command reference).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Each entry gives the symptom, its cause, and a fix you can type. Most of Eden's own errors already name the fix in their message, so read the last line of the traceback first; this page covers the problems whose cause lies outside the message, in the machine, the environment or the install.

Run the commands from the directory that holds your virtual environment: the repository root for a clone, or your project for a PyPI install.

docs.title: Check the install first
docs.text:
python -c "import eden, torch; print('eden', eden.__version__, eden.__file__); print('torch', torch.__version__, 'cuda', torch.version.cuda, 'available', torch.cuda.is_available())"
eden list

The first command should print an eden path inside the clone you are working in (for a source install) and available True on a GPU machine. eden list should print a table of tasks. Include the output of both when you ask for help.

docs.title: torch.cuda.is_available() is False
docs.text:
The NVIDIA driver is not visible, or the torch wheel was built for a newer CUDA than the driver supports:

nvidia-smi                                                 # the driver works and lists your GPUs
python -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)"        # the CUDA version torch was built for

nvidia-smi prints the newest CUDA version the driver supports in its top-right corner, and that must be at least the version torch was built for. If it is lower, upgrade the driver. If nvidia-smi itself fails, the driver is not installed or not loaded, and no change on the Python side fixes that.

To keep working without a GPU, use the CPU backend with a few environments:

eden train --task reacher --cpu --num_envs 64

docs.title: Backend gpu not available on this machine. Falling back to CPU.
docs.text: Genesis tried every GPU backend (CUDA, then AMD, then Metal) and found none, so the run continues on the CPU, much more slowly. On a machine with an NVIDIA GPU this is the same problem as the previous entry: torch cannot see the GPU.

docs.title: CUBLAS_STATUS_INVALID_VALUE after module load cuda
docs.text:
On a cluster, module load cuda-... puts the system's CUDA libraries ahead of the ones torch ships with. A mixed pair of cuBLAS and cuBLASLt then fails, typically in batched matrix products such as the IK solvers. Put torch's own NVIDIA libraries first:

export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$(ls -d .venv/lib/python*/site-packages/nvidia/*/lib | paste -sd:):${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"

The SLURM template in Multi-GPU training already does this.

docs.title: The first run spends a long time before the first step
docs.text:
Genesis compiles its kernels the first time a scene is built and caches them under ~/.cache/quadrants/, so later runs start much faster. Upgrading Genesis invalidates the cache and the first run compiles again. Both are expected.

If a run fails inside kernel compilation after an earlier run was interrupted, clear the cache and retry:

rm -rf ~/.cache/quadrants/qdcache

docs.title: Every multi-GPU rank lands on GPU 0, or CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES has N entries but LOCAL_RANK=...
docs.text:
import eden gives each rank its own GPU, by rewriting CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES from LOCAL_RANK, and it has to do that before anything initializes CUDA. Import eden before genesis and torch in every script:

import eden as en      # first: it pins this rank's GPU
import genesis as gs
import torch

en.init(backend=gs.gpu)   # en.init, not gs.init: it also sets up logging and the run directory

The LOCAL_RANK error means CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES lists fewer GPUs than the launch starts ranks. Make --nproc_per_node match the number of visible GPUs. See Multi-GPU training.

docs.title: An opaque CUDA unknown error, after eden.init() called again
docs.text: Calling eden.init() twice in one process is a common cause of an unexplained CUDA unknown error, and the second call also starts a new run directory. Eden warns when it happens: eden.init() called again in a process where Genesis is already initialized. Call eden.init() exactly once per process, and start a new process for each run.

docs.title: pip install eden installed something else
docs.text:
The PyPI name eden belongs to an unrelated project. Uninstall it and install eden-world:

pip uninstall eden
pip install eden-world

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError for an optional package
docs.text: The feature needs an extra you have not installed. Eden's message for a missing extra names both install commands, for example pip install "eden-world[vis]", or uv sync --inexact --extra vis in a checkout. The extras are listed in Installation.

docs.title: A uv sync removed my extras
docs.text:
uv sync is exact: it installs the extras and groups you name and uninstalls every other one. After uv sync --all-extras --all-groups, a later plain uv sync, or a sync that names a single extra without --inexact, removes everything else, and the next import gsplat or eden pico bridge fails with ModuleNotFoundError.

Repeat the flags you installed with, every time:

uv sync --all-extras --all-groups

Or keep what is installed and only add to it:

uv sync --inexact --extra docs

docs.title: ...and now import torch fails with libcudnn.so.9: cannot open shared object file
docs.text:
Some extras put libraries in the same site-packages/nvidia/ directory as torch's CUDA packages. Uninstalling them can delete files that belong to nvidia-cudnn-cu12, nvidia-nccl-cu12 and similar packages while their metadata stays behind, so uv considers them installed and a new sync changes nothing. Find every package with missing files and reinstall those:

broken=$(.venv/bin/python -c 'import importlib.metadata as m; print(" ".join("--reinstall-package " + d.metadata["Name"] for d in m.distributions() if any(not f.locate().exists() for f in (d.files or []) if f.suffix != ".pyc")))')
echo "$broken"                                  # e.g. --reinstall-package nvidia-cudnn-cu12 ...
uv sync --all-extras --all-groups $broken       # use the flags you normally sync with

If the list is empty and torch still fails to load, reinstall torch itself:

uv sync --all-extras --all-groups --reinstall-package torch

docs.title: onnxruntime ... exposes no InferenceSession
docs.text:
Both ONNX extras are installed and one of their wheels was uninstalled, which deletes files the other one shares. Reinstall the wheel you want, last:

uv sync --inexact --extra onnx --reinstall-package onnxruntime                # CPU runtime
uv sync --inexact --extra onnx-gpu --reinstall-package onnxruntime-gpu        # CUDA runtime

With pip, pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps "onnxruntime==<the installed version>", or the same for onnxruntime-gpu. Installation explains why the two clash.

docs.title: pip install of the soma-retargeter extra fails to resolve
docs.text: That extra installs only with uv in a clone: uv sync --inexact --extra soma-retargeter. Its dependency pins a trimesh version that conflicts with Genesis, and only the clone's [tool.uv] override reconciles the two.

docs.title: import eden resolves to another checkout
docs.text:
A clone installs Eden in editable mode, so import eden loads the source tree that the environment was last synced from. Two clones or git worktrees sharing one virtual environment, uv run --active, or a stale VIRTUAL_ENV variable all send the import to the wrong tree. Give each clone its own environment, and do not use --active:

env -u VIRTUAL_ENV uv sync --all-extras --all-groups
.venv/bin/python -c "import eden; print(eden.__file__)"

docs.title: No task named '...' found in task registry
docs.text: The message suggests the closest name and lists every task. For a task in your own package, the package must be installed and named under the eden.tasks entry-point group of its pyproject.toml; see Your first task.

docs.title: Extra inputs are not permitted
docs.text: A config or option class received a field it does not have, usually a misspelling. Options refuse unknown fields on purpose, so that a typo cannot be silently ignored. The validation error names the field and the class; fix the spelling. To see the fields a term accepts, run eden terms --grep <term name>.

docs.title: A task builds from TASK_REGISTRY.get(name)() and then fails in env.build()
docs.text: get() returns the bare config class, and instantiating it runs none of the task's mods. For a task whose robot or data is chosen by a mod, the config constructs fine and then fails during the build, often on an empty name. Construct registered tasks with TASK_REGISTRY.build(name).

docs.title: cannot register ... as '...': that key is taken by ...
docs.text: Your term's name gives the same registry key as another term, possibly one of Eden's built-ins. Term keys are the term's name in snake case, and register() does not take a name=. Rename your function or class.

docs.title: Task mod flag(s) ... cannot apply to a replay
docs.text: You passed a variant flag to eden inference, eden export or eden deploy together with a checkpoint that has a config.json beside it. The saved config is what the policy was trained with, so it decides the variant. Drop the flag, or pass a saved config of your own with --config.

docs.title: --log-theme came after the subcommand
docs.text: --log-theme belongs to eden itself, so it goes before the subcommand: eden --log-theme human train .... Or set EDEN_LOG_THEME=human for the whole shell.

docs.title: The console output has no color
docs.text: That is the default. Eden's console theme defaults to agent, plain text without ANSI colors or the greeting box, because most of its output is read from log files. Use eden --log-theme human <command> or export EDEN_LOG_THEME=human for colored output, or auto to color only when writing to a terminal.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
See Assets and the download cache for download errors. Two more errors come from the asset root itself:

  • EDEN_ASSETS_DIR=... is a relative path: export an absolute path. The message prints the one it would have meant.
  • Cannot download assets into ... (a PermissionError): the directory is not writable. The message says whether EDEN_ASSETS_DIR chose it; point EDEN_ASSETS_DIR at a directory you can write.

docs.title: Headless machines: servers, SSH, containers
docs.text:
Training never opens a window; only --vis (or --show_viewer) does. On a machine without a display, leave --vis off and record a video instead:

eden inference --task reacher --checkpoint <path/to/model.pt> --rec    # writes an .mp4 into the run directory

A viewer opened without a display fails with No display detected.

Cameras render offscreen through EGL on Linux. When the EGL library is missing and OSMesa is installed, Genesis falls back to OSMesa, a software rasterizer that is much slower. Install EGL (Debian and Ubuntu shown) and select it explicitly:

sudo apt-get install -y libegl1
export PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=egl

Over SSH with X forwarding, a DISPLAY that points at a forwarded or dead X server makes the viewer and offscreen rendering fail or crawl. Unset it for headless runs:

unset DISPLAY
export PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=egl

PYOPENGL_PLATFORM must be set before genesis is imported, so export it in the shell rather than setting it inside a script after its imports. On a machine with several GPUs, EGL_DEVICE_ID picks the one EGL renders on.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub with the exact command, the full traceback, and the output of the install check.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Installation
  • Environment variables
  • Error messages: how Eden's errors are written, for contributors.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text: The action manager turns the policy's action vector into commands for the simulated actuators. This page covers how the vector is split across action terms, the built-in controllers (joint PD and velocity, task-space IK and operational-space control, floating bases, grippers and welds), action modifiers such as delay and motor models, and the rules the manager enforces. Read Writing terms first for the general term contract.

docs.title: How an action reaches the robot
docs.text:
Each entry of action_options is one action term. The manager lays the terms' action widths end to end in declaration order, so the policy's action vector is the concatenation of every term's slice:

flowchart LR
    A["policy action<br/>(num_envs, total_action_dim)"] --> S{"slice per term<br/>(declaration order)"}
    S --> T1["term.compute(actions)<br/>once per control step"]
    S --> T2["term.compute(actions)"]
    T1 --> P1["term.apply_actions()<br/>once per physics step, × decimation"]
    T2 --> P2["term.apply_actions()"]
    P1 --> G["entity.control_dofs_pos / _vel / _force"]
    P2 --> G
  • ActionManager.compute(action) runs once per control step (phase 1 of the step loop). It stores the raw action, hands each term its slice, and each term computes its command — its processed_action.
  • ActionManager.apply_actions() runs once per physics step, EnvOptions.decimation times per control step (phase 4). Each term writes its command to Genesis there.

env.step() also accepts a dict keyed by action-term name, one tensor per term, instead of the flat tensor. A flat tensor of the wrong width raises ValueError listing the expected per-term layout ([joint_pos_controller=7, gripper=1]); env.action_manager.summary() prints the same layout as a table with each term's slice.

A typical config, from the extreme-parkour student task (eden/tasks/extreme_parkour/student/config.py):

import eden as en
from eden.constants import ReferenceSource
from eden.managers.modifiers.actions import ActionDelay
from eden.options.managers.actions import ActionManagerOptions

action_options = ActionManagerOptions(
    dofs_pos_controller=en.actions.ImplicitPDController.configure(
        entity_name="robot",
        dofs_name=_GO2.dofs_name,  # the robot's joint names
        scale=0.25,
        reference_source=ReferenceSource.DEFAULT,
        modifier=ActionDelay.configure(delay_range_s=(0.02, 0.02)),
    )
)

Action terms are class terms only (there is no function-wrapper form). The built-in ones are importable from eden.actions (from eden import actions), which is eden.managers.terms.actions. Every action term takes entity_name and dofs_name; dofs_name accepts a list of names or regex/glob patterns and is resolved against the entity's own dofs_name.

docs.title: Joint controllers
docs.text:
The joint controllers command one DOF per action column. They share one target formula and one set of options.

Term Commands Genesis call Notes ImplicitPDController position target control_dofs_pos Genesis' built-in PD, integrated implicitly — the MuJoCo-like choice for sim-to-sim ExplicitPDController position target → torque kp·(target − q) − kd·q̇ control_dofs_force the torque is computed in Eden, so torque modifiers (friction, effort limits, motor strength) apply VelocityFeedforwardPDController position and velocity targets → torque kp·(q_t − q) + kd·(q̇_t·feed_forward_ratio − q̇) control_dofs_force action width is twice the DOF count: positions first, then velocities (velocity_scale) ImplicitVelocityController velocity target control_dofs_vel reference_source must stay "zero" ExplicitVelocityController velocity target → torque kp·(q̇_t − q̇), kp = (F_max − F_min)·velocity_gain control_dofs_force gain derived from the DOF force range NullJointAction the entity's default positions, always control_dofs_pos draws no action column; pins its DOFs

The explicit controllers read kp and kd from the entity once at build and re-read them on reset when the entity's DOF info is batched per env, so gain randomization (events.RandomizeKpKdGains) is picked up.

Explicit controllers want sim_substeps=1

apply_actions() runs once per scene.step(), and each scene.step() runs EnvOptions.sim_substeps solver substeps. An explicit controller's torque is therefore held constant across those substeps. Its docstring requires sim_substeps=1 so the PD torque is recomputed every physics step; raise decimation instead to keep the control rate. This is not checked for you.

Damping is explicit in torque mode under every integrator

The -kd·q̇ of ExplicitPDController, VelocityFeedforwardPDController and ExplicitVelocityController is computed by Eden, so it is explicit whatever EnvOptions.integrator says. Genesis' implicit integrators only damp the DOFs it drives itself in position or velocity mode (ImplicitPDController, ImplicitVelocityController), and the kd · substep_dt armature fold runs under integrator="euler" only. A kd that is stable through ImplicitPDController at a given substep can diverge through ExplicitPDController. See Entities.

docs.title: The position target
docs.text:
The position controllers build their target additively:

target = raw_action * scale + offset + reference_offset + dofs_pos_offset
  • scale — a float, a {pattern: value} dict over DOF names, or None (the default, which applies no scale and reads as "not set", so a robot-binding TaskMod can fill it). scale_ratio, when set, replaces scale with scale_ratio * (upper − lower) per DOF, from the entity's DOF position limits (an unbounded joint uses 2π).
  • offset — a float or a {pattern: value} dict.
  • reference_offset — chosen by reference_source, below.
  • dofs_pos_offset — a per-env offset set through set_dofs_pos_offset(), zero until something sets it. This is the hook for joint-zero domain randomization such as events.RandomizeDofsPosOffset.

reference_source takes a ReferenceSource (eden.constants) or its string value:

reference_source Reference added Use it for "default" (ReferenceSource.DEFAULT, the default for position controllers) the entity's default_dofs_pos the usual "action is an offset from the standing pose" "zero" (ZERO, the default for velocity controllers) nothing absolute targets "delta" (DELTA) the DOF positions measured at the start of the control step incremental control: target = q_now + scale·a "accumulate" (ACCUMULATE) — the action is integrated onto a persistent target, target_t = clamp(target_{t−1} + scale·a, soft limits), starting from and reset to default_dofs_pos policies that emit per-step increments of a held target "motion_ref" (MOTION_REF) the motion reference's joint positions for this step residual policies on top of a retargeted motion; needs a MimicRLEnvBase whose motion manager tracks the entity

A non-zero offset stacks on top of the reference under "default", "delta" and "motion_ref" (with a warning at build), and is refused under "accumulate", where it would be re-added every step. VelocityFeedforwardPDController refuses "accumulate", and the velocity controllers refuse anything but "zero".

The reacher task uses "delta" to low-pass its targets (eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py):

joint_pos_controller=actions.ImplicitPDController.configure(
    entity_name="robot",
    dofs_name="joint*",
    scale=0.05,
    reference_source=ReferenceSource.DELTA,
),

Dict-valued scale and offset. Keys are DOF-name patterns, applied in dict order (a later key overrides an earlier one on a DOF both match); DOFs no key matches get 1.0 for scale and 0.0 for offset. A key that matches no DOF of the entity always raises. dict_keys_scope decides what happens to a key that matches only DOFs another term controls: "term" (the default) raises; "entity" skips it, which lets the terms that split one robot share its whole-body dict instead of each carrying a filtered copy.

Read what was actually resolved off the term, not the options: effective_scale (a float, or a (1, num_dofs) tensor for a dict or scale_ratio) and effective_offset (the static offset with default_dofs_pos folded in under "default", plus any dofs_pos_offset).

docs.title: Coupled (mimic) joints
docs.text:
mimic_dofs derives extra position targets from the action instead of reading them off it — an underactuated hand whose follower joints track a driver at a fixed ratio. Each entry is follower: (driver, multiplier, offset), and the follower is commanded driver_target * multiplier + offset:

ImplicitPDController.configure(
    entity_name="left_hand",
    dofs_name=InspireRH56DFQ_L.actuated_dofs_name,  # the 6 drivers: the action columns
    mimic_dofs=InspireRH56DFQ_L.metadata.mimic_dofs,  # follower -> (driver, multiplier, offset)
)

The action stays driver-wide (action_dim counts the drivers), while processed_action, dofs_name and dofs_idx_local widen to drivers-then-followers after build. mimic_follower_dofs_name lists the followers, so a deployment whose hardware couples them itself can leave them out. Drivers must be in dofs_name, followers must not be, chains (a follower driven by a follower) are refused, and only ImplicitPDController and ExplicitPDController support it. A follower that Genesis already couples through a joint equality (a URDF <mimic> tag) is refused, because the PD targets would fight the constraint.

docs.title: Task-space controllers
docs.text:
Term Action What it does DifferentialIKController 6: a world-frame (x, y, z, rx, ry, rz) delta, squashed by tanh and scaled by position_scale / orientation_scale damped-least-squares differential IK at a control point (ee_link_name, ee_local_pos); commands q + Δq through control_dofs_pos. damping (default 0.1), max_dq clamps the per-step joint change, orientation_weight=0.0 makes it position-only OperationalSpaceController 3 (control_mode="position") or 6 ("pose"): a clipped, scaled delta applied to the measured control-point pose operational-space control: the absolute target is held while feedback, Jacobian, inertia and the optional nullspace posture term are recomputed every physics step; commands torques through control_dofs_force IKPoseController 7: an absolute base-frame target pose [x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz] (wxyz), optionally at a tool frame offset from the link solves Genesis IK from the measured joint configuration each control step; max_joint_delta, joint_limit_margin, and residual checks that hold the measured pose when IK fails

Use DifferentialIKController for a policy that emits per-step deltas relative to the measured pose, and IKPoseController for one that emits accumulated absolute targets. OperationalSpaceController does not add Coriolis or centrifugal terms; gravity compensation is a material setting on the kinematic-tree root (RigidMaterialOptions(gravity_compensation=1.0)). Its full parameter contract is in its docstring and the Term Catalog.

docs.title: Floating bases: FreeBasePoseController
docs.text:
An entity that stands on nothing — a dexterous hand or a gripper with no arm under it — is driven through its free joint. FreeBasePoseController takes six numbers per env: a world-axis translation (position_scale metres per unit) and a world-axis rotation vector (orientation_scale radians per unit), both applied to the entity's default root pose, so the target is absolute and a zero action holds the default pose. It resolves the free joint itself and takes no dofs_name; it writes its own gains (position_kp, position_kd, orientation_kp, orientation_kd) and limits (force_limit, torque_limit) to the six free-joint DOFs at build.

Gravity is not in its loop. Give the entity RigidMaterialOptions(gravity_compensation=1.0), as a real arm's controller would, or it hangs m·g / position_kp below its target.

docs.title: Grippers and welds
docs.text:
Term Action What it does BinaryJointController 1: > 0 (or True) closes, <= 0 opens drives dofs_name to close_action or open_action (floats or per-DOF dicts) GripperDecisionController 1, in the units input names owns the open/close decision for a policy server's gripper scalar: input ("sign", "open_sign", "closedness", "openness"), thresholds and hysteresis, hold_steps, sticky_repeats latch, continuous interpolation, and on_missing for a NaN command. With the defaults it behaves like BinaryJointController SuctionCupWelding 1: suction on/off welds the link touching ee_link_name to it while on ParallelJawWelding 1: weld on/off welds a link to ee_link_name once both pads (left_gripper_link_name, right_gripper_link_name) press it above grasp_force_threshold

The welding terms command no DOF. List support surfaces (table, floor) in ignore_entities_name; ignore_links_idx takes solver-global link indices (env.entities["table"].get_link("top").idx), not entity-local ones.

ParallelJawWelding is a simulation surrogate (sim_surrogate is True): it stands in for sim contact friction, while on the robot the gripper joints closing — commanded by a separate joint term — hold the object, so a deployment sends nothing for it. SuctionCupWelding is not: it is the vacuum bit, and a deployment that cannot carry it must say so.

docs.title: Action modifiers
docs.text:
The joint controllers take one modifier= — an ActionModifier options object — that transforms the command on its way to the actuator. To use several, wrap them in Compose. Modifiers live in eden.managers.modifiers.actions (TorqueOffset is only in eden.managers.modifiers.actions.actuators).

A modifier overrides up to three hooks, which run at two rates:

Hook Runs Acts on Built-in modifiers modify_processed_action(target) once per control step, in the controller's compute() the target; its output is processed_action GearBacklash, EnvelopeClip modify_applied_target(target) once per physics step, in apply_actions() the command the actuator acts on this physics step ActionDelay modify_ctrl_torque(torque, dofs_vel, pos_err) once per physics step, after the control law the computed torque FrictionModel, EffortClip, MotorStrength, TorqueOffset, ConstantTorqueKick, Deadband

This config from the HOMIE task (eden/tasks/homie/config.py) chains a task-local motor model with a per-episode delay:

from eden import actions
from eden.constants import ReferenceSource
from eden.managers.modifiers.actions import ActionDelay, Compose

dofs_pos_controller=actions.ExplicitPDController.configure(
    entity_name="robot",
    dofs_name=LEG_DOFS,
    scale=HOMIE_ACTION_SCALE,
    reference_source=ReferenceSource.DEFAULT,
    modifier=Compose.configure(
        modifiers=[
            HomieMotorModel.configure(rfi_scale=0.05, offset_scale=0.05),
            ActionDelay.configure(delay_range_steps=(0, DECIMATION - 1)),
        ]
    ),
),

Compose calls its children in list order within each hook, but the hooks run at different points of a step: every modify_processed_action first, then every modify_applied_target, then every modify_ctrl_torque. So a physics-step modifier such as ActionDelay acts after a control-step one such as EnvelopeClip wherever each is listed; listing it first logs a warning.

Torque modifiers do nothing on an implicit controller

ImplicitPDController and ImplicitVelocityController hand a target to Genesis and never compute a torque, so they never call modify_ctrl_torque. FrictionModel, EffortClip, MotorStrength, TorqueOffset, ConstantTorqueKick and Deadband attached to one are silently inert. Use an explicit controller for a motor model.

FrictionModel, EffortClip and EnvelopeClip read their defaults from the entity's actuator spec when a parameter is None; explicit values override it.

docs.title: ActionDelay
docs.text:
ActionDelay delays the command the actuator acts on by d physics steps, drawn uniformly per env at each reset from delay_range_steps (physics steps, inclusive) or delay_range_s (seconds, each end a whole multiple of sim_dt) — not both. Because the unit is the physics step, a latency shorter than one control step is expressible: at sim_dt=0.005 and decimation=4, d=2 keeps the first two physics steps of every control step on the previous command. After a reset the history is backfilled with the first new command.

processed_action stays undelayed — it is the command the policy issued and what a deployment sends. eden deploy never calls apply_actions(), so it never applies the delay: the real robot has only its own latency, and a MuJoCo sim-to-sim run has none. A policy trained against a delay therefore runs there with less latency than it trained with.

docs.title: Clipping actions
docs.text:
The action manager does not clip. Two places do:

  • The runner: clip_actions on the rsl_rl runner options (and on the rl_games options and the env wrappers) clamps actions to [-clip_actions, clip_actions] before the env sees them. It must be a finite positive bound, or None for no clamp. See Training runs.
  • The term: a term can clamp inside its own compute(). Clamping only the target keeps the raw action unclipped, which is what action-rate penalties read — see the example below.

docs.title: Reading what was commanded
docs.text:
Attribute Shape Meaning env.action_manager.action / .prev_action (num_envs, total_action_dim) the raw policy action this step and last step term.action / term.prev_action (num_envs, action_dim) the term's raw slice term.processed_action (num_envs, ...) the command the term issued: a joint PD controller's target raw·scale + offset + reference, after control-step modifiers env.action_manager.processed_actions dict[str, Tensor] every term's processed_action, keyed by term name term.effective_scale, term.effective_offset what the joint controller resolved, see above

Read processed_action rather than recomputing the target at the call site: a recomputation silently drops whatever control-step modifiers are configured. Rewards such as rewards.action_rate_l2 and observations such as observations.last_action read the raw action, by default over the whole vector or, with action_term_name / action_name, one term's slice.

docs.title: Rules the action manager enforces
docs.text:
These raise at env construction, naming the config keys involved:

  • dofs_name must name single-DOF joints. A term's scale / offset dicts and a deployment's motor map are keyed by joint name, so a free or ball joint — whose name Entity.dofs_name lists once per DOF — is refused, naming the joint and its DOF count. No shipped robot lists one; a .* in an entity's own dofs_name is the usual way in. To drive a floating base, use FreeBasePoseController; to place one at reset, write it from an event (events.reset_base_state_uniform).
  • Two terms cannot command the same DOF. Each term writes its own control target to Genesis every physics step, and control_dofs_* replaces a DOF's control mode and target, so an overlap would be last-writer-wins: the losing term is a no-op on the shared DOFs while its slice still costs policy output and still feeds action-rate rewards. Give each term a disjoint dofs_name — the arm/gripper split every manipulation task uses. Reordering the terms is not a fix. The check walks resolved DOF indices, so two FreeBasePoseControllers on one entity are refused too.
  • A term must draw an action column or command a DOF. A term with neither is almost always a forgotten dofs_name (it defaults to [], which matches nothing). NullJointAction draws no column but commands its DOFs; the welding terms command no DOF but draw a column. A term class that applies a per-physics-step disturbance and needs neither declares _acts_without_action_ = True.

On the first step, a joint term whose command width differs from its DOF count raises naming the term, instead of Genesis' shape error.

docs.title: Writing an action term
docs.text:
Subclass ActionTerm (or one of the controllers) and implement compute(actions), called once per control step with the term's slice, and apply_actions(), called once per physics step. Register it with @ACTION_TERM_REGISTRY.register(). Keep self._raw_action and self._prev_action up to date in compute() so the observations and rewards that read action / prev_action see the policy's output.

This task-local controller from the reorientation task (eden/tasks/reorient/custom_terms/actions.py, trimmed) clamps the action for the target only, smooths the target with an EMA, and holds the default pose for a warmup window:

import torch

from eden.managers import ACTION_TERM_REGISTRY
from eden.managers.terms.actions.joint_actions import ImplicitPDController
from eden.utils.string import term_subject


@ACTION_TERM_REGISTRY.register()
class JointPositionOffsetEma(ImplicitPDController):
    ema_alpha: float = 0.5
    warmup_time_s: float = 0.4

    def build(self) -> None:
        super().build()
        if not 0.0 < self.ema_alpha <= 1.0:
            raise ValueError(f"{term_subject(self)}: ema_alpha must be in (0, 1], got {self.ema_alpha}.")
        # effective_offset already folds in default_dofs_pos for reference_source="default".
        self._default_target = self.effective_offset.expand(self.num_envs, -1).clone()
        self._ema_target = self._default_target.clone()
        soft_limits = self.entity.soft_dofs_pos_limits[:, self.entity.find_named_dofs(self.dofs_name).columns]
        self._target_lower = soft_limits[..., 0].expand(self.num_envs, -1)
        self._target_upper = soft_limits[..., 1].expand(self.num_envs, -1)

    def compute(self, actions: torch.Tensor) -> None:
        self._prev_action[:] = self._raw_action
        self._raw_action[:] = actions  # unclipped: the action-rate penalty reads this
        raw_target = self._compute_pos_target(self._raw_action.clamp(-1.0, 1.0))
        raw_target = raw_target.clamp(self._target_lower, self._target_upper)
        self._ema_target = self.ema_alpha * raw_target + (1.0 - self.ema_alpha) * self._ema_target
        in_warmup = (self._env.episode_length_buf * self._env.dt < self.warmup_time_s).unsqueeze(-1)
        self._processed_action = torch.where(in_warmup, self._default_target, self._ema_target)
        self._ema_target = self._processed_action

    def reset(self, envs_idx=None) -> None:
        super().reset(envs_idx)
        idx = slice(None) if envs_idx is None else envs_idx
        self._ema_target[idx] = self._default_target[idx]

apply_actions() is inherited from ImplicitPDController. A term that writes its own apply_actions() must drive the entity with self._applied_command() exactly once per call, so a physics-step modifier such as ActionDelay advances; reading self._processed_action directly skips it. Pass self.genesis_dofs_idx (a range when the DOFs are contiguous) as dofs_idx_local= to the entity's control_dofs_* calls.

docs.text:
• Writing terms — the general term contract
