docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
A command is the goal a policy is asked to reach: a base velocity to track, a target position for an end-effector, a gait phase, a frame of a motion clip. The command manager owns these goals, resamples them on a timer and on every reset, and publishes them for observation and reward terms to read. This page covers the built-in command terms, the per-step timing a command term has to respect, and how to write your own.

Commands exist only on RL environments (RLEnvBase and MimicRLEnvBase), configured through EdenRLConfig.command_options.

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
The velocity-tracking tasks sample a planar base velocity every 3 to 8 seconds (eden/tasks/velocity_tracking/base_config.py):

import math

from eden.managers.terms import UniformVelocityCommand
from eden.options.managers.commands import CommandManagerOptions

command_options = CommandManagerOptions(
    velocity_command=UniformVelocityCommand.configure(
        entity_name="robot",
        resampling_time_range=(3.0, 8.0),
        rel_standing_envs=0.1,
        rel_heading_envs=0.3,
        heading_command=True,
        heading_control_stiffness=0.5,
        lin_vel_x_range=(-1.0, 1.0),
        lin_vel_y_range=(-1.0, 1.0),
        ang_vel_z_range=(-0.5, 0.5),
        heading_range=(-math.pi, math.pi),
    )
)

The key (velocity_command) is the name every other term uses to find the command. The policy sees it through the generated_commands observation, and the tracking rewards read it by the same name:

from eden import observations
from eden.terms import ObsTerm

velocity_command = ObsTerm.configure(
    func=observations.generated_commands,
    params={"command_name": "velocity_command"},
)

Inside a term, read it with env.command_manager.get_command(name) (the command tensor) or env.command_manager.get_term(name) (the term object, for its extra attributes). Both raise a KeyError listing the active command terms when the name is wrong. A task that declares no command terms has env.command_manager is None.

docs.title: Fields every command term has
docs.text:
Field Type Default Meaning resampling_time_range tuple[float, float] \| None None Seconds until the next resample, drawn uniformly per env after every resample. debug_vis bool False Call the term's draw_vis() every step, outside training only.

A resampled term needs resampling_time_range

The base default is None, and there is no check for it: a term that resamples (such as UniformVelocityCommand or UniformT3Command) and is configured without a range fails with a TypeError from uniform_() on the first reset. Terms that never resample set a very long range themselves: ConstantVelocityCommand, OperatorVelocityCommand and GaitPhaseCommand default to (1.0e9, 1.0e9).

docs.title: Built-in command terms
docs.text:
All of them are in eden.managers.terms.commands (also importable from eden.managers.terms or as eden.commands). eden terms --kind command prints each one with every parameter and default, and the full list is in the generated term catalog.

Term Command shape What it does UniformVelocityCommand (num_envs, 3) (vx, vy, wz) in the robot's base frame, sampled uniformly from lin_vel_x_range, lin_vel_y_range, ang_vel_z_range. ConstantVelocityCommand (num_envs, 3) The same command held at command_value (or whatever set_command() was last given), clamped into the configured ranges. OperatorVelocityCommand (num_envs, 3) A ConstantVelocityCommand re-read from a keyboard or gamepad every control step (device_name, device_options). UniformT3Command (num_envs, 3) A target position sampled from x_range, y_range, z_range. UniformSE3Command (num_envs, 7) A target pose: position from x_range/y_range/z_range, then a wxyz quaternion from roll_range/pitch_range/yaw_range. GaitPhaseCommand (num_envs, num_feet) A per-foot phase in [-pi, pi] advancing at gait_frequency Hz, offset by phase_offset between feet. MotionCommand (num_envs, 2 × clip joints) The current frame of one or more motion clips (.npz): the clip's joint positions, then its joint velocities. Link and base poses are separate accessors.

docs.title: Velocity commands
docs.text:
UniformVelocityCommand has two optional behaviours on top of the uniform draw:

  • Heading control. With heading_command=True, a fraction rel_heading_envs of the resampled envs gets a target heading drawn from heading_range instead of a yaw rate; each step their wz is set to heading_control_stiffness * heading_error, clipped to ang_vel_z_range. heading_command=True with heading_range=None raises at construction.
  • Standing envs. A fraction rel_standing_envs of the resampled envs is commanded all zeros.

ConstantVelocityCommand and OperatorVelocityCommand are what a deployment substitutes for a trained UniformVelocityCommand, so that the robot goes where the operator says instead of where the training distribution says. Both clamp into lin_vel_x_range, lin_vel_y_range and ang_vel_z_range, which a deploy fills from the term it replaces. A degenerate range such as (0.5, 0.5) pins that axis: the policy only ever saw one value there. OperatorVelocityCommand opens its input device in build() and is not meant for training, since a training run would sit at whatever the sticks read. See Deployment.

docs.title: Pose and position targets
docs.text:
UniformT3Command can show its goal: set debug_vis=True and either marker_entity_name (a scene entity, for example a non-colliding sphere, that is moved to the goal each step) or nothing (a debug sphere of marker_radius and marker_color is drawn). Prefer the marker entity when you record video: debug draws appear only in the interactive viewer, not in camera recordings. marker_frame_entity names the entity whose frame the command is expressed in (for example the robot base); left empty, the command is world-frame.

The reacher benchmark (eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py) is a complete task built on UniformT3Command.

docs.title: Gait phase
docs.text: GaitPhaseCommand.command holds raw phase angles. Feed them to the policy with the sin_phase / cos_phase observation terms (eden/managers/terms/observations/locomotion.py). With velocity_command_name set, the phase of every foot is pinned to stand_phase_value in the envs whose velocity command is below stand_velocity_threshold, so a gait reward stops asking for steps while the robot is told to stand.

docs.title: Motion clips
docs.text: MotionCommand plays BeyondMimic-format .npz clips (motion_file, or motion_files for one clip per env) and exposes the current reference frame through links_*_w, base_*_w and anchor_*_w accessors. It is the lightweight motion path, used by the frozen-policy ports and single-clip tracking on a plain RLEnvBase; the training-grade path is the motion manager of MimicRLEnvBase. motion_command_options(...) builds the {"motion": MotionCommand} entry for a policy. Both paths, their sampling modes and the clip format are described in Motion tracking.

docs.title: When a command term runs
docs.text:
A command term has three per-step hooks, and which one you put state in decides whether the reward sees it in the same step or a step late. The full step order is the table in Environments; the rows that concern commands are:

Phase Call What belongs there 3 CommandTerm.pre_physics_advance() Advance a time-based reference before physics, so the post-physics robot is graded against the matching frame (MotionCommand advances its clip clock here). 5 CommandTerm.post_physics_refresh() Everything that grades this step: caches of the post-physics robot state, hold counters, contact latches, tracking errors. The metric, termination and reward managers (phases 6–9) read it in the same step. 13 CommandTerm.reset(envs_idx) Runs for the envs being reset: logs stats, then resamples them. 17 CommandTerm.compute(dt) Ticks the resampling clock, calls _resample_command() for expired envs, then _update_command(). This publishes the command the next action is chosen from. 20 CommandTerm.draw_vis() Only for terms with debug_vis=True, and only when the env is not training.

Commands are published at phase 17, after the reward at phase 9, on purpose: the policy chose this step's action from the command it observed at the end of the previous step, so the reward must grade against that command, not a freshly resampled one.

Grading state goes in post_physics_refresh, not _update_command

_update_command() runs at phase 17, below the reward. A value derived from the post-physics robot and written there is read by the reward one control step late, and a value cleared there is never read at all: the step that earned it is graded through the cleared buffer and pays zero. Compute such state in post_physics_refresh(). The test is what the state is, not who reads it — the command itself still belongs in _update_command(). Terms explains the rule in full.

On the deployment path (eden deploy) only some hooks run: advance_reference() (which calls pre_physics_advance() by default), compute() and draw_vis(). post_physics_refresh() never runs there, because there is no physics to bracket and no reward to grade. State the policy's observations read must therefore also be produced from compute(); an idempotent cache refresh can live in both hooks, as MotionCommand's robot-state cache does. A term whose pre_physics_advance() resets or teleports the robot (a clip wrap) must override advance_reference() with a clock-only advance, and rewind_reference() with a clock-only rewind.

docs.title: Resampling
docs.text:
A command is resampled in two situations:

  • On reset. CommandManager.reset() resamples the reset envs (phase 13, after the scene reset and the RESET events). The command an env starts its episode with is therefore always fresh.
  • On its timer. Every step, compute() subtracts dt from each env's time_left; the envs at or below zero are resampled and get a new time_left drawn from resampling_time_range.

command_counter counts each env's resamples since its last reset.

Per-env statistics a term puts in its stats dict (each a (num_envs,) tensor) are averaged over the envs being reset, logged as Commands/<term_name>/<stat>, and zeroed for those envs.

docs.title: Writing a command term
docs.text:
Subclass CommandTerm, register it, and implement three members:

import torch

from eden.managers import COMMAND_TERM_REGISTRY, CommandTerm
from eden.utils.sample import sample_uniform_ranges


@COMMAND_TERM_REGISTRY.register()
class UniformHeightCommand(CommandTerm):
    """A target base height, resampled on a timer."""

    height_range: tuple[float, float] = (0.6, 0.8)

    def __init__(self, env, options):
        super().__init__(env, options)
        self._target = torch.zeros(self.num_envs, 1, device=self.device)

    @property
    def command(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self._target

    def _resample_command(self, envs_idx: torch.Tensor) -> None:
        sampled = sample_uniform_ranges((self.height_range,), self.num_envs, self.device)
        self._target.copy_(torch.where(envs_idx.unsqueeze(-1), sampled, self._target))

    def _update_command(self) -> None:
        pass  # the target is constant between resamples

command_options = CommandManagerOptions(
    base_height=UniformHeightCommand.configure(height_range=(0.5, 0.9), resampling_time_range=(4.0, 6.0)),
)

The contract for each member:

  • command — a property returning the (num_envs, ...) tensor other terms read. Return the same buffer every time and update it in place.
  • _resample_command(envs_idx) — always receives a (num_envs,) bool mask with at least one True, whatever selector reached the manager (the timer mask, the auto-reset's reset_buf, a slice, an index tensor). An empty selection never reaches it, so do not guard for one. Write through torch.where over a full-batch draw, as above, rather than indexing with the mask: self.cmd[envs_idx] = ... is correct but costs a GPU→CPU sync for the gather and another for the write, and this method runs every control step. A scalar fill such as self.flag[envs_idx] = False is fine. len(envs_idx) is num_envs, not the number of selected envs.
  • _update_command() — publishes the command for the next step (phase 17). Closing the loop of a goal state machine (deciding a goal was reached and drawing the next one) belongs here too.

Resolve entities and other terms in build(), so a bad name raises at env construction; see UniformVelocityCommand.build() for the pattern, and Terms for the general rules (state in build(), entity handles re-resolved through resolve_entity, no GPU syncs on the hot path).

docs.title: Replacing a command term after build
docs.text:
CommandManager.swap_term(name, options) builds a new term from options, installs it under name, and returns the old term. It is how a deployment puts an operator-driven or held command in place of the trained generator. The replacement's command must have the same shape as the one it replaces, or swap_term raises a ValueError: the observation layout and the policy's input width were fixed by the old term. restore_term(name, term) puts back the exact object swap_term returned.

swap_term does not repoint terms that cached the replaced term in their own build() (self._command = env.command_manager.get_term(...)). Code that needs those to follow the swap must repoint them itself, as DeploymentBase does.

docs.title: Curricula
docs.text:
A curriculum term changes the task while it trains: it widens a command range on a schedule, ramps a penalty weight up as the policy gets better, or tightens a termination tolerance as the success rate rises. This page covers when curriculum terms run, the built-in terms, what happens to them at evaluation, and how to write one that other terms can read.

Curricula exist only on RL environments, configured through EdenRLConfig.curriculum_options.

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
The velocity-tracking tasks widen the commanded velocity in three stages (eden/tasks/velocity_tracking/base_config.py):

from eden.managers.terms import VelocityCommandCurriculum
from eden.options.managers.curricula import CurriculumManagerOptions

curriculum_options = CurriculumManagerOptions(
    command_vel=VelocityCommandCurriculum.configure(
        command_name="velocity_command",
        velocity_stages=[
            {"step": 0, "lin_vel_x": (-1.0, 1.0), "ang_vel_z": (-0.5, 0.5)},
            {"step": 5000 * 24, "lin_vel_x": (-1.5, 2.0), "ang_vel_z": (-0.7, 0.7)},
            {"step": 10000 * 24, "lin_vel_x": (-2.0, 3.0)},
        ],
    ),
)

step is compared with env.common_step_counter, the number of control steps (env.step() calls) the env has taken. All envs step together, so it is not multiplied by num_envs. With RSL-RL collecting num_steps_per_env=24 steps per iteration (that task's runner setting), 5000 * 24 is reached after 5000 iterations.

The reacher benchmark raises a penalty weight the same way (eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py):

from eden.managers.terms.curricula.rewards import StageRewardWeightCurriculum

curriculum_options = CurriculumManagerOptions(
    reaching_weight=StageRewardWeightCurriculum.configure(
        reward_term_name="joint_vel_hinge",
        weight_stages=[(0, -0.01), (100 * 24, -0.1), (200 * 24, -1.0)],
    )
)

docs.title: When curriculum terms run
docs.text:
Phase Call Runs at eval? 13 CurriculumManager.reset(envs_idx): log every term's last published state, then call each class term's reset(envs_idx) for the envs that finished an episode logging only (there is nothing to log); term reset() does not run 16 CurriculumManager.compute(): call every term's compute() in declaration order and cache what it returns no

Phase 16 is after the auto-reset and before the commands are published (phase 17), so a range a curriculum writes takes effect on the next resample. The full step order is in Environments.

compute() runs on every control step, not once per iteration. A term that moves a level by a fixed amount per call (PenaltyCurriculum moves its scale by degree) moves it once per step.

A term's reset(envs_idx) is where it accumulates the statistics compute() adapts from: an episode-length average, a success rate. It runs during the reset at phase 13, before episode_length_buf is zeroed, so env.episode_length_buf[envs_idx] still holds the finished episodes' lengths.

compute() returns the term's published state: a dict of scalars, logged as Curriculum/<term_name>/<key> (a non-dict value is logged as Curriculum/<term_name>).

docs.title: Curricula are frozen at eval
docs.text:
When the env is built with eval_mode=True (env.training is False), the curriculum manager's compute() and the terms' reset() do nothing. An eval rollout's difficulty is therefore fixed, and no Curriculum/* key is logged for the whole rollout.

What a term holds at eval is what it installed at build. That is the level the config pins, not the level the training run ended at:

  • VelocityCommandCurriculum and StageRewardWeightCurriculum write nothing until their first compute(), so at eval the command ranges and the reward weight are the ones configured on the command and reward terms.
  • PenaltyCurriculum installs initial_scale on its reward terms in build(), so at eval those terms run at initial_scale times their configured weight.

To evaluate at a later level, set that level in the config the eval builds from.

A resumed run restarts every curriculum

env.common_step_counter starts at 0 when an env is constructed, and Eden does not restore it, or any curriculum term's internal state, from a checkpoint. A run resumed from a checkpoint replays its step-scheduled stages from the first one, and adaptive terms restart their averages.

docs.title: Built-in curriculum terms
docs.text:
All built-ins live in eden.managers.terms.curricula (also eden.curricula). eden terms --kind curriculum prints them with every parameter, and the generated term catalog has the same list.

Term Drives Adapts from VelocityCommandCurriculum the lin_vel_x_range, lin_vel_y_range, ang_vel_z_range of command term command_name velocity_stages: dicts with a step and any of lin_vel_x, lin_vel_y, ang_vel_z StageRewardWeightCurriculum the weight of reward term reward_term_name weight_stages: (step, weight) pairs; the latest stage reached wins PenaltyCurriculum a scale on the weights of several reward terms (configured_weight * scale) the average episode length: up by degree above level_up_threshold, down below level_down_threshold, within [min_scale, max_scale] AverageEpisodeLengthTracker nothing; publishes average_episode_length and is_primed an EMA of episode length MotionBasePoseThresholdCurriculum the pos_threshold / rot_threshold of a MotionBasePoseTrackingBreak termination an EMA of the per-episode success rate (an episode succeeds when its clip runs out rather than the pose gate firing) SuccessGuidedSampling which configuration each resetting env draws, for the RESET event that binds it as its sampler each configuration's success rate over its last history episodes (graded by termination success_term); draws peak at target

Each term resolves what it drives in build(), so a wrong command_name, reward_term_name or termination_term_name raises at env construction: the command, termination and reward managers are built before the curriculum manager.

PenaltyCurriculum selects its reward terms either by reward_term_names or by reward_term_tags (matched against each reward term's tags), never both; setting both or neither raises. A tag selection that matches no term logs a warning and does nothing. It normally keeps its own buffer of the last num_episode_average episode lengths; with tracker_name it reads an AverageEpisodeLengthTracker instead, which several penalty curricula can share:

from eden.managers.terms.curricula import AverageEpisodeLengthTracker, PenaltyCurriculum

curriculum_options = CurriculumManagerOptions(
    # Declared first: the consumers below read it in the same step.
    ep_tracker=AverageEpisodeLengthTracker.configure(num_compute_average_epl=1000),
    penalty_torques=PenaltyCurriculum.configure(reward_term_tags=["penalty"], tracker_name="ep_tracker"),
    penalty_smoothness=PenaltyCurriculum.configure(reward_term_tags=["smoothness"], tracker_name="ep_tracker"),
)

The tags are the ones you set on the targeted reward terms (tags=["penalty"] in their configure()), not the curriculum's own key. AverageEpisodeLengthTracker's effective window is max(1, int(num_compute_average_epl * num_envs / 4096)) resets, so the same setting gives the same time constant at any env count; it reports is_primed=False until its first finished episode, and PenaltyCurriculum does not move its scale before then.

Task packages add their own, for example TerrainLevelCurriculum (eden/tasks/extreme_parkour/custom_terms/curricula.py) and GoalRangeCurriculum (eden/tasks/manipulation/custom_terms/curricula.py).

docs.title: Reading another term's state
docs.text:
env.curriculum_manager.get_state(name) returns what the named term published in this step. It never returns None and never serves an older value: every way there can be no current state raises, and each message names the fix.

Situation Raises Fix No curriculum term has that name KeyError, listing the declared terms Use one of the listed keys, or add the term. The env is in eval mode (every step of the rollout) RuntimeError Read the term itself (below). The named term is declared after the term reading it RuntimeError, naming both Move the producer above the consumer in curriculum_options. The read happens before the run's first compute() (in build(), the first reset, task setup) RuntimeError Read the term itself. The named term's compute() returned None RuntimeError Return a dict from that term's compute(). The read runs earlier in the step than phase 16 (a curriculum reset(), a metric, a termination, a reward) RuntimeError, naming both steps Read the term itself, or move the read after phase 16.

Terms compute in declaration order, so a producer must be declared above every curriculum term that reads it. A term must publish on every step: one that returns a dict on some steps and None on others makes get_state raise on exactly the steps it skipped.

Need the level at eval too? Read the term, not the manager

get_state raises for the whole of an eval rollout, by design: a consumer that fell back to a default there would grade the eval at a difficulty no training step used. A term that needs the current level in both modes resolves the curriculum term once in build() with env.curriculum_manager.get_term(name) and reads the attribute it exposes. ObjectVelocityDisturbance does this with AdaptiveEpisodeCurriculum.value (eden/tasks/reorient/custom_terms/). Do not catch the error and substitute a default.

Do not call CurriculumManager.compute() yourself to refresh a value: terms adapt as a side effect of computing, so a second call in one step advances the curriculum twice.

docs.title: Reset-configuration samplers
docs.text:
A curriculum term can also decide which stored start state each env resets to. A RESET event that owns a fixed set of starts, such as ResetFromStateBuffer, names a curriculum term with sampler="<config key>"; that term must subclass ResetConfigSampler (eden/managers/resets/sampling.py) next to CurriculumTerm. The event resolves it in build() (the curriculum manager is built before the event manager), binds it to the set's size once, and asks it for indices on every reset. A name that is missing, or a term that is not a ResetConfigSampler, raises at env construction. Without sampler, rows are drawn uniformly. See Events.

SuccessGuidedSampling is the built-in sampler (Success Guided Sampling, Zhang et al., CoRL 2026). It keeps the last history outcomes of every configuration, grades each finished episode in the RESET event that starts the next, and draws the next configuration from a softmax over a Beta-shaped kernel peaked at target, so most episodes go to configurations the policy solves sometimes. Its defaults are the paper's locomotion settings, it draws uniformly at eval, and a term no reset event binds raises at env construction. Extreme parkour wires it in with --terrain_sampler sgs.

docs.title: Writing a curriculum term
docs.text:
Subclass CurriculumTerm, register it, resolve what it drives in build(), and return a dict from compute():

from eden.managers import CURRICULUM_TERM_REGISTRY, CurriculumTerm


@CURRICULUM_TERM_REGISTRY.register()
class LinearSpeedRamp(CurriculumTerm):
    """Widen a velocity command's x range linearly over ramp_steps control steps."""

    command_name: str = "velocity_command"
    start_speed: float = 0.5
    max_speed: float = 2.0
    ramp_steps: int = 100_000

    def build(self) -> None:
        self._command = self._env.command_manager.get_term(self.command_name)

    def compute(self, *args, **kwargs) -> dict[str, float]:
        frac = min(self._env.common_step_counter / self.ramp_steps, 1.0)
        speed = self.start_speed + frac * (self.max_speed - self.start_speed)
        self._command.lin_vel_x_range = (-speed, speed)
        return {"max_speed": speed}
  • compute() runs every control step in training, so keep it cheap and free of GPU→CPU syncs. A per-episode statistic belongs in reset(envs_idx); reduce it on the device (eden.utils.misc.sum_over_envs), as MotionBasePoseThresholdCurriculum.reset does, because envs_idx is the auto-reset's bool mask on most steps.
  • Install the starting level in build() if eval should see it: compute() never runs at eval.
  • Expose the current level as an attribute if other terms need it in eval as well as in training.

A function term works too, through eden.terms.CurrTerm.configure(func=..., params={...}). Its function is called as func(env=env, **params) once per step and its return value is published the same way.

docs.title: Datasets and recording
docs.text: Any Eden env can record itself: you list recorder terms in the config, start recording, and every finished episode is written to an HDF5 (or NPZ) file. Teleoperation sessions, scripted demonstrations (eden datagen) and policy rollouts all produce the same layout, and eden lerobot convert turns it into a LeRobot dataset. This page is the how-to for demonstration data. The recorder manager itself — the term hooks and how to write a recorder term — is covered in Metrics and recorders.

docs.title: Record a session
docs.text:
Add recorder_options to the env, choose the HDF5 file handler, and bracket the part you want with start_recording() / end_recording():

from eden.constants import DatasetExportMode
from eden.managers.terms.recorders import ActionRecorder, InitialStateRecorder, ObservationRecorder, StateRecorder
from eden.options import RecorderManagerOptions
from eden.utils.file_handler import HDF5FileHandler

recorder_options = RecorderManagerOptions(
    file_handler_options=HDF5FileHandler.configure(),
    dataset_export_dir_path="data/teleop",
    dataset_filename="franka_pick",                 # -> data/teleop/franka_pick.hdf5
    dataset_export_mode=DatasetExportMode.EXPORT_ALL,
    observations=ObservationRecorder.configure(),   # obs/<group>, needs observation groups
    actions=ActionRecorder.configure(),             # action
    state=StateRecorder.configure(entity_name="robot"),
    initial_state=InitialStateRecorder.configure(),
)

Pass it as recorder_options= to the env constructor (or set config.recorder_options on a task config), then:

recorder = env.recorder_manager
recorder.start_recording(reset_scene=True)   # reset first, so the episode starts from a fresh state
...                                          # step the env from your device or policy
recorder.end_recording()                     # exports the episodes in progress
recorder.close()                             # flushes and closes the file

Each key under RecorderManagerOptions other than the manager's own fields is one recorder term; the key name is yours. examples/recipes/teleop/keyboard/teleoperation_keyboard_viser_recorder.py is a complete teleop session with recording and replay of the last demo.

Nothing is recorded until start_recording()

A configured recorder manager stays idle until you call start_recording(); eden train and eden inference never call it. Without any recorder term, start_recording() only logs a warning.

docs.title: Recorder terms
docs.text:
The built-in terms live in eden.managers.terms.recorders. Each writes one key (or a group of keys) per episode.

Term Writes When Notes ActionRecorder action start of each step The raw action vector the action manager received (every term's slice, concatenated). ObservationRecorder obs/<group> start of each step The observations the step's action was chosen from, so row t of obs and action is one (o_t, a_t) pair. groups= limits it; an unknown group raises at build. StateRecorder state/qpos, state/dofs_vel, state/pos, state/quat start of each step One entity (entity_name="robot") or several, concatenated in order along the last axis. pos / quat are the root pose (wxyz). include_qpos, include_dofs_vel, include_pos_quat switch parts off. InitialStateRecorder initial_state/entities/<name>/{qpos,dofs_vel,pos,quat} after each reset Every entity's state at the start of the episode, for replay. RLStepRecorder reward, done, terminated, timeout, timestamp end of each step Reads RLEnvBase buffers, so it records nothing on a plain EnvBase. timestamp is episode_length_buf * dt. SensorRecorder sensor/<name> start of each step (and after reset) Every sensor's read(); use_ground_truth=True reads read_ground_truth(). SysIDRecorder sysid/... reset, start and end of each step The trace Trajectory.from_recorder_episode reloads for system identification; see Planning and system identification.

To record something else, write a RecorderTerm subclass — see Metrics and recorders.

docs.title: Where episodes go
docs.text:
RecorderManagerOptions fields:

Field Default Meaning file_handler_options NPZFileHandler.configure() The file format. Pass HDF5FileHandler.configure() for HDF5. dataset_export_dir_path <tempdir>/eden/logs (/tmp/eden/logs on Linux and macOS) Output directory. dataset_filename "dataset" File name without extension; the handler adds .hdf5 or .npz. dataset_export_mode DatasetExportMode.EXPORT_ALL Which episodes are written (below). override False False appends to an existing file (logged as "Resuming recorder dataset"); True replaces it.

DatasetExportMode (eden.constants):

  • EXPORT_ALL — every episode, in one file.
  • EXPORT_SUCCEEDED_ONLY — only episodes labelled successful.
  • EXPORT_SUCCEEDED_FAILED_IN_SEPARATE_FILES — successes to <filename>, the rest to <filename>_failed.
  • EXPORT_NONE — nothing.

Prefer HDF5 for anything large

NPZ has no incremental write: every flush rewrites the whole archive (atomically, through a temporary file), and the manager flushes after each exported episode. eden datagen and eden lerobot convert use HDF5; Trajectory.from_recorder_episode (system identification) reads NPZ.

Appending to an existing file warns when the stored env_cfg differs from the current env's config: the episodes would mix configurations.

docs.title: When an episode ends, and its success label
docs.text:
The recorder closes and exports an episode whenever its env resets:

  • On an RLEnvBase, an env that terminates or times out is reset inside step(), and its episode is exported with success set from the metric manager's success_buf (the task's metric terms with contributes_to_success).
  • A manual env.reset() or env.reset(envs_idx) exports the episodes of the envs it resets.
  • end_recording() exports the episodes still running, cut short (export_unfinished=False drops them instead).

A plain EnvBase has no terminations, so its episodes end only on a manual reset or end_recording(). Label them yourself with recorder.set_episode_success(envs_idx, success_values) before the reset.

Unlabelled episodes count as failed

An episode with no success label is exported under EXPORT_ALL, but EXPORT_SUCCEEDED_ONLY drops it and the separate-files mode writes it to <filename>_failed. A task without a success metric needs set_episode_success for those modes.

docs.title: File layout
docs.text:
HDF5 (HDF5FileHandler):

<filename>.hdf5
└── data/                          attrs: env_cfg (JSON of the env config), total (episode count)
    ├── demo_0/                    attrs: env_id, success (when labelled)
    │   ├── action                 (T, action_dim)
    │   ├── obs/<group>            (T, ...)            ObservationRecorder
    │   ├── state/qpos             (T, n_qs)           StateRecorder
    │   ├── state/dofs_vel, state/pos, state/quat
    │   ├── reward, done, terminated, timeout, timestamp   RLStepRecorder, (T, 1)
    │   └── initial_state/entities/<name>/...           InitialStateRecorder
    ├── demo_1/
    └── ...

Nested dicts become groups; every array is gzip-compressed. Demos are numbered in the order they finish, across envs, so demo_N says nothing about which env produced it — read the env_id attribute. A resumed file continues after its highest demo_N.

NPZ (NPZFileHandler) stores the same tree as flat, slash-separated keys (demo_0/state/qpos), with __meta__env_cfg / __meta__total for the file and demo_0/__attrs__ (JSON) for an episode's attributes.

docs.title: Reading a dataset back
docs.text:
With h5py:

import h5py

with h5py.File("data/teleop/franka_pick.hdf5", "r") as f:
    for name, demo in f["data"].items():
        actions = demo["action"][:]                 # (T, action_dim)
        success = bool(demo.attrs.get("success", False))

Inside a running session, env.recorder_manager.load_episode("demo_0") returns an EpisodeData whose .data is the nested dict of tensors on the env's device. It refuses before a recording session has opened the file, rather than creating an empty one. The keyboard recorder recipe replays a demo this way: it writes the episode's initial_state back into the entities, then steps the recorded actions.

docs.title: Convert to LeRobot
docs.text:
pip install -U "lerobot[dataset]>=0.4"   # 0.4+ writes LeRobot v3; bare lerobot leaves out its dataset code; no Eden extra
eden lerobot convert \
    --hdf5 data/demos/robosuite_stack.hdf5 \
    --output-dir lerobot/robosuite_stack \
    --repo-id local/robosuite_stack \
    --robot-type panda \
    --task "stack the red cube on the green cube"

Flags: --hdf5 and --output-dir (both required), --repo-id (default local/eden_teleoperation), --robot-type (default eden), --task (the task string stored on every frame; default teleoperate the robot), --image-writer-threads (default 4) and --force. The output is a LeRobot v3 dataset rooted at --output-dir. The same function is importable: from eden.utils.lerobot import convert_hdf5_to_lerobot takes an argv-style list.

What the converter reads and writes:

  • Every demo_<n> group under /data, in numeric order. Each one needs action, timestamp, state/qpos, state/dofs_vel, state/pos and state/quat — that is, ActionRecorder, StateRecorder and RLStepRecorder (for timestamp, so the env must be an RLEnvBase). eden datagen records all three.
  • observation.state is qpos ‖ dofs_vel ‖ pos ‖ quat, with feature names qpos_i, dofs_vel_i, root_pos_{x,y,z} and root_quat_{w,x,y,z} (root0_…, root1_… when StateRecorder recorded several entities). action is the recorded action vector.
  • The frame rate is inferred from the first demo's timestamps.
  • Every demo must have the same feature dimensions; a mismatch raises instead of padding.

Not converted

Images, obs/* groups and the reward/done keys are not carried over: the LeRobot dataset holds observation.state, action and the task string.

--force replaces an existing output directory only if it is empty or already a LeRobot dataset (it has meta/info.json), so a mistyped path cannot delete an unrelated directory.

docs.title: Scripted and teleoperated data together
docs.text: eden datagen records with exactly the recorder set above (ObservationRecorder, ActionRecorder, RLStepRecorder, StateRecorder on the task's arm or arms, InitialStateRecorder) into HDF5 — see Scripted demonstrations. A teleoperated recording made with the same terms on the same task converts the same way, so the two can feed one training set.

docs.title: Multi-GPU Training (DDP)
docs.text: Eden trains on several GPUs, and several nodes, with PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel: one process (rank) per GPU, each simulating its own batch of envs and averaging gradients with the others. This page covers launching a run with torchrun, what Eden does for each rank, the import-order rule DDP depends on, and a job script for SLURM clusters.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
# 4 GPUs on one machine; --num_envs is per GPU, so this run simulates 4 x 4096 envs
torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=4 -m eden train --task velocity_tracking_flat --num_envs 4096

In a checkout, prefix the command with uv run (uv run torchrun ...). A training script of your own launches the same way: torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=4 my_train.py. With --nproc_per_node=1 (or plain eden train) the run is an ordinary single-GPU run; an algorithm that cannot train distributed refuses only when WORLD_SIZE > 1.

docs.title: What Eden does for each rank
docs.text:
torchrun sets WORLD_SIZE, RANK and LOCAL_RANK for every process. When WORLD_SIZE > 1, Eden:

  1. Isolates one GPU per rank, at import eden. Before anything initializes CUDA, it sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (and Quadrants' QD_VISIBLE_DEVICE / TI_VISIBLE_DEVICE) to the rank's GPU: entry LOCAL_RANK of an existing CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, or GPU LOCAL_RANK when none is set. Every rank then sees its GPU as cuda:0, and the runner's device="auto" resolves to it.
  2. Gives each rank its own kernel cache. Each rank compiles into <cache>/rank_<LOCAL_RANK> (under QD_OFFLINE_CACHE_FILE_PATH, by default ~/.cache/quadrants/qdcache/kernel_compilation_manager), because ranks sharing one cache contend for its lock file and crash.
  3. Creates the NCCL process group in en.init(), right after Genesis initializes and before any scene is built.
  4. Shares one run directory. Rank 0 names it and broadcasts the name, so every rank logs under the same logs/<task>/<run>/.
  5. Quiets the other ranks. Genesis logs at warning level on every rank but 0.

eden train builds the DDP variant of the runner (DDPOnPolicyRunner, DDPDistillationRunner, or FlashSAC's), which broadcasts the parameters at the start and averages gradients every update.

Import Eden before Genesis and torch

GPU isolation runs when eden is imported, so import eden must come before anything that can initialize CUDA. Importing torch or genesis first lets CUDA see every GPU, and the ranks end up on the same device.

# Correct
import eden as en
import genesis as gs
import torch

# Wrong: CUDA may already have initialized before Eden can isolate the GPU
import torch
import eden as en

import eden itself imports neither Genesis nor torch (both load in en.init()), so any order that starts with import eden is correct. A module that needs genesis must import it itself rather than rely on Eden having pulled it in.

docs.title: What changes in a distributed run
docs.text:
• num_envs is per rank. The total is num_envs × WORLD_SIZE.
  • Seeds differ per rank. Rank r seeds with runner_options.seed + r, so ranks sample different randomization. config.json and run.json record the base seed and world_size, which together reproduce every rank. See Seeding.
  • Rank 0 writes the run files. config.json, run.json and progress.json are written by rank 0 only. In a script of your own, guard file writes the same way (en.distributed.is_main_process(), or the en.distributed.main_only decorator).
  • Dataset caches are prepared once. A motion dataset with no cache yet is downloaded and processed by rank 0 while the other ranks wait at a barrier, then every rank loads the shared cache.

Some learners cannot train distributed, and eden train refuses them before the build rather than letting each rank train its own copy:

  • an algorithm class with a distributed_unsupported message (the RMA teacher's RmaPPO);
  • the RMA depth-distillation runner (extreme_parkour_student), which is single-GPU;
  • a custom runner (runner_options.class_name as an import path) that does not compose DDPRunnerMixin.

Launch those without torchrun.

docs.title: Distributed helpers
docs.text:
en.distributed (eden.utils.distributed) holds the rank-aware helpers Eden uses itself:

Function Returns / does is_distributed() True when WORLD_SIZE > 1 is_main_process() True on global rank 0 get_global_rank() / get_local_rank() / get_world_size() RANK, LOCAL_RANK, WORLD_SIZE barrier() Synchronize all ranks; a no-op without a process group main_only Decorator: run the function on rank 0 only (others return None) setup(backend="nccl") / cleanup() Create / destroy the process group; en.init() already calls setup

docs.title: Running on a SLURM cluster
docs.text:
One job script covers one or many GPUs and nodes: srun starts one torchrun per node, and torchrun starts one rank per GPU. Fill in the lines marked site-specific, create the slurm/ directory (SLURM will not create it), and sbatch the script from the repository root.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=eden
#SBATCH --nodes=1                  # >1 for multi-node; nothing else changes
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1        # one torchrun per node; it spawns the per-GPU ranks
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:4               # site-specific GPU type, if your cluster needs one; the count must equal NGPU
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=48:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=<partition>    # site-specific
#SBATCH --output=slurm/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm/%x_%j.err
set -euo pipefail
NGPU=4

cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
# module load cuda               # site-specific; drop it if the cluster has no modules
# `module load` puts the system CUDA ahead of torch's bundled libraries, and a mixed cuBLAS / cuBLASLt pair fails
# batched-gemm IK with CUBLAS_STATUS_INVALID_VALUE: put torch's own NVIDIA libraries first.
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$(ls -d .venv/lib/python*/site-packages/nvidia/*/lib | paste -sd:):${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
# Assets download on first use into ~/.cache/eden/assets, which on a cluster is often a small home quota or a
# node-local disk (every node then fetches its own copy). Point it at a shared filesystem with tens of GB free.
export EDEN_ASSETS_DIR=<shared filesystem>/eden_assets   # site-specific

# Several nodes: node 0 hosts the rendezvous store, on a port derived from the job id.
export RDZV_ENDPOINT="$(scontrol show hostnames "$SLURM_JOB_NODELIST" | head -n1):$((20000 + SLURM_JOB_ID % 10000))"

srun --kill-on-bad-exit=1 --cpus-per-task="$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" --cpu-bind=none bash -c '
    if [ "$SLURM_NNODES" -eq 1 ]; then
        rdzv=(--standalone)
    else
        rdzv=(--nnodes="$SLURM_NNODES" --rdzv_id="$SLURM_JOB_ID" --rdzv_backend=c10d
              --rdzv_endpoint="$RDZV_ENDPOINT" --rdzv_conf=is_host=$((SLURM_NODEID == 0)))
    fi
    exec uv run --no-sync torchrun "${rdzv[@]}" "$@"
' torchrun --nproc_per_node="$NGPU" \
    -m eden train --task <task> --num_envs 4096   # or a script: drop -m and give its path

Why the script looks the way it does:

  • The rendezvous must belong to this job alone. When torchrun has to guess whether it hosts the rendezvous store and finds the port taken, it does not fail: it silently joins whatever store holds the port (another job's) and dies mid-run when that job ends. So one node uses --standalone (the OS picks a free port), and several nodes name the host explicitly (is_host), which turns a taken port into an EADDRINUSE at launch.
  • --kill-on-bad-exit=1 stops the other nodes when one fails, instead of leaving them waiting out the join timeout.
  • --cpus-per-task is repeated on srun, because Slurm 22.05 to 23.02 do not pass sbatch's CPU count on to srun, which would confine the step, and every rank in it, to one CPU.
  • uv run --no-sync, so the ranks do not race to rewrite one virtual environment.

Track the job with squeue -j <id> / sacct -j <id> and read slurm/eden_<id>.out. The run's logs and checkpoints land under logs/ as usual, and progress.json there tells you how far it got (see The run directory).

docs.title: Robot setup for deployment
docs.text:
This page is the one-time setup and the robot-specific behaviour of each hardware backend eden deploy drives: the SDK to install, how the robot is reached, its remote, and what its wire does differently. Read Deployment first for the loop, the operator state machine and the safety mechanisms every backend shares. None of this applies to eden deploy --mujoco, which needs no SDK.

Robot Backend SDK (Python import) Operator inputs Unitree G1 UnitreeG1Deployment unitree_sdk2py + CycloneDDS G1 remote, keyboard Unitree Go2 UnitreeGo2Deployment unitree_sdk2py + CycloneDDS keyboard Unitree Go1 UnitreeGo1Deployment robot_interface (legacy unitree_legged_sdk) keyboard LimX Oli LimxOliDeployment limxsdk LimX remote, keyboard Franka Panda / FR3 FrankaPandaDeployment panda_py keyboard RoboTera XHand RoboTeraXHandDeployment xhand_controller keyboard Wuji Hand 1 / Hand 2 WujiHandDeployment wujihandpy / wuji_sdk keyboard

Every SDK is imported at connect() (or guarded at import), so a missing one never breaks import eden; the backend raises with an install hint when it connects.

docs.title: ONNX runtime
docs.text:
On a G1 29-DOF, eden deploy preloads the Holosoma locomotion policy as the boot-active safety slot (--base_policy auto), and Holosoma, like sonic and omnixtreme, is an ONNX policy. Install one of the two mutually exclusive runtime extras:

pipuv (checkout) 
pip install "eden-world[onnx-gpu]"   # onnxruntime-gpu; needs a matching CUDA/cuDNN
pip install "eden-world[onnx]"       # CPU wheel

uv sync --inexact --extra onnx-gpu
uv sync --inexact --extra onnx

Without it, the policy fails at startup, before anything connects, with onnxruntime is not installed and both install commands.

The two wheels share the onnxruntime/ package directory. To switch, reinstall the one you want on top of the other: pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps "onnxruntime-gpu==<its version>", or uv sync --inexact --extra onnx-gpu --reinstall-package onnxruntime-gpu in a checkout (the error Eden prints gives the exact command). Never uninstall either wheel: that deletes files the other needs, and Eden then fails fast on the half-removed install with a message saying so.

The CPU wheel is fast enough for the deployed policies, because Eden bounds every session's thread pool (see Control-loop timing).

docs.title: SDKs live outside the lockfile
docs.text: The robot SDKs below (except Wuji Hand 2's, which is the wuji extra) are installed into the venv by hand and are not declared in pyproject.toml. A plain uv sync removes packages the lockfile does not list, these included: reinstall them after one, or sync with --inexact.

docs.title: State-check recipes
docs.text:
Before running a policy on a new robot, run its state-check recipe under examples/recipes/deployment/: each reads the real robot through its backend, mirrors it in sim and prints a side-by-side comparison of every quantity the observation terms use, flagging mismatches.

Recipe Robot real_g1_states.py Unitree G1 real_oli_states.py, real_oli_teleoperation_slider.py (joint sliders in the viewer) LimX Oli real_franka_states.py, real_franka_teleoperation_keyboard.py Franka Panda real_xhand.py (same sinusoid to sim and real) XHand real_wuji_hand2.py (open and close, reports tracking) Wuji Hand 2

The G1 and Franka recipes are run with LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6, as their headers show. The headers do not say why. If eden deploy on the same machine fails to import the robot's SDK with a GLIBCXX_... not found error, preload the same library.

docs.title: Unitree G1
docs.text: UnitreeG1Deployment drives G1Dofs23, G1Dofs29 and G1Dofs29NoHands over the Unitree SDK2 DDS low-level interface (unitree_hg): LowState_ on rt/lowstate, a CRC-stamped LowCmd_ on rt/lowcmd, joints mapped to motor slots by name.

docs.title: Install the SDK and CycloneDDS
docs.text:
The backend imports unitree_sdk2py, which needs the CycloneDDS native library (libddsc.so.0). When it is missing, connect() raises:

RuntimeError: Unitree SDK (unitree_sdk2py) failed to import. Install it and ensure it
(and its native deps, e.g. libddsc.so.0 from CycloneDDS) are on the loader path.
Underlying error: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'unitree_sdk2py'

  1. Build CycloneDDS once and point CYCLONEDDS_HOME at the install prefix; the cyclonedds Python wheel the SDK pins (cyclonedds==0.10.2) builds against it.

    git clone https://github.com/eclipse-cyclonedds/cyclonedds -b releases/0.10.x
cmake -S cyclonedds -B cyclonedds/build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$HOME/cyclonedds/install -DBUILD_IDLC=ON
cmake --build cyclonedds/build --target install

# persist it (the loader and the cyclonedds build both read this)
echo 'export CYCLONEDDS_HOME=$HOME/cyclonedds/install' >> ~/.bashrc
export CYCLONEDDS_HOME=$HOME/cyclonedds/install

    $CYCLONEDDS_HOME/lib must contain libddsc.so.0.

  2. Install the SDK into the Eden venv, editable so it stays linked to the checkout:

    git clone https://github.com/unitreerobotics/unitree_sdk2_python
CYCLONEDDS_HOME=$HOME/cyclonedds/install uv pip install -e ./unitree_sdk2_python

  3. Verify both import:

    uv run python -c "import cyclonedds, unitree_sdk2py; print('OK')"

If the SDK was installed without its native CRC library (unitree_sdk2py/utils/lib/crc_*.so), Eden falls back to the SDK's pure-Python CRC and logs a warning; it is slower but well within a 50 Hz loop's budget.

docs.title: Network interface
docs.text: The DDS channel binds to the first wired interface (en* / eth*) that is up, skipping loopback and virtual ones (docker*, br-*, veth*, tailscale*, tun*, tap*). Override it with GS_UNITREE_NETWORK_INTERFACE (also read: UNITREE_NETWORK_INTERFACE, CYCLONEDDS_NETWORK_INTERFACE), or the backend option network_interface. With no usable interface, connect() raises naming the variable. The same applies to the Go2.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
connect() first releases any high-level motion mode the robot is running (through the SDK's MotionSwitcherClient), then waits up to connect_timeout_s (eden deploy passes 10 s) for the first LowState_. Nothing goes on the wire before the first command.

Remote: A START, B STOP, Y INIT, L1 + R1 KILL, Select next policy slot (L1 + Select is ignored so it does not collide with other chords). The keyboard keys work alongside it.

docs.title: Publish rate on the G1
docs.text:
The G1 has parallel-linkage joints, the ankles always and, on the 3-DOF-waist 29-DOF build, waist roll and pitch too, driven in PR (pitch/roll) space via LowCmd_.mode_pr. The per-packet PD mechanism described in Republishing the wire command applies, so the backend re-sends the held LowCmd_ between control ticks at publish_rate, default 500 Hz. 500 Hz is the rate both vendor references feed the robot at, independent of any policy rate: Unitree's own g1_low_level_example publishes at control_dt_ = 0.002, and NVIDIA's SONIC G1 deploy runs a dedicated 500 Hz command-writer thread beside its 50 Hz control thread.

Inferred on the G1, measured on the Oli

The per-packet damping fault was measured by a torque fit on Oli hardware captures. Nothing equivalent has been measured on a G1: the mechanism and the 500 Hz default come from the two vendor references. --publish_rate 0 restores one packet per tick, which is the A/B to run before concluding anything about a particular robot. The hardware example scripts under examples/policies/ take the same flag, spelled --publish-rate. --debug_record writes the commanded and measured history (including stamp), and the re-send loop logs the packet rate it achieved when it stops.

On shutdown the backend holds the last pose it read at kp = 0 for shutdown_damping_steps ticks, with the re-send loop still running, before it drops the channel.

docs.title: Unitree Go2
docs.text:
UnitreeGo2Deployment drives Go2 over the same SDK2 DDS stack as the G1 (unitree_go), so the G1 install and network steps apply unchanged. It has no remote reader: use the keyboard.

  • Publish rate. The backend re-sends its held LowCmd_ at publish_rate, default 500 Hz, for parity with the vendor, not to fix a fault: the Go2's twelve joints are all serial (its LowCmd_ has no mode_pr), so the parallel-linkage mechanism does not apply. 500 Hz is what Unitree's own Go2 low-level example feeds the robot (go2_stand_example.py: dt = 0.002, written from a 2 ms RecurrentThread). --publish_rate 0 sends one packet per tick. The re-send loop's health reporting applies unchanged.
  • Go2W inherits this binding but is refused at construction: its wheel motors have no confirmed SDK motor index or velocity-mode mapping, and guessing them on real hardware is unsafe.

docs.title: Unitree Go1
docs.text: The Go1 predates the DDS stack. UnitreeGo1Deployment uses the legacy unitree_legged_sdk, exposed as the robot_interface pybind module (synchronous UDP, not CycloneDDS), so the CycloneDDS setup above does not apply.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Build and install the robot_interface module from the unitree_legged_sdk Python wrapper (python -m build --wheel, then install the wheel into the venv), or point EDEN_GO1_SDK_PATH at the directory holding robot_interface.*.so:

    export EDEN_GO1_SDK_PATH=/path/to/unitree_go1_sdk
uv run python -c "import robot_interface; print('OK')"

    When missing, connect() raises RuntimeError: Unitree Go1 SDK (the legacy 'robot_interface' module) failed to import, with both options. - No ONNX runtime is needed: Holosoma is a G1-only policy, and --base_policy auto loads no base policy on a Go1, so your --checkpoint is slot 1. - Put the robot in low-level mode on the remote: L2 + A → L2 + B → L1 + L2 + start.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
eden deploy --task move_forward --robot go1 --checkpoint /path/to/model.pt
  • connect() primes the bidirectional UDP link: the robot only streams state to a client it has heard from, so the backend sends a limp command (kp = kd = tau = 0) while it waits for the first state. A timeout means the robot is not powered, not in low-level mode, or not reachable at robot_ip:robot_port (default 192.168.123.10:8007) from local UDP port local_port (default 8080).
  • --power_protect_factor N sets the SDK's Safety.PowerProtect factor, 1..10 = 10%..100% of rated motor power, default 10. Lower factors clamp the torque a gait needs (the backend's source records factor 7 freezing the move_forward Go1 mid-stance), and the SDK examples' value of 1 starves locomotion entirely and trips Error: Power Protection. Lower it (for example to 5) only for cautious bench bring-up with the robot supported, then raise it back toward 10.
  • Stand-up. INIT is a joint-space ramp that is blind to where the feet are (see Gains and the INIT ramp). If the robot starts from an awkward stance, some legs fight the ground to reach their target angles; that shows up as a large persistent tracking error on those joints and drives their motors into thermal derating, so the leg goes weak and the robot freezes or sags. Lift the robot and set it down squarely, feet roughly under the hips, before INIT; wait for INIT reached the target pose and confirm full height before START.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
• --debug_record additionally records, per step, each motor's temperature and mode and the battery (x_motor_temp, x_motor_mode, x_battery_v, x_battery_soc).
  • The backend warns, once per joint until it recovers, when a motor reports Overheat mode or reaches motor_temp_warn_c (default 80 °C). A derating motor is the usual cause of a frozen or weak leg: let the motors cool between runs.
  • If a leg is stuck with its measured tau far below the commanded PD demand (kp·(cmd − q) − kd·qd, reconstructable from the record), the motor is limiting itself (temperature, battery), not the controller or the policy.

Go1 safety

connect() touches the real robot. Keep the e-stop in reach and the robot supported for first runs. The default --power_protect_factor 10 (100%) leaves no PowerProtect margin; dial it back while commissioning. Do not disable load-bearing leg joints on an unsupported robot.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The SDK is not on PyPI; install the platform wheel shipped in the limxsdk-lowlevel repo:

git clone https://github.com/limxdynamics/limxsdk-lowlevel
uv pip install limxsdk-lowlevel/python3/amd64/limxsdk-*.whl   # aarch64/ on the onboard PC
uv run python -c "import limxsdk.robot, limxsdk.datatypes; print('OK')"

docs.title: Address
docs.text: The backend connects to the robot_ip option, else the ROBOT_IP environment variable, else 10.192.1.2 (the robot's address on its own network). ROBOT_IP=127.0.0.1 targets the LimX MuJoCo simulator, which speaks the same protocol on localhost.

docs.title: Hardware preparation
docs.text:
Follow LimX's procedure; both steps are required. Hang the robot, power it on, click the right joystick button on the remote to activate the motors, then press R1 + DOWN to enter developer mode (it persists across reboots; exit with R1 + LEFT).

The failure modes are distinctive. Outside developer mode the onboard motion controller keeps commanding the motors, so SDK commands fight it: the motors buzz and shake. In developer mode with the motors not activated, SDK commands are silently ignored: the robot stays limp. From the moment a deploy boots (STOP, holding), the robot should feel stiff; limp means the activation step is missing. The backend prints this at reset() too.

docs.title: Remote
docs.text:
The remote is PS4-style (□ square, △ triangle, ✕ cross, ○ circle); LimX's docs and SDK comments name the same buttons with Xbox-style letters (✕ = A, ○ = B, □ = X, △ = Y). The chords follow LimX's own deploy tooling where it has a counterpart:

Chord Command L1 + △ INIT R1 + □ START L1 + ✕ STOP L1 + □ KILL (soft-damp and exit) L1 + ○ Next policy slot

docs.title: Wire behaviour
docs.text:
• Joint order by name. Motor order is mapped by name from the robot's live getMotorNames() at connect, never by position (LimX's docs and controller files disagree on the head-joint order). If a robot reports names that do not match the URDF joint names even after _joint-suffix normalization, map them with the motor_name_map option (Eden DOF name → SDK motor name).
  • PR space. Commands are sent in PR (serial-joint) space with the SDK's parallel_solve_required flag set, so the SDK handles the parallel ankle and waist linkages, matching Eden's serial HU_D04_01.urdf and LimX's own RL deployment stack.
  • Publish rate is load-bearing on this robot. In PR mode the robot evaluates the PD law of its six parallel-linkage joints (ankle pitch/roll, waist roll/pitch) once per received packet, on that packet's state. Measured on hardware (recorded in eden/extensions/deployment/utils/republisher.py): with one packet per tick their torque fits kp·(q_des − q) − kd·dq[previous packet] at R² 0.92–0.99 while the serial joints fit the same-instant velocity, and the waist-roll linkage rang at 25 Hz once a foot strike kicked it; at 1 kHz the audible buzz is gone and the >10 Hz torque RMS drops from 23.7 to 2.1 N·m. The backend re-sends the held command at publish_rate, default 1000 Hz (LimX's own rate). --publish_rate 0 sends one packet per tick, for A/B only.
  • Torque clamp. Every commanded target is clamped to q ± soft_torque_limit · budget / kp around the measured pose, so the position term of the implied PD torque never exceeds the per-joint budget (soft_torque_limit defaults to 0.95, like LimX's walk controller; 0 disables it). The budget is the robot's default_dofs_force_limits with the clamp_torque_limits option on top, whose default is LimX's deploy-time user_torque_limit where that differs from Eden's training limits: 80 N·m on the six parallel ankle and waist joints (each driven by two 42 N·m motors), while training, and the action scale derived from it, keeps 42. The clamp runs after the target low-pass, on every command path (INIT, hold, policy). Unlike LimX's clamp, the window is not shifted by kd·dq/kp: theirs is re-evaluated every 1 ms with fresh state, Eden's once per 20 ms tick on the previous tick's state, and while the waist rang the SDK's reported velocity for the parallel joints was 8–11× the derivative of the reported position, so that term pinned the command to the window edge on 11–28% of walking ticks and amplified the oscillation.
  • Diagnostics. Error-level robot diagnostics (motor faults, overheat, …) are logged as [deploy] robot diagnostic '<name>': level=… code=… whenever they change. Set the verbose_diagnostics option (--verbose-diagnostics on the slider recipe) to also log warning and OK transitions.

--menagerie under --mujoco loads LimX's own MJCF for the Oli, with the linkages as equality constraints; see Which model is loaded.

docs.title: Franka Panda and FR3
docs.text: FrankaPandaDeployment drives FrankaEmikaPanda, FrankaResearch3 and FrankaEmikaPandaNoHand through panda-python (panda_py): the 7-DOF arm on panda-py's real-time JointPosition controller at 1 kHz inside libfranka, the Franka Hand through libfranka's blocking Gripper API from a worker thread, so a step never blocks on the gripper.

docs.title: Install and prepare
docs.text:
• panda-python wheels ship inside per-libfranka zips on panda-py's GitHub releases, with no direct wheel URL; install the one whose libfranka matches your controller's server version (server v4 → libfranka 0.8.0). The comment above the franka extra in pyproject.toml has the download-and-install commands for that case. Without it, connect() raises panda-python package is not installed.

  • Activate FCI in Desk and release the joint brakes.

  • A PREEMPT_RT kernel is strongly recommended for stable 1 kHz control; without it, expect occasional communication_constraints_violation reflexes.
  • robot_ip defaults to 192.168.1.1.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
• Gains. The arm runs panda-py's own stiffness (arm_stiffness / arm_damping, panda-py's defaults when unset), not the command's, so --deploy_kp_kd_scale and --disable_joints do not reach it, and each policy slot runs at the same gains.
  • Smoothing. arm_filter_coeff (default 0.05; panda-py's own is 1.0) low-passes the setpoint inside the 1 kHz loop: at policy rates the controller sees abrupt setpoint changes, which make the arm buzz under PD. Lower it if it still oscillates, raise it toward 1.0 for responsiveness.
  • Velocity clamp. Each step's commanded joint delta is scaled down, direction preserved, so the implied joint velocity stays within velocity_safety_factor (default 0.5) of the datasheet limits; without it, a differential-IK step near a high-Jacobian configuration can trip libfranka's joint_velocity_violation reflex.
  • Boot. The arm boots in STOP holding its measured pose (the first command starts the controller at that setpoint); INIT ramps it to init_target over init_steps, with the velocity clamp.
  • The gripper is the policy's alone. The hold, INIT and the START tick leave it where the policy last commanded it, so STOP or INIT never opens a grasp. With use_grasp_on_close (default on), a target width below close_width_threshold (0.04 m) closes with force-controlled grasp (gripper_force, default 20 N), which holds objects during arm motion; wider targets use move. target_lpf smooths the arm only. skip_gripper_homing skips homing when an object is already held.
  • Position terms only. Torque-mode action terms (OperationalSpaceController) are refused at construction; use DifferentialIKController or another position-mode term.
  • The arm has no IMU: read_state reports an identity base orientation.

docs.title: RoboTera XHand
docs.text:
RoboTeraXHandDeployment drives XHand1_R / XHand1_L through the vendor's xhand_controller package. It is not on PyPI and no Eden extra installs it: get it from RoboTera with the hand's SDK.

  • Bus. protocol is "RS485" (default; serial_port /dev/ttyUSB0, baud_rate 3000000) or "EtherCAT" (the first EtherCAT port found). hand_id 0 selects the first enumerated hand; a configured ID that is not present raises, listing the ones that are. CRC failures are retried crc_retries times (default 3) before raising.
  • The hand runs its own PD on firmware gains, programmed once at connect from dofs_kp / dofs_ki / dofs_kd (defaults 50 / 0 / 25) and tor_max (300), all in firmware units with no known mapping to N·m/rad; connect logs what it programs. Only positions are sent per command. So --deploy_kp_kd_scale other than 1.0 and --disable_joints are refused at construction: lower the firmware gains instead. finger_mode is 0 powerless, 3 position (default), 5 powerful.
  • Joint velocity is a finite difference of consecutive positions over wall-clock time (the SDK reports none), zero on the first read: noisier and a period later than the simulator's.
  • The hand has no IMU: read_state reports an identity orientation.

docs.title: Wuji Hand 1 and Hand 2
docs.text: WujiHandDeployment (eden/extensions/deployment/wuji_hand.py) is bound to WujiHand1* and WujiHand2Beta2*, left and right.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
• Hand 1 needs wujihandpy (pip install wujihandpy==1.5.1, the version upstream pins).
  • Hand 2 needs wuji_sdk, the wuji extra: pip install "eden-world[wuji]", or uv sync --inexact --extra wuji in a checkout. It is Linux-only (manylinux wheels for x86-64 and aarch64); elsewhere the extra installs nothing.

Both are imported at connect, so neither is needed to construct the backend or to run it against a simulator.

Wuji SDK telemetry

Importing wuji_sdk starts a background worker that sends anonymous usage events to a third-party analytics host. Set WUJI_TELEMETRY_DISABLE=1 in the environment to turn it off; Eden does not set it for you.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
• Side and joint order come from the joint names. Both SDKs speak 20 angles, finger-major and thumb first, the same for either hand. The backend maps {right,left}_finger{1-5}_joint{1-4} (Hand 1 and the wuji-mjlab task models) and {r,l}_thumb_cmc_flex … {r,l}_pinky_dip (Hand2Beta2) onto that order, so a robot may declare its DOFs in any order. A robot outside those classes must name its generation: WujiHandDeployment.configure(hand="hand2").

  • Gains are programmed once, at connect. Hand 2 takes MIT mit_kp / mit_kd (one value, or a pattern-keyed dict covering all 20) and a current limit effort_limit_a (default 1.0 A). Hand 1 runs its own position loop, so it refuses deploy_kp_kd_scale and gains; soften it with effort_limit_a (default 0.5 A). Both refuse --disable_joints.

    Hand 2's default MIT gains are the simulation's

    Left unset, mit_kp / mit_kd default to the robot's default_dofs_kp / default_dofs_kd times deploy_kp_kd_scale, which for WujiHand2Beta2 are 50 / 5, simulation gains. The hand's firmware ships with kp 3.0, kd 0.05, which is what examples/recipes/deployment/real_wuji_hand2.py programs. Set them explicitly on real hardware, and compare them with what your policy trained at: the deploy warns per slot when the two differ.

  • Streaming. stream_mode="sync" (default) interpolates servo_hz (default 200) sub-targets across each control period and blocks until the period's deadline, chained from the previous one, so a tick is one control period and the inference time is absorbed into it (the base rate limiter is not stacked on top). "thread" ramps from a background thread and the rate limiter paces the loop. A tick with nothing to send holds the last target for the period, so a "sync" loop never spins faster than the control rate.

  • Safety. Lost joint feedback always stops the run (raising DeployStop): on Hand 2 a joint feed older than stale_after_s (default 0.5 s), on Hand 1 a position read that gets no answer within it. A latched hardware fault stops it unless stop_on_fault=False. Both are checked before every control tick (hold, INIT and policy alike) and before every waypoint of ease_to. clip_targets_to_joint_limits clamps every target to the built robot's range, ease_to included.
  • Loop order. The backend reads the hand before the commands publish (sync_before_commands), and it advances the env's episode clock once per tick, only while the policy drives, restarting it at every START (advances_episode_clock), so a warm-up gated on it runs from the handover however long the hand held and INITed before.
  • No IMU. The base orientation is the robot's default_root_quat, and joint velocity is a finite difference of consecutive reads (vel_lowpass_hz smooths it).
  • Extending it. A subclass overrides sync_scene() to write anything else it observes into the scene after each read (a camera-tracked object) and check_safety() to add its own stop conditions. use_transport(transport) swaps the hardware for a simulator, for sim-to-sim through the same code path: any HandTransport built with the deployment's dep.stream.

docs.text:
