docs.title: Environments
docs.text: An environment turns a task config into a running, vectorized simulation: it creates the entities, builds the Genesis scene, owns the managers and runs the step loop. This page covers the environment classes, building one from a config, what step() and reset() do and in which order, inspecting a built environment, and writing a new environment class. Read it when you build an environment by hand, write a term whose timing matters, or debug a reset.

docs.title: The environment classes
docs.text:
Each environment class reads exactly one config class (its config leaf). The pairing is fixed, and from_config refuses a config of another leaf:

Environment (eden.envs) Config leaf Adds base.EnvBase EdenConfig the scene, entities, cameras, sensors, and the action, metric, event, observation and recorder managers base.RLEnvBase EdenRLConfig the reward, termination, command and curriculum managers, the RL step with auto-reset, reward_buf / reset_buf base.MimicRLEnvBase EdenMimicConfig the motion manager, which streams a reference motion splat.SplatEnvBase EdenSplatConfig a Gaussian-splat background (gsplat), on a non-RL environment splat.SplatRLEnvBase EdenSplatRLConfig the same splat background, on an RL environment nyx_splat.NyxSplatEnvBase EdenNyxSplatConfig a path-traced splat background (Nyx), on a non-RL environment 
classDiagram
    EnvBase <|-- RLEnvBase
    RLEnvBase <|-- MimicRLEnvBase
    EnvBase <|-- SplatEnvBase
    RLEnvBase <|-- SplatRLEnvBase
    EnvBase <|-- NyxSplatEnvBase

The config classes are described in Task Configuration. API reference: Environments.

docs.title: Building an environment
docs.text:
import eden as en          # import eden before genesis and torch
import genesis as gs
from eden.envs.base import RLEnvBase
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY

en.init(backend=gs.gpu)    # the default backend is gs.cpu

config = TASK_REGISTRY.build("reacher")
env = RLEnvBase.from_config(config)   # constructs only: the scene is NOT built yet
env.build()                           # builds the Genesis scene and the managers
obs, extras = env.reset()             # call reset() once before the first step()

Or let a training wrapper do all of it:

from eden.envs.wrappers.rsl_rl_env import RslRlVecEnvWrapper

env = RslRlVecEnvWrapper.from_config(config)   # seeds, constructs, builds and resets

What from_config() does depends on the class

Call Constructs build() reset() Seeds the RNGs EnvBase / RLEnvBase / MimicRLEnvBase.from_config(cfg) yes no, call it yourself no no: an env has no runner_options to read a seed from RslRlVecEnvWrapper / RlGamesVecEnvWrapper.from_config(cfg) yes yes yes, in the wrapper's __init__ yes, from runner_options.seed, before it constructs the env

A raw environment is unbuilt: its managers, entity handles and buffers do not exist until build(), and build() does not reset. The wrapper path requires cfg.runner_options; a config without one raises ValueError pointing back at RLEnvBase.from_config. A wrapper owns the environment its from_config built: close() destroys the scene, and so does a wrapper that fails to construct. An environment you build yourself and pass to a wrapper's __init__ stays yours to destroy, with env.destroy().

from_config() takes only show_viewer and eval_mode as keywords; a wrapper's also takes apply_seed. eval_mode=True sets env.training = False: curricula freeze and command debug drawing turns on. en.init() also sets up the run's log directory and the console log theme; see Training runs.

from_config() does not copy the config. The environment holds the config's own option objects, so an edit to env.env_options after construction is also an edit to config.env_options.

Seeding is the wrapper's job. Put the seed on the config (cfg.runner_options.seed = ...) instead of seeding around a wrapper's from_config(), which would overwrite it. If you build a raw environment and wrap it yourself, call eden.utils.random.apply_run_seed(cfg.runner_options.seed) before from_config. env.seed(seed) and env.reset(seed=...) seed the RNGs with exactly the value given, with no per-rank offset. Seeds must be non-negative. Per-rank offsets under multi-GPU training are in Training runs.

docs.title: Picking the env class: env_class_for_config()
docs.text:
The environment class and the config leaf must match. An environment's from_config() forwards only the option groups its own config leaf declares, so RLEnvBase.from_config(mimic_cfg) would drop motion_options and train with no motion reference at all. from_config() therefore raises TypeError on a mismatch, naming the class that should build the config. Task subclasses on either side are fine: the check compares leaves, so a ReacherEnv(RLEnvBase) built from a ReacherConfig(EdenRLConfig) is one pairing.

When the config class is not known statically (a CLI --task, a registry lookup, a helper that takes any config), dispatch on the config's type:

from eden.envs.base import env_class_for_config

env = env_class_for_config(cfg).from_config(cfg, show_viewer=True)
env.build()
env.reset()

env_class_for_config (eden/envs/base.py) is the single source of the mapping. It checks the most specific leaf first, because the configs form an inheritance chain:

Config Env class EdenNyxSplatConfig NyxSplatEnvBase EdenSplatRLConfig SplatRLEnvBase EdenSplatConfig SplatEnvBase EdenMimicConfig MimicRLEnvBase EdenRLConfig RLEnvBase EdenConfig EnvBase

A config of none of these types raises TypeError. The splat classes are imported only when a splat config asks for them, so a splat config without the optional renderer dependencies raises ImportError (install the batch-splat or nyx extra), rather than falling back to a plain environment. eden inference, the training wrappers and the smoke harness (eden.utils.smoke.build_and_step) all dispatch through it, and new code should too.

Before it constructs anything, from_config() also calls cfg.check_bindings(), which names any field a TaskMod should have filled (TaskMods).

docs.title: What construction and build() do
docs.text:
Construction (__init__) creates the Genesis scene from env_options, then one Eden entity per scene entry (a composite rig unfolds into its bodies and welds), the welds of attachments_dict, the cameras and the sensors. A parent and the entities welded onto it are created consecutively, as Genesis requires; a weld to an entity that does not exist raises ValueError here.

build() runs three steps:

  1. pre_build_setup(): every entity's, camera's and sensor's pre-build hook, then the hooks registered with register_pre_build_hook().
  2. scene.build(), with env_options.num_envs environments (and env_spacing / center_envs_at_origin, which build() also accepts as arguments).
  3. post_build_setup(): every entity's and camera's post-build hook, then the managers are constructed in manager order and checked against it, the STARTUP events fire, and the hooks registered with register_post_build_hook() run. The scene state at this point is saved as the state every reset restores.

Afterwards build() checks the built scene. A rigid body lighter than 1 g that is not carried by an immobile base gets a warning and its mass set to 0.01 kg (a Mochi body raises instead, since its mass cannot be patched). A scene with equality constraints (closed kinematic loops) and an effective substep sim_dt / sim_substeps above 0.004 s gets a warning.

register_pre_build_hook() must be called before build(). A post-build hook may be registered later, from a manager's construction inside step 3, because the queue is drained at the end of that step; MotionManager registers one that way. Registering one after the drain raises RuntimeError, since it could never run.

register_substep_callback(callback, before=False) registers a zero-argument callback that runs around every scene.step() of a control step, that is decimation times per step: after the physics step, or just before it with before=True (after the action manager has written its controls). It is for a term that has to act between physics steps. Keep callbacks cheap and free of GPU syncs.

docs.title: Stepping and resetting
docs.text:
obs, extras = env.reset()                          # all envs; env.reset(envs_idx) for some
obs, reward, terminated, timeouts, extras = env.step(action)
  • reset(envs_idx=None, *, seed=None) resets the given environments (all of them when None) and returns (obs, extras), where extras["log"] holds the managers' reset logging.
  • step(action) advances one control step and returns (obs, reward, terminated, timeouts, extras). obs maps each observation group to its tensor; reward, terminated and timeouts have shape (num_envs,). extras["log"] holds the logging of the envs that reset this step, and extras["final_observations"] the final observations, when enabled.
  • action may be None: the simulation still advances, with no new controls.
  • On an EnvBase (no RL layer), step() returns (obs, None, None, None, extras).

docs.title: The Step Loop
docs.text:
RLEnvBase.step() runs these phases in this order. The table is the contract, not a summary: tests/envs/test_base.py runs the real step against a recording harness and fails if the code and this table disagree.

# phase call runs when 1 Map the policy action onto the actuators action_manager.compute action 2 Open the recorded step recorder_manager._on_step_started always 3 Advance command references before physics command_manager.pre_physics_advance command_manager 4 ×decimation: apply_actions() + scene.step() _scene_step_with_sensor_gating always 5 Refresh command caches on the post-physics state command_manager.post_physics_refresh command_manager 6 Shared computations for the graded layer metric_manager.compute metric_manager 7 Tick stateful observation terms (once per step) observation_manager.post_physics_refresh always 8 Terminations termination_manager.compute always 9 Rewards reward_manager.compute always 10 Tag the ending episodes with their success flag recorder_manager.set_episode_success metric_manager, recording, episode_ends 11 Close the recorded step (terminal envs still un-reset) recorder_manager._on_step_finished always 12 Snapshot done envs' final obs (opt-in) _record_final_observations record_final_observations 13 Reset done envs: scene reset + RESET events _reset_idx always 14 post_reset() on every term, for the envs phase 13 reset _dispatch_post_reset always 15 Record new-episode data recorder_manager._on_reset_finished always 16 Adapt difficulty (frozen at eval) curriculum_manager.compute curriculum_manager 17 Resample / publish commands command_manager.compute command_manager 18 INTERVAL events event_manager.compute interval_events 19 Observations observation_manager.compute always 20 Command debug draw (eval only) command_manager.draw_vis command_manager, eval_mode

A phase runs only when all of its conditions hold; always means every step of every RL environment. The test switches each condition off in turn to check that the phase disappears with it and nothing else does:

  • action: step() was called with an action. The apply_actions() inside phase 4 is gated the same way; with no action the simulation still advances.
  • command_manager, metric_manager, curriculum_manager: the task declares at least one term for that manager. A task with no command terms has no phases 3, 5, 17 or 20.
  • recording: a recording is active (recorder_manager.is_recording).
  • episode_ends: at least one environment's episode ends on this step.
  • record_final_observations: opted in with EnvOptions.record_final_observations.
  • interval_events: at least one event term uses INTERVAL mode.
  • eval_mode: the environment is not training.

Phase 13 always runs, but it resets only the environments whose episode ended. episode_length_buf and common_step_counter advance right after phase 4.

docs.title: Grade the step, then prepare the next one
docs.text:
Phases 6–9 grade the step that just happened, phases 16–20 prepare the next one, and phases 10–15 close the books in between: the recorder closes the finished step, then the done environments are reset and their terms rebuilt.

  • Phase 5 feeds the grading: it refreshes command-owned state on the post-physics robot, above everything that reads it.
  • Phase 7 is the one call per step a stateful observation term can count on. It comes after the command caches (5) and the metrics (6) that such a term may integrate, and before anything grades or resets. observation_manager.compute() at phase 19 is a read: it also runs at phase 12, at build, in reset() and from get_observations(), so a counter advanced inside it would be wrong.
  • Commands update at phase 17, after the reward at phase 9, on purpose. The policy chose this step's action from the observations computed at phase 19 of the previous step. Grading at phase 9 against the command those observations carried keeps observation, action and reward aligned on one command.
  • Phase 14 is where a term rebuilds per-step caches for the environments phase 13 reset. Without it, phase 19 would read the finished episode's values for those environments. It runs once the whole reset is done, including a subclass's extra work (the motion environment's buffer refill).

Which per-step hook a term's state belongs in follows from this split, and getting it wrong fails silently; the rules are in Terms, and why phase 19 must not advance state is in Terms.

Auto-reset runs before observation

Done environments are reset after the reward and the termination but before the observation, so the observations step() returns for them already show the fresh post-reset state, not the terminal one. This matters to an algorithm that uses the "next observation" of the done step; enable final observations if it needs the terminal one.

docs.title: The step of the other environment classes
docs.text:
• MimicRLEnvBase.step() first advances the motion reference (motion_manager.compute), then runs the twenty phases above.
  • EnvBase.step() is a subsequence of them, with no commands, no terminations or rewards, and no auto-reset: phases 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 11, 18 and 19. It returns no reward.

docs.title: Final observations
docs.text:
Because of the auto-reset, the observation step() returns for a done environment is the first one of its next episode, not the terminal post-physics state. On-policy PPO in RSL-RL does not need the terminal state: it masks natural terminations out of its value targets, and bootstraps time-outs from the value it computed on the previous step. The wrapper reports extras["time_outs"] as truncated and not terminated, so an environment that failed on the step it timed out counts as terminal.

A learner that needs the real terminal state opts in with EnvOptions(record_final_observations=True). Phase 12 then computes the observations of the post-physics state before the reset, and step() returns them in extras next to the reset log:

extras = {
    "log": ...,                    # the managers' reset logging
    "final_observations": {        # one entry per observation group, laid out like obs
        "policy": ...,             # (num_envs, *obs_shape); a nested dict for a group that does not concatenate
        "critic": ...,
    },
}
  • Rows of environments whose episode did not end are zero. Rows of done environments hold the observation of the pre-reset state.
  • For a group with history, the row has the history's shape, with the fresh post-physics frame in the most recent slot. The snapshot is computed with update_history=False, so it does not advance the history buffer; the once-per-step advance still happens at phase 19.
  • The tensors are reused on every step. Copy them if you keep them, for example in a replay buffer.
  • The cost is one more observation pass and one torch.where per group on every step, with no GPU sync.

The consumers it exists for are off-policy learners that bootstrap a timed-out transition from its real next state (the FlashSAC learner of flashdexretarget refuses to run without it, from check_bindings()), estimators whose target is the true next observation (homie turns it on for HIMPPO), and evaluation recording that needs the terminal frame. It is off by default.

To change what counts as the terminal observation, override RLEnvBase._compute_final_observations(), for example to skip a group whose terms are unsafe to evaluate on the post-physics state.

docs.title: Solver errors
docs.text:
A physics solver that leaves an environment's state corrupt (a NaN contact, force or acceleration, or a diverged Mochi solve) does not stop the run:

  • phases 6 and 9 drop what the metric and reward terms read from those environments, so no NaN reaches the learner;
  • phase 8 truncates them, logged as Episode_Termination/solver_error;
  • phase 13 resets them, which clears the flag and zeroes the control force the solver reports for them.

env.get_solver_error_envs_mask() returns the flagged environments. Genesis raises a flag that is still set at the start of its next scene.step(), so phase 4 lets only the first scene.step() of a control step check the flags: an environment flagged during any of the decimation physics steps is reset before the check that would raise for the whole scene. An environment that nothing resets (a plain EnvBase) raises at the next control step.

A misconfiguration of the scene is never reset away. An environment flagged with a contact capacity overflow, an unsupported collision pair or, under requires_grad, a NaN gradient is truncated and its values dropped like any other, but it keeps the flag across the reset. The flag is handed back to the solver right before the first scene.step() of the next control step, which then raises with a message naming the option to change (on CUDA, the step after that, since its check does not wait for the device).

docs.title: Replaying the graded phase from a CUDA graph
docs.text:
Phases 6–9 read the post-physics state and write only the managers' own buffers, in hundreds of small kernels. When a step is limited by the host, launching them is the cost, and EnvOptions(cuda_graph_options=CudaGraphOptions()) replays them from one CUDA graph instead. The module docstring of eden/envs/graded_graph.py gives the scale: about 3 ms of host time for the eager phase on beyondmimic at 4096 envs, a replay that launches in about 5 µs, and about 70 µs of checks before each replay.

It is off by default (cuda_graph_options=None) and needs an RLEnvBase on a CUDA device; any other environment refuses it. It is in EnvOptions.training_only_fields, which eden inference, eden export and eden deploy reset when they replay a run's own config. CudaGraphOptions (eden.options.envs) holds its settings:

Field Default Meaning warmup_steps 2 Eager steps before the first capture, so terms can build their lazy caches. validation_steps 3 Replays after each capture that are also run eagerly and compared bit for bit (at least 1). recapture_window 100 The span, in steps, over which re-captures are counted. max_recaptures_per_window 2 Re-captures allowed within the window; one more raises, naming what changed.

A term the graph cannot reproduce fails a validated replay, and the error names the buffers that differ. Before every replay the graph checks what it baked in, and re-captures (and re-validates) when one of these changed:

  • a graded term's configured field, such as a termination threshold a curriculum moves;
  • an environment constant a term may read: dt, max_episode_length, training;
  • a tensor the graph reads, rebound to a new one (by a term, by load_state_dict, or by replacing the container that holds it). The check walks every object reachable from the environment, except the environment itself, the standard library's objects, and those of genesis, quadrants and torch.

Reward weights are mirrored on the device and copied before every replay, so a weight curriculum needs no re-capture. A curriculum that moves a graded value on every step must keep it in a tensor written in place, or it re-captures too often and raises.

A term is replayable when it follows the term contract: state in buffers written in place, and no value read back to the host. These are not:

  • A host read (.item(), nonzero(), a boolean-mask gather) fails the capture, and the error names the term's source line. Contact queries switch to their padded, fixed-shape form inside the graded phase of graph mode, eager runs included, for this reason (see Entities).
  • env.common_step_counter changes every step, so reading it during the capture raises BakedHostReadError naming the line: a replay would keep the branch the capture took.
  • Python state a term advances outside its configured fields fails validation.
  • Any other Python value read from outside the term's own fields, such as another manager's term attribute or a module global, is not watched: the graph replays the value it read at capture. Keep such a value in a tensor written in place.

docs.title: Events and resets
docs.text:
Event terms fire in one of three modes (eden.constants.EventMode):

Mode When it fires STARTUP once, in build(), after every manager is constructed RESET on every reset of an environment, right after the scene state of the reset environments is restored and before the managers' reset(): in env.reset() and at phase 13 INTERVAL at phase 18 of each step, with the control dt, when the term's interval has elapsed

A reset therefore runs in this order: the scene state of the reset environments is restored, the RESET events fire, every manager's reset() runs in manager order (publishing the finished episode's statistics and clearing accumulators), episode_length_buf is zeroed for those environments, and then every term's post_reset() runs, in the same order. env.reset() ends by computing the observations. How priority orders the terms of one mode, and the fields of each mode, are in Events.

docs.title: Manager order
docs.text:
One declared order, _manager_order(), drives three walks: the construction of the managers in build(), every manager's reset(), and every term's post_reset(). It is checked at build against the managers the environment owns.

env _manager_order() EnvBase action → metric → event → observation → recorder RLEnvBase action → command → metric → termination → reward → curriculum → event → observation → recorder MimicRLEnvBase the RL order, bracketed by the motion manager (below)

The order meets four constraints:

  1. action_manager before event_manager. Reset-mode domain-randomization terms write the action modifiers' per-env buffers in reset(), so that the write lands after action_manager.reset() restores the baselines. With events first, every such draw would be overwritten within the same reset. This is the one constraint the check tests by position.
  2. The metric manager and the curricula may sit anywhere in the loop. They normalize the finished episode by episode_length_buf, which is zeroed only after the loop.
  3. Every build-time handle lookup points backwards. A term that resolves another manager's term in its own build() (an action-rate reward finding the action term, a velocity-tracking reward finding its command, a curriculum finding the reward or termination term it adjusts) needs that manager to exist already. Construction follows this order, so a bad name raises at build, not mid-rollout.
  4. The ended episode's motion is read through motion_manager.ended_episode_validity(). In a motion environment, the reset environments' reference window is refilled for the new episode before the manager loop, so reading motion_manager.data from a manager's reset() raises. A term that grades the ended episode registers with record_ended_episode_validity in build(); a term that wants the new episode's reference reads it in post_reset().

Everything else is a choice of producer before consumer. Commands are the reference every graded term reads, so they come first; metric terms, the shared computations, feed termination and reward; the curriculum reads the graded outcome last. Observation and recorder terms consume every other layer and produce nothing, so they go last, with events just ahead of them.

Two consequences matter to term authors:

  • Every manager before event_manager publishes the finished episode under the domain-randomization draw it actually ran with. The new draw lands at event_manager.reset().
  • curriculum_manager.reset() runs after reward_manager.reset() has cleared its accumulators. A curriculum that adapts on the finished episode's reward must read something published, such as another term's get_state() from its own compute() at phase 16, not the reward manager's internal sums. An evaluation environment never computes a curriculum, so it logs no Curriculum/* keys.

The motion manager brackets the loop. Its reset() must run before the scene reset, because reference-state initialization (RSI) events read the freshly sampled clip, and its buffer is refilled around the scene reset and the RESET events, before every other manager. No position in a flat list expresses that, so MimicRLEnvBase constructs it before the others, calls motion_manager.reset() before the base reset and motion_manager.post_reset() before the others' post_reset(), and declares it in _BRACKETED_MANAGERS so the check knows it is handled.

docs.title: Adding a manager to your own environment
docs.text:
1. Add a "<name>_manager": lambda: ... entry to your _manager_factories() override, merged into super()._manager_factories().
  2. Add "<name>_manager" to your _manager_order() override, in the producer-before-consumer position it belongs in. The order is restated in full per class rather than composed, because the RL managers sit between the base ones.
  3. If the manager may legitimately be absent (no terms declared), add it to _OPTIONAL_MANAGERS as well: it is then left as None, which every consumer's is not None check expects. The metric, command and curriculum managers are optional; the others are always constructed.

Miss a step and the build raises RuntimeError naming the manager: a factory no position in the order calls, an ordered name with no factory, and a *_manager attribute the order does not mention are all refused. Managers are discovered by that _manager suffix, so do not give any other attribute that name. Override _manager_order(), not _reset_idx(): an imperative reset override bypasses the declared order, and the check cannot see it.

docs.title: Inspecting a built environment
docs.text:
env.num_envs              # parallel environments
env.device                # torch device
env.sim_dt                # physics time step
env.dt                    # control step: sim_dt * decimation
env.training              # False when built with eval_mode=True
env.episode_length_buf    # (num_envs,) steps into the current episode
env.max_episode_length    # steps per episode (RLEnvBase and subclasses)
env.max_episode_length_s  # seconds per episode (RLEnvBase and subclasses)
env.common_step_counter   # control steps since construction (RLEnvBase and subclasses)
print(env.summary())      # every manager and its terms

docs.title: Entities, cameras and sensors
docs.text:
robot = env.entities["robot"]                 # by the name given in scene_options
robot = env.get_entity("robot")               # same, but a miss lists the entities that exist
arms = env.get_entities(["robot_.*", "box.*"])  # regex patterns, matched from the start of the name
camera = env.get_camera("wrist")              # also env.cameras["wrist"]
sensor = env.sensors["imu"]

An entity's class follows its options: Terrain for TerrainOptions, ParticleEntity for MPM, SPH and PBD materials, FEMEntity for FEM materials, the Mochi entity classes for Mochi materials, and RigidEntity otherwise. Test it with isinstance. Poses, DOF indexing and contacts are in Entities.

env.scene is the Genesis scene and env.rigid_solver its rigid solver. env.mochi_solver is the Mochi solver, and raises RuntimeError when no entity uses a Mochi material.

docs.title: Managers
docs.text:
env.action_manager, env.observation_manager, env.event_manager, env.recorder_manager
env.reward_manager, env.termination_manager                          # RLEnvBase and subclasses
env.metric_manager, env.command_manager, env.curriculum_manager      # None when the task declares no terms
env.motion_manager                                                   # MimicRLEnvBase
term = env.reward_manager.get_term("action_rate")

The optional managers read None both before the build and after it when the task declares none of their terms, so test them with is not None.

docs.title: Reading what the controller commanded
docs.text:
Three buffers describe an action step, and logging the wrong one is a common mistake:

term = env.action_manager.get_term("joint_pos_controller")

term.action             # the raw policy output this step, (num_envs, action_dim)
term.prev_action        # the raw policy output last step
term.processed_action   # the command the term issued, which deployment also sends

env.action_manager.processed_actions  # {term_name: processed_action} for every term

Read processed_action when you need the controller target, for a rollout export, a sim-to-real comparison or a tracking-error plot. Recomputing raw * scale + offset yourself drops any configured control-step action modifier. A joint controller's resolved multiplier and bias are term.effective_scale and term.effective_offset, the built values rather than the scale / offset config fields. processed_action differs per term in units and width, so only its leading num_envs dimension is guaranteed. An ActionDelay modifier acts later, once per physics step inside apply_actions(), and no deployment applies it. Controllers and modifiers are covered in Actions, and what deployment sends in Deployment.

docs.title: Recovering the config
docs.text:
env.config reconstructs the config that describes the environment. For an environment built with from_config, it is a round trip: an instance of the source config's own class (ReacherConfig, not EdenRLConfig) that carries every field the environment never receives (runner_options, language_instructions, task-specific fields), while the option groups the environment owns are read off the live environment.

config = TASK_REGISTRY.build("reacher")
env = RLEnvBase.from_config(config)

type(env.config)               # ReacherConfig
env.config.runner_options      # kept, though no environment parameter takes it
env.config.save_as_json("config.json")   # reloads into a ReacherConfig

The returned root is a fresh, unlocked object, but its option groups are the live ones, so editing them edits the environment; use env.config.clone() for an independent copy. An environment constructed directly (RLEnvBase(env_options=..., ...)) has no source config, so env.config synthesizes a plain EdenConfig / EdenRLConfig / EdenMimicConfig, and the fields the environment does not own take their class defaults.

The list of option groups is the same in both directions: from_config forwards every field the environment's config leaf declares except runner_options and language_instructions, and env.config reads that same list back. Neither side writes the list out, so they cannot drift apart. A loaded config keeps its concrete class too (Saving and loading configs), which is what lets eden train --config <a saved config.json> rebuild the right environment without being told the task.

docs.title: A task environment: subclass, and do not re-parameterize
docs.text:
To customize an environment for one task, subclass the environment class its config leaf uses, and stop there:

from eden.envs.base import RLEnvBase


class MyTaskEnv(RLEnvBase):   # the config leaf stays EdenRLConfig
    ...


env = MyTaskEnv.from_config(MyTaskConfig())
env.config.grasp_threshold    # a task-specific field, recovered from the source config

Task-specific config fields need no environment parameter, because env.config carries them over from the config the environment was built from.

Leave from_config alone in a subclass that only customizes step(). An override that genuinely needs to exist must declare show_viewer and eval_mode by name: a **kwargs there would swallow a misspelled keyword that the base would have rejected. tests/envs/test_base.py holds every from_config under eden/ and examples/ to this.

docs.title: A new config leaf: parameterize on it
docs.text:
An environment class declares its config leaf by parameterizing on it: class RLEnvBase(EnvBase[EdenRLConfig]), class MimicRLEnvBase(RLEnvBase, EnvBase[EdenMimicConfig]). That binding is the list from_config forwards from and env.config reads back, so it is a promise that the environment's __init__ takes every field the leaf declares. The promise is checked when the class is created:

class MyTaskConfig(EdenRLConfig):
    grasp_threshold: float = 0.03


class MyTaskEnv(RLEnvBase, EnvBase[MyTaskConfig]):   # TypeError, at class creation
    pass

The TypeError names ['grasp_threshold'] as declared by the config and missing from MyTaskEnv.__init__. Unchecked, both directions would fail without naming the config: from_config would pass grasp_threshold=... into __init__, whose **kwargs hands it on to the Genesis scene (Scene.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'grasp_threshold'), and env.config would raise a bare AttributeError.

Re-parameterize only to add a genuinely new leaf with option groups of its own, as the splat configs do. Then declare those groups as constructor parameters, and add the config-to-environment pair to env_class_for_config. The two directions are declared separately (each environment declares its own leaf, and env_class_for_config dispatches), so a new leaf must update both; tests/envs/test_base.py fails if only one of them lands.

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
Eden's design rule "fail fast, fail loud" decides when to raise: at the earliest well-defined point (Pydantic validation, a term's configure() or build()), never deep inside a hot compute() step. This page decides what the error says. It is for anyone writing a raise in Eden, and it assumes the reader of the message is often a coding agent working from a captured traceback, with no running process, no debugger, and no memory of the session that produced the log.

That reader has a narrow loop: grep for a symbol, open one or two files, make an edit. A message earns its keep by removing lookups from that loop. A message that describes the problem well but hands over no identifier costs more than a short one, because the reader still has to find the identifier and now has prose to discount first.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
<what broke>: '<the offending value>'.
<observed state — what was actually there, enumerated>
Fix: <an expression or edit the reader can type>
<the wrong fix, named, when a plausible wrong fix exists>

Not every message needs all four lines. Every message needs the first and the third.

A worked example, from CurriculumManager.get_state (eden/managers/curriculum_manager.py), when a curriculum term reads another that is declared after it:

Curriculum term 'ep_tracker' has not computed yet, so it has no state to read.
curriculum_options order: penalty_torques, ep_tracker
'penalty_torques' is reading 'ep_tracker', but 'ep_tracker' is declared after it
Fix: move 'ep_tracker' above 'penalty_torques' in curriculum_options — CurriculumManager computes terms in declaration order, so a producer declared after its consumer would feed it a value one control step stale.

The reader needs no second lookup: the two config keys, their order, which one is at fault, and the edit are all there.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Quote the offending value, first. 'ep_trackr' in quotes is a grep target; "an unknown term" is not. This extends Eden's base rule that a message names the offending value and the available options.

Enumerate what is there. Declared curriculum terms: level, penalty turns a typo into a one-character edit. The code that raises usually knows the roster, so make it pay. A registry lookup does this for you: Registry.get raises a KeyError that names the missing key, suggests the closest registered key (Did you mean '...'?) and lists the available ones.

Give the fix as something typeable. curriculum_manager.get_term('level') beats "read the level off the term". An expression is copy-pasteable and unambiguous; a description has to be translated, and that translation is where a reader guesses. A command counts too: eden terms --grep <text> is a fix a reader can run.

Resolve the symbol for the reader. A traceback carries the class that raised; it does not carry the config key that built it, and a task can hold a dozen entries of one class (metric_reward twelve times in robosuite PickPlace, two PenaltyCurriculums sharing a tracker). Name the entry to edit and a class name to open. Eden already does this at two layers, so build on them rather than repeating them:

  • build_term in eden/managers/base.py, which every manager's _build_term goes through, adds a note (add_note) naming the config entry and its registry key to any exception a term raises while it is constructed or built: while building RewardManager term 'lift_milk' (name='...'). A term's own message therefore does not need to restate its config key.
  • A term bound to an entity opens its errors with term_subject(self) (from eden.utils.string), which renders "<Class> on entity '<name>'", rather than spelling the class or the entity out by hand. CurriculumManager._term_label does the same inline for curriculum terms (the class name, or func() for a function term).

Name the wrong fix when there is an attractive one. A reader told to make an error go away will reach for a try/except or a default value. If that would reintroduce the bug the raise exists to prevent, say so in the message. Two examples from the code:

  • CurriculumManager.get_state at eval: "Do NOT catch this and fall back to a default: the default would stand for every step of the eval, grading it at a difficulty no training step used, with nothing logged and nothing raised."
  • A term's options built while eden.managers is still importing (eden/options/managers/base.py): "Do not wrap this in try/except and do not make it fall back to ..." — tests/options/managers/test_base.py checks that the message keeps that line.

This is the single highest-value line in Eden's error text: it is the only place the wrong fix can be pre-empted at the moment someone is considering it.

Split conflated causes. Two causes with one message force the reader to work out which applies, and sometimes they pick wrong and edit the wrong file. If the code can tell the causes apart, it must. CurriculumManager records the term it is in the middle of computing for exactly this reason, so "declared after its consumer" and "read before the run's first compute()" — identical empty-cache states — get different text and different fixes.

Point at something that ships. A docs path (docs/guides/environments.md) or a CLI command (eden terms --grep <name>) is readable offline, from the checkout or the installed package. An issue number is not. Issue numbers belong in comments and docstrings, where they record why a rule exists, not in runtime messages, where the reader needs what to do.

Never put a newline in a KeyError. KeyError.__str__ is repr(args[0]), so a multi-line message reaches the reader as one escaped, \n-laden blob — worse than the single line it was trying to improve on. Keep a KeyError to one line, and use ValueError, RuntimeError or TypeError for multi-line text. (Registry.get keeps its KeyError to one sentence on one line for this reason.)

Message-building code must not be able to raise. A helper that formats a label and throws AttributeError replaces the diagnostic with a traceback into the diagnostic, and the original failure is lost. Use isinstance over duck typing and getattr(..., default) over attribute access, and prefer a degraded label to an exception. CurriculumManager._term_label is written this way, and Registry.get computes its "did you mean" suggestion only when the missing key is a string, because a None key would make difflib raise from inside the message.

Render it before you ship it. Nearly every rule above was written after looking at real output rather than at the source. Print the message from a script that triggers it, and read it as the person who will see it. It takes a minute, and it is where the escaped KeyError and the raising label helper were both caught.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text:
Not a request for longer messages. Every line above carries an identifier or an instruction. Filler ("something went wrong", "please check your configuration", a restatement of the exception type) makes a message worse in exactly the way prose does. Shorter is better at equal information.

Not a structured error framework either. Eden raises plain built-in exceptions with hand-written text, tuned per site, and the exception type is part of the contract that callers and tests match on. There is no error-code registry to look values up in.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Terms guide — where validation belongs in a term's lifecycle
  • Testing — asserting on a raised error and its message
  • Contributing

docs.title: Events and domain randomization
docs.text:
Event terms change the simulation at defined moments: once at startup, whenever an env resets, or on a timer while it runs. Resetting a robot to a random pose, pushing it mid-episode and randomizing its friction, mass or PD gains are all event terms. This page covers when events fire and in what order, the built-in reset, placement and domain-randomization terms with the scene settings some of them need, and how to write your own.

Events are configured through event_options (an EventManagerOptions) on any config, RL or not.

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
The velocity-tracking tasks reset the robot's base and joints every episode, push it every 1 to 3 seconds, and randomize its foot friction, centre of mass and encoder offsets once per env (eden/tasks/velocity_tracking/base_config.py, trimmed):

import eden as en
from eden import events
from eden.options.envs import EnvOptions
from eden.options.managers.events import EventManagerOptions
from eden.terms import EventTerm

env_options = EnvOptions(
    batch_links_info=True,  # RandomizeComShift writes per-env link COMs
)

event_options = EventManagerOptions(
    reset_base=EventTerm.configure(
        func=en.events.reset_base_state_uniform,
        mode="reset",
        params={
            "entity_name": "robot",
            "pos_x_range": (-0.5, 0.5),
            "pos_y_range": (-0.5, 0.5),
            "pos_z_range": (0.01, 0.05),
            "yaw_range": (-3.14, 3.14),
        },
    ),
    push_robot=events.PushByVelocity.configure(
        mode="interval",
        interval_range_s=(1.0, 3.0),
        entity_name="robot",
        velocity_range={"x": (-0.5, 0.5), "y": (-0.5, 0.5), "yaw": (-0.78, 0.78)},
    ),
    randomize_friction=events.RandomizeFrictionRatio.configure(
        mode="startup",
        entity_name="robot",
        links_name=[".*_foot"],
        friction_range=(0.3, 1.2),
    ),
    randomize_com=events.RandomizeComShift.configure(
        mode="startup",
        entity_name="robot",
        links_name=["base"],
        com_shift_x_range=(-0.025, 0.025),
    ),
    encoder_bias=events.RandomizeDofsPosOffset.configure(
        mode="startup",
        entity_name="robot",
        dofs_pos_range=(-0.015, 0.015),
    ),
)

(The task fills links_name per robot; the patterns above are placeholders.) Two spellings appear: function terms go through EventTerm.configure(func=..., params={...}), class terms through their own .configure(...) with the parameters as keyword arguments.

Two classes called EventTerm

eden.terms.EventTerm is the wrapper for function event terms (EventTerm.configure(func=...)). The base class you subclass for a class event term is eden.managers.EventTerm (eden.managers.event_manager.EventTerm). Import the one you mean.

docs.title: When events fire
docs.text:
Every event term carries five scheduling fields:

Field Type Default Meaning mode EventMode or its string "reset" "startup", "reset" or "interval". Several class terms change the default (pushes and wrenches default to "interval", RandomizeStartupDofsPosBias to "startup"). priority int 0 Order among the terms of the same mode: lower runs first. interval_range_s tuple[float, float] \| None None Interval mode only, and required there: seconds between fires, redrawn after each fire. is_global_time bool False Interval mode only: one clock shared by all envs instead of one per env. min_step_count_between_reset int 0 Reset mode only: fire for an env at most once every N control steps. Mode Fires Where in the step "startup" Once, for all envs, at the end of env.build() after every manager is constructed — "reset" For the envs being reset, right after the scene reset phase 13 (and every env.reset()) "interval" For the envs whose countdown expired phase 18, after the auto-reset, before observations

The phase numbers refer to the step-order table in Environments.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
STARTUP events run once, with envs_idx=None, before Eden snapshots the scene state that every later reset restores. Two consequences:

  • A property a STARTUP event writes (friction, mass, COM, gains, a joint-zero bias) holds for the env's lifetime. This is the usual choice for physical domain randomization: one draw per env per run.
  • A state a STARTUP event writes (a joint position, a base pose) becomes part of the reset baseline: every scene reset returns to it.

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
RESET events run after scene.reset() has put the reset envs back to the post-build state, for exactly those envs, before any manager's reset(). A task with no reset events therefore starts every episode from the same pose. The events receive envs_idx in whatever form the caller used: the auto-reset in RLEnvBase.step passes the full-length bool reset_buf, env.reset() passes a slice or an index tensor. Index with it; never take its length (see Writing event terms).

min_step_count_between_reset throttles an event for an env that keeps resetting: the event fires for an env only if at least that many control steps passed since it last fired there (or it has never fired there).

docs.title: Interval
docs.text:
An interval term keeps a countdown per env (one CPU-side countdown with is_global_time=True). Each control step subtracts env.dt; when it reaches zero the term fires for those envs and draws a new interval from interval_range_s. The countdown is in control-step time, so an interval equal to env.dt fires every step. A mode-"interval" term without interval_range_s raises a ValueError when the event manager is built.

  • A class term's per-env countdown restarts with a fresh draw when its env resets. A function term's countdown does not restart on reset.
  • A global-time term is called with no envs_idx at all, so a function used that way must give envs_idx a default.

docs.title: Ordering events with priority
docs.text:
Within one mode, terms run in ascending priority; equal priorities keep their declaration order (the sort is stable). Ordering is computed separately for each mode. Set priority whenever one event has to see another's result, and leave gaps (0, 10, 20) so a term can be slotted in later. Examples:

  • An event that converts a world-frame angular velocity through the base orientation must run after the event that randomizes that orientation (reset_base_state_uniform), or it converts against the previous episode's heading. A free base stores its angular DOF velocity in the base body frame; see Entities.
  • Two events that write the same quantity, such as a whole-robot friction pass at priority=0 and a tighter per-foot pass at priority=10.
  • ResetFromStateBuffer must run after any RESET event that writes the same entities, or they overwrite the restored state.

env.event_manager.summary() prints the resolved order, one table per mode with a Priority column. It is the quickest way to confirm what runs.

docs.title: A class term's reset() always runs
docs.text: Separately from firing, the event manager calls reset(envs_idx) on every class event term whenever an env resets, whatever the term's mode. This happens after action_manager.reset(), which the env enforces at build. Several domain-randomization terms rely on it: an action modifier's per-env buffer is restored to its baseline by the action manager's reset, so a randomization written earlier in the same reset would be overwritten. The actuator randomizers write in reset() instead (see below).

docs.title: Events do not stop at eval
docs.text:
The event manager has no eval switch: every event fires in eval_mode=True exactly as in training. (Eval mode turns off observation corruption and freezes curricula; see Observations and Curricula.) To evaluate without a randomization, remove it from the config before building the env:

config.event_options.disable_term("push_robot")

disable_term raises a KeyError listing the declared terms if the name is wrong. The keyboard-driven velocity-tracking player disables every reset and randomization event this way before it runs a trained policy (examples/projects/locomotion/velocity_tracking/main.py).

docs.title: Built-in event terms
docs.text: All built-ins live in eden.managers.terms.events (also eden.events). eden terms --kind event prints every one with its parameters, defaults and requires: line, and the generated term catalog has the same list. The groups below say what each is for and what it needs.

docs.title: Resetting state
docs.text:
Function terms; use them with EventTerm.configure(func=..., mode="reset", params={...}).

Term What it does reset_base_state_uniform The entity's default root pose plus a uniform offset (pos_*_range) and rotation (roll_range, pitch_range, yaw_range, composed as R_rpy @ R_default). Writes the authored root frame (relative=True), so the asset's declared origin lands on the target. Rigid entities only. reset_dofs_by_offset Joint positions default + U(dofs_pos_range), clamped to the soft limits; velocities zero, or U(dofs_vel_range) when given. reset_dofs_by_scale Joint positions default * U(dofs_pos_scale_range), clamped; velocities zero. reset_dofs_by_scale_and_offset default * U(dofs_scale_range) + U(dofs_offset_range), clamped; velocities zero.

Class terms for joint positions: SetRandomDofsPos (default: a fraction of each joint's limit range, apply_as_ratio=True, (0.0, 0.2)) and RandomizeStartupDofsPos (default: absolute radians, ±1°; despite the name its default mode is "reset").

For motion-tracking tasks on MimicRLEnvBase, ReferenceStateInitialization (robot) and ObjectReferenceStateInitialization (a free object) start each episode from the motion reference, with optional pose, velocity and joint noise; see Motion tracking. ResetFromStateBuffer(path=...) restores each resetting env to a stored row of a reset-state buffer file, drawn uniformly, by category_weights, or by a curriculum sampler named in sampler (see Curricula).

docs.title: Placing objects on a surface
docs.text:
These sample a position on another entity's support surface and drop the entity onto it, after resetting its orientation to its default (plus the sampled rotation, where there is one). The support entity must be built with support sampling enabled: is_support_enabled=True on its options, for example en.scenes.Empty(is_support_enabled=True) for the ground plane. See Scenes and terrains.

Term Kind Samples place_constant_xy function A fixed pos_xy (frame="world" or "local" to the support). place_range_xy function Uniform range_x × range_y, plus optional range_roll / range_pitch / range_yaw. place_uniform function Uniformly over the support surface (samples_per_area). PlaceGaussian class Gaussian-weighted around (mu_x, mu_y) with variances var_x, var_y. PlaceFromLayouts class One of a fixed list of layouts, each mapping entity names to (x, y, yaw_deg). Drawing every entity from one layout keeps them from overlapping, which independent ranges over the same area cannot guarantee.

docs.title: Pushes and external wrenches
docs.text:
Term Default mode What it does PushByVelocity interval Adds a random velocity to the free base. velocity_range keys: x, y, z (world frame) and roll, pitch, yaw (added in the base body frame). PushSetPlanarVelocity interval Sets the base's vx, vy to U(velocity_xy_range), keeping vz and the angular velocity. ApplyExternalForce interval A random force (force_*_range, N) on links_name, at ref="link_origin" or "link_com", world or local frame. ApplyExternalTorque interval The same for a torque (torque_*_range, N·m).

The two wrench terms take prob, a per-env probability of applying the wrench at each fire. Each term draws its own mask, so a force term and a torque term configured together gate independently. Genesis applies the wrench over one simulation step (RigidSolver.apply_links_external_wrench).

docs.title: Physical properties
docs.text:
Term Requires What it does RandomizeFrictionRatio — Per-link sliding friction from friction_range, as an absolute coefficient (see the warning below). RandomizeMassShift EnvOptions(batch_links_info=True) Adds U(mass_shift_range) kg to each named link's mass. RandomizeLinkMassScale EnvOptions(batch_links_info=True) Multiplies each named link's mass by U(mass_scale_range). RandomizeComShift EnvOptions(batch_links_info=True) Shifts each named link's centre of mass by an xyz offset (m, link frame). RandomizeKpKdGains EnvOptions(batch_dofs_info=True) Scales the joint PD gains by U(kp_range) / U(kd_range) per env and DOF. set_contact_sol_params STARTUP only Sets the constraint-solver parameters (7 values: timeconst, dampratio, dmin, dmax, width, mid, power) on the collision geoms of entity_links.

batch_links_info defaults to False and batch_dofs_info to True (EnvOptions). A term whose flag is off raises a ValueError naming the term and the flag when the env is built, rather than failing on its first write.

The mass and COM terms also refuse, at build:

  • A link fixed to the world (a fixed-base arm's base, a mounted hand's palm, a fixed=True prop), whose mass and COM the solver never reads. The error suggests a links_name that selects exactly the moving links, so links_name=["*"] suits only an entity with no world-fixed link.
  • A body Genesis re-anchored at build. By default a single free rigid body is aligned: its frame is put on its centre of mass and principal axes, and Genesis then does not support writing its COM (or, for a body of several links, its mass). The fix is to load the asset with align=False; primitives always align, so load the shape from a file instead. batch_links_info=True does not help here.
  • A range that can make a mass non-positive (RandomizeMassShift checks the lightest selected link, RandomizeLinkMassScale requires a positive lower bound).

RandomizeKpKdGains has two paths. With action_term_name=None it writes the entity's gains (set_dofs_kp / set_dofs_kd), which is what Genesis' built-in PD (ImplicitPDController) reads. With action_term_name set to an ExplicitPDController or VelocityFeedforwardPDController, it scales that controller's own gain caches and leaves the entity alone; the factors are re-applied after every action-manager reset so they survive it.

set_contact_sol_params rejects any envs_idx other than all envs, because Genesis stores geom solver parameters unbatched. Genesis mixes a contact pair's parameters as the mean of its two geoms, so stiffening one object's geoms also stiffens its contacts with everything else (the table, say). To stiffen an object without an event, set default_geoms_sol_params on it; see Entities.

Friction randomization has absolute semantics, and contact friction combines as max

Every RandomizeFrictionRatio fire first sets the whole entity's base friction to 1.0 — discarding any authored default_geoms_friction, including on links outside links_name — and then writes per-link ratios on links_name. friction_range is therefore the absolute coefficient range, whatever the asset authored; convert a source config written as "scale × authored value" before porting it. Where torsional and rolling friction are enabled, the same ratio scales them too.

Genesis resolves a contact pair's friction as max(a, b), so the randomized value only matters against surfaces whose friction is below it. Author the ground low (for example PlaneOptions(default_geoms_friction={"*": 0.01})) so the robot side decides. The full porting recipe is in Entities.

docs.title: Actuator and controller randomization
docs.text:
These randomize an action term or one of its action modifiers rather than the simulator. Each names its action term with action_term_name and raises at build if the term, or the modifier it needs, is missing. Modifiers are configured in the action term's modifier chain; see Actions.

Term Needs What it randomizes RandomizeMotorStrength MotorStrength The torque scale, one factor per env from motor_strength_range. RandomizeGearBacklash GearBacklash The backlash per env and DOF (backlash_range, rad, or multipliers of the configured value with apply_as_ratio=True). RandomizeConstantTorqueKick ConstantTorqueKick The kick magnitude (torque_kick_range, or multipliers). RandomizeDeadbandEpsilon Deadband The position-error deadband (deadband_epsilon_range, or multipliers). RandomizeTorqueNoise TorqueOffset Random force injection: per-DOF torque noise in [-rfi_scale, rfi_scale] at each fire. Interval mode; set interval_range_s to the control period. ERFI50 TorqueOffset Per env, either a constant actuation offset for the episode or per-step random torque noise (erfi_ratio splits the envs). Interval mode, interval_range_s set to the control period. RandomizeDofsPosOffset a joint position controller A per-env joint-position offset added to the controller's target (encoder bias). action_term_name=None selects every joint position controller on entity_name. RandomizeStartupDofsPosBias — Bakes a per-env constant bias into entity.default_dofs_pos at startup (calibration drift).

The first four randomize in reset(), not in their event compute(), so their draw lands after the action manager has restored the modifier's baseline. They therefore support only mode="reset" with min_step_count_between_reset=0, and reject anything else at construction. Managers that reset before the event manager (action, command, metric, termination, reward, curriculum) still see the previous episode's draw in the modifier buffers.

RandomizeStartupDofsPosBias and RandomizeDofsPosOffset compose: a fixed drift baked in at startup plus per-episode jitter on top, in either event order. Because the bias moves default_dofs_pos, every PD controller on the entity with reference_source=DEFAULT must be listed in action_terms_name so its cached offset moves in lockstep; build() raises for a controller left out, for duplicates, and for a NullJointAction on the same entity (which caches the default with no refresh path).

docs.title: Function terms
docs.text:
An event function takes the env and the env selector, then keyword-only parameters:

import torch

from eden.managers import EVENT_TERM_REGISTRY
from eden.terms import EventTerm
from eden.utils.misc import sanitize_envs_idx


@EVENT_TERM_REGISTRY.register()
def my_reset(env, envs_idx: slice | torch.Tensor | None, *, entity_name: str, scale: float = 1.0) -> None:
    envs_idx = sanitize_envs_idx(envs_idx, env.num_envs)
    entity = env.get_entity(entity_name)
    ...  # write the selected envs' state through the entity's setters, with envs_idx=envs_idx


reset_thing = EventTerm.configure(func=my_reset, mode="reset", params={"entity_name": "robot", "scale": 0.5})

The built-ins in eden/managers/terms/events/resets.py are complete examples. Points to get right:

  • envs_idx is None at startup (all envs), a full-length bool mask on the auto-reset and on interval fires, and a slice or index tensor from env.reset(). sanitize_envs_idx turns None into a slice. Index with it; len(envs_idx) on the step path is num_envs, not the reset count.
  • Sample for every env and keep the selected rows (sample_uniform(..., (env.num_envs, n), ...)[envs_idx], or pass every row with the mask where the setter accepts it), rather than gathering through the mask, which costs GPU→CPU syncs on every step that resets anything. Terms covers the sync rules.
  • A function used with is_global_time=True is called without envs_idx; give it a default.
  • A function that needs an EnvOptions flag declares it at registration: @EVENT_TERM_REGISTRY.register(_requires_env_options=("batch_links_info",)). The env then refuses to build without it, and eden terms shows it on the term's requires: line.

docs.title: Class terms
docs.text: Subclass eden.managers.EventTerm when the term needs state resolved once (link indices, a cached controller) or a reset() hook. Declare parameters as annotated class attributes (they become configure() arguments), resolve names in build() so a typo raises at env construction, and implement compute(self, envs_idx=None). Set _requires_env_options = ("batch_links_info",) as a class attribute for a scene-wide flag. RandomizeComShift in eden/managers/terms/events/domain_rand.py is a short, complete example.

docs.title: Firing several reset terms as one write
docs.text: Each Genesis state setter resets the selected envs' collider state and runs forward kinematics, so N terms that each seed one entity pay N passes. A class term can override the classmethod EventTerm.compute_batch(terms, envs_idx) to fire several terms of its kind in one write. The event manager hands a run of RESET terms to one call when they are adjacent in priority order, each term's class takes compute and compute_batch from the same class, and none sets min_step_count_between_reset. A term of another kind between them breaks the run, and a subclass that overrides compute alone runs alone. A batch must leave exactly what firing its terms one after another would leave: the same random draws in the same order, last write winning. The reference-state-initialization terms do this through StagedStateWrite (eden/entities/rigid.py). EventManager.iter_reset_batches() lists the batches; their terms' own compute never runs on a reset.

docs.text:

  • Terms — the general term lifecycle, validation and performance rules.
  • Entities — pose frames, free-base velocity frames, friction and contact parameters.
  • Physics — EnvOptions batching flags and solver settings.
  • Actions — the action modifiers the actuator randomizers write to.
