docs.title: Physics
docs.text:
This page covers the simulation settings of an Eden environment: time stepping, the backend and floating-point precision, which physics solver an entity runs in, the rigid solver's contact and integrator settings, the Eden-hosted Mochi solver, and what happens when a solver fails. Read it when you write the env_options of a task, port a task from another simulator, or add deformable bodies to a scene.

Almost everything here is a field of EnvOptions, which EnvBase turns into Genesis' SimOptions, RigidOptions and the per-solver options when it creates the scene. Per-entity physical properties (mass, armature, friction, contact softness, gains) live on the entity options instead: see Entities.

docs.title: Time stepping
docs.text:
Three fields decide how simulated time advances:

Field Default Meaning sim_dt 0.005 Length of one scene.step(), in seconds. sim_substeps 1 Genesis substeps inside one scene.step(). Every solver integrates at sim_dt / sim_substeps. decimation 4 scene.step() calls per control step (action repeat).

The control step is env.dt = decimation * sim_dt, so the control frequency is 1 / (sim_dt * decimation). With the defaults a policy acts at 50 Hz on 200 Hz physics. The episode horizon episode_length_s (default 20.0) becomes max_episode_length = ceil(episode_length_s / env.dt) control steps on an RLEnvBase; it must be positive and finite.

The reacher task (eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py) runs physics at 100 Hz with two substeps and acts on every physics step:

from eden.options.envs import EnvOptions

env_options = EnvOptions(
    num_envs=4096,
    episode_length_s=9.0,
    iterations=10,
    ls_iterations=20,
    sim_dt=0.01,
    sim_substeps=2,
    decimation=1,
    max_collision_pairs=30,
    multiplier_collision_broad_phase=12,
    enable_multi_contact=True,
)

LIBERO (eden/tasks/libero/config.py) does the opposite: sim_dt=0.002 and decimation=25, a 20 Hz policy on 500 Hz physics.

Two things are easy to get wrong:

  • The substep dt is what stiff constraints see. Genesis clamps every constraint time constant to 2 * sim_dt / sim_substeps, so a stiff contact only takes full effect when the substep is short enough. Closed-loop grippers such as the Robotiq 2F-85 need a substep dt of 0.001 s or less (see Closed-loop grippers).
  • A substep callback runs per scene.step(), not per Genesis substep. env.register_substep_callback(fn) runs fn around each of the decimation scene steps; Genesis' own sim_substeps happen inside one call and are never visible to it.

num_envs (default 4096) is the number of parallel environments. Under multi-GPU training it is the count per rank (see Multi-GPU training).

docs.title: Backend and precision: eden.init()
docs.text:
eden.init() initializes Genesis and torch for the process. Call it once, before you build an environment; a second call warns, does not re-initialize Genesis, and moves the run's log directory.

import eden as en
import genesis as gs

en.init(backend=gs.gpu)                     # the common case
en.init(backend=gs.gpu, precision="64")     # double precision (Mochi at its default stiffness, SAP)
Argument Default Meaning backend gs.cpu Genesis backend. The eden CLI commands pass gs.gpu unless you give --cpu. precision "32" Floating-point precision of the simulation, "32" or "64". eps 1e-8 Genesis' global epsilon, chosen for rigid-solver stability. allow_tf32 True Let torch use TF32 matmuls on Ampere and newer GPUs. deterministic False Use deterministic torch and Genesis algorithms. performance_mode False Passed to gs.init. The CLI training and evaluation commands set it.

After eden.init(), torch's default dtype is Genesis' float type, so a dtype-less torch.zeros(n) matches Genesis' tensors under precision="64". The default device is not set: a tensor created without device= is a CPU tensor. Use env.device (or gs.device).

When you need precision="64":

  • Mochi at its default contact stiffness. The Mochi materials default to penalty_coefficient=1e9 Pa/m, which makes the Newton system ill-conditioned in single precision; the solver warns at build when a stiffness of 1e8 or more runs at 32 bits. Either initialize with precision="64" or lower the stiffness, as the Mochi tasks do (see Mochi).
  • The SAP coupler. examples/recipes/physics/sap_franka_grasp_cube.py initializes with en.init(backend=gs.gpu, precision="64", eps=1e-15): SAP needs double precision, and Eden's default eps=1e-8 is coarser than SAP's convergence tolerances, which makes contacts explode.

The eden train / eden inference commands always initialize at precision="32"; there is no CLI flag for it. A task that only works in double precision has to run from its own script. Some tasks refuse double precision outright: the art tasks raise at build when Eden was initialized at precision="64".

docs.title: Which solver an entity runs in
docs.text:
Genesis has one solver per physics family. You never pick a solver directly: the material of an entity decides it, and with it the Eden entity class that wraps the entity.

Material options (eden.options.materials) Solver Eden entity class RigidMaterialOptions (the default), KinematicMaterialOptions rigid RigidEntity MPMElasticMaterialOptions, MPMElastoPlasticMaterialOptions, MPMLiquidMaterialOptions, MPMSandMaterialOptions MPM ParticleEntity SPHLiquidMaterialOptions SPH ParticleEntity PBDLiquidMaterialOptions, PBDClothMaterialOptions, PBDElasticMaterialOptions, PBDParticleMaterialOptions PBD ParticleEntity FEMElasticMaterialOptions, FEMClothMaterialOptions, FEMMuscleMaterialOptions FEM FEMEntity MochiRigidMaterialOptions Mochi MochiRigidEntity MochiElasticMaterialOptions, MochiShellMaterialOptions, MochiRodMaterialOptions Mochi MochiSoftEntity

A terrain (TerrainOptions) always builds as a Terrain, a rigid entity. There are no separate "MPM entity" or "FEM entity" options: you put the material on an ordinary entity (BoxOptions, SphereOptions, EntityOptions(file=...)). Solver-wide settings go on EnvOptions as Genesis option objects: mpm_options, sph_options, pbd_options, fem_options (gs.options.MPMOptions and so on), mochi_options (MochiOptions, Eden's own), and coupler_options.

From examples/recipes/physics/mpm_tutorial.py, three MPM bodies on a rigid plane:

import genesis as gs

from eden.options import EnvOptions, SceneOptions
from eden.options.entities import BoxOptions, PlaneOptions, SphereOptions
from eden.options.materials import MPMElasticMaterialOptions, MPMElastoPlasticMaterialOptions, MPMLiquidMaterialOptions

env_options = EnvOptions(
    num_envs=1,
    sim_dt=4e-3,
    sim_substeps=10,
    mpm_options=gs.options.MPMOptions(lower_bound=(-0.5, -1.0, 0.0), upper_bound=(0.5, 1.0, 1.0)),
)
scene_options = SceneOptions(
    plane=PlaneOptions(),
    elastic=BoxOptions(
        size=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2),
        default_root_pos=(0.0, -0.5, 0.25),
        material=MPMElasticMaterialOptions(),
        surface=gs.surfaces.Default(color=(1.0, 0.4, 0.4), vis_mode="visual"),
        vis_mode="visual",
    ),
    liquid=BoxOptions(
        size=(0.3, 0.3, 0.3),
        default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.25),
        material=MPMLiquidMaterialOptions(),
        surface=gs.surfaces.Default(color=(0.3, 0.3, 1.0), vis_mode="particle"),
        vis_mode="particle",
    ),
    plastic=SphereOptions(
        radius=0.1,
        default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.5, 0.35),
        material=MPMElastoPlasticMaterialOptions(),
        surface=gs.surfaces.Default(color=(0.4, 1.0, 0.4), vis_mode="particle"),
        vis_mode="particle",
    ),
)

examples/recipes/physics/ has one script per solver and coupler (rigid, FEM, MPM, SPH, PBD, IPC, SAP); its README.md lists them. They run on backend=gs.gpu, except the rigid collision tower and the keyboard-teleop variant of the MPM dragon cut, which run on the CPU.

Deformable bodies are posed at creation

ParticleEntity.set_pos() / set_quat() raise (MPM, SPH, PBD), and so does FEMEntity.set_quat(). Give the pose through default_root_pos / default_root_quat, which is baked into the morph when the entity is created. The DOF and constraint-solver fields of the entity options are refused on a non-rigid material. See Deformable entities for their API.

docs.title: Couplers
docs.text:
coupler_options decides how the solvers of one scene exchange forces. None (the default) is Genesis' legacy coupler; gs.options.SAPCouplerOptions and gs.options.IPCCouplerOptions are the alternatives. Two-way coupling of a rigid body is configured on its RigidMaterialOptions (needs_coup, coup_friction, coup_softness, coup_restitution, and, under IPC only, coup_type, coup_links, enable_coup_collision, coup_collision_links, contact_resistance).

EnvOptions refuses two IPC settings at construction: batch_dofs_info=True (set it False) and num_envs > 1 (the IPC coupler can only reset the whole scene). The IPC recipes also need the libuipc Python bindings installed.

docs.title: The rigid solver
docs.text: Every robot, object, terrain and ground plane with a rigid material runs in Genesis' rigid solver. These EnvOptions fields configure it.

docs.title: Constraint solver
docs.text:
Field Default Meaning solver "newton" Constraint solver: "newton" or "cg". iterations 50 Maximum constraint-solver iterations. tolerance None Convergence tolerance, as a ratio against the scene's free-motion cost. None lets Genesis pick from the precision (1e-6 single, 1e-9 double). ls_iterations 50 Line-search iterations. ls_tolerance 1e-2 Line-search tolerance. noslip_iterations 0 Iterations of the noslip post-pass, which suppresses slip and drift. 0 disables it.

The noslip pass is a cheap fix for objects creeping in a grasp; the LIBERO, SimplerEnv and PolaRiS ports run with noslip_iterations=5.

docs.title: Integrators and implicit damping
docs.text:
integrator selects how the rigid solver advances velocities:

  • "approximate_implicitfast" (default): Genesis' own fast scheme.
  • "implicitfast": MuJoCo's integrator of that name. It integrates joint damping and the position actuators' velocity gain implicitly, as MuJoCo does. Use it for tasks ported from a MuJoCo stack.
  • "euler": MuJoCo's explicit Euler. The PD controller's damping is integrated explicitly.

Implicit damping changes armature under euler only

Under integrator="euler", an actuated entity's post_build() adds kd * substep_dt to the armature of its DOFs, which emulates implicit damping and keeps the PD loop stable. The armature the solver holds then differs from the configured default_dofs_armature. Under the two implicit integrators nothing is added.

Only damping Genesis applies itself is ever implicit: the kv of a DOF Genesis drives in position or velocity mode. A torque-mode action term (one that calls control_dofs_force, such as ExplicitPDController or OperationalSpaceController) computes -kd * qdot in Python, so its damping is explicit under every integrator. Read entity.get_dofs_armature() on the built entity to see what the solver actually uses. See Implicit damping and Actions.

docs.title: Collision detection
docs.text:
Field Default Meaning use_gjk_collision True Use GJK for convex collision; False uses MPR+GJK. max_collision_pairs 50 Contact capacity per environment. multiplier_collision_broad_phase 8 Broad-phase capacity multiplier. enable_multi_contact True Generate several contact points per pair. enable_self_collision True Collide the links of one entity with each other. enable_neutral_collision False Keep self-collision pairs that already overlap at the neutral pose.

A contact capacity that overflows is a misconfiguration: the env keeps its error flag across the reset and the next control step raises with a message naming the option to raise (see Solver errors).

enable_neutral_collision is scene-wide

With the default False, Genesis drops every self-collision pair that overlaps at an entity's neutral configuration (qpos0), using a voxel approximation that can also drop a pair that only comes within millimetres. True keeps the asset's full collision set, but for every articulated entity in the scene: a second robot whose collision meshes genuinely interpenetrate at qpos0 then fights itself from the first step.

docs.title: Friction
docs.text:
Field Default Meaning friction_cone "pyramidal" "pyramidal" (robust, easy to solve) or "elliptic" (the exact isotropic cone). contact_resolution None "signorini" or "convex". None resolves to "signorini" with the elliptic cone and the Newton solver, "convex" otherwise. impratio None Ratio of frictional to normal constraint impedance (MuJoCo's impratio). None lets Genesis pick: 100 with the elliptic cone, 1 otherwise. enable_torsional_friction False Add one constraint axis per contact that resists spin about the normal. enable_rolling_friction False Add two axes that resist rolling. Requires enable_torsional_friction.

"signorini" bounds friction by the normal force the contact has developed, so fast sliding never inflates the normal force: a body launched horizontally decelerates at mu times g instead of lifting off. It needs friction_cone="elliptic" and solver="newton", and costs extra solver iterations. The elliptic cone is not supported with the noslip pass (noslip_iterations > 0) or with requires_grad.

Friction coefficients themselves are per geom, on the entity and its material; the entities guide covers them. In short:

  • A contact pair takes the max of the two coefficients, not the minimum or the mean (Friction combines as max).
  • The two switches above only add constraint axes. The strength is per geom (friction_torsional / friction_rolling, in meters), MJCF geoms without condim >= 4 parse to 0, and a coefficient set while its switch is off raises at build (Torsional and rolling friction).

docs.title: Contact softness
docs.text:
constraint_timeconst (default None) is the rigid solver's global constraint time constant. None resolves to max(0.01, 2 * sim_dt / sim_substeps).

Stiffen contacts per object, never globally

Lowering EnvOptions.constraint_timeconst to stiffen one grasp ejects mesh objects on contact elsewhere in the scene. Stiffen the objects that need it through the entity's default_geoms_sol_params instead, on both sides of the pair: see Closed-loop grippers and constraint fidelity.

docs.title: Per-environment physical properties
docs.text:
Genesis stores link, joint and DOF properties once for the whole batch unless asked otherwise. Randomizing them per environment needs the matching switch:

Field Default Needed for batch_links_info False Per-env link mass, inertia and center of mass. batch_joints_info False Per-env joint properties. batch_dofs_info True Per-env DOF gains, armature, damping, limits.

An event term that writes one of these declares the flag it needs, eden terms lists it on the term, and the env refuses to build without it, naming the flag. For example RandomizeLinkMassScale, RandomizeMassShift and RandomizeComShift need batch_links_info=True. See Events.

docs.title: Other rigid-solver switches
docs.text:
• use_hibernation (default False) is passed to Genesis' RigidOptions.use_hibernation.
  • Gravity compensation is a material field, RigidMaterialOptions(gravity_compensation=1.0) cancels gravity on the entity. It is not a morph, RigidOptions or add_entity argument (Gravity compensation).
  • requires_grad (default False) turns on Genesis' differentiable mode. The Mochi solver and the elliptic cone do not support it.

docs.title: Mochi: the Eden-hosted implicit solver
docs.text:
The MochiSolver is a fully implicit multi-physics solver that Eden hosts on stock Genesis (eden/engine/solvers/mochi). Every substep it solves one nonlinear system over all rigid and articulated bodies, tetrahedral solids, thin shells and discrete elastic rods, with a smooth signed-distance penalty contact model. Contact is re-detected at every Newton iterate and enters the same system as the inertia, which keeps large time steps stable and couples deformable bodies to rigid ones without a coupler. Genesis does not ship it; how Eden installs it on one scene at a time is described in Engine add-ons. This section covers the scene and solver settings; the Mochi entity API (fixing and driving vertices, attaching soft bodies, contact parameters per link) is in Mochi entities.

A Mochi scene is configured like any other: give every entity a Mochi material, and optionally tune the solver through EnvOptions.mochi_options. From examples/recipes/mochi/rigid_bodies.py:

from eden.engine.solvers.mochi.options import MochiOptions
from eden.options import EnvOptions, SceneOptions
from eden.options.entities import BoxOptions, PlaneOptions, SphereOptions
from eden.options.materials import MochiRigidMaterialOptions

env_options = EnvOptions(
    num_envs=1,
    sim_dt=1.0 / 60.0,
    mochi_options=MochiOptions(n_newton_iterations=8),
)
scene_options = SceneOptions(
    plane=PlaneOptions(material=MochiRigidMaterialOptions()),
    table=BoxOptions(
        size=(1.6, 1.0, 0.1),
        default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.75),
        is_fixed_base=True,
        material=MochiRigidMaterialOptions(collider_type="sdf"),
    ),
    sphere=SphereOptions(radius=0.2, default_root_pos=(-0.5, 0.0, 1.5), material=MochiRigidMaterialOptions()),
)

The solver is installed when the first entity with a Mochi material is added, whether or not mochi_options is set. env.mochi_solver returns it, and raises if no entity of the scene takes a Mochi material.

docs.title: Rules of a Mochi scene
docs.text:
• A Mochi scene is all-Mochi. Every entity, the ground plane included, needs a Mochi material (kinematic entities are allowed). SceneOptions rejects the mix and names the offending entities; remember that an entity with no material defaults to RigidMaterialOptions.
  • Double precision at the default stiffness. Run with en.init(precision="64"), or lower every penalty_coefficient. The Mochi tasks (eden/tasks/mochi/) use 1e7 Pa/m so they train under eden train's single precision. Light cloth also uses 1e7.
  • Leave MochiOptions.dt unset. The solver substep is sim_dt / sim_substeps, as for every other solver; unset dt and gravity are filled from the scene's SimOptions.
  • No requires_grad. EnvOptions refuses requires_grad=True with mochi_options set, and the env refuses it when the first Mochi entity is added.
  • Rasterizer or Nyx only. The solver refuses a scene whose renderer is the ray tracer or the batch renderer. Use the rasterizer, or render through a Nyx camera (examples/recipes/mochi/_nyx.py is the bridge). See Sensors and rendering.
  • Options refused at validation. A MochiRigidMaterialOptions entity rejects default_dofs_frictionloss, default_dofs_force_limits and the constraint-solver (sol params) fields, since the solver clamps no drive force, models no joint friction loss and has no constraint solver. Support-surface fields, visualize_contact=True, GroupedEntityOptions and TerrainOptions are refused with a Mochi material too.
  • Per-env DOF properties are MochiOptions.batch_dofs_info (default False), not EnvOptions.batch_dofs_info, which configures the rigid solver only.

docs.title: Mochi materials
docs.text:
Material Body Entity MochiRigidMaterialOptions rigid and articulated bodies; keeps the rigid-entity API (DOFs, PD control, IK, attach_to) MochiRigidEntity MochiElasticMaterialOptions tetrahedral solids (stable neo-Hookean, StVK or linear); primitives and meshes are tetrahedralized, .node / .vtk files are read as they are MochiSoftEntity MochiShellMaterialOptions thin shells and cloth on a mesh's surface triangles MochiSoftEntity MochiRodMaterialOptions discrete elastic rods; needs a RodOptions morph MochiSoftEntity

All four share the contact fields of MochiMaterialOptions: friction (default 0.5, combined per pair as the geometric mean), penalty_coefficient (1e9 Pa/m), penalty_smoothing_half_distance (5e-3 m), penalty_threshold (1e-3 m), friction_falloff_vel, viscous_friction, normal_viscous_damping (the restitution knob), max_alignment_normals, has_gravity and contact_layer. Contact between two layers is switched at runtime with env.mochi_solver.enable_layer_contact(layer_a, layer_b, is_enabled), and the contact parameters of a built entity with its set_contact_params(...).

docs.title: Solver options
docs.text:
MochiOptions carries the Newton loop (n_newton_iterations, default 4; newton_abs_tol, newton_rel_tol), the line search, the linear solver (linear_solver: "auto", "ldlt" or "pcg"), the time integrator (integrator: "backward_euler" or "bdf2"), friction regularization, contact quadrature (boundary_element_type), soft joint limits (joint_limit_stiffness, default 1e4), body sleeping (use_sleeping), divergence handling (explosion_control, default True) and the step kernel (step_kernel). The API reference documents every field. With explosion_control, a substep whose residual blows up is flagged: the env is put back to its previous pose with zero velocity and the error reaches Eden's solver-error handling below.

The scripts in examples/recipes/mochi/ cover each body type, articulated grasps, cloth and rods; the Mochi tasks are trainable examples.

docs.title: Solver errors and recovery
docs.text:
A physics solver latches an error flag per environment. Eden splits them in two:

  • A corrupt state (a NaN contact force, acceleration or force in the rigid solver, a diverged Mochi solve) is recovered: the termination manager truncates the affected envs, the reward and metric managers drop what their terms read of them, and the reset clears the flag before Genesis' error check would raise for the whole scene. env.get_solver_error_envs_mask() returns these envs, (num_envs,) bool.
  • A misconfiguration (contact capacity overflow, an unsupported collision pair, a NaN gradient under requires_grad) is reset and dropped the same way, but the env keeps its flag across the reset, and the next control step raises it (on CUDA, the one after) with Genesis' message naming the option to change.

So a training run survives an occasional exploding env, but not a scene that is too small for its contacts.

docs.title: Throughput switches
docs.text:
These EnvOptions fields change speed, not physics:

  • update_sensors_every_substep (default False) skips sensor updates on the intermediate scene steps of a control step. See Sensors and rendering.
  • cuda_graph_options (default None) replays the graded phase of RLEnvBase.step (metrics, terminations, rewards) from a CUDA graph; CudaGraphOptions() turns it on. CUDA only. It is a training-only field: eden inference, eden export and eden deploy reset it when they replay a run's config. See Environments.
  • The batch_*_info switches above cost memory and some speed; leave them off unless a term needs them.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Entities: mass, armature, gains, contact parameters, deformable entities.
  • Sensors and rendering: cameras, renderers, sensors.
  • Engine add-ons: how the Mochi solver and Eden's sensors are hosted on stock Genesis.
  • Environments: the step loop and where physics runs in it.
  • EnvOptions API and material options API.

docs.title: Planning and system identification
docs.text: Three extensions sit beside the RL stack: motion planners that compute collision-free joint paths for an arm (cuRobo, OMPL), offline motion optimization that adapts a recorded clip to terrain (TCRS), and system identification that fits a robot's joint dynamics in simulation to measurements from the real robot. This page covers what each one does, how to call it, and its limits.

docs.title: Motion planning
docs.text:
A motion planner takes a built env and the name of an entity, and returns joint-space waypoints that you feed to a joint-position action term. Both planners subclass MotionPlannerBase (eden/extensions/motion_planning/base.py), register in MOTION_PLANNER_REGISTRY, and are configured through PlannerOptions (entity_name, default "robot"; backend fields arrive as extras).

CuroboPlanner OMPLPlanner Module eden.extensions.motion_planning.curobo eden.extensions.motion_planning.ompl Goal end-effector pose (ee_goal_pos, ee_goal_quat, wxyz) joint configuration (qpos_goal) Batched over envs yes no (one env per call, envs_idx) Collision world meshes of the entities in collision_entities_name the entity's own contacts in the live scene (detect_collision) Install cuRobo (see cuRobo's install guide); no Eden extra pip install ompl (OMPL 1.7 or 2.x; see OMPL releases); not available on Windows; no Eden extra Recipe examples/recipes/planning/path_planning_curobo.py examples/recipes/planning/path_planning_ompl.py

Both raise an ImportError with the install pointer when their library is missing.

docs.title: cuRobo
docs.text:
# excerpt from examples/recipes/planning/path_planning_curobo.py
import torch
from curobo.util_file import get_robot_configs_path, join_path

from eden.extensions.motion_planning.curobo import CuroboPlanner
from eden.options.extensions.motion_planning import PlannerOptions

planner = CuroboPlanner(
    env,
    PlannerOptions(
        entity_name="robot",
        robot_config_file=join_path(get_robot_configs_path(), "franka.yml"),  # cuRobo's own Franka config
        ee_link_name="hand",
        collision_entities_name=["table", "plate"],
    ),
)
target_pos = env.entities["plate"].get_pos()
target_pos[:, 2] += 0.2
waypoints = planner.plan_motion(
    ee_goal_pos=target_pos,
    ee_goal_quat=torch.tensor([[0, 1, 0, 0]] * env.num_envs).to(env.device),
)
# waypoints: one (num_waypoints, n_dof) tensor per env

CuroboPlanner fields: robot_config_file (a cuRobo robot YAML; its cspace joints minus lock_joints are the planned DOFs), ee_link_name, collision_entities_name (default none) and interpolation_dt (default 0.05 s).

  • The collision world is built on the first plan_motion call. When the scene has changed since, call planner.update_world(carried_entities=[...], num_envs=..., envs_idx=...) first; entities in carried_entities (an object in the gripper) are left out of the obstacles.
  • The goal pose is in the world frame; the planner converts it into the robot's base frame.
  • Per env, a failed plan returns the start configuration as its single waypoint. Different envs return different waypoint counts, so the recipe pads the shorter paths while stepping.

docs.title: OMPL
docs.text:
# excerpt from examples/recipes/planning/path_planning_ompl.py
from eden.extensions.motion_planning.ompl import OMPLPlanner
from eden.options.extensions.motion_planning import PlannerOptions

# robot = env.entities["robot"]; target_pos (num_envs, 3) and target_quat (num_envs, 4, wxyz) are the hand's goal
planner = OMPLPlanner(env, PlannerOptions(entity_name="robot"))
qpos_goal = robot.inverse_kinematics(links_name="hand", poss=target_pos, quats=target_quat)[0]
waypoints = planner.plan_motion(qpos_goal=qpos_goal, envs_idx=0)
for waypoint in waypoints:            # each an (n_qs,) tensor
    env.step(waypoint[:7].unsqueeze(0).repeat(env.num_envs, 1))

plan_motion(qpos_goal, qpos_start=None, resolution=0.01, timeout=5.0, max_retry=1, smooth_path=True, num_waypoints=100, ignore_collision=False, planner="RRTConnect", envs_idx=0). planner is the name of any ompl.geometric planner class.

  • The return shape differs from cuRobo's: a list of waypoints for the one env, each an (n_qs,) tensor, not a list per env. An infeasible problem returns an empty list (with a warning); one that does not converge within max_retry attempts returns the approximate path, or an empty list.
  • Collision checking moves the entity: each sampled state is written with set_qpos and checked with detect_collision. Contacts already present at the start configuration (a gripper welded to its flange, an object resting in the hand) are ignored. The entity is put back at qpos_start when planning ends.
  • Start or goal outside the joint limits relaxes the limits to contain them, with a warning.

docs.title: Motion optimization (TCRS)
docs.text:
eden.extensions.motion_optimization.tcrs is Eden's port of the TCRS terrain-adaptive motion optimizer: it turns a flat-ground biped clip into one that walks on a terrain height field (footstep planning with MPPI, support-aware pelvis height, whole-body Jacobian IK on a MuJoCo model of the robot). It is env-free and offline. Use it directly through TCRSMotionAdapter, or on a whole motion dataset through the TCRSTerrainAdapt dataset modifier.

TCRS terrain adaptation is the full guide; examples/recipes/motion_optimization/tcrs/ holds the runnable recipes (adapt_clip.py, adapt_dataset.py, render_on_terrain.py).

docs.title: System identification
docs.text:
eden.extensions.sysid fits per-DOF dynamics parameters of an Eden robot — damping, armature, stiffness, frictionloss, and the PD gains kp / kd — so that the simulated response to a recorded action trace matches the measured one. The workflow:

flowchart LR
    A["excite the robot<br/>(DeploymentRecorder or SysIDRecorder)"] --> B["Trajectory (.npz)"]
    B --> C["fit a ParameterSet<br/>(SciPyLeastSquares or CMAES)"]
    C --> D["params_identified.yaml"]
    D --> E["verify on a held-out trajectory"]

examples/projects/sysid/xhand1/ is the complete worked example for a real XHand1 (collect, identify, verify), and its README.md is the step-by-step guide, including the troubleshooting list.

docs.title: 1. Record a trajectory
docs.text:
A Trajectory (eden/extensions/sysid/trajectory.py) holds times and (n_steps, dim) arrays: action (the action the action manager received, which the replay re-injects), dofs_pos, dofs_vel, dofs_torque, base_quat, base_ang_vel, base_lin_acc, plus dof_names and an initial_state (qpos, dofs_vel, and optionally pos, quat). Fields the measurement lacks are None and skipped. save(path) / load(path) use NPZ.

From a real robot, drive a connected eden deploy backend with an excitation:

from eden.extensions.sysid import ChirpExcitation, DeploymentRecorder

# deployer: a connected DeploymentBase at its start pose; safety_limits: (num_dofs,) offset clamp in rad
excitation = ChirpExcitation(
    num_dofs=deployer.num_dofs, dof_indices=range(deployer.num_dofs),
    f_start=0.2, f_end=3.0, duration=30.0, amplitude=0.2,
)
recorder = DeploymentRecorder(deployer, excitation, kp_scale=0.5, safety_limits=safety_limits)
trajectory = recorder.run()
trajectory.save("data/chirp.npz")
  • deployer must be connected and already at its start pose (its INIT finished). The recorder writes the wire directly, outside the deployment's operator state machine.
  • The excitation is an offset added to a centre pose — the robot's measured pose at the start, or center_dofs_pos. safety_limits clamps the offset per DOF (radians), and the recorder warns, per DOF, when the centre ± peak offset leaves the joint limits: a joint driven into its stop clips on the real robot, and the fit then explains the clipping with friction.
  • Excitations: ChirpExcitation (a swept sine, stagger_phase to decorrelate DOFs), PRBSExcitation (a pseudo-random binary sequence; good for stiction and friction) and PlaybackExcitation (replay recorded offsets with a zero-order hold).

In simulation (for a sim-to-sim check, or to test the pipeline on known parameters), add SysIDRecorder to the env's recorder options and load an episode back with Trajectory.from_recorder_episode(path, dof_names=..., demo="demo_0"); it reads the sysid/* keys of the recorder's default NPZ file. SysIDRecorder(entity_name="robot", include_torque=True, include_base=True) records the action, a timestamp, joint state, the control force and the base orientation and angular velocity; set include_base=False for a fixed-base arm. See Datasets and recording.

docs.title: 2. Build the sim twin
docs.text:
Fit on a dedicated sysid env: an RLEnvBase holding the robot, built (env.build()), with no task logic it needs. The rollouts call the action manager and scene.step() directly (replay_rollout), so terminations, rewards, resets, commands, events and recorders never fire: a trajectory longer than the episode is not cut by an auto-reset, and a domain-randomization event cannot change the parameters being fitted. Each rollout starts by writing initial_state into the entity.

  • Match the cadence: sim_dt * decimation must equal the trajectory's dt, or the replay runs at another rate than the robot did. The XHand1 example warns above a 2 % mismatch.
  • Use a torque-mode controller such as ExplicitPDController (as the XHand1 sim twin does), so the PD damping is computed explicitly and the fitted kd and armature mean what they say. Under EnvOptions(integrator="euler") a position-mode controller's kd · substep_dt is folded into the armature at build — see Entities.
  • num_envs: 1 for the serial optimizers, the population size for batched CMA-ES, n_params + 1 for parallel_fd least-squares.

docs.title: 3. Fit the parameters
docs.text:
from eden.extensions.sysid import ParameterSet, SciPyLeastSquares, Trajectory, make_parameter_from_default
from eden.extensions.sysid.report import write_summary
from eden.options.extensions.sysid import SystemIdentificationOptions

# env: the built sim twin (step 2); dof_names: the joints to fit, in the trajectory's column order
trajectories = [Trajectory.load("data/chirp.npz"), Trajectory.load("data/prbs.npz")]
params = ParameterSet([
    make_parameter_from_default(env, prop, prop, dof_names, per_dof=True)   # name, property, DOFs
    for prop in ("damping", "armature", "kp", "kd")
])
sysid = SciPyLeastSquares(
    env=env,
    options=SystemIdentificationOptions(entity_name="robot", signals=("dofs_pos",), max_iters=200, diff_step=1e-2),
)
initial = params.copy()
identified, result = sysid.fit(params, trajectories)
write_summary("results/sysid", initial, identified, result)   # params_identified.yaml, params_initial.yaml, summary.txt
  • Parameters. A Parameter(name, property, dof_names, entity_name="robot", per_dof=False, nominal, min_value, max_value, frozen=False) targets one property on a set of DOFs, one scalar shared by all of them or one value per DOF. make_parameter_from_default(env, name, property, dof_names, min_scale=0.1, max_scale=10.0, ...) takes the built entity's current value as the nominal and bounds it multiplicatively; when that value is zero (an asset with no frictionloss), the bounds collapse, so construct that Parameter explicitly. Frozen parameters are kept but not optimized. ParameterSet.save_yaml / load_yaml round-trip a set.
  • Residual. SystemIdentificationOptions: entity_name, signals (any of dofs_pos, dofs_vel, dofs_torque, base_quat, base_ang_vel; default the first three), signal_weights, normalize (default True: each signal block is divided by its measured RMS so units mix fairly), max_iters (200), verbose. Fit only the signals the robot really measures: a velocity finite-differenced from positions, or a torque in firmware units, biases the fit. Several trajectories are fitted jointly, which improves conditioning (a chirp and a PRBS trace have complementary spectra).
  • Optimizers (both work in a unit hypercube over the parameter bounds):
    • SciPyLeastSquares — trust-region reflective least squares with box bounds. diff_step (default 1e-2, a fraction of each bound range) is the finite-difference step: too small and the Jacobian is numerical noise, so the optimizer stops at iteration 0. parallel_fd=True scores all Jacobian columns in one batched replay and needs env.num_envs == n_params + 1 exactly (any other count raises).
    • CMAES — for noisy, contact-heavy or saddle-shaped residuals. Needs the cma package (pip install cma; no Eden extra declares it). sigma0 (default 0.25), population_size (default CMA's own), and batched=True to score the whole population in one replay on an env with num_envs == population_size. When warm-starting from a previous fit, lower sigma0 (the XHand1 example uses 0.05) or the first population scatters away from it.
  • fit() returns the identified ParameterSet and a FitResult (cost, nfev, x, jacobian, message, history, extras). sysid.evaluate(params, trajectories) returns the residual of one parameter set without optimizing.

docs.title: 4. Apply and verify
docs.text: apply_parameters(env, params) writes a parameter set into every env (through set_dofs_damping, set_dofs_armature, set_dofs_stiffness, set_dofs_frictionloss, set_dofs_kp, set_dofs_kd); apply_candidates(env, params, candidates) writes one candidate per env. To verify, replay a held-out trajectory with single_candidate_rollout(env, params, trajectory, entity_name) under the nominal and the identified set and compare the error. eden.extensions.sysid.report.signal_plots(...) overlays measured and predicted signals. Carry the identified values into a task through its robot's default_dofs_* fields.

docs.title: Adding an optimizer
docs.text: Subclass SystemIdentificationBase, implement fit(params, trajectories) -> (ParameterSet, FitResult) with the rollout helpers (single_candidate_rollout, batched_candidate_rollout) and multi_trajectory_residual, declare backend options as class attributes (they arrive as SystemIdentificationOptions extras), and register it with @SYSID_REGISTRY.register().

docs.title: Exporting a Policy for Your Own Runtime
docs.text:
eden deploy runs a checkpoint on a robot, but it needs Eden installed on the robot's computer. To run a trained policy on your own stack instead (ROS 2, a Jetson, a C++ controller), export it with eden export. The export is a graph that any ONNX or TorchScript runtime can load, plus a policy_spec.json that describes the observation the graph expects, how its output becomes joint targets, and the control rate. This page explains the command, the graph's inputs and outputs, and every field of the spec.

eden export --task <task> --checkpoint logs/<task>/<run>/model_1500.pt

logs/<task>/<run>/exported/model_1500/
├── policy.onnx         # ONNX graph
├── policy.pt           # TorchScript module
└── policy_spec.json    # the contract around the graph

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
Flag Default What it does --task TASK required The task the checkpoint was trained on. --checkpoint PATH required An rsl_rl model_<iteration>.pt. --format FORMATS onnx,jit Comma-separated: onnx writes policy.onnx, jit writes policy.pt (TorchScript). --out DIR exported/<checkpoint name>/ beside the checkpoint Where the files go. An earlier export there is replaced, including a graph of a format not exported this time. --no_verify off Skip the parity check (below). --config, --override, --cpu As for every task command.

The ONNX graph needs the onnx package, and its parity check needs onnxruntime. Install both with the onnx extra: pip install 'eden-world[onnx]', or uv sync --inexact --extra onnx --reinstall-package onnxruntime in a checkout (eden export --help prints the full command for your install, including the step that repairs an onnxruntime wheel the GPU extra overwrote). A missing package is reported before anything is built; --format jit needs neither.

How the env is built:

  • From the checkpoint's own config.json, with --config / --override on top, exactly as eden inference builds it. One env, in eval mode.
  • Event terms that bias the default joint pose at startup (RandomizeStartupDofsPosBias) are disabled first, because the spec records that pose. An env built with one is refused by the export function itself.

What exports:

  • Only rsl_rl checkpoints. An rl_games checkpoint is refused; export it with rl_games' own tooling.
  • Only under rsl-rl-lib 4 or newer, whose models have export hooks. A 3.x checkpoint loads into a 4.x / 5.x runner, so upgrade rather than export under 3.x.

docs.title: The graph
docs.text:
policy.onnx policy.pt input obs, shape (batch, obs_dim) obs, shape (batch, obs_dim) output actions, shape (batch, action_dim) the actions recurrent state explicit: h_in → h_out (and c_in → c_out for an LSTM), shaped (num_layers, batch, hidden); start from zeros and feed each output back as the next input inside the module, batch 1; call reset() at the start of each episode
  • obs is raw. It is the actor's observation groups concatenated in the order the spec lists them. The observation normalizer is baked into the graph, so do not normalize the input yourself.
  • actions is the raw policy output, before any action term scales it. The deterministic mean is exported, never a sample.
  • The ONNX batch axis is dynamic. TorchScript's is dynamic only for a non-recurrent policy.

docs.title: Parity check
docs.text: Before writing the spec, the export steps the env for a few control steps with the policy eden inference runs, then replays those observations through every exported graph, threading the recurrent state, and fails if any action disagrees (tolerance 1e-4, since the graph runs on the CPU and the reference on the env's device). This catches a learner whose export hook exports something other than what its model runs. The files are written to a staging directory and moved into --out only after the check passes, so a failed export leaves --out as it was. Keep the check on unless you have no onnxruntime.

docs.title: Learners with their own graph
docs.text: The graph comes from the policy model's own as_onnx() and as_jit() hooks; rsl-rl-lib's MLPModel and RNNModel define them. (Before rsl-rl-lib 5.5.2 the ONNX hook was as_onnx(verbose); the export passes verbose=False only to a hook that declares it, so a model written against either form exports.) A learner whose deployed policy is more than an MLP over the observation defines both hooks on its model, each returning a module that runs the deployed composition on the flat observation, and sets obs_groups (the groups it concatenates). For an example see RmaActorModel in eden/learning/wrappers/rsl_rl/rma/model.py, which injects its estimator's prediction. A model with neither hook (HIMLoco's HIMActorCritic) is refused, and the error names what to define.

docs.title: policy_spec.json
docs.text: Every per-DOF list in the spec is in the entity's column order: its configured dofs_name, given under entities, not the order of the asset file. The top-level keys are schema_version, model, observations, actions, entities, rate and provenance. schema_version changes whenever a consumer would have to change with it.

docs.title: model
docs.text:
The exported files, with the ONNX graph's tensors as it declares them (a dynamic axis appears as "batch"):

{"onnx": {"file": "policy.onnx",
          "inputs": [{"name": "obs", "shape": ["batch", 25]}],
          "outputs": [{"name": "actions", "shape": ["batch", 6]}]},
 "jit": {"file": "policy.pt"}}

docs.title: observations
docs.text:
{"dim": 25, "groups": [{"name": "policy", "slice": [0, 25], "history_length": 0, "backfill": null,
  "nan_policy": "disabled", "terms": [
  {"name": "dofs_pos", "term": "dofs_pos", "slice": [0, 8], "frame_dim": 8, "history_length": 0,
   "backfill": null, "clip": null, "scale": 1.0, "modifiers": [],
   "config": {"entity_name": "robot", "...": "..."}}]}]}

To build obs, compute each term and lay it into its slice of obs. Groups follow each other in groups order, and each term's slice is relative to its group. Process a term's frame in this order:

  1. Compute the term. term is its registry key; eden terms --grep <term> documents what it measures, and config holds the parameters it was configured with (entity, link and DOF names, frames).
  2. Apply modifiers. These also run on hardware, so a delay or a filter listed here must be reproduced.
  3. clip, then multiply by scale. A list scale is per component.
  4. Apply the group's nan_policy. Under sanitize and warn, NaN and ±inf become 0. Under error, Eden raises on them; under disabled they pass through.
  5. Stack the history. With a term history_length H > 0, the term's slice holds its last H frames, oldest first, each frame_dim wide. A group with its own history_length stacks whole group frames instead: the term slices then index one frame, and the group's block is H frames, oldest first. At an episode start the window is filled with copies of the first frame when backfill is true, and with zeros when it is false. backfill is null where there is no history.

Training noise is never part of the contract: the export reads the env in eval mode.

docs.title: actions
docs.text:
{"dim": 6, "clip": null, "terms": [
  {"name": "joint_pos_controller", "term": "implicit_pd_controller", "class": "ImplicitPDController",
   "slice": [0, 6], "entity_name": "robot", "target": "position", "reference_source": "default",
   "dofs_name": ["joint1", "..."], "scale": 0.25, "offset": [0.0, "..."], "mimic_dofs": {},
   "config": {"...": "..."}}]}
  1. If clip is [lo, hi], clamp the raw actions to it (the runner's clip_actions).

  2. Each term reads its slice. A joint controller turns its first len(dofs_name) columns into a target (a position or a velocity) for dofs_name: target = action * scale + offset + reference, where reference follows reference_source:

    reference_source reference zero 0 default 0: the default pose is already folded into offset delta the joint positions measured at the start of the control step accumulate the previous step's target, clamped to the soft joint limits (offset is 0) motion_ref the reference motion's joint positions, which only an Eden motion manager provides

  3. A follower in mimic_dofs (follower: [driver, multiplier, offset]) is commanded driver_target * multiplier + offset.

  4. A term with velocity_feedforward (VelocityFeedforwardPDController) has a second block of columns at velocity_feedforward.slice, a target velocity for the same DOFs: target_velocity = action * velocity_feedforward.scale. The PD law is then kp * (target - q) + kd * (feed_forward_ratio * target_velocity - q̇).

offset is the nominal one. A per-env joint-zero offset drawn by domain randomization (RandomizeDofsPosOffset) is never part of it.

Other action terms (task-space controllers, binary grippers) carry only their class and config, as does a joint controller whose columns do not map one-to-one onto DOFs as above. A runtime implements those itself.

docs.title: entities, rate, provenance
docs.text:
• entities.<name>: dofs_name in column order, with default_dofs_pos, kp and kd as built for training. Hold the DOFs that no action term drives at their default pose with these gains.
  • rate: control_dt (run the policy once every control_dt seconds), with the decimation and sim_dt it was built from.
  • provenance: the task, its config class, the checkpoint path and SHA-256, the rsl-rl-lib version (rl_library) and the torch version. eden and genesis each record a version and a commit, null when unknown: Eden's commit is the HEAD of the clone it ran from (null for an installed package), Genesis's the one a git+ or editable install records. eden.dirty says whether that clone had uncommitted changes.

docs.title: Loading an export back into Eden
docs.text:
OnnxModule from eden.extensions.policies.onnx runs a non-recurrent ONNX export on a batch of observations, which is a quick way to check an export inside Eden:

import json

from eden.extensions.policies.onnx import OnnxModule

spec = json.load(open("exported/model_1500/policy_spec.json"))
policy = OnnxModule(
    "exported/model_1500/policy.onnx", "obs", "actions",
    expected_input_dim=spec["observations"]["dim"],
    expected_output_dim=spec["actions"]["dim"],
)
actions = policy(obs)   # (batch, obs_dim) -> (batch, action_dim)

docs.title: Porting a Pretrained Policy
docs.text:
A frozen policy trained in another stack (IsaacGym, Isaac Lab, mjlab, MuJoCo, rl_games, an exported ONNX graph) runs in Eden for inference and sim-to-sim as a policy extension, not as a task. The policy keeps its weights and its observation and action contract; Eden supplies the robot, the scene and the control loop. This page is the checklist for reproducing such a policy faithfully, and the order in which to verify it. How to package the result (the class, its files, the registry) is in Adding a Policy to the Zoo.

Training a new policy is a different job

This page is for reproducing a policy someone else trained. To train in Eden, write a task config instead: see Task Configuration.

The ports that ship with Eden are worked examples, all under eden/extensions/policies/:

  • husky (G1 skateboarding, ONNX) declares its observation and action through the training task's own terms: the model to follow for a new port.
  • holosoma, homie, sonic assemble their input from raw simulator state, which is what lets them ride along as extra slots in a deployment.
  • twist2, omnixtreme, humanoid_gpt (ONNX motion trackers), protomotionv3 (a torch actor loaded from a training checkpoint), and simtoolreal (a 29-DOF arm and hand with an rl_games LSTM actor reimplemented in torch).

The Policy Zoo lists every one with what it needs.

docs.title: The shape of a port
docs.text:
A port is one PolicyBase subclass whose classmethods describe the world the policy was trained in:

Member What to put there robot_options() The robot, as an eden.robots options object (G1Dofs29(...), KukaSharpa(...)) with the source's default pose, gains and armature. scene_entity_options() Every other entity the policy reads: the object it manipulates, the board it rides, a goal marker, or a plane entity that replaces the flat ground (for example with terrain). env_options() sim_dt, decimation and solver settings: the control rate and physics the policy expects. action_options() The action terms its output drives. observation_options() The observation groups it reads. command_options() The command terms it consumes, if any (a velocity command, a motion reference). step(obs) One inference call, returning {action_term_name: tensor}. reset(envs_idx) Clear recurrent state and per-episode buffers.

robot_options() and scene_entity_options() together are the scene: eden inference --policy <name> without a --task builds an empty scene from exactly those two. A policy whose observation is defined against something other than its robot (SimToolReal's tool on its table, HUSKY's skateboard) must declare that entity, or a task-less run spawns a lone robot and the policy fails resolving the entity. Resolve each entity with self.require_entity(name) in __init__ so a scene that lacks it fails at construction, and keep reading it through self.env.entities[name] in step(), because deployment swaps the entity for a live-robot stand-in.

docs.title: Declare the observation; don't assemble it in step()
docs.text:
A policy that owns its env (the task-less eden inference --policy case) should state its input as observation_options(), with command_options() for any command or clock it observes and action_options() scaled so that last_action is the actor's raw output. It then sets reads_env_observations = True, and its step() just feeds obs[<group>] to the network. The layout is explicit and reusable, and it gets the observation manager's history, scale, NaN and reset handling for free.

husky is the worked example. Its observation_options() and action_options() reuse the training task's actor group and action term (eden/tasks/husky/config.py), so the released checkpoint and a policy trained in Eden share one layout, and a held ConstantSkateCommand carries the command and the phase clock. tests/extensions/policies/husky/test_policy.py pins that env against a hand-written formula of the source's observation.

A command term that ticks must tick in pre_physics_advance

A deployment never runs post_physics_refresh, so a command term a frozen policy observes (a phase clock, a held command) must advance its state in a hook that runs on hardware too. HUSKY's ConstantSkateCommand ticks in pre_physics_advance for that reason.

Assembling the input from raw sim state inside step() is for policies that have to ride along as extra slots on someone else's env: the Holosoma safety policy eden deploy inserts on a G1, and controllers stacked next to it. One env publishes one observation layout, so only one env-reading policy can be loaded at a time (see Deployment). Such a policy's observation_options() may return {}: no groups at all builds and steps fine, as holosoma does. What is not allowed is declaring a group and leaving it empty: a group with concatenate_terms=True and no terms fails at construction with Unable to concatenate observation terms in group `<name>`. Declare one real term or no group.

docs.title: The porting checklist
docs.text: Match the source exactly, in this order. Each step's failure is invisible to the steps before it, which is why the order matters.

docs.title: 1. The I/O contract
docs.text:
Reproduce the observation layout and order, any input normalization, and the action transform bit for bit.

  • Index every DOF and link by name. Genesis' native DOF order differs from the source's. Resolve the names once with robot.find_named_dofs(POLICY_JOINT_NAMES), then hand its .columns to tensor reads (default_dofs_*, full-width get_dofs_*()) and its .dofs_idx_local to Genesis calls (dofs_idx_local=). Never index a default_dofs_* tensor with local indices: they are a different index space (see DOF ordering).
  • Check the built robot's frozen constants by name, in every env. robot.get_default_dofs_pos(POLICY_JOINT_NAMES) returns (num_envs, n) in the policy's order; compare it against the source's default pose at construction, as HuskyPolicy.__init__ does.
  • Quaternions are wxyz in Eden, while many sources put xyzw in their observation vector.
  • Mind world vs. base frame for every absolute term.
  • Read object and free-body poses with get_pos(relative=True) / get_quat(relative=True). The default returns Genesis' solver frame, re-originated at the center of mass, not the declared root pose the source reports (see Which frame?). This one fails quietly.

docs.title: 2. The network
docs.text: Use OnnxModule from eden/extensions/policies/onnx.py for feedforward ONNX actors (twist2, sonic and humanoid_gpt wrap it). Reimplement exotic backends in plain torch, as simtoolreal/network.py does for an rl_games LSTM. Carry recurrent state across step() and clear it in reset(). When you load weights, confirm there are no missing or unexpected keys.

docs.title: 3. The dynamics
docs.text: Match the robot's base pose, PD gains (default_dofs_kp / default_dofs_kd), armature (default_dofs_armature: Eden fills armature=0.1 on every URDF joint whose asset armature is zero, often far too high for a low-stiffness finger; see Armature defaults), joint friction, control rate (sim_dt × decimation) and gravity compensation. The objects and the scene must match the world the policy trained in.

docs.title: 4. Verify, in layers
docs.text:
This is what catches the bugs.

  1. Observation parity. Feed the same state (q, q̇, …) to the source's observation function and to your assembly, and diff field by field (expect differences around 1e-7). This validates the math given a state, so synthetic poses never reveal that you read the sim in the wrong frame: also diff a few sim-measured states against the source's convention.
  2. Action parity. Feed the same observation to the source's policy and to yours, and diff the action. A faithful network reimplementation is bit-identical.
  3. Dynamics audit. Dump the built robot's per-DOF kp, kd and armature (get_dofs_armature()), plus object mass, placement and control rate, and compare them with the source. Passing observation and action parity does not mean the rollout matches: mismatched dynamics make the trajectory diverge while both parity checks stay green. When a ported policy underperforms with parity passing, look here first.
  4. Sim-to-sim rollout. Only after the above, run the closed loop and render it. Two rungs: eden inference --policy <name> --async replays the loop in Genesis with deployment-style timing, and eden deploy --policy <name> --mujoco --menagerie replays it against MuJoCo, which catches dynamics assumptions only Genesis satisfies (see Sim-to-sim validation).

Why the closed loop cannot be the first check

A policy servos whatever pose it is shown, so a frame or gain mismatch still converges: it just converges to the wrong place. A constant offset between object and goal is the classic symptom of the relative= mistake. A rollout that "mostly works" is not evidence of a correct port.

docs.title: The Policy Zoo
docs.text: Eden ships published controllers that run as released, with no training: humanoid locomotion and motion tracking, skateboarding, dexterous tool use, insertion, and clients for server-hosted vision-language-action models. This page lists every policy in eden/extensions/policies/, what each one needs to run, and how eden inference --policy builds its world.

docs.title: Run a policy
docs.text:
eden inference --policy sonic --motion_file examples/projects/mimic/beyondmimic/sample/G1_gangnam_style_V01_bvh_60hz.npz --vis
eden inference --policy holosoma --base_command 0.5 0.0 0.0 --vis     # walk forward at 0.5 m/s
eden inference --policy beyondmimic_moves --clip_name B_DadDance --vis
eden inference --policy husky --rec                                   # record an mp4

Weights download on first use from the policy's Hugging Face dataset into the asset cache (policies/ under EDEN_ASSETS_DIR, by default ~/.cache/eden/assets), and are checked against the MD5 the policy pins. Policies with ONNX weights need the onnx extra: pip install 'eden-world[onnx]', or uv sync --inexact --extra onnx in a checkout.

--policy accepts the package name (holosoma), the registry key (holosoma_locomotion_policy), or the key without its _policy suffix. The flags that matter for a policy run:

Flag What it does --policy NAME The policy to roll out. Mutually exclusive with --checkpoint. --task TASK Run the policy on a task's env instead of the policy's own world (below). Optional. --robot NAME The eden.robots class for a task-less run of a policy that does not pin its own robot (default G1Dofs29). Ignored when the policy pins one, and with --task. --entity_name NAME The scene entity the policy controls (default robot). --motion_file PATH The reference motion for a motion-tracking policy. Required when the policy takes one. --clip_name CLIP The clip for a per-clip policy (beyondmimic_moves); ignored by the others. --base_command VX VY WZ A constant command for a command-driven policy (default: stand). Padded or truncated to the policy's command width. --steps N Steps to run (default 1000). --episodes is not available with --policy. --num_envs N Parallel envs, with --task only: a task-less run builds one env. --vis, --rec, --async, --cpu As for a checkpoint replay (Training Runs).

docs.title: Task-less runs and --task runs
docs.text:
Without --task, Eden builds the policy's own world from its spec: one env, an empty scene holding the robot robot_options() returns plus every entity scene_entity_options() declares (the skateboard, the tool and its table), the policy's env_options() (its control rate and solver settings), and its observation, action and command terms. This is the run the policy was ported for, and the one to start with.

With --task, the policy runs on that task's env, and the policy's command terms are merged into the task's. The task must provide what the policy reads: the entities (checked at construction), and, for a policy that reads the env's observations, the exact observation group it was built for. A policy that observes its command through the task's own command terms ignores --base_command, and passing a non-zero one is an error.

docs.title: Humanoid locomotion
docs.text: --policy What it is Robot Needs Control holosoma Holosoma velocity-tracking locomotion (ONNX); also the safety base eden deploy preloads on a G1 G1Dofs29 at Holosoma's default pose --base_command VX VY WZ; onnx extra 50 Hz homie OpenHomie walk/stand tracker for the lower body (walk and stand torch checkpoints) G1Dofs29 with HOMIE's pose and gains --base_command: a 4-D [vx, vy, wz, height_delta] command, padded with zeros 50 Hz amo AMO adaptive whole-body control (TorchScript) G1Dofs29NoWristDof (23 DOF) Nothing: its command term resamples its own commands 50 Hz husky HUSKY humanoid skateboarding (ONNX) HuskyG1 (23 DOF) plus a skateboard --base_command: a 2-D [lin_vel_x, relative_heading]; onnx extra 50 Hz limx_oli_loco Velocity-tracking loco/stand controller for LimX Oli (rsl_rl actor) Oli No released weights: a local velocity_tracking_flat checkpoint trained for Oli (see Local checkpoints) the env default

docs.title: Humanoid motion tracking
docs.text:
These track a reference motion. Each takes --motion_file (an Eden motion .npz, see Motion Tracking) except where noted.

--policy What it is Robot Needs Control sonic GEAR-SONIC universal-token whole-body controller (encoder + decoder ONNX) G1Dofs29 at SONIC's standing pose --motion_file; onnx extra 50 Hz twist2 TWIST2 whole-body tracker (ONNX) G1Dofs29, knees bent --motion_file; onnx extra 50 Hz humanoid_gpt Humanoid-GPT tracker, Transformer by default or MLP (ONNX) --robot (default G1Dofs29) --motion_file (a 50 Hz motion); onnx extra 50 Hz protomotionv3 ProtoMotions v3 g1-bones-deploy tracker (torch actor from the training checkpoint) G1Dofs29 --motion_file 50 Hz omnixtreme OmniXtreme flow-matching base policy plus residual correction (three ONNX graphs) OmniXtreme_G1 --motion_file; onnx extra 50 Hz gmt GMT general motion tracking (TorchScript) G1Dofs29NoWristDof (23 DOF) --motion_file: GMT's own .pkl format (samples in examples/policies/gmt/motions/) 50 Hz beyondmimic_moves 60 BeyondMimic tracking policies from the exptech/g1-moves dataset, one per clip G1Dofs29 at the g1-moves pose --clip_name (default B_DadDance); the clip's checkpoint and motion download on first use 50 Hz metamotivo Meta Motivo (FB-CPR) behavior foundation model for an SMPL humanoid; behavior set by a context vector z SmplHumanoid The metamotivo package (pip install "metamotivo[huggingface]@git+https://github.com/facebookresearch/metamotivo.git"); the model loads from Hugging Face (facebook/metamotivo-S-1 by default) 30 Hz

The sample motion examples/projects/mimic/beyondmimic/sample/G1_gangnam_style_V01_bvh_60hz.npz is what the sonic, humanoid_gpt and omnixtreme examples default to; examples/policies/twist2/resources/greeting.npz is TWIST2's.

docs.title: Manipulation
docs.text: --policy What it is Robot Needs Control simtoolreal SimToolReal object-centric tool manipulation (rl_games LSTM actor reimplemented in torch) KukaSharpa (KUKA iiwa14 arm + SharPa hand, 29 DOF) plus a table, a DexToolBench tool and a goal ghost Nothing extra; the tool defaults to long_screwdriver 60 Hz omnireset UWLab OmniReset state-based insertion expert OmniResetUR5e2f85 (UR5e + Robotiq 2F-85) plus the object pair The peg pair is the one released expert 10 Hz

docs.title: Server-backed clients (VLAs and world models)
docs.text:
These policies run inference on a separate server and only exchange observations and actions with it. They need the policy-client extra (pip install 'eden-world[policy-client]'), a running server, and a manipulation scene with the cameras their setup reads; see Remote Policy Clients.

--policy Server Transport Default address Setups (policy_setup) pi OpenPI (pi0, pi0-FAST, pi0.5) openpi_websocket localhost:8000 widowx_bridge (default), google_robot, libero, droid, droid_jointpos, aloha gr00t NVIDIA Isaac-GR00T zmq_msgpack localhost:5555 simpler_env_widowx (default), libero_sim, oxe_droid_relative_eef_relative_joint galaxeavla GalaxeaVLA (G0.5) galaxea_websocket localhost:8765 galaxea_r1lite (default), galaxea_r1pro, droid_franka cosmos3 Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID (world action model) openpi_websocket localhost:8000 DROID only molmoact2 MolmoAct2 DROID server (absolute joint control) http_json_numpy localhost:8000 DROID only octo Octo, through an HTTP server http_json localhost:9010 WidowX only

eden inference --policy <client> constructs the client with its defaults (the address, setup and no instruction above), so to choose a server, a setup or a language instruction, drive the client from Python as Remote Policy Clients shows.

docs.title: Local checkpoints
docs.text:
Every policy's file locations are class constants, not options. To run your own weights in place of the released ones, call use_local_checkpoint on the class before constructing it; it also clears the MD5 pinned to the released file, which your file would fail:

from eden.extensions.policies.limx_oli_loco.policy import OliVelocityLocoPolicy

OliVelocityLocoPolicy.use_local_checkpoint("logs/velocity_tracking_flat/<run>/model_3000.pt")

A policy that loads several files names the one to redirect: SonicPolicy.use_local_checkpoint(path, checkpoint_attr="decoder_checkpoint_path"). On the command line, eden deploy --policy NAME --policy_checkpoint NAME=PATH does the same for a deployment.

To fetch every policy's files from a mirror (an offline cluster, a shared read-only cache), export EDEN_ASSETS_DIR=/data/mirror: policies then cache under /data/mirror/policies/.

docs.title: Policies on hardware and in MuJoCo
docs.text: eden deploy --policy NAME loads any of these as a switchable slot on a real robot or, with --mujoco, in MuJoCo. On a G1, Holosoma is preloaded as the safety base slot. Which policies can share one deployment, and how slots switch, is in Deployment. examples/policies/policy_switch/main.py shows the sim-side counterpart: Holosoma and SONIC hot-swapping on one G1.

docs.title: Example scripts
docs.text: Most policies also have a standalone script under examples/policies/<name>/main.py that builds the same world and adds policy-specific controls (a keyboard command, a clip picker, recording): amo, beyondmimic_moves, gmt, holosoma, homie, humanoid_gpt, husky, metamotivo, omnireset, omnixtreme, protomotionv3, simtoolreal, sonic and twist2. Each script's header gives the command to run it.

docs.title: Pose Estimation from Video
docs.text:
eden pose recovers human motion from ordinary monocular video, so a phone clip can become a robot trajectory without a motion-capture studio. It writes an AMASS-style SMPL-X clip, which is exactly what eden retarget soma reads. This page covers installing the estimator, running it, the frame and timing conventions of its output, and the Python API.

eden pose gvhmr --src clip.mp4 --out motions/clip.npz --static-cam
eden retarget soma --src motions/clip.npz --out qpos/ --body-model smplx \
    --body-model-path /data/body_models/smplx/SMPLX_NEUTRAL.npz --snap-to-ground

The backend is GVHMR (world-grounded human motion recovery, SIGGRAPH Asia 2024), installed from the eden-gvhmr package (import name hmr4d). It is the only eden pose subcommand.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
GVHMR installs into the same environment as Eden, through the pose extra:

pipuv (checkout) 
pip install 'eden-world[pose]'

uv sync --inexact --extra pose

Then download the model weights and provide the body models:

gvhmr-download-checkpoints          # GVHMR, HMR2, ViTPose and YOLO weights, from eden-gvhmr
export GVHMR_CHECKPOINT_ROOT=/data/gvhmr/checkpoints   # or pass --checkpoint-root on every run

The checkpoint root holds gvhmr/, hmr2/, vitpose/, yolo/ and body_models/. The SMPL and SMPL-X body models in body_models/ are licence-gated and are not downloaded for you: register at smpl.is.tue.mpg.de and smpl-x.is.tue.mpg.de and place them there as GVHMR's own install instructions describe. Without --checkpoint-root or the environment variable, GVHMR looks in ./inputs/checkpoints.

GVHMR runs on CUDA only; pick a GPU with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. hmr4d is imported lazily, so import eden never needs it, and a missing install reports the extra to install instead of a bare ModuleNotFoundError.

docs.title: Running eden pose gvhmr
docs.text:
eden pose gvhmr --src videos/ --out motions/ --pattern '*.mp4' --static-cam --skip-existing
flag default effect --src required one video, or a directory searched recursively --out required output directory (the source tree is mirrored), or a .npz file for a single video --pattern *.mp4 glob for a directory --src --checkpoint-root GVHMR's own resolution weights directory (see Install) --ckpt <root>/gvhmr/gvhmr_siga24_release.ckpt GVHMR checkpoint file --static-cam off assume the camera does not move, skipping visual odometry --use-dpvo off use DPVO instead of SimpleVO for camera motion (needs GVHMR's DPVO install and checkpoint) --f-mm estimated full-frame-equivalent focal length in mm, when you know the lens --output-root GVHMR's outputs/demo where GVHMR writes, and reuses, its per-video intermediates --skip-existing off skip a video whose output exists --verbose off also save GVHMR's bounding-box and keypoint preprocessing overlays

One model load serves the whole batch. GVHMR keeps each video's intermediates (tracking, ViTPose features, the raw hmr4d_results.pt) under --output-root and reuses them, so a re-run of the same video is nearly free.

--static-cam only for a fixed camera

For tripod footage --static-cam is correct and much faster. For handheld video it is wrong: the camera's own motion would be absorbed into the body motion.

docs.title: The output
docs.text:
Each video becomes one .npz:

key shape content poses (T, 165) SMPL-X axis-angle pose, AMASS layout: root (3), body (63), then jaw, eyes and hands, which are zero because GVHMR does not estimate them trans (T, 3) root translation, Z-up betas (10,) body shape, averaged over the clip gender "neutral" (GVHMR predicts with the neutral SMPL-X model) mocap_frame_rate always 30 surface_model_type "smplx" gvhmr_* the raw Y-up estimate (gvhmr_global_orient, gvhmr_transl, gvhmr_betas, gvhmr_pelvis_j0, gvhmr_K_fullimg, gvhmr_video_fps), for provenance source_video the input path

Three properties of the output matter downstream.

Up axis. GVHMR predicts in a gravity-aligned frame whose +Y is up; Eden, Genesis and AMASS are Z-up. The clip is rotated into Z-up before it is written. Only the root changes (SMPL joint rotations are parent-relative), and its translation is corrected for SMPL-X's rest-pose pelvis offset J0, because the body rotates about J0 rather than the world origin:

trans' = R @ (trans + J0) - J0

Rotating trans alone, as GVHMR's own get_tgtcoord_rootparam does, offsets the whole clip. J0 comes from GVHMR's own SMPL-X model.

Frame rate. GVHMR re-encodes every input to 30 fps without resampling frames and integrates root motion at that rate, so the clip is always stamped 30 fps. There is deliberately no --fps flag: any other stamp would relabel a clip whose motion was already integrated at 30 fps. A 60 fps video therefore gives a time-warped trajectory; the command warns before running the pipeline, and the fix is to re-encode the video to 30 fps first.

Height. GVHMR's world translation is only defined up to a vertical offset, so the clip may float or sink by a few centimetres. Retarget with eden retarget soma --snap-to-ground, which applies one constant vertical shift so the robot's lowest collision point touches z = 0.

docs.title: No overlay videos
docs.text: Eden does not expose GVHMR's in-camera and world overlay rendering. That path needs pytorch3d (built against your torch and CUDA) and chumpy from git, neither of which can be declared as a dependency, so the pose extra does not install them; a flag that failed after the whole pipeline had run would be worse than none. To look at an estimate, install those two and use GVHMR's own CLI, python -m hmr4d.demo --video clip.mp4 -s. --verbose works from Eden: its overlays are drawn with OpenCV.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: In Eden's environment GVHMR runs on Eden's video decoder (av) and person detector (ultralytics), not the versions its checkpoint was tuned with. The estimator's module docstring records the effect, measured one change at a time on GVHMR's bundled tennis clip: av 13 → 17 moves body joints by up to 3.6°, and ultralytics 8.2.42 → 8.4.113 moves the detected boxes by 8.5 px and body joints by 3.4°; numpy (including the 1.x → 2.x jump), timm and imageio are bit-identical. The estimate stays valid, but it is not bit-comparable with the published reference stack. To reproduce published numbers, install GVHMR in its own environment with its pinned versions and run it there.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
No Eden scene or entity is involved: estimation is offline preprocessing, and the robot only enters at retargeting.

from eden.extensions.pose_estimation.gvhmr import GvhmrEstimator, save_amass_npz

estimator = GvhmrEstimator(
    options=GvhmrEstimator.configure(
        # checkpoint_root is optional: $GVHMR_CHECKPOINT_ROOT is used when unset.
        static_cam=True,
    )
)
try:
    clip = estimator.estimate_clip("tennis.mp4")   # AMASS-style, Z-up
    save_amass_npz(clip, "motions/tennis.npz")

    raw = estimator.estimate("tennis.mp4")         # GVHMR's own output: Y-up world and camera frame
finally:
    estimator.close()
  • The shared options (PoseEstimatorOptions): checkpoint_root, ckpt_path, output_root, motion_fps (must stay 30; any other value raises), verbose. GVHMR's own: static_cam, use_dpvo, f_mm.
  • The model loads on the first estimate call and is reused; close() frees it and its GPU memory.
  • estimate(video, **overrides) returns global and incam SMPL-X parameters, pelvis_j0, K_fullimg, output_dir and video_fps. It accepts per-call overrides of static_cam, use_dpvo, f_mm, output_root and verbose; anything else raises.
  • estimate_clip converts that result with to_amass_smplx_clip (in eden.extensions.pose_estimation.gvhmr).

A runnable script: examples/recipes/pose_estimation/gvhmr/video_to_motion.py.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text: GVHMR is released for non-commercial research use (see the licence in its repository), and the SMPL and SMPL-X body models carry their own licences. Eden ships no GVHMR code or weights, only this wrapper; check those terms before using recovered motion in a product.
