docs.title: Remote Policy Clients
docs.text:
Some policies do not run inside the Eden process: a server (on another GPU, in another framework or another repository) computes the actions, and Eden sends it observations. This page covers the client policies Eden ships for such servers, how to run one in an evaluation loop, and the machinery they share (transports, action chunking, per-embodiment setups, gripper conventions), which is also what you build on to wire a new server in.

Eden ships six clients under eden/extensions/policies/, for vision-language-action models (OpenPI pi, GR00T gr00t, GalaxeaVLA galaxeavla, Octo octo, MolmoAct2 molmoact2) and a world action model (Cosmos3 cosmos3). The shared layer is family-neutral: nothing in it assumes images, language or grippers.

Install the client dependencies (ZMQ, msgpack, WebSockets, json-numpy, Pillow) with pip install 'eden-world[policy-client]', or uv sync --inexact --extra policy-client in a checkout. Each transport imports its own dependencies only when it is used.

docs.title: The shipped clients
docs.text:
Policy Server transport Default host:port Setups (policy_setup) pi (PiPolicy) OpenPI: pi0, pi0-FAST, pi0.5 openpi_websocket localhost:8000 widowx_bridge (default), google_robot, libero, droid, droid_jointpos, aloha gr00t (Gr00tPolicy) NVIDIA Isaac-GR00T zmq_msgpack localhost:5555 simpler_env_widowx (default), libero_sim, oxe_droid_relative_eef_relative_joint galaxeavla (GalaxeaVlaPolicy) GalaxeaVLA (G0.5) galaxea_websocket localhost:8765 galaxea_r1lite (default), galaxea_r1pro, droid_franka cosmos3 (Cosmos3Policy) Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID openpi_websocket localhost:8000 — (DROID) molmoact2 (MolmoAct2Policy) MolmoAct2 DROID server, absolute joint control http_json_numpy localhost:8000 — (DROID) octo (OctoPolicy) Octo, behind an HTTP server http_json localhost:9010 — (WidowX)

A setup is the per-robot half of a client whose server serves several embodiments; it decides the observation groups and action terms the env must provide (see Per-embodiment setups).

docs.title: Wire a client into an evaluation loop
docs.text:
A client needs an env whose observation groups and action terms are the ones its setup reads and writes, so build the task config, replace its observation and action options with the client's, and then construct the client:

import eden as en
import genesis as gs

from eden.envs.base import env_class_for_config
from eden.extensions.policies.gr00t.policy import Gr00tPolicy
from eden.options.managers.actions import ActionManagerOptions
from eden.options.managers.observations import ObservationManagerOptions
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY

en.init(backend=gs.gpu)

setup = "simpler_env_widowx"
cfg = TASK_REGISTRY.build("simpler_put_carrot_on_plate")
cfg.env_options.num_envs = 1
cfg.observation_options = ObservationManagerOptions(**Gr00tPolicy.observation_options(policy_setup=setup))
cfg.action_options = ActionManagerOptions(**Gr00tPolicy.action_options(policy_setup=setup))
env = env_class_for_config(cfg).from_config(cfg, show_viewer=False, eval_mode=True)
env.build()

policy = Gr00tPolicy(env, Gr00tPolicy.configure(host="localhost", port=5555, policy_setup=setup))
policy.set_task(cfg.language_instructions[0])

for episode in range(5):
    obs, _ = env.reset()
    policy.reset_server()
    for _ in range(100):
        obs, *_ = env.step(policy.step(obs))

observation_options(policy_setup=...) and action_options(policy_setup=...) are classmethods, so the env is wired without a live server. Constructing the client connects to the server and checks it (below); a wrong setup, a missing gripper term or a control rate the checkpoint was not trained at fails there, before the first step.

eden inference --policy gr00t also runs a client, but builds it with configure()'s defaults (the address and setup in the table, no instruction), so use the loop above to choose a server, a setup or an instruction.

docs.title: How a client works: ClientMixin
docs.text:
A client is a PolicyBase whose step() comes from ClientMixin (eden.extensions.policies.client):

from eden.extensions.policies.base import POLICY_REGISTRY, PolicyBase
from eden.extensions.policies.client import ClientMixin
from eden.options.extensions.policies import RemotePolicyOptions
from eden.utils.common import ConfigurableMixin


@POLICY_REGISTRY.register()
class MyClientPolicy(ClientMixin, PolicyBase, ConfigurableMixin[RemotePolicyOptions]):
    transport = "http_json"          # a TRANSPORT_REGISTRY key
    response_action_key = "action"   # where the reply carries the chunk

    def pack_observations(self, obs): ...   # Eden observations -> server payload
    def unpack_actions(self, raw): ...      # one (D,) row -> {action_term: tensor}

    @classmethod
    def observation_options(cls, **kwargs): ...
    @classmethod
    def action_options(cls, **kwargs): ...

ClientMixin sits left of PolicyBase so its concrete step() satisfies the abstract one, and the third base re-parameterizes ConfigurableMixin with RemotePolicyOptions (the policy fields plus the client fields), so configure() accepts both.

Every step runs the same pipeline:

obs -> observe(obs)                                   per-step hooks (frame history, measured pose)
    -> [if needs_inference]
          payload = pack_request(obs)                 default: pack_observations(obs)
          reply   = transport.infer(payload, request_options())
          chunk   = decode_response(reply)            -> (num_envs, T, D)
          scheduler.accept(chunk)
    -> row = scheduler.pop()                          -> (num_envs, D)
    -> unpack_actions(row)                            -> {action_term: tensor}

The mixin owns three things:

Piece Where What it does Transport eden/utils/policy_client/transport.py Moves a payload to the server and decodes the reply; selected by transport="<key>". Scheduler ActionChunkScheduler in client.py Queues server chunks, applies pred_action_horizon / exec_horizon, optional temporal ensembling. Lifecycle ClientMixin in client.py set_task, reset_server, reset(envs_idx): each clears the queue and local state, then tells the server.

reset(envs_idx) resets the server only when it covers every env the client serves (with one env, every reset). A partial reset of a batched client raises NotImplementedError, because the server's episode state is shared by all of them. Everything the server returns besides the action chunk is kept on policy.last_response_info (GR00T's info, a world model's predictions), so recorders and evaluators can log it, and policy.action_metadata reports where the last executed row sat in its chunk.

docs.title: Running inference asynchronously
docs.text:
step() is also available as its stages: observe, needs_inference, pack_request, infer_payload, accept_chunk and pop_action. An asynchronous evaluator can run the blocking round-trip on a worker thread while the simulator keeps stepping, so the robot moves on during the wait as much as the latency would let it. Two rules:

  • observe must still run on every step: it records the frame histories and measured poses the next request reads.
  • Keep one request in flight: accept or discard its chunk before the next pack_request, and do not call reset, reset_server or set_task while a request is in flight. Nothing in the client locks the transport.

docs.title: Transports and serializers
docs.text:
Both are chosen by registry key, a plain string that survives config serialization, never by passing instances through configure().

transport Wire Default serializer Used by http_json requests POST, JSON body and reply requests' JSON octo http_json_numpy POST with a json_numpy text body json_numpy molmoact2 http_multipart multipart form; the policy's pack_request returns (data, files) — — openpi_websocket msgpack WebSocket with OpenPI's numpy hook msgpack_openpi pi, cosmos3 galaxea_websocket as above, with str-keyed records and a {"__reset__": True} message msgpack_galaxea galaxeavla zmq_msgpack ZMQ REQ/REP with an {"endpoint", "data"} envelope msgpack_numpy (or msgpack_npy_blob) gr00t

A transport is built from a TransportConfig that ClientMixin.transport_config() fills from the policy's attributes: the address, timeouts, endpoints, and the transport-specific knobs each transport declares, read from policy attributes of the same name:

Transport Knobs (defaults) http_json, http_json_numpy, http_multipart set_task_as_query (False), reset_with_payload (True) openpi_websocket api_key (None), ws_ping_timeout (20.0), wait_for_server_s (600.0) galaxea_websocket api_key (None), ws_ping_timeout (None), ws_timeout_s (60.0) zmq_msgpack timeout_ms (60000), api_token (None)

docs.title: Set-task and reset endpoints
docs.text:
set_task_endpoint and reset_endpoint name the server's set-task and reset API and default to None. With None the server has no such API (it takes the task with every request), so set_task, reset_server and an env reset only clear local state. A policy declares one only when its official server exposes it:

Policy set_task_endpoint reset_endpoint octo "/set_task" (HTTP) "/reset" (HTTP) gr00t — "reset" (a ZMQ endpoint name) galaxeavla — "__reset__" (the reset message key) pi, cosmos3, molmoact2 — —

A transport whose protocol has no such message rejects a non-None value at construction; openpi_websocket, for example, has no reset message.

docs.title: The server address
docs.text:
The address is host plus port, joined by eden.utils.policy_client.server_url:

  • A bare hostname such as localhost gets the transport's scheme: http, ws or tcp.
  • host may be a full URL whose scheme fits the transport, such as wss://example.com/ws or https://node/api. Pass port=None to use the port in the URL, or the scheme's default when the URL has none.
  • A port in the URL that disagrees with port raises at construction.
  • ZMQ (tcp://) needs a port and no path.

Errors map onto one hierarchy in eden.utils.policy_client.errors: an unreachable server or a timeout is a TransportError (also a ConnectionError; a timeout is the subclass TransportTimeoutError), a server-side failure is a ServerError, and a payload that cannot be encoded or decoded is a SerializationError. All derive from ClientError (a RuntimeError).

docs.title: Action chunking
docs.text:
Servers usually return a chunk of T actions per request. The scheduler's rules are client options:

Option Meaning chunk_mode client: buffer the chunk and re-query when it drains. server: the server caches the chunk and serves one row per call (GalaxeaVLA). single: one action per call (Octo). pred_action_horizon The expected chunk length; None accepts any. exec_horizon Rows executed open-loop before re-querying; None executes the whole chunk. short_chunk error: a chunk shorter than pred_action_horizon is a truncated prediction and raises. accept: use it. chunk_temporal_ensemble_steps / chunk_temporal_ensemble_dims Blend the previous chunk's unused tail into the new head (OpenPI's optional smoothing); 0 disables. response_action_key The key that holds the chunk in a dict reply ("action" or "actions").

docs.title: Per-embodiment setups
docs.text:
A server that serves several robots (OpenPI: WidowX, Google Robot, LIBERO, DROID, ALOHA; GR00T: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, DROID; GalaxeaVLA: R1 Lite, R1 Pro, a DROID Franka) uses SetupClientMixin and a SETUP_REGISTRY of PolicySetupBase subclasses, selected by policy_setup:

from typing import ClassVar

from eden.extensions.policies.client import PolicySetupBase, SetupClientMixin


class MySetup(PolicySetupBase):
    pred_action_horizon: ClassVar[int | None] = 8   # checkpoint defaults, used when the policy leaves them None
    exec_horizon: ClassVar[int | None] = 4
    default_image_size: ClassVar[tuple[int, int] | None] = (224, 224)

    @classmethod
    def observation_options(cls, **kwargs): ...
    @classmethod
    def action_options(cls, **kwargs): ...
    def pack_observations(self, obs): ...
    def decode_response(self, response): ...   # optional: reply -> (T, D)
    def observe(self, obs): ...                # optional: per-step state (a frame history)
    def unpack_actions(self, raw_action): ...  # optional: default is self.adapter(row, env=...)


@POLICY_REGISTRY.register()
class MyPolicy(SetupClientMixin, PolicyBase, ConfigurableMixin[RemotePolicyOptions]):
    SETUP_REGISTRY = {"my_robot": MySetup}
    policy_setup = "my_robot"
    transport = "zmq_msgpack"

MyPolicy.observation_options(policy_setup="my_robot") and action_options forward to the setup.

docs.title: Server configuration checks
docs.text:
The upstream servers own checkpoint and embodiment selection (serve_policy.py --env for OpenPI, --embodiment-tag for Isaac-GR00T, a per-request embodiment_type for GalaxeaVLA), and the client's policy_setup has to agree with them. Right after the transport connects, SetupClientMixin hands transport.server_config() to the setup's validate_server_config:

  • GR00T setups declare a ModalitySchema (video, state and action keys, action horizon, video window) and compare it with the server's get_modality_config reply. A server started with another embodiment tag fails at construction, with both sides named.
  • OpenPI servers advertise free-form metadata (kept on transport.metadata). Every setup also declares action_dim, so a chunk of the wrong width is rejected before it is queued.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
Manipulation servers consume some composition of three core observation terms (all in eden.observations), so setups declare their groups from these instead of writing per-policy functions. The terms resolve link and DOF names once in build() (a wrong name fails at env construction) and read entities through resolve_entity, so a deployment's entity swap works.

Term Output Options EndEffectorPose [pos(3), rotation] of a link in the base or world frame rotation: quat / euler_xyz / axis_angle / rot6d; a virtual tool offset (offset_pos, offset_quat); frame_correction_quat (for example DROID's rot6d correction) DofsPos Joint positions of the named DOFs, in the declared order entity_name, dofs_name, offset_from_default GripperState Raw, openness or closedness of the gripper DOFs normalize, open_pos, close_pos, scale

Terms in one group concatenate in declaration order: an 8-D DROID state is DofsPos plus GripperState. Builders in eden/extensions/policies/adapters.py cover the recurring layouts: make_ee_pose_group ([pos, quat_wxyz, openness]), make_droid_joint_state_group ([q(7), gripper]) and make_image_groups. Camera images, resizing and channel order go through eden.utils.image (to_uint8_hwc, to_chw_uint8, resize_uint8, resize_with_pad).

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
eden/extensions/policies/adapters.py holds the reusable action decoders for manipulation. Each is an ActionAdapter: a setup assigns one to self.adapter, and the policy calls adapter.bind(env) once the setup is built, so an adapter that reads the env fails at construction on a bad name.

Adapter Row layout Drives EEDeltaAdapter [dxyz, drot(3), gripper], Euler or axis-angle rotation, handed to the IK controller as a rotation vector ee_controller (differential IK), gripper_controller JointPositionAdapter [q(n), gripper] absolute targets ee_controller (implicit PD, zero reference), gripper_controller JointVelocityAdapter [qd(n), gripper] in rad/s, optional lag, compensation and integration ee_controller (implicit velocity or PD), gripper_controller BimanualJointPositionAdapter [left(n), right(m)] left_arm_controller, right_arm_controller

A policy that emits accumulated Cartesian targets drives the core IKPoseController (eden.actions) with a 7-D base-frame pose. Other policy families add their own decoder module beside adapters.py.

docs.title: Gripper conventions
docs.text:
Gripper conventions differ per server and are the most common porting bug. The client does not decide open or close: unpack_actions forwards the server's gripper scalar raw (one column; NaN means "no command this step, hold the previous target"), and the env's GripperDecisionController (a BinaryJointController in eden.actions) applies the rule declared in the policy's action_options():

input Rule Used by sign (default) raw > 0 closes RL policies open_sign raw > 0 opens octo openness raw > threshold opens OpenPI Bridge, GR00T SimplerEnv WidowX closedness raw > threshold closes DROID-style servers (OpenPI DROID, cosmos3, molmoact2, GalaxeaVLA)

Optional knobs, each matching a reference client:

Knob Behavior open_threshold / close_threshold with hold_steps Hysteresis, then hold the new state. sticky_repeats SimplerEnv's Google Robot latch on openness: a jump beyond ±0.5 is repeated for N steps, otherwise the small relative command is sent, integrated into a continuous finger target (OpenPI google_robot). zero_holds With a sign input, exactly 0 keeps the state (robosuite-style sign commands). continuous with snap_threshold Continuous closedness, snapped to closed above the threshold (GalaxeaVLA's DROID Franka). on_missing="measured" A NaN commands the measured closedness (continuous mode only). The default hold keeps the previous target, seeded from the measured position on a first NaN.

build() rejects settings the chosen mode would ignore (for example hold_steps without hysteresis), and the term's reset(envs_idx) clears its state per env. Every client that forwards a raw gripper scalar calls adapters.check_env_gripper_term(env, "gripper_controller", ...) at construction: it raises when the env has no such term, when the term is not a GripperDecisionController (a task's own BinaryJointController would silently misread the scalar), or when its settings disagree with the policy's. make_droid_gripper_action builds the Robotiq [0, close_pos] term every DROID-family setup uses.

The LIBERO setups (OpenPI libero, GR00T libero_sim) do not use this term: they drive the stock libero task's own stateful LiberoPandaGripperController (+1 closes, -1 opens, 0 holds, ramping the fingers as robosuite does), which construction requires by exact type. OpenPI forwards robosuite's command as it is; GR00T's [0, 1] openness becomes -sign(2g - 1), as Isaac-GR00T's LIBERO client maps it.

docs.title: Writing a new client
docs.text:
The /wire-vla skill (.claude/skills/wire-vla/SKILL.md) walks a coding agent through analyzing a policy server's repository and generating the client files. By hand, the checklist is:

  • class MyPolicy(ClientMixin, PolicyBase, ConfigurableMixin[RemotePolicyOptions]) (or SetupClientMixin for several embodiments), decorated with @POLICY_REGISTRY.register(), in eden/extensions/policies/<name>/policy.py.
  • Pick transport (and serializer if the default is wrong); declare the knobs the transport reads as class attributes.
  • Set the chunk rules: chunk_mode, pred_action_horizon, exec_horizon, short_chunk, response_action_key.
  • Implement pack_observations and unpack_actions. Override decode_response if the chunk is not under one key, observe for per-step history, and request_options / reset_options for server sessions.
  • Implement observation_options / action_options from the core terms, the adapters.py builders and eden.utils.image before writing new code.
  • Check the env at construction: the gripper term (check_env_gripper_term) and the control rate the checkpoint was trained at (check_control_rate), both in adapters.py.
  • State the gripper convention in a comment, and verify it against the server's reference client.
  • Pin the wire contract with a golden case in tests/extensions/policies/<name>/test_policy.py (payload, decoded actions, inference-call count for a fixed observation sequence), using record_golden / assert_matches_golden from tests/extensions/policies/conftest.py and a fake server from tests/support/policy_servers.py.

docs.title: Motion Retargeting
docs.text: Retargeting maps motion recorded on one body (a person, a MANO hand) onto a robot with different proportions and joints. eden retarget runs Eden's retargeting backends as batch jobs from the shell; this page covers each subcommand, the data it needs, what it writes, and the Python API behind it. For hand-only retargeting from keypoints in Python (live teleoperation included), see Dex retargeting.

docs.title: Pick a backend
docs.text:
eden retarget omniretarget --src <OMOMO .pt dir> --task-name <clip> --out <dir>
eden retarget otretarget   --source omomo|seed --src <clip(s)> --body-model-path <path> --out <dir>
eden retarget soma         --src <SMPL .npz or dir> --body-model-path <path> --out <dir>
eden retarget dex          --src <keypoints .npz or dir> --out <.pkl or dir>
eden retarget flashdex import    --source taco --raw <release> --mano-dir <dir> --dataset <dir>
eden retarget flashdex kinematic --dataset <dir> --robot xhand
subcommand backend input output target omniretarget OmniRetargeter: interaction-mesh (Laplacian) IK one OMOMO (Holosoma) sequence, body only <clip>.npy, (T, 7 + 29) qpos G1, 29 DOF otretarget OTRetargeter: surface interactions carried by optimal transport, robot and objects solved together canonical OMOMO SMPL-X sequences with objects, or SOMA-rig .bvh <rig>_<clip>.npz (RetargetResult) G1 or LimX Oli, with or without Wuji hands soma SomaRetargeter: the eden-soma-retargeter library AMASS-style SMPL / SMPL-H / SMPL-X .npz .npz with qpos, dof_names, fps G1 or LimX Oli dex DexRetargeter: position optimizer MANO keypoints (T, 21, 3) .pkl of per-frame qpos XHand (right) flashdex FlashDexRetarget kinematic pipeline a released hand-object dataset (TACO, OakInk2, HOT3D, DexYCB) <dataset>/<robot>/motion.pt bimanual XHand or Sharpa Wave

Rules of thumb: use soma for large body-only libraries (AMASS and video estimates), otretarget when the human touches objects or the floor matters and you want the object moved with the robot, omniretarget for a quick body-only OMOMO clip, and flashdex to turn hand-object datasets into training data for dexterous hands. No motion capture at hand? eden pose gvhmr recovers an AMASS-style SMPL-X clip from a video that soma then retargets.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Every subcommand's --help works without its backend; a missing backend fails with the command to install it.

subcommand extra omniretarget all (it needs cvxpy, which only that extra brings) otretarget ot-retargeter soma soma-retargeter (checkout only, see below) dex dex-retargeter flashdex flashdexretarget uv (checkout)pip 
uv sync --inexact --extra ot-retargeter
uv sync --inexact --extra soma-retargeter
uv sync --inexact --extra dex-retargeter
uv sync --inexact --extra flashdexretarget
uv sync --inexact --extra all

pip install 'eden-world[ot-retargeter]'
pip install 'eden-world[dex-retargeter]'
pip install 'eden-world[flashdexretarget]'
pip install 'eden-world[all]'

soma-retargeter is uv-only

eden-soma-retargeter pins a trimesh version that conflicts with Genesis's, and only the checkout's uv override reconciles them, so pip cannot install this extra. Use uv sync --inexact --extra soma-retargeter in a checkout.

docs.title: Shared --src / --out conventions
docs.text:
soma, dex and otretarget --source seed accept a single file or a directory for --src:

  • A directory is searched recursively. soma and dex mirror the source tree under --out, one output per input. otretarget writes flat <rig>_<clip>.npz files and refuses two clips with the same name in different folders.
  • With a single file, soma and dex accept a file or a directory for --out.
  • soma and dex refuse to write onto their own input, so --src equal to --out raises instead of overwriting clips.

Batch flags:

flag subcommands effect --skip-existing omniretarget, otretarget, soma, dex skip a clip whose output exists, so a long batch can resume --num-frames N omniretarget, otretarget, soma keep the first N frames of each clip (quick tests) --cpu otretarget, soma run on the CPU backend instead of the GPU

docs.title: omniretarget: OMOMO human motion → G1
docs.text:
Retargets the body motion of one OMOMO sequence onto the 29-DOF G1 with OmniRetarget's interaction-mesh IK (Laplacian deformation, foot sticking, ground and joint-limit constraints). The manipulated object is ignored.

eden retarget omniretarget \
    --src /data/omomo_holosoma \
    --task-name sub3_largebox_003 \
    --out results/omni
  • --src is the directory of OMOMO Holosoma .pt sequences, the files OMOMOHolosomaDataset downloads.
  • --task-name picks the sequence by file stem; a trailing .pt is accepted.
  • The human is scaled by the G1's height over the subject's (from the dataset's human_height).
  • The output <out>/<task-name>.npy has shape (T, 7 + 29): [base_pos(3), base_quat_wxyz(4), joints(29)].

Retargeting the object together with the body is not in the CLI; see examples/recipes/retargeting/omniretarget/retarget_object_interaction.py.

docs.title: otretarget: humans, hands and objects onto a humanoid
docs.text:
OTRetarget (arXiv 2609.36602) reads the demonstration's interactions off surfaces rather than skeletons. Dense probes on the human, the robot links and the objects measure a signed distance, a closest point and a direction to every channel (the floor and each object). An entropic optimal-transport plan, solved once per (human part, robot link group) in a T-pose, carries each robot probe's targets from the human probes it corresponds to. A per-frame constrained IK (a trust-region SQP solved with ProxQP) then solves the robot pose and every object pose together, at native scale: nothing is rescaled.

# OMOMO: hands, body and object onto a G1 with Wuji hands
eden retarget otretarget --source omomo \
    --src /data/eden_omomo/sequences_canonical/sub3_largebox_003 \
    --objects-dir /data/eden_omomo/objects \
    --body-model-path /data/body_models/smplx \
    --rig g1_wuji --out results/otr

# BONES-SEED: a folder of SOMA-rig BVH clips, body only, onto a LimX Oli
eden retarget otretarget --source seed --src /data/seed_bvh \
    --body-model-path /data/soma/SOMA_neutral.npz --rig oli --out results/otr

Inputs:

--source --src --body-model-path also needs omomo one canonical OMOMO sequence directory (<clip>/human.npz + object.npz) or the folder holding them the directory with SMPLX_NEUTRAL.npz, SMPLX_MALE.npz, SMPLX_FEMALE.npz --objects-dir: the release's objects/ (<name>/<name>.obj, metres) seed a SOMA-rig .bvh or a directory of them SOMA_neutral.npz from the SOMA release

The SMPL-X model files are licence-gated: download them from smpl-x.is.tue.mpg.de.

--rig (default g1_wuji) selects the embodiment and its preset (eden.extensions.retargeting.otretarget.PRESETS): g1_wuji and oli_wuji have dexterous Wuji hands, g1 and oli have moulded hands and retarget the body only. A preset holds the T-pose, the human-part ↔ robot-link groups and the style links.

Further flags:

flag effect --shard K/N retarget every N-th clip of the sorted list starting at the K-th, to split a library across jobs (default 0/1) --clip-list FILE retarget only the clip names listed in FILE, one per line (applied before --shard); an unknown name raises --supports omomo only: add the untracked tables the object rests on as fixed plates, and write <rig>_<clip>.supports.json --keep-going on a clip that raises, write <rig>_<clip>.error.txt, continue, and exit non-zero at the end

Each clip writes <out>/<rig>_<clip>.npz (RetargetResult.save), first under a temporary name so a killed job never leaves a truncated file that --skip-existing would take as done. Its arrays:

  • qpos: (T, n_q) rig configuration, root [pos, quat_wxyz, joints] then each welded hand's joints;
  • entity_qpos/<entity>: the same split per scene entity, ready for entity.set_qpos;
  • object_poses/<name>: (T, 7) solved [pos, quat_wxyz] per object;
  • fps, info/* (per-frame solver diagnostics: iterations, cost, qp_relaxed, penetration_mm, ...) and stats/* (timings and problem size).

The loaders move the human vertically so its feet stand on z = 0 (some OMOMO body fits float several centimetres above the floor the object rests on, and OTRetarget would copy that gap onto the robot). Objects are never moved.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
The recipe README (examples/recipes/retargeting/otretarget/README.md) shows the API:

from eden.extensions.retargeting.otretarget import PRESETS, OTRetargeter, for_body_model
from eden.extensions.retargeting.otretarget.sources import load_omomo_sequence

human, box = load_omomo_sequence(seq_dir, objects_dir, smplx_dir)
retargeter = OTRetargeter(env, OTRetargeter.configure(**PRESETS["g1_wuji"].retargeter_options()))
result = retargeter.retarget_motion(human, [box])     # robot + box solved jointly
env.entities["robot"].set_qpos(result.entity_qpos["robot"][t])

env is a built single-env scene holding the rig (the CLI builds it at precision="64", the precision OTRetarget was tuned in). For SOMA BVH input use sources.load_soma_bvh and for_body_model(PRESETS[rig], "soma").

OTRetargeter is the paper's method alone; embodiment-specific stages are add-ons named in its addons option. floor_stance keeps a legged robot's stance width on the floor and keeps planted feet from sliding; hand_grasp closes dexterous fingers on held objects and corrects a hand that ends up on the wrong side of a thin part. The presets give every rig floor_stance, and a rig with palms hand_grasp. A new embodiment needs a RigPreset; a new body model needs only a HumanSurfaceMotion (posed vertices, faces, skinning weights, joint frames).

The recipe README lists every departure from the paper, the option behind it and the failure it fixes, plus the interaction metrics (eden.extensions.retargeting.otretarget.metrics.evaluate_retarget) and a script that renders the demonstration and the robot side by side.

docs.title: soma: SMPL-family motion → a humanoid
docs.text:
Batch-retargets AMASS-style SMPL, SMPL-H or SMPL-X clips to a floating-base robot through the eden-soma-retargeter library, which fits each clip to the SOMA rig and solves IK. The library runs in a worker subprocess without Genesis.

eden retarget soma \
    --src /data/amass/smplx \
    --body-model smplx \
    --body-model-path /data/body_models/smplx/SMPLX_NEUTRAL.npz \
    --robot unitree_g1 \
    --out results/soma
flag default effect --body-model smplx source model: smpl, smplh or smplx --body-model-path required the model file (e.g. SMPLX_NEUTRAL.npz) or a directory of per-gender files --robot unitree_g1 unitree_g1 or limx_oli --gender neutral default gender; a clip's own gender field overrides it --target-fps 30 rate every clip is resampled to --source-fps override the clip's rate when its metadata is missing or wrong --snap-to-ground off shift each clip by one constant height so the robot's lowest collision point over the clip touches z = 0 --cpu off run the fit on the CPU (default: GPU)

Each input .npz must hold poses, trans, betas and a frame rate (mocap_framerate or mocap_frame_rate), optionally gender. AMASS clips and eden pose gvhmr output both qualify. The SMPL-family model files are licence-gated: download them from their project pages (SMPL, SMPL-H via MANO, SMPL-X).

Each input writes one .npz mirroring the source tree, with qpos of shape (T, 7 + N) ([x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz, joints...], Z-up, radians, joints in the robot entity's dofs_name order), dof_names (so readers can select columns by name), fps and source_path. No shipped dataset loader reads these files as they are; to train on them, write a small loader (see Writing a loader).

The fit targets the public 78-joint SOMA rig: SomaRetargeter passes enable_procedural_transforms=False because the library's expanded twist-joint rig (its own default) also needs SOMA_procedural_transforms.json and SOMA_template_rig.usda, which the public nvidia/soma-x assets do not ship. Both modes emit the same 78-joint interface; the fitted rotations differ slightly. If you have those files, pass SomaRetargeter.configure(enable_procedural_transforms=True); there is no CLI flag for it.

Before building anything, the command checks the installed backend and refuses one it cannot fit with: an eden-soma-retargeter older than 0.4.0 (no enable_procedural_transforms), or py-soma-x 0.1.0, which fits near-zero rotations and reports them as a GPU problem.

In Python, SomaRetargeter (eden.extensions.retargeting.soma_retargeter) also takes body_model="soma" for native SOMA arrays, retarget_bvh(path) for SOMA BVH files, and retarget_motions(clips) to solve many clips in one batched IK. Call close() when done to stop the worker. examples/recipes/retargeting/soma_retargeter/ covers those and rendering to mp4.

docs.title: dex: MANO keypoints → a dexterous hand
docs.text:
Offline position retargeting of MANO-ordered hand keypoints onto a hand:

eden retarget dex --src /data/keypoints --preset xhand1_right_position --out results/dex
  • Each --src .npz holds keypoints of shape (T, 21, 3) in MANO order and, optionally, a scalar fps (default 30).
  • --preset must be a position preset; xhand1_right_position (the default) is the one that ships. Position presets match absolute keypoints, so the keypoints must already be in the robot's wrist frame.
  • Each input writes a .pkl: {"data": [qpos per frame], "meta_data": {"preset", "dof", "joint_names", "fps"}}.

Video (MediaPipe) input and DexYCB-direct retargeting are covered in Dex retargeting.

docs.title: flashdex: hand-object demos → bimanual robot hands
docs.text:
The kinematic half of FlashDexRetarget, without Isaac Sim: it turns a released human hand-object dataset into the motion.pt that the flashdexretarget task trains a multi-motion policy on. Two commands share one dataset directory:

# 1. a release → <dataset>/human_demo/<clip>.npz + <dataset>/objects/<id>/visual.obj
eden retarget flashdex import --source taco --raw /data/taco \
    --mano-dir /data/mano_v1_2/models --dataset /data/taco_fdr
# 2. support disks, reject rules, convex parts, MuJoCo physics IK, object URDFs and SDF grids
#    → <dataset>/xhand/{report.csv, retargeted/, motion.pt}
eden retarget flashdex kinematic --dataset /data/taco_fdr --robot xhand

Each robot's outputs go to <dataset>/<robot>/, so one import retargets to both robots (--robot xhand, then --robot sharpa) and each keeps its own motion.pt; clips and objects are shared. motion.pt names its object meshes relative to its own directory (../objects/<id>).

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
--source read by --raw holds notes taco TacoDataset Hand_Poses/, Object_Poses/, object_models_released/ each hand takes the object it stays nearest to oakink2 OakInk2Dataset anno_preview/, program/, object_repair/ one clip per program stage; the desk is fitted over the whole recording hot3d Hot3dDataset dataset/<recording>/, _assets/assets/ cut into segments where the hands hold objects dexycb DexYCBDataset <subject>/<sequence>/ (with the master camera's labels_*.npz), calibration/, models/ one hand per clip: needs --sides right or --sides left (both is refused)

Each release is read by its eden.datasets loader with its MANO parameters (body_model_params): the loader cuts the clips and picks the object each hand holds, and the import runs MANO, levels the table and resamples to fps (default 60). Loader settings go under source.dataset. For example, to also keep HOT3D segments where the two hands hold two objects (mode C):

eden retarget flashdex import --source hot3d --raw /data/hot3d --mano-dir /data/mano_v1_2/models \
    --dataset /data/hot3d_fdr --override "source: {name: hot3d, dataset: {modes: [B, C], min_frames: 45}}"

A one-hand segment (mode A) holds nothing in its idle hand, so it needs --sides right or --sides left.

The MANO models are licence-gated and never shipped: register at mano.is.tue.mpg.de, download Models & Code, and pass its models/ directory as --mano-dir.

Objects are exported from their geometry alone, which is all retargeting reads (a mesh with UVs gets trimesh's grey placeholder texture). --textures also exports the release's materials and textures, for rendering visual.obj; it costs every import a decode of each object's textures (a 4096² texture decodes to about 50 MB, one object at a time).

docs.title: Kinematic retargeting
docs.text:
The steps, in order (eden/extensions/retargeting/flashdexretarget/pipeline.py):

step does writes (under the dataset) preprocess support disks, reject rules <robot>/report.csv convex convex decomposition (CoACD or CuACD) objects/<id>/convex/*.obj retarget MuJoCo physics IK <robot>/retargeted/<clip>.npz pack kept clips into one file <robot>/motion.pt urdf object URDFs for simulation objects/<id>/object.urdf sdf object SDF grids objects/<id>/.sdf_cache/

The IK runs in CPU MuJoCo on the robot MJCFs under hands/flashdexretarget/<robot>/ of the asset store, so motion.pt's joint_pos columns follow that MJCF's joint order; motion.pt also carries robot, joint_names and fps. --workers sets the process count (default: half the CPU cores).

Every setting is an option in eden.options.extensions.flashdexretarget (FDRImportOptions, FDRKinematicRetargetingOptions and the groups under it: steps, desk, filters, convex, retarget, pack, sdf) with FlashDexRetarget's defaults. Set them from a --config file and repeated --override YAML mappings, as with eden train:

# Review report.csv before running the IK
eden retarget flashdex kinematic --dataset /data/taco_fdr --override "steps: {retarget: false, pack: false}"
# GPU convex decomposition, fewer IK attempts, keep every clip
eden retarget flashdex kinematic --dataset /data/taco_fdr \
    --override "convex: {name: cuacd}" --override "retarget: {attempts: 3}" --override "filters: {enable: false}"

Each step is a cache, redone when anything it was made from changes:

  • Convex parts are keyed on the object's visual.obj and the convex settings; an SDF grid on the mesh, grid_n and extent. A re-import whose release has another geometry for an object replaces its visual.obj, and warns.
  • A retargeted clip is keyed on the robot model files, the imported clip, its support disks, its objects' convex parts, and the retarget settings other than the quality flags, which are rescored every run. pack refuses a clip made from other inputs. A clip whose IK fails is left out of motion.pt.
  • force: true (on convex or retarget) redoes the step anyway.

Every file is written through a temporary file, so an interrupted run never leaves a truncated one. The IK model overrides every contact's parameters (mjENBL_OVERRIDE, as FlashDexRetarget does), so contacts take retarget.contact's o_solref, o_solimp and o_friction.

The convex parts and the IK match FlashDexRetarget's own pipeline on the same inputs and settings, with two deliberate differences: the kept IK run is smoothed by a moving average centred on each frame (one ending on it held the hand a frame behind the object), and fingertip contact is measured to the object's surface rather than to its nearest mesh vertex. Its Isaac-only USD conversion is replaced by the urdf step (convex parts collide, density 800 kg/m³ with the mass clamped to [0.05, 0.5] kg, as FlashDexRetarget authors it).

docs.title: Training on the result
docs.text:
The RL stage (one policy over every clip, whose completed rollouts are the physically valid trajectories) is the flashdexretarget task:

eden train --task flashdexretarget --motion /data/taco_fdr/xhand/motion.pt --robot xhand

See Manipulation tasks and eden/tasks/flashdexretarget/README.md.

docs.title: Rewards and Terminations
docs.text:
The reward manager turns a set of weighted reward terms into the scalar reward of each step, and the termination manager decides which episodes end — and whether each ending is a true terminal state or a time-out. This page covers how the reward is computed, weights, time windows, tags and reward groups, what gets logged, how terminations split into terminated and truncated, and the built-in terms. The general term contract is in Writing terms.

Both managers belong to the RL env (RLEnvBase). In the step loop terminations run at phase 8 and rewards at phase 9, both on the post-physics state of the step that just happened and before the auto-reset, so a reward term can read this step's termination verdicts.

docs.title: The step reward
docs.text:
Each entry of reward_options is one reward term with a weight. The step reward is

reward = dt * Σ_i  weight_i * mask_i * term_i

where dt is the control step (EnvOptions.sim_dt * EnvOptions.decimation), term_i is the term's (num_envs,) output and mask_i is 1 except outside the term's range_s window. The reward is multiplied by dt, so weights are per second: a term that outputs 1 every step with weight 1 contributes 1 over each second of episode, whatever the control rate. When you port weights from a framework that does not scale by dt (or does), convert them.

An excerpt of the velocity-tracking rewards (eden/tasks/velocity_tracking/base_config.py):

import math

from eden import rewards
from eden.options.managers.rewards import RewardManagerOptions
from eden.terms import RewardTerm

reward_options = RewardManagerOptions(
    track_linear_velocity=RewardTerm.configure(
        func=rewards.track_lin_vel_with_z_penalty,
        weight=2.0,
        params={"command_name": "velocity_command", "entity_name": "robot", "std": math.sqrt(0.25)},
    ),
    joint_pos_limits=RewardTerm.configure(
        func=rewards.dofs_pos_limits,
        weight=-1.0,
        params={"entity_name": "robot"},
    ),
    action_rate_l2=RewardTerm.configure(func=rewards.action_rate_l2, weight=-0.1),
    action_rate_l2_smooth=rewards.ActionRateL2Smooth.configure(weight=-0.05),
    # feet_link_names is filled in per robot by the task's robot-binding TaskMod.
    foot_slip=rewards.FeetSlip.configure(
        weight=-0.1,
        entity_name="robot",
        feet_link_names=[],
        command_name="velocity_command",
        command_threshold=0.05,
    ),
)

Penalty terms output a non-negative cost and take a negative weight; the sign lives in the weight, not in the term.

A few things happen around the sum:

  • A weight of 0.0 means the term is not built. The manager logs a warning naming the entry, the term never runs and gets no log key, and reading it (get_term_value) raises a KeyError that says why. To keep a term that a curriculum will switch on later, give it a small non-zero weight.
  • Envs Genesis flagged as corrupt this step (a NaN contact force, a diverged solve) contribute 0 for every term. Those envs are reset in the same step; see Terminations.
  • Term names must be unique across the whole reward manager, groups included.

Reward terms are importable from eden.rewards (from eden import rewards); the full list is in the Term Catalog and from eden terms --kind reward.

docs.title: Reward term fields
docs.text:
Every reward term — function or class — has these fields beside its own parameters:

Field Default Meaning weight 1.0 multiplies the term's output in the sum range_s None a time window (start_s, end_s) in seconds since the episode began, or a list of them, during which the term is active; both ends inclusive. Outside the window the term contributes 0 and is not accumulated in its episode sums. None is active for the whole episode tags [] labels for grouping terms (["penalty"], ["tracking", "feet"]), so curricula and other consumers can select terms by tag instead of by name

range_s is converted to integer step bounds once at build, round(start_s / dt) to round(end_s / dt), and compared against the env's episode_length_buf. The getup task (eden/tasks/mujoco_playground/getup/config.py) only rewards resembling the default pose between 1 and 6 s:

similar_to_default=RewardTerm.configure(
    func=rewards.similar_to_default,
    weight=-1.0,
    params={"entity_name": "robot"},
    range_s=[(1.0, 6.0)],
),

docs.title: Changing weights during training
docs.text: A term's weight can change between steps; the manager compares the terms' weights with its device copy each step and uploads them only when one moved. Curricula are the usual way to move them — for example StageRewardWeightCurriculum (stepwise weights for one term, used by the reacher task) and PenaltyCurriculum (scales a set of terms selected by reward_term_names or by reward_term_tags). Curricula are frozen during evaluation. See Curricula.

docs.title: Reward groups
docs.text:
Entries of reward_options may be flat terms, named groups of terms (RewardGroupOptions), or a mix. Groups never change the scalar reward — the manager always sums every term — but they add a per-group readout for multi-channel consumers: a CMDP-style task/style/penalty split, a multi-critic algorithm, per-group logging. The ConTrack task (eden/tasks/contrack/config.py) splits its reward three ways, abridged:

from eden.options import RewardGroupOptions
from eden.options.managers.rewards import RewardManagerOptions
from eden.terms import RewardTerm

reward_options = RewardManagerOptions(
    rg=RewardGroupOptions(  # object tracking (task)
        tracking_obj_pos=RewardTerm.configure(
            func=motion_base_position_tracking_exp,
            weight=500.0,
            params={"entity_name": "object", "std": _OBJ_POS_STD},
        ),
    ),
    rs=RewardGroupOptions(  # joint and contact imitation (style)
        contact_match=MotionContactMatchReward.configure(weight=100.0, ...),
    ),
    rp=RewardGroupOptions(  # smoothness penalties
        qvel_penalty_arm=RewardTerm.configure(func=contrack_dofs_vel_penalty, weight=-1.0, params={...}),
    ),
)

Flat terms belong to an implicit group named "default" (eden.managers.DEFAULT_REWARD_GROUP), which exists only when at least one flat term is declared; iterate reward_manager.group_term_names rather than assuming it. Unlike observation groups, reward groups partition one flat set of terms: a term name may appear only once across all groups.

To override a grouped term, address it through its group — {"rg": {"tracking_obj_pos": {...}}} in a config override, config.reward_options.rg.tracking_obj_pos in code. A flat-name override of a grouped term raises, naming the group to go through. reward_options.disable_term(name) removes a flat term, a whole group, or a term nested in exactly one group; an ambiguous name raises and tells you to call disable_term on the group.

docs.title: Reading rewards
docs.text:
env.reward_manager exposes the last step's values and the running episode sums. Every per-term readout raises KeyError listing the active terms for an unknown name.

Method Returns get_term_value(name) the term's output at the last step, (num_envs,): masked, zero for corrupt envs, without weight and dt — what an off-policy learner that weights its own reward channels stores get_group_reward(group) the group's share of the last step's scalar reward: weighted, masked and dt-scaled. The groups' shares add up to the scalar reward get_episode_sum(name, raw=True) the running episode sum of one term; raw=True is unweighted, raw=False weighted get_group_episode_sum(group, *, raw) the same for a group; raw is keyword-only and has no default iter_terms(), group_term_names the active terms, flat, and the active term names by group summary() a table of the active terms with their weights (and groups)

The per-step readouts are the manager's own buffers, overwritten in place by the next step: clone a value to keep it. After an auto-reset they still read the step that just ended, consistent with the reward env.step() returned.

docs.title: What gets logged
docs.text:
When envs reset, the reward manager reports, averaged over the envs that reset and divided by episode_length_s:

Key Value Emitted Episode_Reward/<term> the weighted episode sum when per-term logging is on Episode_Reward_Raw/<term> the unweighted episode sum when per-term logging is on Episode_Reward_Group/<group> the sum of the group's Episode_Reward values whenever the config declares groups

RewardManagerOptions.log_per_term_rewards controls per-term logging. None (the default) turns it on for a config with no groups and off for one that declares groups, where the group sums are the intended readout — and logs an info line at build saying so. Set True to always emit per-term keys, or False to never. It changes logging only, never the reward.

The termination manager reports Episode_Termination/<term>: how many of the envs that reset this step were ended by that term (an env can be counted by several). Episode_Termination/solver_error counts the envs reset because a solver flagged them.

docs.title: Terminations
docs.text:
Each entry of termination_options is a termination term returning a (num_envs,) bool. An env whose episode any term ends is reset at phase 13 of the same step, so the observation env.step() returns for it is already its next episode's first frame. Set EnvOptions.record_final_observations=True to also get the terminal frame, in extras["final_observations"].

The velocity-tracking tasks use the two most common terms:

import math

from eden import terminations
from eden.options.managers.terminations import TerminationManagerOptions
from eden.terms import DoneTerm

termination_options = TerminationManagerOptions(
    time_out=DoneTerm.configure(func=terminations.time_out, time_out=True),
    fell_over=DoneTerm.configure(
        func=terminations.fell_over,
        params={"entity_name": "robot", "limit_angle": math.radians(70.0)},
    ),
)

docs.title: Terminated or truncated: time_out
docs.text:
Every termination term has a time_out field (default False), and it decides what kind of ending the term reports:

  • time_out=False — the episode reached a true terminal state (the robot fell, the object dropped). The env lands in terminated, and a learner does not bootstrap the value of the next state.
  • time_out=True — the episode was cut off by a deadline, not by anything the agent did. The env lands in truncated (the manager's timeouts), and a learner bootstraps from the value of the final state.

env.step() returns (obs, reward, terminated, timeouts, extras). An env can be in both on one step — it failed on the step its episode timed out — and is then terminal. The rsl_rl wrapper reports extras["time_outs"] = truncated & ~terminated on every step, which is what rsl_rl bootstraps from.

Mark a term time_out=True only when the ending is genuinely not the agent's doing. A deadline you want treated as a real terminal — a task that must be finished within the episode — is declared with time_out=False.

env.termination_manager exposes dones, terminated, timeouts, solver_errors, get_term_dones(name) and summary().

docs.title: Episode length and the time_out term
docs.text:
The episode horizon is EnvOptions.episode_length_s (default 20.0 s); the env converts it to max_episode_length = ceil(episode_length_s / dt) control steps. Nothing ends an episode at that length on its own: the built-in terminations.time_out term does, by returning episode_length_buf >= max_episode_length. So include it, with time_out=True, in every task that should time out.

episode_length_s must be positive and finite. For an unbounded episode, keep a finite horizon and leave the time_out term out — truncation then never fires. (max_episode_length still sizes integer buffers and the rsl_rl runner, and episode_phase observations and the per-episode log averages divide by it.)

docs.title: Corrupt envs
docs.text: When a physics solver flags an env as corrupt (a NaN contact force, a diverged implicit solve), the termination manager resets it as truncated, never terminated, regardless of what any term says about its state: the simulator failed, not the task, so the learner bootstraps the step instead of reading it as a terminal outcome. The reward and metric managers drop what their terms read of that env on that step. The name solver_error is reserved for the log key; a termination term named solver_error raises at build.

docs.title: Built-in termination terms
docs.text:
Termination terms are importable from eden.terminations (from eden import terminations); the full list is in the Term Catalog and from eden terms --kind termination.

Family Terms Time and success time_out, on_success, on_failure, OnMetricSuccess, MetricAbove, cumulative_reward_below_threshold Contact illegal_contact (which entities touched), IllegalLinkContact (which links of one entity carry force above force_threshold — the knee-and-torso fall detector) Pose and limits fell_over, base_orientation_roll_greater_than, base_orientation_pitch_greater_than, root_height_below_minimum, dofs_pos_limit_exceeded, dofs_vel_limit_exceeded, dofs_torque_limit_exceeded Manipulation object_out_of_reach, and the success conditions also registered as metrics: object_lifted, object_in_region, object_above_height, object_a_is_on_b, entity_near_target, entity_near_entity_xy, joint_angle_at_target Motion tracking bad_anchor_ori, bad_anchor_pos_z_only, bad_base_ori, BadMotionLinkPosZOnly, motion_ends, MotionBasePoseTrackingBreak, and the motion_*_tracking_error_above family

The success conditions in the manipulation row are registered both as metric terms and as termination terms, so one function can count a success and end the episode on it. To end an episode on a metric you already compute, use OnMetricSuccess (the metric's own success check) or MetricAbove (its value against a threshold); see Share a computation across terms.

docs.title: Built-in reward terms
docs.text:
Family Terms Action smoothness and effort action_l2, action_rate_l2, ActionRateL2Smooth, DofsAccL2, dofs_torques Joint limits and posture dofs_pos_limits, dofs_vel_limits, similar_to_default, VariablePosture, WeightedPosePenalty Contact UndesiredContacts, self_collision_cost Velocity tracking and base track_lin_vel_with_z_penalty, track_ang_vel_with_xy_penalty, TrackingLinVel, TrackingAngVel, lin_vel_z, FlatOrientationL2, Upright, BodyAngVelXYPenalty, base_height_l2, constant_base_height, is_terminated_penalty Feet FeetAirTime, FeetClearance, FeetSlip, FeetPhase, FeetContactBalancePenalty, FeetOrientationPenalty, CloseFeetPenalty, CloseFeetYawProjectedPenalty, StumblePenalty Motion tracking the motion_*_tracking_exp family, MotionRelativeBodyPositionErrorExp, MotionGlobalBodyLinearVelocityErrorExp and siblings, MotionContactMatchReward, MotionContactDistanceReward, MotionContactChamferReward Metrics and success MetricReward, TaskSuccess

action_rate_l2 and action_l2 penalize the whole action vector by default; pass action_term_name to restrict them to one action term's slice. is_terminated_penalty returns 1 for envs the termination manager marked terminated this step — time-outs excluded.

docs.title: Writing a reward or termination term
docs.text:
Both kinds take the function form for a pure function of state and the class form (subclass eden.managers.reward_manager.RewardTerm or eden.managers.termination_manager.TerminationTerm) for anything resolved once or carried between steps. Writing terms has the rules; the ones that matter most here:

  • Return (num_envs,) — float for a reward, bool for a termination.
  • RewardManager.compute runs under torch.inference_mode(), so a class term's persistent buffers must be allocated in build() and written in place (Term state lifecycle).
  • Grade the step that just happened. A command term's measurement of this step (a hold counter, a contact latch) must be computed in its post_physics_refresh(), or the reward reads it a step late (Which hook).
  • When a reward, a termination and an observation need one quantity, compute it once as a metric and pull it with MetricReward, MetricAbove / OnMetricSuccess and MetricObservation.

docs.title: Using Eden with Another RL Library
docs.text:
eden train drives rsl_rl and rl_games through a task's runner_options (Training Runs). Any other RL library reaches an Eden task through a wrapper around the RLEnvBase. This page covers the gymnasium vector env (for CleanRL or a loop of your own), stable-baselines3 and skrl, and how to add a wrapper for another library.

Library Entry point Install CleanRL, or any loop of your own gym.make_vec("Eden/<task>", num_envs=N) or GymnasiumVecEnvWrapper (a gymnasium VectorEnv of torch tensors) core stable-baselines3 Sb3VecEnvWrapper (numpy, one observation group) pip install 'eden-world[sb3]' skrl SkrlVecEnvWrapper (torch, optional critic state) pip install 'eden-world[skrl]'

In a checkout, install the extras with uv sync --inexact --extra sb3 or uv sync --inexact --extra skrl.

Runnable examples train the reacher task with each library: examples/recipes/rl_libraries/cleanrl_ppo.py, sb3_ppo.py and skrl_ppo.py.

docs.title: The gymnasium vector env
docs.text:
import eden as en
import genesis as gs
import gymnasium as gym

from eden.envs.wrappers.gymnasium_env import register_gymnasium_envs

en.init(backend=gs.gpu)
register_gymnasium_envs()                     # every registered task, as "Eden/<task>"
envs = gym.make_vec("Eden/reacher", num_envs=4096, seed=0)

obs, info = envs.reset(seed=0)
obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = envs.step(actions)   # actions: (4096, action_dim)

docs.title: Registration
docs.text: register_gymnasium_envs() registers every task in the task registry as Eden/<task> and returns the ids it added. It builds nothing and imports no task module or Genesis, so it is cheap, but import eden does not run it: call it once. Calling it again registers only tasks added since (a task registered at runtime, or one from an installed package).

docs.title: make_vec, not make
docs.text:
Every Eden env is batched, so gym.make("Eden/<task>") raises and names make_vec, as does gym.make_vec with vectorization_mode="sync" or "async". Do not wrap a num_envs=1 env to fake a single one: its tensors keep the leading env dimension. make_vec needs eden.init() first and takes:

  • num_envs: replaces the task's env_options.num_envs. Gymnasium passes its own default of 1 if you leave it out, never the task's.
  • seed: seeds every RNG before the build (Seeding), so the build, the first reset and domain randomization are reproducible. Without it the process RNG is left alone.
  • clip_actions: clamps actions to [-clip_actions, clip_actions] and bounds the action space by it. Without it actions reach the action manager unclamped and the space is unbounded.
  • final_observations (default on): report final_obs in info (below). Turning it off saves an observation compute per step.
  • random_episode_starts (default off): stagger the episode clocks on every reset (below).
  • show_viewer, eval_mode: as for any env's from_config.
  • Any other keyword: the task's TaskMod parameters, as TASK_REGISTRY.build(task, **kwargs) takes them, for example gym.make_vec("Eden/reacher", num_envs=64, difficulty="hard").

From a config you already hold, GymnasiumVecEnvWrapper.from_config(cfg, clip_actions=..., seed=...) does the same, as do the SB3 and skrl wrappers' from_config. cfg needs no runner_options and is left untouched. Each wrapper also wraps an env you built yourself: GymnasiumVecEnvWrapper(env).

docs.title: Tensors stay on the device
docs.text:
Observations, rewards, terminated and truncated are torch tensors on the sim's device (envs.device); actions may be a tensor or a numpy array. Gymnasium's own vector wrappers (RecordEpisodeStatistics, NormalizeObservation, …) are numpy-based and do not apply; the wrapper reports episode statistics itself (below).

Everything step and reset return is a copy, so a learner may keep a step's tensors past the next step (the env itself reuses its buffers in place). That costs one copy of the observation per step, two with final_obs. The SB3 and skrl wrappers copy, and return, only the groups they read.

docs.title: Observations are the env's observation groups
docs.text: obs is a dict with one entry per observation group, and single_observation_space is a gymnasium.spaces.Dict of them: the actor reads obs["policy"], an asymmetric critic another group. A group that concatenates its terms is a Box; one with concatenate_terms=False is a Dict of its terms. The spaces are read off a real observation when the wrapper is constructed (which resets every env), so shapes and dtypes are the manager's.

docs.title: Done envs reset in the same step
docs.text:
metadata["autoreset_mode"] is gymnasium's SAME_STEP: as in RLEnvBase.step(), the observation step returns for a done env already starts its next episode. info carries what the episode ended with:

Key Value final_obs / _final_obs (with final_observations) The observation each done env ended its episode on, and the mask of envs it is valid for: done, and not a state Genesis flagged as corrupt (a solver error, which Eden reports as truncated). Rows outside the mask are zero. episode / _episode {"r": return, "l": length} of each episode that ended this step (zero elsewhere), and the done mask. log The managers' episode statistics, as the rsl_rl and rl_games wrappers log them.

terminated and truncated split the done envs by the termination terms' time_out flag. An env can be both on one step (a failure on the step the episode timed out); treat it as terminal. To bootstrap a time-out correctly, value info["final_obs"], not the returned observation, for the envs in truncated & ~terminated & info["_final_obs"]. Select with torch.where rather than multiplying by the mask, so no other row's value can leak in; cleanrl_ppo.py shows the two lines it takes.

final_obs needs env_options.record_final_observations, which costs one extra observation compute per step (for a camera task, a second render). from_config and make_vec set it to match final_observations. Wrapping an env built without it raises and says so, unless you pass final_observations=False. Turn it off for a loop that never reads final_obs: an evaluation rollout, or skrl, whose wrapper leaves it off by default. The SB3 wrapper always needs it.

docs.title: Staggered episode starts
docs.text: Every env resets together and the episode length is fixed, so without help the envs that never terminate early all time out on the same step, and a learner's per-episode work (SB3 values each ended episode separately) arrives in bursts. random_episode_starts=True starts each env's episode clock at a random step in [0, max_episode_length) on every reset, as eden train does (rsl_rl's init_at_random_ep_len). The first episodes are then shorter, and end as real time-outs. The clocks are drawn after reset(seed=...) seeds the RNGs, so they are reproducible. The three recipes turn it on.

docs.title: Seeding and closing
docs.text:
reset(seed=s) seeds the env's RNGs before resetting every env. Eden's envs share one set of RNGs, so a list of per-env seeds is refused, as are reset options (configure the task through its config or TaskMod keywords).

close() destroys the scene only when the wrapper built the env (from_config, make_vec); an env you passed to GymnasiumVecEnvWrapper(env) stays yours to destroy. No wrapper destroys anything on garbage collection, because a finalizer can run after Genesis has shut down.

docs.title: stable-baselines3
docs.text:
from stable_baselines3 import PPO

from eden.envs.wrappers.sb3_env import Sb3VecEnvWrapper
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY

cfg = TASK_REGISTRY.build("reacher")
cfg.env_options.num_envs = 256
env = Sb3VecEnvWrapper.from_config(cfg, clip_actions=1.0)
model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, n_steps=24, batch_size=256 * 6)
model.learn(total_timesteps=1_000_000)

(Call eden.init() first, as above.)

  • The action space must be bounded. Every SB3 algorithm asserts finite action bounds, so clip_actions is required; use the task's runner_options.clip_actions when it has one. SB3 clips each sampled action to that bound.
  • One observation group, obs_group (default "policy"). A Box group trains with "MlpPolicy"; a group with concatenate_terms=False is a Dict and needs "MultiInputPolicy".
  • Episode ends. Each done env's info carries terminal_observation (SB3 bootstraps time-outs from it, and the off-policy algorithms store it as the transition's next observation), TimeLimit.truncated (truncated and not terminated) and episode, which SB3 logs as rollout/ep_rew_mean; no VecMonitor is needed. A solver-error env gets no terminal_observation, so SB3 does not value its corrupt state. The wrapper therefore refuses an env that does not record final observations; from_config turns them on.
  • No reset options. set_options with anything in it raises at the next reset.
  • Throughput. SB3 is numpy-based and single-device: each step copies observations, rewards and dones to the host, and SB3 builds one info dict per env. Expect a fraction of eden train's throughput, and use a few hundred envs rather than thousands.

get_attr returns the batched env's attribute once per env index; set_attr and env_method raise, since there are no per-env objects to address.

docs.title: skrl
docs.text:
from skrl.utils.runner.torch import Runner

from eden.envs.wrappers.skrl_env import SkrlVecEnvWrapper
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY

env = SkrlVecEnvWrapper.from_config(TASK_REGISTRY.build("reacher"), state_group="critic")
Runner(env, cfg).run("train")   # cfg: skrl's YAML layout, as a dict
  • The wrapper keeps everything on the device. The policy observes obs_group (default "policy"); with state_group set, that group is skrl's state, what a value network with input: STATES reads. Both are flattened to (num_envs, D).
  • Rewards, terminated and truncated are (num_envs, 1), and truncated leaves out an env that also terminated.
  • info is the shared core's, with every log value a 0-d tensor, so a trainer environment_info: "log" puts Eden's per-term episode statistics (Episode_Reward/<term>, …) in skrl's TensorBoard.
  • skrl values a time-out from the observation step returns, which here (as in Isaac Lab) already starts the next episode, whether time_limit_bootstrap is on or off. Its agents never read final_obs, so the skrl wrapper leaves final observations off (final_observations=True to have them).
  • skrl's Wrapper answers any attribute the wrapper lacks from the wrapped env, so wrapper.episode_length_buf works here but raises AttributeError on the gymnasium and SB3 wrappers. Reach the env through wrapper.env to keep code portable between them.

Normalize the inputs

On reacher, skrl's PPO needed RunningStandardScaler for the observation, state and value preprocessors; without them it stayed at a do-nothing policy's reward. skrl_ppo.py carries a configuration that learns.

docs.title: CleanRL
docs.text: CleanRL is a set of single-file algorithms, not a library, so there is nothing to adapt: its continuous PPO runs on gym.make_vec(...) as it is, once it indexes obs["policy"]. The tensors never leave the device, as in CleanRL's ppo_continuous_action_isaacgym.py, which cleanrl_ppo.py follows.

docs.title: What these entry points do not do
docs.text:
• eden train, eden inference, eden export and eden deploy stay rsl_rl/rl_games-only. The libraries above take no runner_options and write their checkpoints in their own formats.
  • They run on one device: Eden's DDP setup is rsl_rl's.
  • The wrappers do not split multi-agent tasks; rl_games' agents option does.

docs.title: Adding another library
docs.text:
All five wrappers (rsl_rl, rl_games, gymnasium, SB3, skrl) live in eden/envs/wrappers/ and share core.py's EnvWrapperMixin: the build and env ownership, the action clamp and space, the observation spaces and the split of terminated from timed-out envs. The gymnasium, SB3 and skrl wrappers add VecEnvMixin (vec_env_mixin.py): final observations, episode statistics and the copies. To add a library:

  1. Mix VecEnvMixin in beside the library's base class: class FooVecEnvWrapper(VecEnvMixin, FooVecEnv).
  2. In __init__, call _init_vec_env(env, ...), after the base class's own __init__ if that routes attribute lookups to the env (as skrl's does). The mixin sets no num_envs or device: those names belong to the library's base class.
  3. Build reset, step and close on what _reset_env, _step_env and _close_env return, converted to the library's types. A learner that bootstraps time-outs reads core.time_outs(terminated, truncated), which leaves out an env that also terminated.
  4. Have from_config call _from_config.
  5. Put the wrapper in eden/envs/wrappers/<library>_env.py, import the library at module level, declare it as an extra in pyproject.toml, and pytest.importorskip it in the wrapper's test.

docs.title: Robots
docs.text: Eden ships robot presets: options classes that load a robot asset with its joint order, default pose, PD gains, armature and effort limits already set. This page covers using and overriding a preset, the full catalog, composite rigs (an arm with a gripper or hand, a humanoid with a hand per wrist), the actuator specs gains are derived from, and how to add a robot or a new asset family. The physics behind the fields (DOF ordering, the armature default, gains vs passive springs) is on Entities.

docs.title: Using a robot
docs.text:
Every preset is importable as en.robots.<Class> (the lazy namespace for eden.options.robots) and is placed in a scene like any other entity:

import eden as en

scene_options = en.scenes.Empty(robot=en.robots.Go2())   # a Go2 on a ground plane, named "robot"

A preset is a Pydantic options class, so override any field at construction. The class's values are the defaults; what you pass replaces them:

robot = en.robots.G1Dofs29(
    default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.8),
    default_dofs_armature={"*": 0.01},
)

A DOF dict you pass replaces the class's dict

default_dofs_kp, default_dofs_kd and every other default_dofs_* dict you pass replace the preset's dict rather than merging into it. A DOF your dict does not cover falls back to the simulator's value, which for a URDF's kp / kd is 0. Re-state every entry you are not deliberately changing; see Actuator gains.

Presets are also registered by name in ROBOT_REGISTRY, keyed by the snake-cased class name:

from eden.options.robots import ROBOT_REGISTRY

cls = ROBOT_REGISTRY.get("go2")      # -> Go2
robot = cls(default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.4))

To look at a robot without writing a task, open it in the viewer or render a snapshot. Both take a class name or an index key such as robot/go2:

eden view Go2                 # interactive viewer; -c shows collision geometry
eden snap G1Dofs29 -o g1.png  # one image
eden arrange FrankaEmikaPanda YCB003CrackerBox   # pose entities with sliders, export a SceneOptions snippet

docs.title: What a preset declares
docs.text:
A preset subclasses RobotOptions, an EntityOptions with is_articulated=True and is_actuated=True. It sets ordinary fields (validated, serialized with the config, overridable) and class-level facts about the asset (ClassVars, read by terms, rigs and deployment but not stored in configs).

Field Kind Meaning file field The asset's repo path (see Where file comes from). is_fixed_base field Arms and grippers are fixed, mobile robots and hands are free. For an MJCF it must match the file (rule). dofs_name field The controlled joints, in the order every DOF-indexed tensor uses (DOF ordering). default_root_pos, default_root_quat field The root link's spawn pose, authored frame, wxyz. default_dofs_pos field Joint positions at reset, and the zero point of position actions. default_dofs_kp, default_dofs_kd field PD gains of Genesis' position / velocity controller. default_dofs_armature, _damping, _stiffness, _frictionloss, _force_limits field Joint dynamics; anything unset comes from the asset or the actuator spec. links_to_keep field URDF links Genesis must not merge away (feet, sensor frames). dofs_spec class Actuator spec per DOF pattern (Actuators). actuated_dofs_name class The DOFs a policy drives; defaults to all of dofs_name. A hand with coupled joints lists only its drivers. ee_links_name class End-effector links; ee_links_name[0] is the IK frame. feet_links_name class Links the robot stands on. The deploy-time base-velocity estimator uses them; empty means "no feet" and makes it refuse (as Go2W does, whose feet are wheels). gantry_links_name class Where eden deploy --mujoco --gantry hangs the robot. open_dofs_pos, close_dofs_pos class Gripper presets only: the open and closed targets of the binary gripper action. tcp_offset, stroke class Gripper facts: the pad midpoint in the gripper's base frame, and the pad-to-pad opening (m). max_substep_dt class The coarsest sim_dt / sim_substeps the asset's constraints stay stiff at (Robotiq2f85: 0.001). metadata class A MetadataOptions bag: hands declare target_hand_links (fingertips) and, for coupled fingers, mimic_dofs (follower -> (driver, multiplier, offset)).

Several robot modules also export per-joint action scales computed from the same actuator specs, for a joint action term's scale (for example ImplicitPDController.configure(scale=GO2_ACTION_SCALE, ...)): G1_ACTION_SCALE, GO1_ACTION_SCALE, GO2_ACTION_SCALE, GO2W_ACTION_SCALE, OLI_ACTION_SCALE, YAM_ACTION_SCALE.

The Inspire RH56 hands are marked unstable

eden/options/robots/inspire_rh56.py flags its base class as a placeholder whose setup is unstable: the Inspire hand is non-backdrivable with high joint friction, which the physics does not model yet. The InspireRH56DFQ hands couple six follower joints to six drivers through metadata.mimic_dofs, which an action term's mimic_dofs takes (see Actions).

A few robots are defined outside the catalog because only one task or policy uses them: the LIBERO Panda and its mounted rig (LiberoPanda, LiberoMountedPanda in eden/options/robots/libero.py) and the HUSKY G1 (eden/extensions/policies/husky/policy.py).

docs.title: Composite robots
docs.text:
A composite robot bundles several unit robots into one rig. It is itself a validated options object (CompositeEntityOptions), so it round-trips through the config system and is placed in a scene under one name; when the environment is constructed it expands into its unit robots plus the welds that join them.

import eden as en
from eden.options.robots import Droid, COMPOSITE_ROBOT_REGISTRY

droid = Droid(base_pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.4))                     # hand-less Panda + Robotiq 2F85
scene_options = en.scenes.Empty(is_support_enabled=True, robot=droid)
# -> entities "robot" (the arm) and "gripper", welded at the arm's "attachment" link

cls = COMPOSITE_ROBOT_REGISTRY.get("ur5e_2f85")             # -> UR5eRobotiq

The scene key must equal the rig's primary body name (arm_name / robot_name, "robot" by default), or SceneOptions raises. Two rigs in one scene need distinct names, for example Droid(arm_name="left", gripper_name="left_gripper").

docs.title: Rig shapes
docs.text:
Base class Bodies For ManipulatorOptions arm + gripper, welded at ee_link an arm with a two-finger gripper DexManipulatorOptions arm + hand, welded at ee_link an arm with a dexterous hand HumanoidOptions robot + left_hand + right_hand, welded at left_ee_link / right_ee_link a humanoid with an end-effector per wrist

The rigs expose what a controller needs as properties over their parts, so DOF lists and link names cannot drift from the robot definitions:

from eden.managers.terms.actions.task_space_actions import DifferentialIKController

DifferentialIKController.configure(
    entity_name=droid.arm_name, ee_link_name=droid.ee_link, dofs_name=droid.arm_dofs,
)
# droid.grasp_links, droid.gripper_dofs, droid.gripper_open, droid.gripper_close,
# droid.tcp_offset, droid.stroke, droid.max_substep_dt
  • Arm rigs have arm_dofs, grasp_links (the links whose midpoint is the grasp point) and base_pos (places the arm base; None leaves arm.default_root_pos alone). ManipulatorOptions adds gripper_dofs, gripper_open / gripper_close, stroke, tcp_offset (the tool point in the ee_link frame, through the mount), max_substep_dt (the stricter of the two parts), hold_width(width) and preset_hold(width) (start the gripper closed on an object welded into it; refuses a width the gripper cannot close on). DexManipulatorOptions adds hand_dofs and fingertip_links; a dexterous hand has no open / close target.
  • Humanoid rigs have robot_dofs, left_hand_dofs / right_hand_dofs, left_hand_actuated_dofs / right_hand_actuated_dofs, left_hand_mimic_dofs / right_hand_mimic_dofs, left_grasp_links / right_grasp_links, base_pos (the pelvis) and feet_links (the humanoid's own feet unless the rig's feet_links_name overrides them; () declares no feet).

docs.title: Mount transforms
docs.text:
An arm rig welds the end-effector at its own default_root_pos / default_root_quat unless the rig sets attach_offset / attach_quat (position and wxyz orientation of the end-effector's base link in the ee_link frame). Setting only one component keeps the end-effector's own value for the other; a rig whose class defaults a component refuses a caller who sets only the other one, since the weld would mix two mounts. A humanoid rig uses mount_offset / mount_quat for both wrists, with per-side left_mount_* / right_mount_* overrides for wrist frames that are not mirror images.

Hands with rotated axes

Genesis applies a weld's quaternion before the child's up / front alignment, so a hand whose up / front rotate its asset (the Wuji hands are rotated 180°) would end up pointing back up the forearm. The rigs pass every mount quaternion through weld_quat(child, mount_quat), which cancels the alignment so the quaternion means the child's base-link orientation in the parent link frame. Use it when you write a weld for such a hand yourself; has_frame_alignment(child) tells you whether one is needed.

Every welded end-effector must have is_fixed_base=False (the rigs refuse one that is also pinned to the world), and the industrial-arm rigs gravity-compensate both parts, while the humanoid rigs do not (the arms must carry the payload).
