docs.title: Art: calligraphy and painting
docs.text:
Seven RL tasks in which a Panda copies a work on a sheet of paper: four of calligraphy, with a Chinese brush or a pointed pen, and three of acrylic painting, with a round brush and a palette. The tool models and the works are Eden's own; the copies are graded by the picture and hand rules that the RoboPaint benchmark publishes. Read this page to train or record the tasks, generate demonstrations, or understand the tool and paint models. The code is in eden/tasks/art/.

These two README clips show the tool and paint models on works that are not registered tasks.

docs.title: The tasks
docs.text:
Task (--task) Work Tool Strokes Episode Envs art_calligraphy_dai 大 (big), kaisho (楷書), 12 cm Chinese brush 3 60 s 256 art_calligraphy_san 山 (mountain), kaisho, 12 cm Chinese brush 3 60 s 256 art_calligraphy_ei 永 (eternity), kaisho, 12 cm Chinese brush 5 60 s 256 art_calligraphy_lettering_minimum minimum, round hand, 14 mm x-height pointed pen 9 120 s 256 art_painting_sunset a sea, a sky and a low sun (3 paints) paintbrush 7 90 s 64 art_painting_fuji_study a study of Hokusai's Fine Wind, Clear Morning (5 paints, two layers) paintbrush 116 800 s 64 art_painting_fuji Hokusai's Fine Wind, Clear Morning (10 paints, four layers) paintbrush 333 1200 s 64 
eden smoke --task art_calligraphy_ei
eden train --task art_calligraphy_dai
eden train --task art_painting_sunset
eden datagen --task art_painting_fuji_study --num_episodes 10 --num_envs 4 --output_dir data/demos

The art tasks run in 32-bit precision only

The tool models, the plans and the grading run in float32, and the published plans are pinned as planned in float32. The copy metric refuses eden.init(precision="64") when it is built; initialize Eden at the default precision="32" instead. Casting the samples down would not do: the plan guide and the scripted demonstrators read the float64 poses too.

docs.title: The workcell
docs.text:
Shared by both families (eden/tasks/art/workcell.py). The robot faces +x.

  • The desk and the sheet. A Panda stands on a desk 0.75 m high; the sheet lies on a felt pad in front of it, its centre 0.50 m out (workcell.SHEET_CENTER). The sheet frame is (u, v) from that centre: u to the robot's right, v up the page, away from the robot.
  • The tool is welded in the Franka Hand, its fingers closed on the handle, and held 35 mm from its back end so the back end clears the palm.
    • The brush: a Chinese writing brush, a 13.5 cm bamboo handle and ferrule and a 30 mm tuft 9 mm thick at the ferrule. It points straight down.
    • The pen: an 11.5 cm holder and a 22 mm nib. It leans 45 degrees along round hand's 55-degree slant, so the nib's slit runs along the downstrokes: they come out shaded and the upstrokes hairline.
    • The paintbrush: a round painting brush, a 15 cm handle and ferrule and a 15 mm tuft 8 mm thick, held so its tip is where the Chinese brush's is. It points straight down.
  • What marks does not collide. The hairs, the tuft and the nib are drawn but have no collision; what they mark is the tool model's, read from where the tip would be undeformed. The rest of each tool collides, so pressing deeper than the hairs are long drives the ferrule into the paper.

Why the tool is welded, not held by friction

The whiteboard tasks hold their marker by friction alone. Over a 30–60 s writing episode a friction grip creeps: a pen held that way turned 29 degrees about its axis and slid 5 mm out of the pinch in 50 s, and a pen's shading depends on how its nib is turned. The tool is welded to the arm's flange link, as the hand itself is. A DOF-less body welded one attachment further down, to the hand link, reads an all-zero pose after build and reset until the first physics step.

docs.title: Plans and works
docs.text: Every work is a plan of the tool's tip (eden/tasks/art/plans.py): stroke by stroke, key points (u, v, depth) joined by a centripetal Catmull-Rom spline, where depth is how far below the paper the tip goes (negative in the air). Every stroke starts and ends in the air, and between strokes the tip rises to 1 cm (plans.TRAVEL_HEIGHT). A work's target is what its own tool model lays along its plan, so a copy can match it, and a plan replayed through the robot shows the work can be made.

docs.title: Calligraphy
docs.text:
eden/tasks/art/calligraphy/. The success metric is CalligraphyWriting, keyed writing.

Each work's target (left) and the scripted writer's copy through the task's own IK action (right), run to the end of its plan (Genesis CPU, one env). These are the metric's ink grids.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Both tools are kinematic, as RoboPaint's are: what a tool lays down follows from where its tip is and its depth, not from a contact force. The tip is sampled after every 5 ms sim step (eden/tasks/art/calligraphy/tools.py).

  • The Chinese brush (DynamicBrush) is the dynamic virtual brush of Wang, Chen, Deng, Hutchinson and Dellaert, Robot Calligraphy using Pseudospectral Optimal Control in Conjunction with a Novel Dynamic Brush Model (IROS 2020), with that paper's fitted width, drag and offset as functions of depth z (in cm): Width(z) = 1.187 z - 0.03, Drag(z) = 1.075 z + 0.138 and Offset(z) = -0.967 z² + 2.11 z - 0.036. It deforms no further than 1.5 cm deep, and the width's and drag's inertia is 0.02 per sample.
    • The mark is a teardrop: its flat end w wide at the hairs' root, narrowing on a parabola over d.
    • The root stays where the hairs touched until the tip has moved Offset(z) from it, then is dragged after the tip, so the hairs trail the stroke and swing round its turns.
    • One deviation from a literal reading of the paper: the root's direction updates only once the tip is more than 0.1 mm (in the air) or 1 mm (on the paper) from it. A brush lowered onto the paper then starts with its hairs trailing the way it came in, at any speed.
  • The pointed pen (PointedPen) marks an ellipse at the tip: a 0.4 mm hairline along the slit, and across it 0.4 mm up to 1 mm deep, swelling linearly to 2 mm at 3.5 mm deep. A stroke pulled along the slit comes out shaded, one across it a hairline.

docs.title: The works
docs.text:
The three characters are kaisho (楷書, regular script) as Japanese schools teach it, 12 cm, in the standard Japanese stroke order and direction. Their shapes are those of Klee One (Fontworks, SIL Open Font License 1.1), a 教科書体 (textbook) kaisho:

  1. Key points are authored along each glyph's strokes with a brush's pressure: pressed in at the start (起筆), lighter through the stroke (送筆), then pressed to a stop (止め) or lifted into a sweep (払い).
  2. The points are then moved, at most 4.8 mm each, so the ink the brush model lays along them matches the glyph. The fitted plans' IoU with the glyphs is 0.90 (大), 0.86 (山) and 0.81 (永).

minimum, the copybooks' drill for the pointed pen's shaded downstrokes, is built from round hand's basic strokes (hairline entries, swelling shaded downstrokes, overturns and underturns), slanted 55 degrees.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
• Ink is a byte per cell on a grid over the whole sheet: 0.5 mm cells for the brush works, 0.2 mm for the pen. A cell is inked once a footprint covers its centre. Ink only exists on the sheet, and the brush never runs dry: RoboPaint counts dips, but nothing here makes a dip necessary.
  • The picture rules are RoboPaint's, judged at the placement shown (RoboPaint first registers a copy to its target within 5 mm; here the copy must be where the target is). Each work can set its own thresholds (its rule); the defaults (WritingRule in eden/tasks/art/calligraphy/grading.py) are:
    • the IoU of the ink with the target (≥ 0.8);
    • the boundary F-measure, matching outlines within 1 mm (≥ 0.75), read in a crop round the target;
    • each stroke's share of the target covered (≥ 80 %);
    • stray ink farther than 1 mm from the target, as a share of the target's area (≤ 4 %).
  • The hand rules are counted as the tool moves (eden.tasks.art.terms.CopyMetric):
    • Strokes: no more than the work has. A stroke is a touch-down after the tool was lifted at least 1 mm clear of the paper or off the sheet; a tip grazing on and off within that is still the same stroke.
    • Path: the tip's path on the paper within 2.5 times the plan's.
    • Mark width: the mean width of the mark along that path at least a third of the plan's.
  • The grade is the IoU while every rule passes, and is held just under the IoU threshold otherwise, so the written termination (OnMetricSuccess) means all rules are met.

Lettering's IoU threshold is 0.7, not RoboPaint's 0.85

RoboPaint sets its own thresholds for pen lettering: IoU 0.85 and boundary F 0.8 (stricter than the defaults above), stroke coverage 0.75 (looser). A pen's hairline is two 0.2 mm cells wide, so a copy that wanders 0.1 mm either side of it inks half as much again. The scripted writer's copies, faithful by eye and on every other rule, score 0.80 at its 1.5 cm/s and 0.77 at 2 cm/s. The minimum work's rule (works.LETTERING_RULE) keeps RoboPaint's boundary F (0.8) and stroke coverage (0.75) with an IoU of 0.7.

docs.title: The policy's view
docs.text:
• Actions. One term, arm: differential IK at the tool's undeformed tip, 20 Hz, up to 1 cm and 0.05 rad a step.
  • Observations (identical policy and critic groups, no noise): the arm's joint positions and velocities, the tip's (u, v, depth) and the tool's axis in the sheet frame (TipPose), the tool's last mark (for the brush, where its bent hairs lie: ToolMark), the next plan points with depth, each flagged where a new stroke starts (NextPlanPoints), the strokes left, the grade (CopyGrade) and the last action.
  • Rewards. inked (the target first inked, 100 for all of it), progress (the plan's points the touching tip first reaches, 20 for all of them), stray (ink off the target, -50 per target area), reach / reach_fine (the tip toward the next plan point at its depth), success (a bonus of 50), and small action-rate and joint-speed penalties.
  • Terminations. timeout and written.

docs.title: Painting
docs.text:
eden/tasks/art/painting/. The success metric is PaintingCopy, keyed painting.

The three works' targets: what the paint model lays along each plan. For the Hokusai works, the woodblock print they were planned from, cropped to the sheet (left).

fuji's target (left) and the scripted painter's copy through the task's own IK action, dipping as the plan does, run to the end of its plan (Genesis GPU, one env). These are the metric's canvases.

docs.title: The palette
docs.text: A tray on the desk to the robot's left of the sheet, its face level with the paper's, with a 22 mm well of each of the work's paints in columns of five, 3 cm apart (eden/tasks/art/painting/palette.py). It is the work's own (PaletteOptions(work=...)): the metric reads a dip off the work's wells, and refuses a scene whose palette is another work's. The paint in the wells is drawn and does not collide.

docs.title: The brush and the paint
docs.text:
The brush is kinematic: what it lays follows from its tip and depth, sampled after every 5 ms sim step (eden/tasks/art/painting/paint.py).

  • The mark is a disc at the tip, 1 mm across at a touch and growing linearly to 18 mm at 15 mm deep (fully pressed), with a 0.5 mm soft edge (RoundBrush). RoboPaint's four acrylic brush sizes, 16, 9.4, 5.2 and 3 mm, are presses of this one brush.
  • The paint is wet acrylic (Acrylic), and the brush and the sheet exchange it as the brush moves. Each rate is per brush diameter travelled on the paper, not per second or per sample, so what is laid does not depend on the brush's speed or the sampling rate.
    • Paints mix as pigments do. A paint is a Kubelka-Munk pigment (an absorption per colour channel and a scattering). Pigments mix in proportion to the amount of each, and the colour shown is the mix's reflectance, so blue and yellow make green, not grey.
    • The brush lays its paint over paper or dry paint, covering all but exp(-20) of a cell it passes over the middle of (deposit_rate). Laid into wet paint it covers far less (wet_resistance, 0.85): it mixes in.
    • The brush picks up the wet paint it drags through (pickup_rate, 0.25 per diameter), so its colour drifts toward it until the next dip.
    • The bristles streak what is laid into wet paint, or from a brush running dry (streaks). A full brush on paper or dry paint covers evenly.
    • Wet paint blends across a stroke's sides. Within 2.5 mm of either side (blend_width) the paint is smoothed with the paint beside it (blend_rate, 3 per diameter), as freely as both are wet. So a stroke laid beside wet paint meets it in a gradient, and keeps a sharp edge against bare paper and dried paint.
    • The paint dries. Its wetness falls by e every two minutes of the episode (open_time, 120 s).
  • The brush carries a load and holds one paint at a time (PaintLoad). A dip, the tip pressed more than 1 mm into a well, fills it with that well's paint at the end of the control step the dip began in (the brush is taken as clean: there is no rinse). A full load covers 3000 mm², a 25 cm stroke 12 mm wide. The paint stays opaque while the load is above a fifth, then fades to nothing: a stroke with too little paint is a dry brush.
  • Paint only exists on the sheet. A brush pressed past the sheet's edge paints the part of its mark on the paper.

fuji's target in paint that dries at once (each stroke flat and opaque over the last) and in wet acrylic: where a stroke meets one still wet the two blend, its bristles streak it, and the brush carries the colour it picked up into the strokes after.

Stripes 10 mm wide laid 9 mm apart, each a fresh dip, without and with the blending across the sides: laid while the last is wet, neighbours meet in a gradient; laid once it has dried, each keeps its edge.

docs.title: The works
docs.text:
• sunset is authored: three 16 mm sweeps of sky, three of sea, and a short sweep of sun on the horizon.

  • The Hokusai works are planned (eden/tasks/art/painting/planner.py) from the Metropolitan Museum of Art's scan of the woodblock print (accession JP2960, which the Met titles South Wind, Clear Sky; released as CC0), cropped to a square round the mountain. The planner paints first the ground in broad strokes, then the forms, then the details:

    1. The palette is k-means in CIELAB over the picture.
    2. Each layer has a brush size. Where the canvas so far is further than the layer's ΔE threshold from the picture blurred to that size, each paint's region is swept with horizontal strokes, each at most as long as a load lasts above its reserve. The ground layer goes on lightest paint first and later layers darkest first, so light details (clouds, snow) go on top.

    fuji has four layers (16, 9.4, 5.2 and 3 mm brushes), fuji_study the first two.

Every stroke is a sweep: it comes down before its start, runs level at the depth that makes its brush size, and lifts off past its end. A target is painted at the scripted painter's pace, so its paint dries between strokes as a copy's does at that pace; a copy painted faster blends more, one painted slower less.

Planned works are fetched, planned once and pinned

A Hokusai work is a PlannedPainting recipe in eden/tasks/art/painting/works.py. Its picture is in the Kashu7100/eden_art dataset at a pinned revision (PICTURES_REVISION). The plan is made on the CPU the first time a task needs it (some 10–20 s; one process plans and any other waits for it) and kept under ~/.cache/eden/art/plans/ (under $XDG_CACHE_HOME when it is set), in a file named for the recipe, the picture and the plan's digest. A kept plan is found without fetching the picture, so an offline run needs only that cache directory.

Each recipe pins plan_sha256, the digest of its plan as published. A change to the planner or the paint model does not re-plan a kept work; re-pinning the digest does. A plan made on another machine is checked against the digest and, if it differs, used with a warning, since its target and stroke count are not the published task's. tests/tasks/art/painting/test_works.py re-plans the works from scratch and checks the digests (marked slow).

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
The canvas is per env, over the whole sheet, in 0.5 mm cells, each with its dry paint's colour and the wet paint over it. It is float32 whatever Eden's precision.

  • The picture rules are RoboPaint's acrylic ones, judged at the placement shown (eden/tasks/art/painting/grading.py). The copy and the target are blurred by a 1 mm Gaussian, then:

    • the CIELAB colour difference per cell (ΔE*ab, CIE 1976): mean ≤ 2 and 90th percentile ≤ 6;
    • the SSIM of the lightness L*: ≥ 0.92;
    • the correlation of the lightness gradients' magnitudes (Sobel), the edges: ≥ 0.8;
    • the IoU of the cells painted at all with those the target paints: ≥ 0.95.

    The colour, the SSIM and the edges are read in a crop round the target's paint, the coverage over the whole sheet: RoboPaint's paintings cover their canvas, and a small work's bare paper would otherwise dilute every measure. - The hand rules are counted as the brush moves: - Strokes: at most 1.3 times the plan's. A dip is not a stroke, but going to the palette lifts the brush off the sheet. - Path: the tip's path on the paper within 3 times the plan's. - Scribbles: a stroke at least 1 cm long whose path is over 2.5 times the distance from its start to its end (a zigzag, a loop, a there-and-back) is a scribble; scribbles may take at most a tenth of the path. - The grade is the lightness SSIM while every rule passes, and is held just under the SSIM threshold otherwise, so the painted termination (OnMetricSuccess) means all rules are met. - sunset's mean ΔE is 1, not 2. It is a small work on a bare sheet: its sun is a small part of the crop, and a copy would meet a mean ΔE of 2 as soon as the brush touched down for the sun.

Envs per GPU

Each env carries a full-sheet canvas of dry and wet paint, so the painting tasks default to 64 envs (the calligraphy tasks to 256). Raise --num_envs only as far as your GPU memory allows.

docs.title: The policy's view
docs.text:
• Actions. One term, arm: differential IK at the brush's undeformed tip, 20 Hz, up to 1 cm and 0.05 rad a step.
  • Observations (identical policy and critic groups, no noise): the arm's joints, the tip's pose (TipPose), the paint on the brush, its load and colour (BrushPaint), the paint the plan's next point needs, its well's offset from the tip and whether the brush holds another paint (NextPaint), the next plan points, the strokes left, the grade (CopyGrade: a reset env's is its bare sheet's, not 0) and the last action.
  • Rewards. error_drop (the copy's mean ΔE brought toward the target, 100 for all of the bare sheet's error), progress (the plan's points the touching tip first reaches with their paint on the brush, at full opacity, 20 for all of them; a point passed with a dry brush or another paint stays unreached), reach / reach_fine, success (a bonus of 50), and small action-rate and joint-speed penalties.
  • Terminations. timeout and painted.

docs.title: Recording the marks
docs.text:
The ink and the paint live in the metric, not in the scene, so a plain camera shows a blank sheet. eden inference --rec records each task's recording_camera(), which carries a PlanePaintOverlay painting the metric's marks where the camera sees the sheet, shaded as the renderer shaded the sheet (so the tool's shadow falls across them) and hidden by the tool and the hand in front of them. The calligraphy camera looks down from above the robot's right side; the painting camera from high over the arm, so the painting reads upright. The training configs declare no camera, so training builds none.

To show the marks in another camera, give its CameraOptions the same overlay. Ink takes a colour; paint is drawn in its own colours, so the painting overlay takes none:

from eden.entities.camera_overlays import PlanePaintOverlay
from eden.options.camera import CameraOptions
from eden.tasks.art.calligraphy.grading import INK_COLOR

ink_camera = CameraOptions(cam_pos=..., cam_lookat=..., overlays=[PlanePaintOverlay.configure(metric_name="writing", color=INK_COLOR)])
paint_camera = CameraOptions(cam_pos=..., cam_lookat=..., overlays=[PlanePaintOverlay.configure(metric_name="painting")])

docs.title: Scripted demonstrators
docs.text:
Each task has a privileged demonstrator registered under its name (ScriptedWriter in eden/tasks/art/calligraphy/scripted_demos.py, ScriptedPainter in eden/tasks/art/painting/scripted_demos.py), which is also the proof that each work can be made. Both follow the work's tip path through the task's own action with the suite's TipFollower (eden/tasks/art/scripted.py): each step commands a gain times the offset from the tip to the path, and the path's clock waits while the tip trails it. They read the tip and the plan and never touch the tool or the marks.

eden datagen --task art_calligraphy_ei --num_episodes 100 --num_envs 16 --output_dir data/demos
  • They have no randomness and make no deliberate mistakes, so --seed changes nothing and --p_mistake must be 0.
  • The writer draws at 2 cm/s with the brush and 1.5 cm/s with the pen (each tool's ToolSpec.draw_speed); the painter paints and dips at 3 cm/s. The painter dips where the plan dips: before the first stroke, before a change of paint, and before a stroke that would leave the brush under its reserve.
  • An episode ends when the task does, on success, which can come before the last stroke is finished.
  • tests/tasks/art/calligraphy/test_scripted_demos.py pins all four calligraphy works and tests/tasks/art/painting/test_scripted_demos.py pins sunset (marked slow).

See Scripted demonstrations.

docs.title: Not ported
docs.text:
• RoboPaint's brush engine. Its acrylic brush is libmypaint's; this paint model is Eden's own, so RoboPaint's thresholds hold for it as rules, not as calibrated equivalents.
  • RoboPaint's exemplars, plans and targets. Its calligraphy rubbings and copybook pages and its reference painter's runs are not released; the works here are Eden's.
  • Registration. RoboPaint aligns a copy to its target within 5 mm before scoring it.
  • Dipping for ink and rinsing. The calligraphy brush never runs dry; a paint dip replaces the paint on the brush however dirty it was, and the wells stay clean.

docs.title: LIBERO
docs.text: Eden runs the 130 tasks of the LIBERO benchmark through one registered task, libero, which builds any catalog task from its upstream BDDL file. Read this page to evaluate a policy on LIBERO in Eden, including a generalist policy served by a remote server. The code is in eden/tasks/libero/.

docs.title: What is ported
docs.text:
• The catalog. All five suites, by their upstream names: libero_spatial, libero_object, libero_goal and libero_10 (10 tasks each) and libero_90 (90 tasks), plus the derived libero_100 (libero_90 followed by libero_10). The 10-task suites also carry LIBERO's official continual-learning task orders.
  • The tasks. Each task's scene, fixtures, movable objects, language instruction and goal come from its BDDL file, which is fetched on first use from the Kashu7100/eden_libero dataset along with the objects.
  • The robot and controller. LIBERO's mounted Panda (eden.options.robots.libero.LiberoPanda), driven by an OperationalSpaceController in robosuite's OSC_POSE convention (0.05 m and 0.5 rad per unit action) and a stateful LiberoPandaGripperController (+1 closes, -1 opens, 0 holds).
  • The goal check. LiberoGoalMetric evaluates the task's BDDL goal predicates (On, In, Open, ...) with the upstream semantics.
  • The protocol. 20 Hz control (a 2 ms step, decimation=25), five zero-action settling steps (LIBERO_RESET_WARMUP_STEPS) and then 600 policy actions (LIBERO_POLICY_HORIZON_STEPS). The episode ends on goal success or after those 605 steps.

The task defines no rewards: it is an evaluation task, not an RL training task.

docs.title: Fixed-state bundles
docs.text:
LIBERO evaluates every task from a fixed set of initial states. Eden resets from a fixed-state bundle per task, which holds the exact poses, joint positions and velocities of each init ID. Eden does not ship, generate or download these bundles: you provide them.

The layout is:

<bundle_root>/<suite>/<task>/state-bundle/task.json
<bundle_root>/<suite>/<task>/state-bundle/states.npz

task.json names the task, its init IDs and its entities; states.npz stores the arrays under semantic keys such as entity/robot/root_pos_world and entity/robot/joint/joint1/qpos, so each array is bound to the entity or joint it restores rather than to a position in a list. Both are validated when the env builds (eden.tasks.libero.state_bundle.load_state_bundle).

If you omit bundle_root, the task looks under libero/fixed_states in the asset directory. Nothing populates that path for you, so in practice you pass bundle_root.

BDDL :init is not the reset state

The BDDL :init predicates are kept as symbolic catalog facts (LiberoTaskSpec.initial_state) for inspection and tooling. They are not used to reconstruct simulator state; the bundle is the only reset source.

docs.title: Selecting a task and its init states
docs.text:
libero takes three TaskMod flags (LiberoTaskMod):

Flag Meaning Default --task_name A catalog task name pick_up_the_alphabet_soup_and_place_it_in_the_basket (the first libero_object task) --bundle_root Root of the <suite>/<task>/state-bundle directories libero/fixed_states in the asset directory --init_ids Comma-separated init IDs, one per env empty: the first num_envs states of the bundle 
eden smoke --task libero \
    --task_name pick_up_the_alphabet_soup_and_place_it_in_the_basket \
    --bundle_root /path/to/libero-fixed-states

--init_ids may name any nonempty subset of the bundle's init IDs. Because it assigns one state per env, it sets num_envs.

--init_ids and --num_envs must agree

Every num_envs override is applied after the task's modifiers run, so a later override can contradict the count --init_ids set. eden smoke --num_envs defaults to 2 and always applies, so a single-state smoke run needs both flags. A mismatch is rejected when the env builds, naming both values.

eden smoke --task libero --init_ids 7 --num_envs 1   # one env, fixed state 7
eden smoke --task libero                              # num_envs envs, the first num_envs states

To list tasks, use the catalog functions:

from eden.tasks.libero import get_suite_names, get_suite_task_names, get_task_spec

get_suite_names()                       # ('libero_spatial', ..., 'libero_90', 'libero_100')
get_suite_task_names("libero_goal")     # in task order 0; pass task_order_index= for another
spec = get_task_spec("turn_on_the_stove")
spec.language_instruction, spec.goal_state

docs.title: Running an episode in Python
docs.text:
import torch

import eden
from eden.envs.base import RLEnvBase
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY
from eden.tasks.libero import LIBERO_RESET_WARMUP_STEPS

eden.init()
config = TASK_REGISTRY.build(
    "libero",
    task_name="pick_up_the_alphabet_soup_and_place_it_in_the_basket",
    bundle_root="/path/to/libero-fixed-states",
    init_ids="7",
)
env = RLEnvBase.from_config(config)
env.build()
observations, _ = env.reset()

# The benchmark protocol: five exact zero-action settling steps before the 600 policy actions.
zero_action = {
    "osc_pose": torch.zeros((env.num_envs, 6), device=env.device),
    "gripper": torch.zeros((env.num_envs, 1), device=env.device),
}
for _ in range(LIBERO_RESET_WARMUP_STEPS):
    observations, _, _, _, _ = env.step(zero_action)

The policy observation group is not concatenated. It holds agentview_rgb and eye_in_hand_rgb (128 × 128 by default), arm_joint_pos and gripper_joint_pos. The language instruction is config.language_instructions[0].

docs.title: Evaluating a generalist policy
docs.text:
Two remote-policy clients ship a LIBERO setup that matches the upstream evaluation client end to end:

Client policy_setup Upstream client it matches PiPolicy (eden.extensions.policies.pi.policy) libero OpenPI examples/libero/main.py Gr00tPolicy (eden.extensions.policies.gr00t.policy) libero_sim Isaac-GR00T's LIBERO eval

Both drive the task's own osc_pose and gripper terms, mirror the images left-right as LIBERO's training images are, and step at 20 Hz. The clients need the policy-client extra (pip install 'eden-world[policy-client]', or uv sync --inexact --extra policy-client in a checkout).

Render at 256 × 256 for these checkpoints

The stock task renders 128 × 128, but OpenPI's and GR00T's LIBERO checkpoints were trained on 256 × 256 renders, and both clients refuse a camera at another resolution rather than upsample. Set both cameras before building:

config.cameras_options.agentview.cam_resolution = (256, 256)
config.cameras_options.eye_in_hand.cam_resolution = (256, 256)

Do not resize the frames in the client instead: an upsampled render is off the training distribution.

A minimal OpenPI loop:

import torch

import eden
from eden.envs.base import RLEnvBase
from eden.extensions.policies.pi.policy import PiPolicy
from eden.options.managers.observations import ObservationManagerOptions
from eden.tasks import TASK_REGISTRY
from eden.tasks.libero import LIBERO_RESET_WARMUP_STEPS

eden.init()
config = TASK_REGISTRY.build("libero", task_name="turn_on_the_stove", bundle_root="/path/to/libero-fixed-states")
config.env_options.num_envs = 1
config.cameras_options.agentview.cam_resolution = (256, 256)
config.cameras_options.eye_in_hand.cam_resolution = (256, 256)
config.observation_options = ObservationManagerOptions(**PiPolicy.observation_options(policy_setup="libero"))
env = RLEnvBase.from_config(config, eval_mode=True)
env.build()

policy = PiPolicy(env, PiPolicy.configure(host="localhost", port=8000, policy_setup="libero"))  # your server
policy.set_task(config.language_instructions[0])

observations, _ = env.reset()
policy.reset_server()
zero = {"osc_pose": torch.zeros((1, 6), device=env.device), "gripper": torch.zeros((1, 1), device=env.device)}
for _ in range(LIBERO_RESET_WARMUP_STEPS):
    observations, *_ = env.step(zero)
for _ in range(600):
    observations, _, terminated, _, _ = env.step(policy.step(observations))
    if terminated.any():
        break

PiPolicy's default port is 8000. See Remote policies for the client architecture, the gripper conventions and the construction checks that refuse a mis-wired env.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
The 130 benchmark tasks use one of five reusable LIBERO scene presets, chosen from the BDDL problem name (tabletop, floor, kitchen tabletop, living-room tabletop and study tabletop); a sixth, the coffee table, covers additional tasks. The presets are in eden.options.scenes.libero (see Scenes and terrains). A preset holds only the workspace and the robot; the task layer adds the declared fixtures and objects, the cameras, the reset term and the goal metric. Constructing a preset on its own does not give a runnable LIBERO task: use TASK_REGISTRY.build("libero", ...).

Build task-specific LIBERO scenes from BDDL metadata.

Build a family preset with the fixtures and movable objects declared by BDDL.

Source code in eden/tasks/libero/scenes.py 
def make_libero_scene_options(
    task_spec: LiberoTaskSpec,
    **extra_entities: BaseEntityOptions | CompositeEntityOptions,
) -> SceneOptions:
    """Build a family preset with the fixtures and movable objects declared by BDDL."""
    family_spec = _get_libero_family_spec(task_spec.problem_name)
    objects: dict[str, BaseEntityOptions] = {}
    staging_origin = (2.5, -0.8, 1.25)
    staging_step = 0.24
    staging_columns = 6
    staging_index = 0
    for entity_name, category_name in task_spec.entity_categories.items():
        if entity_name == family_spec.workspace_entity_name:
            continue
        entity_options = LIBERO_OBJECT_REGISTRY.get(category_name)(
            default_root_pos=(
                staging_origin[0] + (staging_index % staging_columns) * staging_step,
                staging_origin[1] + (staging_index // staging_columns) * staging_step,
                staging_origin[2],
            ),
            batch_fixed_verts=entity_name in task_spec.fixture_names,
        )
        if entity_name in task_spec.fixture_names and not entity_options.is_fixed_base:
            raise ValueError(f"LIBERO fixture {entity_name!r} ({category_name!r}) must use a fixed-base registry entry")
        objects[entity_name] = entity_options
        staging_index += 1
    return family_spec.scene_factory(**objects, **extra_entities)

def __init__(self, **data):

    # __pydantic_extra__ (no-op for extra="forbid" classes, which use

    data.update(option_metadata(self))

def apply(self, config: LiberoConfig) -> LiberoConfig:
    raw_init_ids = self.init_ids.strip()
    try:
        init_ids = tuple(int(value.strip()) for value in raw_init_ids.split(",")) if raw_init_ids else None
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise ValueError("init_ids must be a comma-separated list of integers") from exc

    task_spec = get_task_spec(self.task_name)
    if init_ids is not None:
        # An explicit selection is one state per env, so it *defines* num_envs rather than
        # being checked against it. Every CLI num_envs override lands after the mods run, so a
        # caller that passes both must keep them consistent; LiberoFixedStateReset.build()
        # raises and names both knobs when they disagree.
        config.env_options.num_envs = len(init_ids)
    indicators = {
        f"{entity_name}_burner_indicator": CylinderOptions(
            radius=0.0625,
            height=0.001,
            default_root_pos=(0.0, 0.0, LiberoStoveBurnerVisualization.hidden_z_offset),
            fixed=True,
            batch_fixed_verts=True,
            collision=False,
            surface=EmissionSurfaceOptions(color=(0.9, 0.05, 0.05, 1.0)),
        )
        for entity_name, category_name in task_spec.entity_categories.items()
        if category_name == LiberoFlatStove.category_name
    }
    config.scene_options = make_libero_scene_options(task_spec, **indicators)
    family_spec = _get_libero_family_spec(task_spec.problem_name)
    lights = [
        {
            "type": "point",
            "pos": (1.0, 1.0, 4.0),
            "color": (0.8, 0.8, 0.8),
            "intensity": 1.0,
        },
        {
            "type": "point",
            "pos": (-3.0, -3.0, 4.0),
            "color": (0.8, 0.8, 0.8),
            "intensity": 1.0,
        },
    ]
    if family_spec.has_directional_light:
        lights.insert(
            0,
            {
                "type": "directional",
                "dir": (0.0, 0.0, -1.0),
                "color": (0.8, 0.8, 0.8),
                "intensity": 1.0,
            },
        )
    camera_to_world = trans_quat_to_T(
        np.asarray(family_spec.agentview_pos_w),
        np.asarray(family_spec.agentview_quat_w),
    )
    image_resolution = (128, 128)
    config.cameras_options = CamerasOptions(
        agentview=CameraOptions(
            cam_extrinsic=np.linalg.inv(camera_to_world),
            cam_resolution=image_resolution,
            cam_fov=45.0,
            sensor_options=RasterizerCameraOptions(lights=lights),
        ),
        eye_in_hand=CameraOptions(
            cam_resolution=image_resolution,
            cam_fov=75.0,
            attach_entity_name=LIBERO_ROBOT_ENTITY_NAME,
            attach_link_name=LiberoPanda.ee_links_name[0],
            attach_offset=(0.05, 0.0, 0.0),
            attach_quat=(0.0, 0.7071067811865475, 0.7071067811865475, 0.0),
            sensor_options=RasterizerCameraOptions(),
        ),
    )
    bundle_root = self.bundle_root or get_assets_dir(LiberoObjectOptions.assets_subdir, "fixed_states")
    bundle_path = Path(bundle_root).expanduser() / task_spec.suite_name / task_spec.name / "state-bundle"
    event_terms = {
        "libero_fixed_state": LiberoFixedStateReset.configure(
            task_name=task_spec.name,
            bundle_path=str(bundle_path),
            init_ids=[] if init_ids is None else list(init_ids),
        ),
    }
    policy_dt = config.env_options.sim_dt * config.env_options.decimation
    for entity_name, category_name in task_spec.entity_categories.items():
        if category_name != LiberoFlatStove.category_name:
            continue
        indicator_name = f"{entity_name}_burner_indicator"
        event_terms[f"{indicator_name}_reset"] = LiberoStoveBurnerVisualization.configure(
            stove_entity_name=entity_name,
            indicator_entity_name=indicator_name,
        )
        event_terms[f"{indicator_name}_interval"] = LiberoStoveBurnerVisualization.configure(
            mode="interval",
            interval_range_s=(policy_dt, policy_dt),
            stove_entity_name=entity_name,
            indicator_entity_name=indicator_name,
        )
    config.event_options = EventManagerOptions(**event_terms)
    config.metric_options = MetricManagerOptions(goal=LiberoGoalMetric.configure(task_name=task_spec.name))
    config.language_instructions = [task_spec.language_instruction]
    return config

def get_suite_task_names(suite_name: str, task_order_index: int = 0) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    if suite_name == "libero_100":
        return get_suite_task_names("libero_90", task_order_index=0) + get_suite_task_names(
            "libero_10",
            task_order_index=task_order_index,
        )
    try:
        task_names = _TASKS_BY_SUITE[suite_name]
    except KeyError as exc:
        raise KeyError(f"Unknown LIBERO suite: {suite_name!r}") from exc
    if suite_name == "libero_90":
        if task_order_index != 0:
            raise IndexError("libero_90 supports only task_order_index=0")
        return task_names
    if not 0 <= task_order_index < len(_TASK_ORDERS):
        raise IndexError(
            f"task_order_index={task_order_index} out of range [0, {len(_TASK_ORDERS)}) for suite {suite_name!r}"
        )
    order = _TASK_ORDERS[task_order_index]
    return tuple(task_names[index] for index in order)

@functools.cache
def get_task_spec(task_name: str) -> LiberoTaskSpec:
    """Resolve, parse, and memoize one task without loading unrelated BDDL files."""
    suite_name = next((name for name, task_names in _TASKS_BY_SUITE.items() if task_name in task_names), None)
    if suite_name is None:
        raise KeyError(f"Unknown LIBERO task: {task_name!r}")

docs.title: Locomotion Tasks
docs.text:
Eden's locomotion tasks train legged robots to walk, recover, balance and ride. This page gives, for each task, the robot, what the policy learns, its variant flags, what it needs installed, and the commands to train and replay it. The commands shared by every task (eden smoke, --resume, eden export) are on the task index.

Task Robot Flags Default num_envs velocity_tracking_flat Unitree G1 29-DOF or LimX Oli --robot, --obs_preset 4096 velocity_tracking_terrain Unitree G1 29-DOF or LimX Oli --robot, --obs_preset 4096 extreme_parkour_teacher Unitree Go2 — 4096 extreme_parkour_student Unitree Go2 — 192 mujoco_playground_getup Unitree Go1 — 4096 mujoco_playground_handstand Unitree Go1 — 4096 homie Unitree G1 29-DOF — 4096 husky Unitree G1, 23-DOF skater model — 4096 move_forward Unitree Go2 or Go1 --robot, --controller, --runner 4096

num_envs is per GPU rank. Override it with --num_envs N.

docs.title: Velocity tracking
docs.text:
A bipedal humanoid follows a random planar velocity command (forward, lateral, yaw rate) while staying upright and moving smoothly. velocity_tracking_flat runs on a ground plane; velocity_tracking_terrain runs on a procedurally generated grid of stairs, inverted stairs, slopes, random bumps and waves, and adds a 17 × 11 height scan to both observation groups and an out-of-terrain-bounds termination. Both share one config base, eden/tasks/velocity_tracking/base_config.py.

eden train --task velocity_tracking_flat                          # Unitree G1 29-DOF
eden train --task velocity_tracking_terrain --robot oli           # LimX Oli 31-DOF
eden train --task velocity_tracking_flat --obs_preset privileged  # the policy also reads base_lin_vel
eden inference --task velocity_tracking_flat \
    --checkpoint logs/velocity_tracking_flat/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --rec
Flag Choices (default first) Effect --robot g1, oli Which humanoid. The mod binds the robot's joints, action scale, torso and feet links, and prefixes the experiment name (g1_velocity_tracking_flat). --obs_preset proprioceptive, privileged proprioceptive: sensor-only policy input, 5 frames of history. privileged: the policy also reads the simulator's base_lin_vel, single frame, unscaled joint velocities.

The command range widens over training (VelocityCommandCurriculum): forward speed starts at ±1 m/s and reaches −2 to 3 m/s. Training uses rsl_rl PPO, 30 000 iterations at 50 Hz control.

privileged needs a velocity estimator on the robot

A humanoid has no sensor for base linear velocity. A policy trained with --obs_preset privileged must run with eden deploy --estimate_lin_vel (a contact-aided Kalman filter) on hardware. The default proprioceptive policy needs no estimator. See Deployment.

To drive a trained policy with the keyboard in the viewer, use the example script:

uv run python examples/projects/locomotion/velocity_tracking/main.py play --model <path/to/model_<iter>.pt>

The reasons behind the robot binding, the observation split, the posture tolerances and the smoothness penalties are on Velocity tracking: design notes.

docs.title: Extreme Parkour
docs.text:
A port of Extreme Parkour with Legged Robots (Cheng et al. 2023) on the Unitree Go2, in two phases.

  • extreme_parkour_teacher — the Go2 follows waypoint goals across a grid of parkour courses (gaps, hurdles, flat lanes, steps, stepping stones), with a walked-distance terrain-level curriculum. The policy reads one 753-wide policy group: proprioception, terrain scan dots, privileged state and a 10-frame history. It trains with the RMA stack in eden.learning.wrappers.rsl_rl.rma (scan, privileged and history encoders, a base-velocity estimator, periodic DAgger updates of the history encoder, a left-right mirror loss). The config selects that stack itself; stock PPO with a plain MLP does not learn this task.
  • extreme_parkour_student — the same environment plus a forward depth camera (106 × 60, mounted on the base link and pitched 20° down), a one-control-step action delay and camera-mount pitch randomization. The policy is distilled from a teacher checkpoint (DAgger), so --checkpoint names the teacher.
eden train --task extreme_parkour_teacher --logger wandb
eden train --task extreme_parkour_student \
    --checkpoint logs/extreme_parkour_teacher/<run>/model_<iter>.pt
eden inference --task extreme_parkour_student \
    --checkpoint logs/extreme_parkour_student/<run>/model_<iter>.pt

Both tasks take one flag:

Flag Choices (default first) Effect --terrain_sampler level, uniform, sgs Which terrain cell each episode starts on. level: the walked-distance curriculum moves the env up or down a difficulty row and keeps its course column. uniform: every cell of the grid, uniformly. sgs: Success Guided Sampling over every cell, graded by all_goals_reached (see Curricula).

All three modes log Commands/parkour_command/terrain_level (the row each finished episode ran on) and Metrics/parkour_goal_progress, whose all-goals episodes make up Metrics/Success; compare the modes on those. The feet_edge penalty applies only above its min_terrain_level, and uniform and sgs place envs on those rows from the first episode, so the reward differs between the modes as well as the sampling.

The student renders depth with the gs-madrona batch renderer, which is not an Eden extra: install gs-madrona (Linux x86-64 only) before training it. The teacher needs nothing beyond the core install.

examples/projects/locomotion/extreme_parkour/ has a viewer playback script and a full description of the observation slot table and the network architecture.

docs.title: MuJoCo Playground: getup and handstand
docs.text:
Two Go1 tasks reimplemented from MuJoCo Playground's locomotion/go1 (no MuJoCo involved):

  • mujoco_playground_getup — fall recovery. At reset the Go1 is dropped from 0.5 m with a random orientation and random joint angles (with probability 0.6; otherwise it starts standing), and it must stand up and hold its default pose at a torso height of 0.275 m. 42-wide observation; the action is 12 joint-position targets offset from the default pose.
  • mujoco_playground_handstand — the body's x-axis points down, the torso is held at 0.55 m, and the rear feet are penalized for touching the floor. 45-wide observation; the action is a joint-position delta accumulated onto the previous target (ReferenceSource.ACCUMULATE, scale 0.3, clamped to the soft joint limits).

Both run at 50 Hz control (sim_dt 0.004, decimation 5) and train with rsl_rl PPO for 3000 iterations.

eden train --task mujoco_playground_getup
eden inference --task mujoco_playground_getup \
    --checkpoint logs/mujoco_playground_getup/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --rec

The handstand config also declares the upstream action-rate, torque, joint-acceleration, stay-still, energy and termination rewards at weight 0, for fine-tuning. examples/projects/locomotion/mujoco_playground/ has train-then-play scripts for both tasks.

docs.title: HOMIE
docs.text:
A port of OpenHomie's G1 lower-body controller. The policy tracks a 4-D command [lin_vel_x, lin_vel_y, ang_vel_z, base_height] with the 12 leg joints, while the 3 waist and 14 arm joints are driven to random poses by an upper-body pose curriculum, so the legs stay robust to whatever the upper body does. It trains with OpenHomie's HIMLoco learner (eden.learning.wrappers.rsl_rl.him), which the config selects.

eden train --task homie
eden inference --task homie --checkpoint logs/homie/<run>/model_<iter>.pt

The differences from OpenHomie are listed in the module docstring of eden/tasks/homie/config.py. The main ones: the full 29-DOF G1 (OpenHomie welds the waist to one DOF), actions delayed by less than one control step, an upper-body curriculum on a fixed step schedule, and friction ranges remapped because Genesis combines contact friction as max. The frozen OpenHomie release checkpoints are a separate, inference-only port: eden inference --policy homie (see the policy zoo).

Licence

OpenHomie is released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial), and this task inherits that licence.

docs.title: HUSKY skateboarding
docs.text:
A training port of HUSKY (humanoid skateboarding). A G1 rides a free-floating skateboard whose trucks steer when the deck tilts. A 6 s phase clock cycles push (the left leg strokes the ground), transition, steer (both feet on the deck) and transition; the command is [board speed, relative heading]. The robot is HuskyG1, the 23-DOF skater model (wrists welded) used by the frozen HUSKY policy.

The config trains PPO with an adversarial motion prior (RslRlAmpPpoAlgorithmOptions) over retargeted human pushing clips, which is the full HUSKY recipe. The clips are an asset file fetched on first use.

eden train --task husky --logger wandb
eden inference --task husky --checkpoint logs/husky/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --rec

To train the same MDP without the style reward, replace runner_options.algorithm with a plain RslRlPpoAlgorithmOptions(...) (setting class_name alone is not enough). The SkatePushFlag observation warns at the start of such a run, because the result is not comparable to a HUSKY result. The frozen published policy runs with eden inference --policy husky; examples/projects/locomotion/husky_skate/main.py adds a play script with rough terrain.

Licence

HUSKY is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial).

docs.title: Move forward
docs.text:
A small Go2 task that rewards walking forward, used as a benchmark and as the worked example of composing several TaskMods.

eden train --task move_forward
eden train --task move_forward --robot go1 --controller explicit --runner rl_games
Flag Choices (default first) Effect --robot go2, go1 Which quadruped. --controller implicit, explicit Genesis's built-in PD, or user-space torques (halves sim_dt and sets decimation=2). --runner rsl_rl, rl_games The RL library. rl_games replaces the runner options with the rl_games schema and needs the rl-games extra. pipuv (checkout) 
pip install "eden-world[rl-games]"

uv sync --inexact --extra rl-games

docs.title: Manipulation Tasks
docs.text:
Eden's own manipulation tasks: arm-and-gripper reaching and lifting, a dexterous-hand lift, in-hand cube reorientation, piano playing, two-part assembly, and hand-object tracking with dexterous hands. This page gives, for each task, the robot, what the policy learns, its flags, what it needs installed, and the commands to train and replay it. The ported benchmark suites (robosuite, LIBERO, SIMPLER, PolaRiS, Mochi, ...) have their own pages, linked from the task index, which also has the commands every task shares.

Task Robot Flags Default num_envs reacher I2RT YAM arm --difficulty 4096 manipulation_reach_droid Franka Panda + Robotiq 2F-85 — 4096 manipulation_lift_box Franka Panda + Robotiq 2F-85, or UR5e / UR10e + 2F-85 --manipulator, --reset_buffer 4096 manipulation_lift_box_rgb Franka Panda + Robotiq 2F-85 — 1024 manipulation_lift_ycb_rgb Franka Panda + Robotiq 2F-85 --object_properties 1024 manipulation_dex_lift Franka + XHand1 (left) — 4096 reorient Wuji Hand 1 (simplified collision model) --hand 4096 piano Two Wuji Hand 2 (beta2) --song 1024 omnireset UR5e + Robotiq 2F-85 --robot 4096 flashdexretarget XHand, or two Sharpa Wave hands --motion, --robot, --learner 4096

num_envs is per GPU rank. Override it with --num_envs N.

docs.title: Reacher
docs.text:
The canonical Eden task config (eden/tasks/benchmark/reacher/config.py) and the template every other task follows: a YAM arm moves its end effector to a target sampled in a box, with an exponential reaching reward, action-rate, joint-limit and joint-velocity penalties, and a curriculum that stages the weight of the joint-velocity penalty. The arm uses incremental joint position control (ReferenceSource.DELTA, target = current position + 0.05 × action).

eden train --task reacher --difficulty hard
eden inference --task reacher --checkpoint logs/reacher/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --rec

--difficulty sets three things together, because shrinking the target without sharpening the reward or shortening the episode just makes a longer, sparser task:

--difficulty Target half-extent, xy / z (m) reaching_std Episode (s) easy 0.15 / 0.075 0.30 12 medium (default) 0.10 / 0.05 0.20 9 hard 0.05 / 0.025 0.10 6

The target box is centred on (0.4, 0.0, 0.3) m. Your first task builds a task like this one from scratch.

docs.title: Reach (Droid)
docs.text:
manipulation_reach_droid is the reacher on the Droid rig (Franka arm + Robotiq 2F-85): joint-position arm control, a uniform 3D target, an exponential reaching reward and the same penalties and curriculum. The end effector is the midpoint of the gripper's finger pads. It mirrors mjlab's Reach-{Robot}.

eden train --task manipulation_reach_droid

The Droid rig's arm is a Panda

Droid is a hand-less Franka Emika Panda with a Robotiq 2F-85, not the FR3 that mjlab pairs the gripper with: the rig was tuned on that arm and kept on it so trained policies stay valid. Droid(arm=FrankaResearch3()) gives the FR3 pairing. See Robots.

docs.title: Lift box
docs.text:
A port of mjlab's Lift-{Robot}, trained from scratch: every episode starts at the arm's ready-to-grasp home pose with the cube spawned in a region on the table, so the policy learns reach → grasp → move to target with no warm start. Arm control is 6-DOF differential IK (DifferentialIKController); the gripper is a binary open/close controller on the Robotiq drivers, which are force-limited so closing on the cube makes a friction grip instead of crushing through it. The rewards follow mjlab's lift_env_cfg: shaped reaching, lifting, and coarse (std 0.3) and fine (std 0.05) goal tracking gated on the lift.

eden train --task manipulation_lift_box
eden train --task manipulation_lift_box --manipulator ur5e_2f85
eden inference --task manipulation_lift_box --checkpoint logs/manipulation_lift_box/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --rec
Flag Choices / default Effect --manipulator droid (default), ur5e_2f85, ur10e_2f85 The arm. Every rig carries the same Robotiq 2F-85, so the grasp point, gripper action and gripper rewards are unchanged; only the arm entity, the IK frame and joint set, and the experiment name change. The observation width follows the arm's DOF count, so checkpoints do not transfer between arms. --reset_buffer none A reset-state buffer file to restore every reset from, replacing the cube placement and the arm-joint jitter. Capture one with capture_reset_states(env, ["robot", "gripper", "cube"]) (eden.utils.buffers.reset_states). Rows are drawn uniformly; the goal command still draws each episode's goal.

docs.title: Lift box from RGB
docs.text:
manipulation_lift_box_rgb keeps the lift-box physics, actions, rewards, terminations, events and curricula, and changes the perception. A 128 × 72 wrist RGB camera on the tool flange feeds a spatial-softmax CNN (one conv stack per image group ending in a soft-argmax that emits each channel's expected image location). The actor loses the privileged object pose and must find the cube in the image; the critic keeps the full privileged state. Both read the shared camera group.

eden train --task manipulation_lift_box_rgb

It renders with the gs-madrona batch renderer, which is not an Eden extra: install gs-madrona (Linux x86-64 only) first.

Two Madrona traps this config avoids

Either one leaves the actor effectively blind, with no error. Madrona renders ambient light only until lights are added, and it fixes the light count when the scene is built, so the lights are declared on BatchRendererOptions and applied before scene.build(). And BoxOptions defaults to a grey surface, which is invisible on a grey table, so the cube is coloured red and the table darkened. Reuse both in any vision task on the batch renderer.

docs.title: Lift YCB from RGB
docs.text:
manipulation_lift_ycb_rgb extends the RGB lift with a different rigid YCB object in each env: master chef can, tomato soup can, tuna can, pudding box, gelatin box, potted meat can, apple and foam brick. The objects are one GroupedEntityOptions entity still named cube, so every inherited term works unchanged; Genesis distributes the variants in contiguous blocks across the envs (128 envs per object at 1024 envs), and the variant an env holds is fixed at build. Because each object rests at a different height, an ObjectRestHeight metric latches each env's actual resting height after the reset settles, and the four lift rewards use it instead of one scalar.

eden train --task manipulation_lift_ycb_rgb --object_properties ycb
--object_properties Effect uniform (default) Every object at the default density and friction 2.0. ycb Each object at its published YCB mass (scaled with the mesh) and a friction by surface material.

docs.title: Dexterous lift
docs.text:
manipulation_dex_lift keeps the lift-box structure (shaped reach, dense lift, grasped-and-lifted gate, coarse and fine goal tracking, a goal-range curriculum, staged smoothness curricula, contact stiffening) and swaps the gripper for a 12-DOF XHand1 (left). The rig is FrankaXHand: the hand on a right-angle coupling, palm down at the ready pose. The arm uses differential IK and the hand a joint-space PD over its 12 DOFs. The end effector is the centroid of the five fingertips, and a per-fingertip approach reward replaces the gripper's grasp bonus.

eden train --task manipulation_dex_lift

The policy is trained to be deployed on the real rig:

  • It observes only what the rig measures: joint encoders, its own last action, the goal, forward kinematics of those, and the cube pose a camera would estimate from AprilTags on the cube, with that estimate's noise and a 3-frame history. The cube's orientation is a 6D rotation, so the sign a pose estimator picks does not matter. Simulator-only state (hand joint velocities, cube velocity, fingertip-to-cube offsets) is critic-only.
  • The hand keeps the URDF effort limits (0.4 / 1.1 N·m), every hand link meets the cube with stiffened contact, hand friction is drawn per env from U(0.8, 2.0) against a 0.5 cube and table, lift goals are 10–30 cm above the cube's rest position in the arm's base frame, and the action-rate penalty is 5× the lift-box task's.

Deployment is not complete yet

The cube pose reaches the policy through the cube entity, so a deployment writes the camera's estimate into it each control step. The Franka and XHand backends ship with Eden; the AprilTag observer that does that write is not in Eden yet, and MuJoCo sim-to-sim cannot load this rig yet (the module docstring of eden/tasks/manipulation/dex_lift/config.py explains why).

docs.title: In-hand reorientation
docs.text:
A port of wuji-mjlab's reorient task: a palm-up, fixed-base 20-DOF Wuji Hand 1 holds a 54 mm cube and rotates it to a target orientation given in the wrist-tag frame, holds it there, then chases the next target, without dropping it.

eden train --task reorient --hand right --num_envs 4096 --logger wandb
eden inference --task reorient --checkpoint logs/reorient/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --rec

--hand (right, default, or left) swaps the chirality; the grasp keyframe is mirrored for the left hand.

What to know before changing it (the module docstring of eden/tasks/reorient/config.py has the full list):

  • The goal is a state machine, not a timer. Reaching a goal opens a success window that pays an escalating hold reward before the next goal is drawn. The success state is measured in InHandReorientCommand.post_physics_refresh and only the goal switch is published in _update_command, following the hook rule in Writing terms.
  • Drop detection is one metric term that the reward, the termination and the critic observation all read.
  • The goal is drawn: a kinematic twin of the cube, invisible to the physics, floats over the palm at the target orientation in a recorded rollout.
  • The policy group is reproducible on hardware: joint angles, joint tracking error and the cube pose relative to the wrist tag. Everything privileged is critic-only.
  • The hand is soft. Its actuator table is the manufacturer's (kp about 0.2–0.7 N·m/rad), and blanket gains break it.

docs/assets/reorient/reorient.mp4 is a recording of a trained policy. It was trained before the success-window fix above, so reproducing its numbers needs a retrain.

docs.title: Piano
docs.text:
Eden's take on RoboPianist's PianoWithShadowHands, with two Wuji Hand 2 (beta2) hands on a simulated 88-key keyboard. The policy sees the key states of the current control step and the next ten (half a second at 20 Hz control over 200 Hz physics), and is paid for pressing the keys that are due, and nothing else, at the moment they are due. Each hand is a free body whose 6-axis wrist pose is driven by FreeBasePoseController with its weight carried, so each hand has 26 action axes (20 finger joints and 6 wrist axes).

eden train --task piano --song twinkle_twinkle
eden train --task piano --song chpn-p7.mid          # a MIDI file, by name if it is in the scores directory
eden inference --task piano --checkpoint logs/piano/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --rec

--song takes a built-in song (five_finger_scale, ode_to_joy, twinkle_twinkle, the default) or a .mid file: its path, or its file name alone if the file is in the scores directory ~/.cache/eden/scores (under $XDG_CACHE_HOME when that is set). The file-name form keeps the saved config portable. Where the MIDI file says which hand plays what, each hand is placed over its own part. The episode is as long as the score.

The task itself is silent. To hear a policy, add a PianoAudio sensor and a microphone at evaluation time; the example does that:

uv run python examples/projects/manipulation/piano/main.py play --song twinkle_twinkle --vis --play
uv run python examples/projects/manipulation/piano/main.py play --song twinkle_twinkle --record -o /tmp/twinkle.mp4

The module docstring of eden/tasks/piano/config.py lists every difference from RoboPianist (the free-flying hands, actions as offsets from a rest pose, a softer key-press margin, a lighter energy penalty, the rewards dropped and added, and annotation-free fingering).

docs.title: OmniReset
docs.text:
UWLab's OmniReset stage-1 task (OmniReset-Ur5eRobotiq2f85-RelCartesianOSC-State-v0): a UR5e with a Robotiq 2F-85 assembles an object pair, each episode starting from one of four recorded reset-state families drawn with equal probability, with UWLab's scene, observations, relative Cartesian OSC controller, rewards, startup randomization and PPO recipe. The recorded states are downloaded from UWLab's Hugging Face dataset on first use.

eden train --task omnireset
--robot Rig uwlab (default) UWLab's UR5e + 2F-85 (OmniResetUR5e2f85), the rig the released expert drives. ur5e_2f85 Eden's own ur5e_2f85 composite, for training a policy of your own. Run python -m eden.tasks.omnireset.retarget --pair peg once first, to retarget UWLab's states onto it.

UWLab evaluates with every episode from the ObjectAnywhereEEAnywhere family. To evaluate a checkpoint that way, override the reset weights:

eden inference --task omnireset --checkpoint logs/omnireset/<run>/model_<iter>.pt --num_envs 256 --episodes 256 \
    --override "event_options: {reset_states: {category_weights: {ObjectAnywhereEEAnywhere: 1.0,
    ObjectRestingEEGrasped: 0.0, ObjectAnywhereEEGrasped: 0.0, ObjectPartiallyAssembledEEGrasped: 0.0}}}"

The released expert runs with uv run python examples/policies/omnireset/main.py. Genesis combines contact friction as max where PhysX averages, so only the insertive object's friction is randomized (0.9–1.6). The config's docstring reports the released expert at 94 % success from ObjectAnywhereEEAnywhere over that range, and 87 % over UWLab's 0.65–1.3 averaged span.

docs.title: FlashDexRetarget
docs.text:
The RL half of FlashDexRetarget on Genesis. One policy, trained across every clip of a retargeted dataset, drives one or two robot hands (6 actuated forearm joints plus fingers each) so the objects follow their recorded trajectories while the hands follow the human (MANO) wrists and fingertips. A PD wrench pulls each object toward its reference at first and is withdrawn as the policy improves (FDRAssistCurriculum). The clips a policy completes are physically valid robot hand-object trajectories — the retargeting's real output.

The task trains on a motion.pt that eden retarget flashdex builds from a released hand-object dataset:

# 1. Build the dataset (needs the flashdexretarget extra and the licence-gated MANO models).
eden retarget flashdex import --source taco --raw /data/taco --mano-dir /data/mano_v1_2/models --dataset /data/taco_fdr
eden retarget flashdex kinematic --dataset /data/taco_fdr --robot xhand

# 2. Train. The robot is the one motion.pt was retargeted to.
eden train --task flashdexretarget --motion /data/taco_fdr/xhand/motion.pt
eden train --task flashdexretarget --motion /data/taco_fdr/xhand/motion.pt --learner flashsac

# 3. Roll out with the assist off; prints per-episode completion and tracking errors.
eden inference --task flashdexretarget --checkpoint logs/flashdexretarget/<run>/model_<iter>.pt
Flag Default Meaning --motion required The <dataset>/<robot>/motion.pt that eden retarget flashdex kinematic wrote, next to its object URDFs. --robot the motion's own xhand or sharpa. --learner ppo ppo (rsl_rl PPO) or flashsac (FlashDexRetarget's off-policy learner).

Install what each step needs:

pipuv (checkout) 
pip install "eden-world[flashdexretarget]"   # the dataset pipeline (eden retarget flashdex)
pip install "eden-world[flashsac]" "rsl-rl-flashsac @ git+https://github.com/Holiday-Robot/rsl_rl_flashsac@9822b1b7e0b5cce45e7f79d6b3e2c169fa042faa"

uv sync --inexact --extra flashdexretarget
uv sync --inexact --extra flashsac --group flashsac-git

A held-out evaluation cannot use --motion on the run's checkpoint

eden inference replays the run's saved config.json, and a task flag such as --motion cannot apply to a saved config. To roll a policy out on other clips, copy the checkpoint out of its run directory first, so no config.json sits beside it:

cp logs/flashdexretarget/<run>/model_<iter>.pt /tmp/policy.pt
eden inference --task flashdexretarget --motion /data/held_out/xhand/motion.pt --learner <learner> \
    --checkpoint /tmp/policy.pt --num_envs 512 --episodes 2048

With FlashSAC the replay buffer holds whole observations in float16: 50M rows with one XHand need about 154 GB of GPU memory, so set runner_options.algorithm.replay_buffer_size for your GPU (the task README gives 10M rows, 31 GB, as fitting a 48 GB card). eden/tasks/flashdexretarget/README.md lists every piece of the port and every difference from the original. Building its dataset (eden retarget flashdex) is covered on Retargeting.

docs.title: Mochi deformable tasks
docs.text:
Three batched RL tasks in which two arms handle a soft body: a foam sponge, a terry towel and a cable. They run on the Mochi solver, Eden's host of the Genesis port of Meta's SuperDex implicit solver. Read this page to train or replay them, and for what Mochi changes about contact-rich deformable manipulation. The code is in eden/tasks/mochi/.

Each task is Eden's version of one of RoboSimStudio's three demos (examples/08_demos in that project), built at that demo's numbers on its bimanual i2RT YAM workcell and scored with the demo's own goal. Every env carries its own soft body in one Mochi solve.

The README labels the wiping clip as a trained policy and the folding and routing clips as scripted runs.

docs.title: The tasks
docs.text:
Task (--task) Demo Soft body Goal (success) Episode mochi_wipe_the_bar wipe_the_bar (surface_prep) 50 × 75 × 30 mm FIRM_FOAM sponge (E 80 kPa) 90 % of a 243-cell marker stripe on a grab bar's crown worn clean 15 s mochi_fold_the_towel fold_the_towel (cloth_fold / towel_half) 30 cm terry towel, 500 g/m², 30 × 30 cells fold score ≥ 0.85, fold extent ≤ 0.6, the towel at rest, both hands clear 12 s mochi_route_the_cable route_the_cable (VABAR cable_route/port_easy) 600 mm, 7 mm cable of 50 segments, welded at one end two segments in each spool's seat, three in the port with the free end, hands clear, at rest 20 s 
eden smoke --task mochi_wipe_the_bar
eden train --task mochi_wipe_the_bar        # 256 envs, default fp32 precision

Each task trains 256 envs with PPO at 30 Hz control: one 1/30 s Mochi step (decimation=1) with 4 Newton iterations (MochiOptions(n_newton_iterations=4)).

docs.title: mochi_wipe_the_bar
docs.text:
A 25 mm chrome tube with a 340 mm straight run on two 32 mm elbows, its legs 50 mm into 76 × 80 × 70 mm blocks on a 10 mm mat; the sponge lies on the mat 70 mm past the near block. The stripe is the middle 200 mm of the bar's crown, 9 degrees either side: 243 cells of 2.5 mm, each wearing by Preston's law with the demo's constants (custom_terms.wipe.BarStripeWipe).

The right arm does the job: it takes the sponge off the mat with its jaws across the 50 mm side, carries it over the near block and strokes the stripe. Its jaws squeeze at most 8 N a finger, the demo's cap. Once the grip has settled, the demo's latch (SettledGraspLatch) pins the foam under the pads to the hand until the jaws open. The left arm stands at its ready posture. The episode ends on success.

docs.title: mochi_fold_the_towel
docs.text:
The towel lies flat at (-0.05, +0.06) on the bench; the crease is its centreline across y, and the far half is carried over onto the near half. The fold is scored with the cloth suite's measures (custom_terms.fold: ClothFoldScore, SoftGym's ClothFold with a drag term and one layer's 7.5 mm forgiven, and ClothFoldExtent). "At rest" means a 95th-percentile particle speed under 0.02 m/s; "hands clear" means no particle within 2 cm of a tool centre.

The left arm takes the far edge and carries it over. The right arm, its jaws shut, presses the near half to the bench so the flap does not drag it along.

docs.title: mochi_route_the_cable
docs.text:
The cable is welded under an anchor bracket and lies along +y. Two ManipulationNet F1 spools stand 240 mm apart (a 4.75 mm shaft between 12.5 mm flanges); the cable must pass the first on the far side and the second on the robot's side. A port 61 mm out from the second spool is a 10 mm channel between 12.5 mm walls, facing the run. The goal is the board's routed (custom_terms.route), counted on the rod's segments; "at rest" means no node faster than 50 mm/s and "hands clear" more than 50 mm from the cable.

Both arms act: the right makes the three placements and the left plugs the end. The jaws hold the cable by friction at the demo's 6000 N/m servo.

docs.title: Rewards and terminations
docs.text: The rewards stage the demo's job: reach the part, hold it (gated on the grip or the latch), bring it to the goal, and the task's own measure. The wipe ends on success. The fold and the routing hold a state, so they do not terminate on success: they pay a bonus every step the goal holds (custom_terms.MetricsHold) and run to the time-out. Ending those episodes on success forfeited the dense terms' remaining pay, and the policy learned to keep hold of the towel.

docs.title: The workcell
docs.text:
Positions are in RoboSimStudio's work-surface frame: the origin at the middle of the bench top, +x away from the arms, +y toward the left arm, z up from the bench top, which is the ground plane. Two Eden Yam arms (eden.options.robots.i2rt_yam.Yam) stand at the demo's mounts, 0.3475 m behind the middle and 0.62 m apart (eden.tasks.mochi.common.YAM_BASES).

  • Gravity-free arms, as the demo's gravity-compensated arms are (Mochi has no compensation term).
  • The demo's servo gains, not the asset's sim-to-real defaults: kp 300 / kv 30 for the arm (1600 / 70 for the wiping arm, which the demo stiffens), and each demo's calibrated squeeze for the jaws.
  • A squeeze cap is a gain. Mochi clamps no drive force, so the asset's effort limits are dropped and the cap is set through kp: closed on a part w wide, each finger squeezes with finger_kp × w / 2. 320 N/m puts the demo's 8 N cap on the 50 mm sponge.
  • Actions. Each acting arm moves its tool centre (between the fingertip pads) by differential IK with its tilt held pointing down, turns it about the vertical where the demo does (the cable), and opens and closes its jaws.
  • No fingertip micro-spheres. The YAM's MJCF carries six 0.6 mm collision spheres per finger for MuJoCo's point contacts. Mochi samples every collision triangle, so they were 55 % of the arm's contact samples and slowed a step sevenfold when a policy pushed its hand into the sponge. The task loads a copy without them (common.yam_mochi_file); the pads' boxes carry the grip.

docs.title: Replaying the demo routines
docs.text:
examples/recipes/mochi/rss_demo_routines.py plays each demo's own routine (the same moves, speeds and marks) through env.step and the task's own actions. A routine that meets the goal shows the goal is reachable from the policy's action space.

uv run python examples/recipes/mochi/rss_demo_routines.py --task mochi_wipe_the_bar
uv run python examples/recipes/mochi/rss_demo_routines.py --task mochi_route_the_cable -b 4

docs.title: Recording the wipe
docs.text: The stripe is the metric's ink, not geometry, so a plain camera shows a clean bar. eden inference --rec records the task's recording_camera(), whose PlanePaintOverlay paints each cell as dark as the ink it holds, in STRIPE_COLOR, shaded as the renderer shaded the bar. The training config declares no camera. See Sensors and rendering for camera overlays.

docs.title: Where Mochi differs from the demos' physics
docs.text:
Mochi solves the arms, the parts and the fixtures in one implicit Newton system. RoboSimStudio runs MuJoCo for the arms and couples SuperDex (the sponge) or VBD (the towel, the cable's capsules) to it. Where that mattered:

  • The sponge needs the latch, for the demo's reason. Friction alone picks and carries the sponge, but a stroke drags it out of the jaws, as it did in the demo.
  • The towel is taken by the benchmark's latch, not the demo's pinch. The demo's jaws gather the two faces of a 5 mm VBD slab. A Mochi shell is one surface (here with a 2.5 mm collider either side), and the fingertips press it into the bench instead of gathering it. So closing the jaws seizes the edge strip within 3 cm of the tool centre (FeatureGraspLatch, RoboSimStudio's attach); a close with nothing in reach seizes nothing.
  • The cable lies on its own bed. A rod touches through its centreline, so the bench must push back at the cable's radius; the same plane would also stop the fingertips at the centreline, and the jaws would ride over the cable. So the cable lies on an invisible bed in the bench's plane, the arms stop on the bench, and each plane's pairs with the other's bodies are off.
  • The cable bed is grippier than the demo's bench (0.3 combined friction against the demo's 0.02): the demo's contacts are sticky, which is static friction, and Mochi's friction grows with slip below its falloff.
  • The arms collide, where the demo's pass through each other. So the right hand presses the towel at (0.08, -0.04), 80 mm farther out than the demo's mark: at the demo's mark the folding arm stopped against the pressing one 45 mm short of its place.
  • The sponge is meshed 6 × 9 × 4 (350 nodes, about 8 mm apart) rather than the demo's 9 × 13 × 6 (980): twice as fast.
  • The cable is a Mochi discrete elastic rod with the demo cable's bending rigidity (its per-joint stiffness times the segment length) and an axial stiffness that keeps it all but inextensible, as rigid capsules are.

docs.title: Physics notes
docs.text:
• Contact stiffness is 1e7 Pa/m (common.CONTACT_STIFFNESS), which Mochi conditions well in single precision, so the tasks train under the default fp32. Mochi's 1e9 default needs eden.init(precision="64").
  • A Mochi scene is all-Mochi. Every entity, the bench plane included, takes a Mochi*MaterialOptions. See Physics.
  • Pins survive resets. Mochi keeps a pin, and where it holds the vertex, outside the state a reset restores. So the cable's weld is re-pinned at every reset (PinSoftBodyVertices), and the latches release their pins.
  • A diverged env is reset alone. An env whose implicit solve fails is truncated and reset (Episode_Termination/solver_error) while the others go on (EnvBase.get_solver_error_envs_mask); its reward is zeroed for that step.
